News.title: Childminder who left 27 children alone in her home pleads guilty to neglect
News.content:
A Dunfermline childminder has admitted leaving more than 20 children she was caring for alone and unsupervised in her home.

Amanda Mathewson, 55, pleaded guilty at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court to neglect and abandoning children in her care.

Her offending took place at a number of locations in Dunfermline and elsewhere in Fife.

The court heard Mathewson had 27 children in her home, 19 more than she was licensed to look after.

Mathewson, who has been a self-employed childminder for 30 years, was arrested by police following allegations of cruelty towards children.

The court heard she had provided childcare services at her home in Dunfermline for children under the age of 16.

At the time of her arrest she had 15 children aged under 12, 10 children under primary school age, and two children under the age of one in her care.

News.title: Rise in babies in care proceedings raises fears of unnecessary adoptions, experts tell BBC
News.content:
Broadhurst acknowledges that term is "politically loaded" and the modern care system is very different from the coercive practices that took place mainly between 1949 and 1976 - and for which the government recently apologised for cases in England.

But she says it "is actually what's happening because parents do not agree".

"They want to continue to be in contact with a child," she says. "Even parents who feel they couldn't look after a child at that point find it particularly brutal that they're going to have no contact, or very little contact, with that child until they're 18."

One birth mother, Jean, tells us she never wanted to give up her daughter, Tye, for adoption - and describes it as "forced". Her local council says it followed a lawful process.

Jean was separated from her daughter for 16 years, after Tye was taken into care at 11 weeks' old and then adopted at the age of two.

Now, with Tye an adult, they are reunited. When she turned 18, having struggled with adoption and questions about her identity, Tye looked for her mother on social media.

"I knew I had a mum somewhere and it wasn't the people I was growing up with," she says - describing her adoption as something that had left her "completely alone" without a "whole chunk of heritage".

When Jean became pregnant, she was looking forward to being a mother. But she had concerns too: "The only thing I knew for certain was that I was disabled, I couldn't look after myself properly, so I wasn't sure how I was going to be able to look after a baby, so I needed help."

Her local authority at the time, Newham Council in east London, told her such help was not available, she says. Tye was put into foster care, but Jean was able to see her often.

There had been multiple assessments and residential placements as Jean tried to keep Tye. But professionals, including doctors and social workers, ultimately advised the court that Tye needed a stable, permanent family and that Jean could not provide it.

Jean says she fought and "gave it my all" through years of court proceedings. She even asked if she could have visiting rights, in a similar way to a parent in a divorce. "I was told that was an unrealistic expectation," she says.

News.title: One million UK people who have never smoked are now vaping
News.content:
More than a million people who say they have never smoked are now vapers, latest data for 2025 reveals, external - up from around 940,000 in 2024.

People aged 25-34 are vaping more than any others, overtaking 16 to 24-year-olds, with 16.4% using e-cigarettes daily or occasionally.

For the second year in a row, more over-16s in Great Britain are using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Meanwhile, the number of smokers in the UK continues to fall to nearly one in 10 adults, or 4.9 million people, down from 5.3 million in 2024, with more over-16s now vaping than smoking at 5.4 million.

News.title: Queen pays tribute to 'irrepressible' Jeffrey Archer
News.content:
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as "devastating news".

"We will miss him very much," she told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday, adding that he had texted her earlier on Monday.

Badenoch said he was "very much loved by the Conservative family", adding: "I'm glad that I saw him recently."

Speaking about what she described as "other parts of his life", she said: "He did serve his time, he made amends, and he wanted to do a lot of good in the world."

Former Conservative prime minister Sir John Major said "we have lost a man who lived one of the most remarkable lives of our age", and that he will be "much missed â and long remembered".

Archer's last novel, Adam and Eve, was released on Tuesday.

Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told BBC Breakfast that he was with Archer on Sunday. "I mean, literally 72 hours ago, doing a show in the West End of London celebrating this book, the publication, and he was in great form.

"He didn't really acknowledge that he'd changed much since being in prison, but I think he became a nicer person in some ways, a gentler, a milder person after the prison experience."

Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as "a remarkable man who did everything at full bore", adding: "There were simply no half measures with him."

Other former ministers also paid tribute. Sajid Javid said Archer had been a "dear friend", while Sir Jeremy Hunt said Archer had "showed enormous kindness with his advice about how to become a writer".

James Cleverly said the author and politician had been "a huge personality and fantastic storyteller", and that he had been very supportive when his wife Suzie was recovering from cancer.

Reform UK member and former Conservative minister Nadim Zahawi, wrote: "Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company."

News.title: Tories pledge £10bn for British anti-missile defence system
News.content:
The Conservatives have pledged to invest Â£10bn in a system to defend Britain against long-range missiles and drones, if they win the next general election.

The party said the "Britannia Shield" would offer the UK an integrated network of radar, command and control systems, as well as interceptor missiles.

The Tories initially said the system would be "in essence a British 'Iron Dome'", likening it to Israel's missile shield, however party leader Kemi Badenoch drew back from the comparison in broadcast interviews.

She said the plan would be funded from within their commitment to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, paid for by welfare reform and reprioritisation of other spending.

Badenoch said that the Â£10bn cost would be split over 10 years, with Â£1bn allocated each year for the project.

Earlier this year, Gen Sir Richard Barrons told MPs on the Commons defence select committee "the cost of an iron dome at entry level is probably Â£80bn over 10 years".

Speaking to the BBC, Badenoch said: "We are not building the iron dome... we are designing something specific for the kind of threat that we face here."

She added: "It is not going to be the daily onslaught that Israel has, so we don't need that level of capability."

News.title: Student admits murdering woman in 'Dexter' kill room
News.content:
The first day of the trial heard that after causing 78 knife wounds to sex worker Saceanu, who he contacted through a website using a burner phone, Day abandoned the "gruesome task" of dismemberment because he cut himself.

Prosecutors claim Day left the Airbnb after the killing, walked some distance away, and called 999 at 00:50 on 21 December asking for medical help.

On body cam footage played to jurors on Tuesday, Day could be seen sitting in a police car with his hand wrapped in duct tape.

He said he had been going to drink in Dudley and had been looking for a "random girl" in a bar when he claimed he had been injured near a bush by an animal that "might have been a fox".

Questioned as to where he had got duct tape to wrap around his hand, Day told police it was in his car, although he could not remember where it was parked.

A male officer told him that his story did not quite check out, to which Day responded: "I don't know if it was a wild dog or a fox."

Police were alerted to the scene at the Airbnb by the property's landlord, who had been contacted by another resident who had booked into a different room and had discovered a trail of blood.

In a statement the resident told jurors they had pushed open the door and saw "a lot of blood on the floor" and what appeared to be a doll.

"The doll was lying on the floor on its back," they added.

When Day was arrested on suspicion of murder at Russells Hall Hospital in Dudley in the early hours of the morning of 21 December he was wearing a khaki top resembling one worn by Dexter.

A Home Office pathologist said Saceanu, originally from Romania, probably died as a result or wounds to her neck, causing damage to her carotid arteries, with a number of wounds to her hands "consistent with efforts to protect herself".

Defence barrister Gurdeep Garcha KC said of Day: "He is well aware of the nature and inevitability of the sentence that must follow.

"It seems to us that given his age and the absence of (previous) criminal offending, the court would be assisted by a pre-sentence report."

News.title: Katie Price's ex told teenager to 'take it to the grave', rape trial hears
News.content:
The former husband of Katie Price told a teenager after allegedly raping her that she should "take it to the grave", a court has heard.

Kieran Hayler, 39, is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies.

The complainant, who was 13 at the time of the alleged offences, wept during a police interview shown to jurors when she admitted lying to her mum about what happened because she "didn't want her to think I was disgusting".

She said: "I thought it was my fault for ages," adding that she told her mum Hayler had touched her but not that it was sex as she feared that "maybe I'd led him on".

The complainant told police that Hayler had called her two or three years after the alleged incidents had taken place.

She said: "He said something like 'you promise you won't tell anyone? What we had was special - you better take it to the grave', and that it might get me into trouble."

The complainant recalled him saying it might end badly for her, but that she had not felt frightened of him.

Asked by police how she felt following the three alleged rapes she said: "At the time I thought he really cares about me so he's not doing something horribleâ¦ because of the way he described it, he said it was a good thing."

The complainant remembered having "four showers a day after that" and said her mum recalled her "always washing" and changing her underwear "several times" a day.

She said: "I definitely remember thinking he's a lot older than me, is this something he should be doing?

"I remember crying and wondering if it should have been happening."

After the jury was shown the video of the police interview, the alleged victim gave evidence in person in court from behind a screen.

She was asked if she remembered anything else, and, speaking about the third incident, the complainant said Hayler had messaged her saying, "I love you, goodnight".

"I replied, 'I love you too'," she added.

In 2021, the complainant contacted the NSPCC charity which referred her to the police, prompting the investigation.

Hayler was first interviewed by police in January 2022 and denied any of the allegations took place and that anything sexual occurred.

He was married to media personality Price at the time of the alleged incidents, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021.

Hayler suggested his ex-wife had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended, and the allegations form part of this, the court heard.

The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families.

Price is expected to be a witness in the trial which is expected to last about a week.

The trial continues.

News.title: Iranian men accused of spying targeted journalists for 'serious violence', court hears
News.content:
Three Iranian men have gone on trial in London accused of spying for Iran on UK-based journalists, who were being targeted so "serious violence" could be inflicted on them.

The prosecution said Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, was to carry out the attack, with Farhad Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Noori, 57, doing the surveillance and reconnaissance. All three were born in Iran but were living in London.

The jury at Woolwich Crown Court heard that Sepahvand does not deny his involvement but said he did it out of fear of the consequences of refusing.

The prosecution said that is "an entirely bogus claim", adding that he did it for money and to have a criminal conviction for theft in Iran "fixed".

Sepahvand was in contact with two men with Iranian telephone numbers.

According to the prosecution, Manesh and Noori are expected to say they did not know they were carrying out surveillance on behalf of Iran.

All three face charges under the National Security Act, including "assisting a foreign intelligence service".

Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones KC said the men's targets were journalists working for Iran International - a Persian-language satellite channel that is critical of the Tehran regime and has its headquarters in London.

Jones said at least two journalists linked to Iran International were targeted in the surveillance.

He said at least one of them was to be "subjected to serious violence" as retribution and "to try to silence and deter others who might dare to voice their criticism".

Iran International, which broadcasts into Iran, has been declared as a "terrorist organisation" by Tehran.

"The evidence we will call illustrates that these three defendants carried out surveillance and reconnaissance, visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos, taking videos, doing online research about them," Jones said.

"The defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying," he added.

The men also allegedly had a "briefing sheet" on a barrister, Jonathan Turner, who was a founding member of a group called UK Lawyers for Israel.

One Iran International journalist who was allegedly targeted was Mojtaba Pourmohsen.

Images of him, his workplace and a hotel where he had lived were found in a "briefing document" on Sepahvand's mobile phone.

The prosecution says Noori took pictures of the block of flats Pourmohsen lived in in Brentford, southwest London, in December 2024.

It is also alleged that Sepahvand and Manesh went there to take photos and videos.

Another man targeted for surveillance was Kambiz Hosseini, the court heard.

The men even knew the name of his dog and the colour of his car, Jones said: "You can imagine the fear and psychological impact caused to him by discovering that all of those details about him, including the name of his dog, were known to the intelligence services."

Jones said Sepahvand's motivation was to try to resolve a criminal conviction he had in Iran for theft.

"He was not just in it for money. He quite explicitly wants something very particular in return for his work - he wanted his criminal conviction in Iran to be fixed," Jones told the jury.

The prosecution said Sepahvand's relationships with his contacts on Iran were not always good.

In one voice note he let out his frustration, saying: "This job is about committing an offenceâ¦ I'm supposed to put up my own money, put my own life at risk, put my car into it, put my time into it, leave my wife, leave my home, go chasing after their business, and in the end get completely screwed because of them."

He later said: "This is an illegal job. It's something that constitutes a criminal offence and it carries a heavy prison sentence.

"At the absolute minimum, they should transfer Â£10,000 for now."

The prosecution said that in total Sepahvand was to be paid Â£150,000 to find a target and to "finish them off".

The three men, who each had an interpreter in the dock, deny all the charges.

All three were granted temporary leave to remain in the UK after claiming asylum. They arrived in the UK between 2016 and 2022.

Sepahvand arrived in 2016 concealed in a lorry. The other two arrived in small boats.

The trial continues.

News.title: I had to crawl on my hands and knees to get off train, says disabled woman
News.content:
A wheelchair user was left in tears as she crawled on her "hands and knees" through a train after being told a ramp could not be used to help her off.

Phoebe Tesoriere, 24, who lived in Caerphilly at the time, was on a Great Western Railway (GWR) train from London Paddington to Bath Spa when it happened.

Her family spoke to the assistance desk and were taken to the only designated wheelchair space on the train. Phoebe said she was assured a ramp and assistance would be waiting, but was told she was in a carriage beyond the platform and could not get off.

GWR said it was "really sorry" and admitted "we let her down, both when we helped her board and at several points during her journey".

Cardiff Met student Phoebe, who has hereditary spastic paraplegia, external which causes weakness and stiffness in the leg muscles, said: "My mum specifically asked if a ramp and assistance would be waiting at Bath Spa. We were assured it would be."

While on the train, staff checked which station she would be getting off at numerous times during the incident in December 2025, she added.

Despite this, Phoebe was not told the carriage she was directed to would stop beyond the platform, leaving her unable to use a ramp to get off.

News.title: Mexico asks for evidence after US official says shots were fired at border personnel
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said her administration has formally requested proof from U.S. authorities regarding allegations that gunfire was aimed at U.S. personnel from the Mexican side of the border, emphasizing that domestic security forces detected no such event.

"We asked for all the evidence because we have no evidence," Sheinbaum said during her daily press conference on Monday.

She explained that personnel from Mexico's Army, Navy, and National Guard found no indication of shots being fired from Mexican territory toward the United States.

Her remarks came a day after U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson stated on X that "shots were fired at US Coast Guard personnel" in a border region connecting the Mexican state of Tamaulipas with Texas, where Mexico announced the deployment of Army and National Guard troops on Sunday.

Ronald Johnson ( Reuters )

Johnson's comments followed Mexico's announcement late Sunday of a joint border initiative titled "Operation Mirror," under which 500 troops, helicopters, drones, and anti-drone technology will be stationed along the frontier.

The dispute comes amidst growing security cooperation between Mexico and the US, though Sheinbaum has firmly and repeatedly rejected any potential US military intervention within Mexico.

Sheinbaum noted that Mexican authorities suggested "mirror operations" alongside US agencies as a precautionary measure after being notified of the reported incident.

"To avoid any of these situations, what was proposed was that mirror operations be carried out so there would be no problems," she said. "We have not been given any evidence that these shots actually occurred, but to prevent any situation a mirror operation has already been carried out."

News.title: Measles outbreak mapped: New York declares state of emergency after virus wreaks havoc in Pennsylvania
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Measles is surging at historic levels in the United States with nearly 3,900 cases reported in 47 states and Washington, D.C. this year so far.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency due to the virus Monday after 109 cases were reported - the most since a 2019 outbreak.

Pennsylvania has experienced the nation’s largest measles outbreak in over three decades with infections surpassing the 1,000 case threshold this week.

The state has reported five deaths linked to measles but that has been disputed by federal health officials who only confirmed two fatalities. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. claimed in August that Pennsylvania’s measles deaths were “fabricated” and ordered the CDC to change how it counts such fatalities.

Cases have surged over the past year in largely unvaccinated communities. Health experts say vaccine hesitancy and misinformation have led to falling child vaccination rates. The majority of 2025 and 2026 cases are in children and teens, CDC data shows.

open image in gallery Measles is surging at historic levels nationwide. This federal map, last updated October 2, shows which states are reporting more than 500 cases in the darkest blue. The lightest blue indicates states reporting between 1-9 cases ( CDC )

open image in gallery New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency this week as cases spread to the highest levels New York has seen since 2019 ( Reuters )

South Carolina had a six-month outbreak of nearly 1,000 cases between October 2025 and April 2026. An ongoing outbreak in Utah has led to 724 infections since June 2025.

Measles is a highly-contagious virus that can cause high fever, rash, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. If it becomes a serious case, it can cause brain-swelling, pneumonia and death.

The majority of infections are in people who are unvaccinated.

Infections spread easily after a person with measles coughs or sneezes, but the viral droplets they produce can linger in the air for up to two hours or contaminate surfaces.

Receiving two doses of the MMR vaccine, that targets measles, mumps and rubella, provides lifelong protection against infection.

open image in gallery This CDC map, last updated October 2, shows vaccination rates among U.S. kindergarteners. The turquoise states have most coverage, with vaccinate rates above 95 percent, the level needed for immunity. Those in burnt orange have rates below 90 percent and those in light orange are in between 90-94.9 percent ( CDC )

Only 10 states have reported kindergarten vaccination levels at 95 percent - the level needed to ensure sufficient immunity to the disease so that it no longer spreads easily.

Vaccination against measles has been proven effective and the virus was declared eliminated from the U.S. in 2000 after most Americans had been vaccinated.

It’s likely that the U.S. will lose its elimination status this year, according to medical experts in Boston. This status indicates there has not been continuous spread of the disease for more than a year.

It has been the most active year for measles in the U.S. since the 1990s.

“Strengthening vaccination efforts, reducing exemption rates and interrupting ongoing local transmission will be essential to reverse this trajectory,” the researchers said in a letter in May.

News.title: Trump won’t reimburse taxpayers for money already spent on campaign ads, White House says
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump will not reimburse the federal government for money already spent on a series of campaign-like ads using taxpayer dollars.

On Monday night, facing threats of legal action and complaints from Republican and Democratic lawmakers for using public money to promote his administration before critical midterm elections, the president said he will “pay for them myself” and through a Trump-connected political action committee.

“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” the president wrote on his Truth Social account.

“This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.” he added.

The White House said Tuesday that the president “was not referring to reimbursement.”

open image in gallery Homeland Security has reportedly budgeted $20 million for series of ads promoting the Trump administration ( White House )

“Presidential public service announcements” are used to “explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction,” the White House told The Independent.

The White House has argued that previous administrations have launched similar ad campaigns, comparing Trump’s messages to ads promoting Medicare prescription drug benefits, anti-drug campaigns, Affordable Care Act enrollment, and COVID-19 vaccinations.

Trump’s ads — one of which appears to be directly lifted from one of the president’s 2024 campaign videos — promote a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.”

Another video promotes his administration with the song “Love Me” by singer-songwriter JMSN, who has issued a cease-and-desist notice demanding the Trump administration immediately stop using it.

Each of the ads ends with the caption “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

The ads have reportedly already cost $10 million, as part of the Department of Homeland Security’s reported $20 million budget to produce the ads, according to members of Congress investigating the campaign. The administration has also spent more than $2 million to buy up airtime on national TV networks, where they have already aired hundreds of times.

Legal experts and members of Congress have argued that the ads are a blatantly illegal use of taxpayer dollars that violates ethics laws against public money being wielded for partisan political messages and propaganda.

“This is an unlawful and outrageous misuse of public funds,” former White House ethics lawyer and Democracy Defenders Action co-founder Norm Eisen told The Independent last week.

“Federal law forbids using taxpayer dollars for political propaganda, which this clearly is,” he said. “This is yet another corrupt attempt to advance a partisan agenda ahead of the midterm election, paid for by average American taxpayers who are already suffering from high costs caused by this administration’s failed policies.”

Senator Maggie Hassan, a top Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, has pushed the White House to detail the costs of the ads and where the money was pulled from, as well as any outside contractors, federal agencies and government employees who were involved.

“These campaign ads never should have run on the taxpayer’s dime to begin with,” she said in a statement shared with The Independent on Tuesday.

“They were clearly wrong and clearly illegal, which is why the president should also immediately repay the taxpayers for the amount already spent on these ads,” she added.

News.title: Boy, 13, dies after his shirt gets caught on playground slide screw, mom says
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A grieving mother said her 13-year-old son died after his shirt was caught on a loose screw on a playground slide, strangling him.

Olvin Daniel Cabrera Valladares went to Shenandoah Park in Miami’s Coral Way neighborhood on September 25 to play.

The boy was found inside the slide by a man who was visiting the park with his own children, Olvin’s mother Estefanía Valladares told Local 10.

​“He told me he pulled on him, but he was caught on a screw,” Valladares said. “He pulled again, and my son fell out. His arm was inside of his shirt, and his collar was tight around his neck.”

​“He was my baby, my youngest, just 13 years old. He had his whole life ahead of him. He just wanted to play and, sadly, it was playing that took his life.

open image in gallery The boy was found hanging from a slide at Shenandoah Park in Miami's Coral Way neighborhood ( Local 10 )

​The mom said her son was a student at Miami’s Citrus Grove K-8 Center and should have been at school when the tragic accident happened.

“I have a message for parents,” Valladares told the outlet. “Be careful taking your children to these parks. Look at the tragedy that happened to my son.”

Olvin’s sister Stephany said medics tried to treat her brother at the scene, before rushing him to hospital.

“At the hospital, the doctors and medical team did everything possible to bring Olvin back,” she wrote in a GoFundMe appeal. “Our family held onto hope and prayed for a miracle. Sadly, on October 1, Olvin was declared brain dead.”

In one of the images of Olvin shared on the campaign page, the boy is seen lying in a hospital bed, surrounded by medical machines.

Others showed the boy posing with his family in front of a Christmas tree, wearing festive pyjamas. ​As of October 6, the GoFundMe campaign has raised more than $10,000 for Olvin’s funeral arrangements.

open image in gallery Olvin Daniel Cabrera Valladares died after his shirt caught on a screw on a playground slide ( GoFundMe )

​On the day Olvin was discovered, Miami District 3 Commissioner Rolando Escalona said on social media Shenandoah Park had been closed for a “non-criminal investigation.”

​When a Local 10 crew visited the park, they said they found visible screws were flat. The park reopened a day after it was shut and it was unclear if repairs to the slide had been made.

“The matter is under investigation, and the city cannot comment further,” a city spokesperson told the outlet.

​Footage captured by NBC 6 South Florida showed investigators examining the playground, looking both inside and outside the slide.

The Independent has contacted Escalona and the City of Miami for further comment.

News.title: Student loan borrowers have more time to reduce their interest rate. Here's what to know
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Student loan borrowers now have until the end of 2026 to enroll in auto pay and have their interest rate reduced by 1%.

The original deadline was Sept. 30, but the U.S. Department of Education extended it to give borrowers more time to enroll. The rate reduction will last through June 2028.

Borrowers who currently use auto pay already receive an interest-rate discount of 0.25%, so the new reduction takes off just 0.75%.

This temporary benefit is meant to support borrowers, along with those who are returning to repayment, and ensure they can stay on top of the new Repayment Assistance Plan that requires on-time payments, according to the Education Department.

The interest reduction can benefit borrowers who have large balances and are on fixed payments, said Lesley J. Turner, associate professor of public policy at the University of Chicago.

“For a limited time, borrowers are now able to get a full percentage point reduction in their interest rate if they 

Since the interest reduction was announced this summer, nearly 2 million borrowers have enrolled in auto pay.

Around 9 million Americans are in default on their federal student loans as of June, according to the Education Department. Hundreds of thousands more are behind on loan payments and at risk of default this year.

If you're looking to enroll your student loans in auto pay, here's what you need to know:

If you're new to auto pay, enroll by the end of the year

In order to get the 1% interest reduction, you must enroll in auto pay by Dec. 31.

First, log in to your student loan servicer account and select auto pay. You'll need to enter your bank information to automatically withdraw the monthly payment from your checking or savings account.

Even without the rate reduction, auto pay is a good way to stay on top of your student loans, Turner said.

“We all know life gets busy and if you have to log in every month and manually make your payment there may be a chance that you forget and then you end up having your loans go delinquent," she said.

If you're already enrolled, you already have the reduction

Borrowers who were enrolled in auto pay before the announcement in July have had their interest rate automatically reduced by 1%, according to the Education Department.

If you're currently in default, consolidate your loans

If your student loans are in default, you must log in to studentaid.gov and consolidate your eligible loans in order to 

Involuntary collections on federal student loans remain on hold. The Trump administration announced earlier this year that it is delaying plans to withhold pay from student loan borrowers who default on their payments. Borrowers are considered in default when they are at least 270 days behind on payments.

The online application for loan consolidation is available at studentaid.gov/loan-consolidation. If you have multiple federal student loans, you can combine them into a single loan with a fixed interest rate and a single monthly payment. The consolidation process typically takes around 60 days to complete. You can only consolidate your loans once.

If your student loans are in default, you can also contact your loan holder to apply for a loan rehabilitation program. Through this program, borrowers are enrolled in a reduced payment plan and, after five successful payments, wage garnishment ends.

Borrowers can find more information about loan rehabilitation here.

News.title: The big unknowns limiting how US will respond to possible Russian plague outbreak
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The pneumonia death of a lab technician at a plague research facility in Russia is raising crucial questions for American officials — with Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling Tuesday for greater transparency from Moscow.

“I ​think it's incumbent upon Russia to share more information with the world,” Rubio told reporters after arriving in Reykjavik, Iceland, for an official visit.

Rubio also said U.S. officials were monitoring the situation “very closely, hour by hour.”

The scarcity of details surrounding the death of the worker, identified by Russian media as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, leaves unanswered why she fell ill and whether others have been infected by whatever sickened her.

“It's really critical to get the diagnosis right. There are conflicting stories around it,” Tom Inglesby, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, told Axios. “Getting the real story, the true facts of the situation out in the open is critical to everything else that follows in the response.”

open image in gallery A photo released in 2019 shows workers at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, where a lab technician’s pneumonia death has sparked fear that she was infected with pneumonic plague ( Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East )

Russian officials haven’t publicly identified the pathogen that sickened Shipilova, who worked at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk.

It's also unclear where and how she was infected, with Russia's national health agency, Rospotrebnadzor, disputing social media rumors that she dropped a laboratory test tube containing live bacteria.

The available information has raised fears that she contracted pneumonic plague, the most virulent form of the disease that killed an estimated 50 million people during Europe's infamous Black Death during the 14th century.

Russian health officials said in a memo Tuesday that they had tested the dead woman's contacts and found “no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens,” according to The Associated Press, which said it got the note from the World Health Organization.

“Based on available data, laboratory test results, and health status, medical monitoring for 100% of the contacts has now been concluded,” the memo said. “The epidemiological situation is stable and remains under monitoring.”

open image in gallery Darya Shipilova has been identified by Russian media as the lab technician who died of pneumonia ( Social media )

A WHO spokesperson said Tuesday that the research facility in Irkutsk “studies dangerous pathogens, including plague, in a part of Siberia where plague occurs naturally in wild animals.”

Russia hasn't asked the WHO to send experts to help determine whether the lab worker died of pneumonic plague, spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said during a video briefing to the United Nations.

“The WHO initial risk assessment, from the information available, estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region,” Lindmeier said.

On Monday, President Donald Trump called the situation a “big problem for Russia” but said he hadn't spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about it.

Trump also told reporters that the U.S. would “help anybody that has that kind of a problem.”

“It's a rough disease, you know,” he said. “That's a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They're like an army ... and things that used to work on pneumonia don't work as well anymore.”

Dr. Glenn Wortmann, the section director of infectious diseases at MedStar Washington Hospital Center, said Tuesday that the bacteria that cause plague don’t “travel very far” and that a person would “really need to be face-to-face” with an infected person to get pneumonic plague.

“The chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen, not with this type of bacteria, because it’s not spread easily and we have antibiotics to stop it from spreading,” Wortmann told the AP.

News.title: Jim Furyk’s fighting talk shows USA path to Ryder Cup redemption in Ireland
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

This time it will be different, Jim Furyk maintains, both in his second outing as USA captain at a Ryder Cup and off the back of consecutive defeats at the hands of his European counterpart Luke Donald.

Misery at Marco Simone and bedlam at Bethpage Black has left the Americans spinning and embracing, according to Furyk, a newfound status.

“We’re the underdogs,” Furyk unmistakably uttered, despite possessing Scottie Scheffler, the best player of a generation, yet one that continues to struggle when representing the stars and stripes. “I know it’s always been played, we come in, the Americans seem to be the favourites.

“This year, there’s no chance that that could happen. We’re the underdogs. We understand that. We’ve got a lot of work ahead of us. And you know, I’m excited about that process. I’m a process guy, getting our ducks in a row, putting these guys in a good position and letting our guys go out and show their talent.

“It’s going to be difficult. The fans here – Irish fans, Irish sports are amazing but folks are going come in droves from all over Europe to support their favourite countrymen. I’ve been saying it all week, I need 12 guys that love that atmosphere and love walking into that type of arena because it takes a certain mentality. Those are the guys I’ll be looking for.”

open image in gallery Jim Furyk, Team USA Captain, and Luke Donald, Team Europe Captain, pose for a photograph with the Ryder Cup Trophy ( Getty )

It was at Le Golf National in 2018 when Furyk’s dream first fizzled out. After Phil Mickelson’s tee shot plunged into the water, pandemonium overcame the 16th tee box with Francesco Molinari, the first man to win a major and all five matches at a Ryder Cup, drowned in flat beer. Amid European euphoria, perhaps Furyk’s character shone through the American despair.

He broke into a stride to catch counterpart Thomas Bjorn, en route to soak in the celebrations, clenching his hand in respect after three engrossing days of golf.

So it will be 34 years since the last American win on European soil when the first ball is struck in anger at Adare Manor on 17 September next year.

The resounding success of Donald’s ability to harness team chemistry, bonding a group of men from nine different countries and six different languages, has been undoubtedly impressive, hence a third term as skipper, yet the USA continue to flounder on one of golf’s biggest stages, grossly underperforming when considering the exorbitant talent at their disposal.

open image in gallery Furyk (left) and Donald (right) will go head to head at Adare Manor ( PA )

The key, perhaps, is team golf’s most iconic format: Foursomes. Both Furyk, specifically, and the USA remain baffled by alternate shot golf, with the International team routing the USA 5-0 in last month’s Presidents Cup to move to the brink of a stunning victory, only for a rousing comeback in singles to negate an embarrassing home American defeat.

It has also been the foundation of European success: Donald’s tenure has seen Europe win 13 of 16 foursomes matches across Rome (7-1) and New York (6-2). Furyk’s own tenure as captain in the 2018 Ryder Cup and 2024 Presidents Cup has seen 0-4 and 0-5 sessions. There is simply no mystery to the USA’s painful defeats in this storied competition.

“I know those numbers very, very well. I’ve lived them the last four,” a candid Furyk remarked. “What’s interesting is it’s a recent thing for us in the United States. When I started playing the Ryder Cup, we felt and in mathematical terms we actuallt had an advantage in the foursomes. At that time we were really struggling in the four-ball.

“So there’s an ebb and a flow. But it’s not an anomaly. There’s some issues. We understand that. Not something I’m very happy with. I plan on making some changes. I would say, one, as captains, we need to do a better job, not only put the folks into good pairings in good positions but I don’t think we are preparing for those matches in a proper way.

open image in gallery Furyk opposed Thomas Bjorn as captain in the 2018 Ryder Cup ( Getty )

“And I will promise you, we will be prepared. I’m going to ask this team to do more than any other United States team has in the past. We’ll be prepared. We’ll be ready to go in that format, and hopefully we can showcase our talent. We have too much depth to have that poor record in alternate shot.”

USA detractors might query just why their players need to be asked to fully commit to team golf and a collective goal. Yet it was certainly fighting talk from Furyk in Limerick and almost a year away from the latest instalment, the captains will begin tinkering with their methods in pursuit of glory.

“It’s obviously no secret that we’ve done very well in the foursomes,” Donald countered. “It’s been a big part of the success of the last two Ryder Cups and hopefully that continues. But I would be naive to think that we would be able to have the same success, keeping going forward. I think any time you have that success, it’s great.

“But every time you don’t have that success, you’re learning, as well. You can tell from the way Jim is talking and what preparations they are doing, they are very focused, and we know we’ll have our work cut out.

“But I’m also focused on that I don’t particularly want to feel like I did on Sunday at Bethpage. You know, it was tough to experience the US coming back so strong. It just shows how much grit, resilience this team will have.

“And it’s certainly something I’m thinking about, how do we get these guys not only prepared as best for foursomes but all sessions, and that includes the singles. There’s 12 points in the singles. There’s a lot of points. So you’d better have some focus on that, as well.”

News.title: UK not prepared for food shortages, experts warn
News.content:
Britain has no way to feed its population of 66 million people in a crisis, a letter addressed to the Prime Minister has warned.

Climate change, cyber-attacks, geopolitical shifts, and energy shocks could put Britain’s food supply at great risk – and the UK is “complacent”, the letter says.

The document was delivered to Andy Burnham on Monday and was signed by 180 experts including academics, farmers, local council leaders, and foodbank workers.

Britain’s food supply is now heavily globalised, with roughly 45-50 per cent of food imported from countries like Spain, the Netherlands and France, as well as South Africa, Columbia and Brazil.

The system provides a cheap and constant supply of food – seasonal or not – but if international supply chains are disrupted, the UK’s home production is “woefully inadequate in [being able to produce] many different food types” , the letter argues.

It adds that “international food supplies can be weaponised”.

Crucially, the UK operates a ‘just-in-time’ food system – meaning hardly any food is stocked and stored in reserves, but is constantly moving from farms and ports directly to supermarket and wholesale shelves when needed.

“When you go to a supermarket and check out, you think, well, ‘it’s adding up the bill’ – it is, but what it’s also doing is reordering,” Tim Lang, emeritus professor of food policy at City University, a signatory of the letter and author of the Just in Case report – a major review that analysed the UK’s food system for the National Preparedness Commission, previously told The Telegraph.

News.title: Kenya confirms first ever case of Ebola after man dies in Nairobi
News.content:
Kenya confirmed its first ever case of Ebola on Tuesday after a Kenyan citizen who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo died in Nairobi.

Kenya is the third country to record a case linked to the Ebola epidemic in eastern Congo, the second largest on record. Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year but was declared Ebola-free in August.

The patient had been ill for about a month before travelling ‌by road ‌from Congo to ⁠Uganda’s capital, Kampala, and then flying to Nairobi on Saturday, health minister Aden Duale told a news conference.

After arriving at Nairobi’s international airport, he passed through health screening and was later taken by a relative to Nairobi ⁠Hospital. He was admitted with fever, chills and bleeding beneath the skin and was quickly placed in isolation, Duale said.

He died late on Monday.

News.title: Tories promise to scrap Labour’s mansion tax
News.content:
The Tories have pledged to scrap Labour’s “mansion tax” on homes worth more than £2m.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, pledged to abolish the “vindictive levy” in his keynote speech to the Conservative Party conference, warning it would hit people living in “ordinary homes”.

Under the tax, which was announced by Labour last year, properties valued at more than £2m face an extra levy on their council tax from 2028.

The shadow chancellor said: “They pretend it’s a mansion tax, but it will hit people here in Birmingham, in Manchester, and those living in ordinary homes making long commutes to our capital city. For many, it will be simply unaffordable.”

He pledged to follow in the footsteps of Nigel Lawson, Margaret Thatcher’s chancellor, and cut one tax at every Budget if the his party returns to power.

Elsewhere in his speech, Mr Griffith promised to scrap a net zero “grocery tax” which pushes up the cost of the weekly shop and cut the cost of a new build by £50,000.

The shadow chancellor also accused previous Tory leaders of failing to govern as free market conservatives, and said Andy Burnham and John Healey want to take Britain back to a “socialist fever dream of the 1970s”.

News.title: How worried should we be about the Russian plague lab leak?
News.content:
A fire breaks out at a laboratory in Siberia where secretive research into infectious diseases is taking place. A technician, racked with guilt over the accident, disappears into the tundra and shoots himself. Hunters discover his body, but what they don’t realise is it is infected with a manipulated version of the plague bacterium. The pathogen quickly spreads around the world, wreaking death and destruction at a scale unprecedented in human history.

This is the plot of Biological War: A Scenario, a recent book by US author Annie Jacobsen which imagines what could happen if a weaponised bacterium escaped from a laboratory.

The book describes an absolute worst-case scenario but the beginnings of this fictionalised pandemic share an eerie similarity with events in Russia over the last week. Reports have emerged about the death of a 28 year old female worker at the Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Shelekho, a city in Irkutsk. Rospotrebnadzor, the country’s infectious disease agency, said the woman was diagnosed with a “pneumonia of unknown origin”.

However, according to reports in Russian media the woman, identified as Daria Shipilova, died of pneumonic plague after dropping a test tube filled with live samples of the pathogen, Yersinia pestis. She was taken to hospital on Tuesday September 29 but died two days later. Nearly 200 contacts are now being monitored for signs of the disease, according to media reports.

So how worried should we be?

News.title: Extreme heat is increasing risks for pregnant women and babies, experts warn
News.content:
Soaring temperatures are increasing birth complications and defects in newborns, a new report has warned.

The report, which surveyed 1,000 doctors and midwives, found that at least 73 per cent of healthcare workers across Australia, Brazil, Britain, India and Zimbabwe had seen an uptick in heat-related complications in pregnancy and birth.

High temperatures can cause surface-level blood vessels to dilate, which in pregnant women can significantly decrease blood flow to the placenta and reduce oxygen and nutrients reaching the foetus.

This phenomenon can increase the risk of stillbirth, premature births, and low birth weight, the report, released by the Wellcome Trust, said.

Heat can also make it hard for newborn babies, whose bodies are already extremely fragile, to regulate their internal temperatures – which can significantly impact both their ability to breathe properly and feed from their mothers.

Extreme heat can also severely affect the health of a pregnant woman, placing heavy demands on the cardiovascular system and inadvertently increasing the risk of gestational diabetes, dangerously high blood pressure, and pre-eclampsia.

The effects are more severe on women who live in places where temperatures are newly or rapidly increasing, as opposed to women who have always lived in hot climates and whose bodies have acclimatised to the heat over time.

Insufferable heat can also impact women’s access to critical healthcare during pregnancy.

More than a quarter of healthcare workers surveyed by Wellcome said they had seen first-hand how fewer women travel to hospitals and clinics during heat waves, particularly in the developing world where millions access healthcare on foot.

The world experienced its hottest August on record in 2026, when the average global surface air temperature reached 16.96 degrees Celsius – roughly 1.65 degrees above pre-industrial levels.

Britain also saw its hottest summer since records began, with five heatwaves recorded over the course of just 40 days, and temperatures reaching 38 degrees in some parts of the country.

A Wellcome-funded project studying pregnant women in Wales, known as MAGENTA, has found that women in the UK have experienced negative birth outcomes as a result of the persistent heat.

Initial research has linked exposure to elevated temperatures exceeding 25 degrees with higher rates of premature births and stillbirths. A 1-degree increase in heat exposure can boost the chances of a preterm birth by around 5 per cent, the research found.

Climate change has been identified by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the greatest threat to global public health.

Between 2030 and 2050, experts project climate change will cause an additional 250,000 deaths every year.

The deaths will be due mostly to heat stress, malnutrition, and an increase in the prevalence of infectious diseases like malaria, which is spreading into new areas where mosquitoes can now more easily survive and spread disease, according to the WHO.

Dr Madeline Thomson, head of climate impacts and adaptation at Wellcome, said: “Extreme heat, fuelled by climate change, is impacting our way of life and our health - and yet many countries are not prepared. With El Niño pushing temperatures higher, the failure to act is costing lives.

“We already know many of the solutions to protect people - from early warning systems to cooler buildings.

“But the challenge is providing solutions to those who need them most, including pregnant women and newborns, who face serious risks but often receive inadequate information and support.”

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: ‘The dogs were eating their bodies’: Thousands of Yemenis flee war across the sea
News.content:
The Houthi militiamen had barely chased the government forces out of Alia Mohammad’s coastal village when the bombing began in a Saudi-backed attempt to recapture it.

Caught in the middle were Ms Mohammad, her family and their neighbours near the town of Dhubab, overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb strait, or ‘Gate of Tears’.

As the roar of planes split the sky over their heads and explosions shook their village, it took little time for them to decide what to do.

Born from generations of fishermen, they resolved to take to the sea and flee their homes in Yemen, to seek refuge across the strait in Djibouti.

More than 4,000 Yemeni refugees have arrived in the coastal Djibouti town of Obock in the past month, fleeing an offensive which has redrawn Yemen’s battle lines and strengthened Tehran’s hand in the Middle East energy crisis.

The offensive last month saw the Iranian-backed Houthi advance around 90 miles along the Red Sea coast in a 48-hour blitz that delivered what analysts have called the most consequential shift in Yemen’s front lines in years.

News.title: This is when to upgrade your tech (and when not to bother)
News.content:
The tech giants’ attempts to persuade people to upgrade to new gadgets every two years are proving less and less effective. According to YouGov polling, Brits are increasingly deciding to stick with the devices they have for longer, and it isn’t altogether surprising.

As well as the inherent wastefulness of the bi-annual upgrade cycle, year-on-year improvements are less dramatic than they used to be, and tech prices are sky-rocketing thanks to the growing needs of AI data centres.

Inevitably, however, there will come a time when you need to bite the bullet and buy a new model. These are the questions to ask yourself to decide whether that should be today, or whether you can kick the can a little further down the road.

How’s the performance?

A good place to start is to evaluate how your device functions day-to-day versus the day you bought it. Tech inevitably slows down over time, but the drop isn’t equal among devices: a five-year-old flagship smartphone may still outperform a budget model from last year.

If it’s still running smoothly enough, and isn’t broken in an unfixable way, then it probably pays to wait until it no longer passes this test. The longer you wait, the more appealing the upgrade choices will be.

The exception to this is if you’re bumping up against storage problems. If there’s no way to add more, and cloud storage isn’t cutting it, then you may need to upgrade early.

Are you missing key features?

News.title: Jibulu emerges as England World Cup bolter in Sale defeat of Saracens
News.content:
Could Nathan Jibulu, the Sale Sharks hooker, emerge as a bolter for England’s World Cup squad? With Steve Borthwick, the England head coach, watching from the stands, the 23-year-old produced the kind of “wrecking-ball” performance in this surprise victory for the North West side that suggested he is on course to do so.

After their tame defeat by Bristol Bears in the opening round, few had predicted that Alex Sanderson’s side had much hope against Saracens, who were looking to back up their impressive win at Welford Road last weekend. But Jibulu’s powerhouse display on either side of the ball typified their stout and physical resistance, backed up by a masterly display by George Ford.

Given the age and injury profile of England hookers Jamie George and Luke Cowan-Dickie, who both missed this contest, and the fact that Theo Dan has yet to make a forceful challenge for the position in the national side, Sanderson is in no doubt that Jibulu has the X factor required to break into Borthwick’s squad this season.

“This is the player that any time you watch him play, he impacts – he takes metres either side of the ball – and we knew that he had that in him,” Sanderson said.

“It shows he’s of international class. He nailed his line-outs, on the back of that he was a wrecking-ball runner causing havoc around the field.

“This is the person that we knew, this is the player that we knew we had in him. It could be the year where he explodes onto the international scene. I hope it is, but it’s early days.

“He’s that quality, he’s that kind of an athlete. You can get away with being fast and skilful in the Prem, but it’s another level again in terms of the power that’s required at international level. And he’s got that ability, he’s immensely strong.”

Borthwick will have left the StoneX Stadium on Sunday evening with a full notebook. Ben Bamber, Sale’s 6ft 9ins lock, has also been attracting his interest and it was Bamber who crossed for the decisive try, Sale’s third, hitting a great line off Ford to finish like an outside centre.

Sports.title: UEFA monitoring Man City case as it considers potential action
Sports.content:
UEFA is monitoring developments and will wait until the end of the Premier League's disciplinary process before deciding whether to take any potential action against Manchester City.

City have been found guilty by an independent commission of breaking the Premier League's financial rules between 2009 and 2018, including five charges of failing to comply with UEFA's Financial Fair Play rules.

UEFA financial rules at the time meant clubs were effectively limited to spending what they earned within set break-even requirements.

The independent commission found that City's owners put in £830m of their own money and disguised it as sponsorship income for nine seasons.

City are appealing against the decision and maintain they have a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence which will clear their name.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kaveh Solhekol explains how the other Premier League clubs are reacting to Manchester City's rule breaches ahead of the appeal process

In 2014, City entered into a settlement agreement with UEFA which included a £49m (£32m of which was suspended) fine after they were charged with breaking Financial Fair Play rules.

In 2020, City were found guilty of breaking UEFA's Financial Fair Play rules, fined €30m (£25.4m) and banned from playing in European competitions for two years.

City appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sports and the ban was overturned, with CAS ruling that UEFA had not established that City's owners had disguised equity funding as sponsorship contributions, while other breaches were time-barred.

CAS reduced City's fine from €30m (£25.4m) to €10m (£8.5m) for failing to co-operate with the UEFA investigation and stated that most of the alleged breaches "were either not established or time barred".

UEFA has a statute of limitations of five years for financial rule breaches, whereas the Premier League does not have a statute of limitations.

UEFA's case was triggered by hacked City emails which were published by German magazine Der Spiegel in 2018.

City said the internal documents were "out-of-context materials purportedly hacked or stolen" as part of an "organised and clear attempt to damage the club's reputation".

The Premier League investigation had access to documents and evidence which were not available to UEFA when it were building its case against City.

City and UEFA have been contacted for comment.

Analysis: How long will Man City's appeal take?

Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol:

"The appeal went in on Thursday at 7pm and so, according to the Premier League's rules, the appeal has to be done and dusted in 12 weeks from then, which takes us into the week before Christmas.

"The appeal can only last five days and those five days can only be in one block.

"The appeal panel, which has to be a different three-person panel from the original panel, would have 30 days to make up their minds and deliver their judgement. That would take you into the third week of January.

"Now that is the speeded-up timeline which has been introduced into the Premier League's rules this season.

"Now, Man City could argue that this speeded-up timeline should not apply in this case because this case has been going on for years and this new rule has only been introduced this season. That is something to look out for."

Details of Man City's appeal strategy explained

Latest from Sky Sports News' Lyall Thomas:

Manchester City are likely to argue as part of their appeal that the extra funding for their sponsorship deals came from the Abu Dhabi government rather than the club's owners, Sky Sports News understands.

City's lawyers argued during the 2024 hearing that the funding had come from the Abu Dhabi government, but this was rejected by the independent commission, which "concluded it was an explanation that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to conceal the realities of the Disguised Funding Scheme".

However, it is understood City are expected to continue contesting this argument.

Manchester City is majority owned by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan's Newton Investment and Development LLC. Sheikh Mansour is also a member of the ruling family of Abu Dhabi and he is the vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.

The separation of UAE state investment and those that are private from the Abu Dhabi royal family has long been a subject of debate and criticism.

What did the independent commission find?

Manchester City arranged "sham" contracts with a number of its commercial partners as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to artificially inflate the club's revenues by £830m.

The club filed accounts that concealed the true state of its finances.

Manchester City were significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits and broke "well over 100" Premier League regulations.

Manchester City failed to co-operate and act in good faith towards the league during the investigation, with three out of four alleged breaches upheld and one charge not proven.

The commission also said it was "regrettable" that a decision had taken so long to reach, with the hearing having taken place between September and December 2024.

City: Process was not impartial

Following the publication of the guilty verdict on September 29, a Manchester City statement read: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League commission, that has been published today.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

"The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Manchester City's statement erroneously refers to a Premier League commission. It is an independent commission.

Why Man City's appeal could drag into 2027

Latest from Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol and Amar Mehta:

Manchester City's appeal could drag on into next year if they argue that the process should not be run according to Premier League rules which were introduced for this season.

City have filed their appeal and the new rules about appeals state that this part of the disciplinary process has to be concluded within 12 weeks and the appeal hearing can last no longer than five days.

City's lawyers could argue that they were charged in 2023 and a hearing was held in 2024 - when the rules about a speeded-up appeals process were not in the Premier League Handbook.

A legal expert told Sky Sports News Manchester City would have a strong case for arguing that the new rules should not apply in this case.

The new rules were introduced to ensure that clubs, where possible, were punished in the same season as relevant rule breaches.

Sports.title: Djokovic wins China Open without needing a match point in semi-final and final
Sports.content:
Former world No 1 Novak Djokovic won his seventh China Open title without needing a match point in his semi-final and final.

Djokovic, who was awarded a win after his semi-final opponent Daniil Medvedev was disqualified after hitting a spectator with the ball, claimed the 102nd title of his career following the retirement of De Minaur in the final.

De Minaur, who left the ​court for ⁠a medical ⁠timeout after the first set, ‌continued playing with a heavy bandage on ‌his left thigh. But he could not continue after winning ⁠the first game ​of the second ​set.

Djokovic narrowly won ​the first set, ⁠with the match poised at ⁠7-6 (7-3) 0-1 when ​De Minaur retired.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Daniil Medvedev was defaulted against Novak Djokovic during the China Open after hitting a ball at a spectator

Novak Djokovic in Beijing

34 wins



0 losses



5 sets dropped in 34 matches



12 top 10 wins



7 titles



"It's been 11 years since I last played here," Djokovic explained during the trophy ceremony. "I always have high expectations of myself and always want to visualise myself with the trophy, particularly here in Beijing, a place where I have never lost. But I was also aware that reality is a little bit different these days."

The 102nd tour-level title of Djokovic's career moves him within one of Roger Federer's 103 for second-most in the Open Era, behind only Jimmy Connors' 109.

The 39-year-old Serbian also extended his perfect record at the ATP 500 event to 34-0.

It has also significantly strengthened his hopes of returning to the Nitto ATP Finals this year.

The two had gone toe to toe in the first set, targeting the baseline to pressure each other.

De Minaur ⁠almost broke Djokovic in the fifth game but the Serbian ​saved the break point with a full-stretch backhand down ​the sideline.

The Australian held firm but the 27-year-old's error count increased ​during the tie-break to hand the first set to Djokovic.

Sports.title: Alcaraz wins Japan Open in first final since wrist injury
Sports.content:
Carlos Alcaraz has won his first final since coming back from a long injury lay-off for a right wrist injury with success at the Japan Open.

Alcaraz, who hadn't played a showpiece since getting beat by Jannik Sinner at the Monte-Carlo Masters in April successfully defended the title he won last year in Tokyo defeating Jiri Lehecka 7-6 (7-4) 6-4.

The Spaniard returned from injury in late August and made a run to the US Open quarter-finals, where he lost to Ben Shelton in a match that ended at 3:33am.

Alcaraz was kept on his toes by Czech star Lehecka, but he did enough to earn his first tour-level trophy since Doha in February.

"It's extra special to win a title again. It's been a while," said the 23-year-old Alcaraz, who is the first man to successfully defend his Japan Open title since Pete Sampras in 1994. "To win a trophy in my second tournament back is amazing. I didn't find my best tennis all week, but I found the right solutions to win. Today I played the best match of the entire tournament. I'm really happy."

Lehecka, ranked 19th, was sharper at the start and led 3-1 but Alcaraz, who has been wearing a compression sleeve on his right arm since his return, hit back to level at 3-3 and showed his full repertoire of crowd-pleasing shots in the tie-break, winning five points in a row from 2-4.

He made his move in the seventh game of the second set with a break to lead 4-3 and looked delighted after clinching victory.

Alcaraz began the season by winning his seventh major title to complete the career Grand Slam at the Australian Open and also lifted the trophy in his next tournament in Doha before his injury lay-off.

"Obviously a lot of negative thoughts come to your mind," Alcaraz said, when asked if he ever feared not tasting trophy success again during his time out injured. "If you are going to come back healthy, if you are going to come back the same as I was before. If I will be able to hit the ball normally without pain at all. A lot of thoughts came to my mind, but I tried to put those thoughts away all the time.

"My team and I knew that if I come back I was going to feel 100 per cent. If I feel something, [the comeback is] not going to be anything, so I just have to go full for every shot, every ball, and I trust [my team], I trust myself, and it worked out."

Image: Alcaraz appears to be 'gathering momentum' towards the back-end of the season

Speaking on Sky Sports Tennis, British tennis star Liam Broady hailed the importance of Alcaraz's victory in Asia, saying: "You can see the gratitude and jubilance in the team and for somebody like Carlos Alcaraz and his team. You might forgive them for not being too bothered about winning an ATP 500 but everything he's been through the last few months, I'm sure this is a very special one for him.

"He was stuttering and struggling to find his game at the start of the week with a few three-set matches which he might normally have won easier.

"This is exactly what the future opponents of Alcaraz do not want to see is him gathering momentum whilst not potentially playing his best tennis."

Sports.title: Packer to miss Red Roses' tour of North America
Sports.content:
England's most-capped active player Marlie Packer will miss the WXV Global Series matches against Canada and the USA in North America later this month.

Two-time World Cup winner Packer, who has made 119 appearances for her country, will remain at home with partner and Red Roses team-mate Rosie Galligan due to give birth.

England play Canada in Toronto and Ottawa on October 17 and 24 respectively before a game versus USA in New Jersey on October 30.

Delaney Burns, Haidee Head and Sophie McQueen are ruled out through injury.

Image: England head coach John Mitchell: 'Playing quality opposition and learning to adapt under pressure will help us raise our level and improve our game'

The Red Roses played three times in September, beating Australia and New Zealand around a 26-26 draw with Canada in Exeter that ended the hosts' 39-match winning streak.

Head coach John Mitchell said: Our last two Tests against Canada and New Zealand have been humdingers that could have gone either way. They were hugely important to our development towards [the 2029 World Cup].

"Playing quality opposition and learning to adapt under pressure will help us raise our level and improve our game.

"The 32 players travelling to North America have a great opportunity to elevate our connections as a squad because playing away from home requires togetherness.

"We have shown a real hunger to compete and improve, and we're excited to rip into our preparations and continue our rivalry with Canada in Toronto."

Sports.title: Russell set for Singapore GP grid penalty after engine failure
Sports.content:
George Russell is set to start from the back of the grid at Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix due to a power unit change in a further blow to his championship hopes.

Russell suffered a power unit failure late in Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia when running third, forcing him to retire while his Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli finished second to extend his lead over the Brit at the top of the Drivers' Championship to 84 points with seven rounds remaining.

Sky Sports News understands Russell will take on a new power unit on Friday in Singapore, which will see him exceed the season allocation of four for each driver, therefore incurring a penalty that will drop him to the rear of the grid.

Russell was expected to have a new power unit at the United States Grand Prix later this month that was going to include an upgrade, with Mercedes taking up the opportunity they were granted by the FIA's ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) system to improve their engine.

The ranking of Mercedes' engine performance below Red Bull's by the sport's governing body has caused some dispute, with the Milton Keynes squad arguing that the Silver Arrows, who are dominating the Constructors' Championship, already have the best power unit.

It is now understood that Mercedes' upgraded power unit could be fast-tracked to be ready for Russell at the Singapore Grand Prix, which would at least prevent him having to incur further penalties later in the season for taking more new parts.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell believes winning his first World Championship title this year is exceptionally unlikely after another DNF

Both Mercedes drivers have suffered power unit problems throughout this season, with Antonelli having to start at the back of the grid at the Italian Grand Prix, where he stormed through the field from 19th to win.

Monza is one of the easiest tracks on the F1 calendar to overtake at whereas the Marina Bay Street Circuit in Singapore is one of the toughest.

Singapore is a Sprint weekend so Russell's back of the grid start will only apply to the Grand Prix on Sunday and not Saturday's Sprint.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Toto Wolff fumes after George Russell's retirement in Malaysia

Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord says the Brackley-based outfit are unsure what caused their latest issue in Malaysia with Russell.

"Our investigation so far, we've got the car back, we've been able to do a first inspection, it's clearly a mechanical failure on the power unit side," he said in Mercedes' race debrief video.

"Exactly what the root cause is we still need to determine, but the consequence was clear for all to see."

Formula 1 2026 remaining races Singapore* This weekend Las Vegas November 20-22 USA October 23-25 Qatar November 27-29 Mexico Oct 30-Nov 1 Abu Dhabi December 4-6 Brazil November 6-8 *denotes Sprint weekend

'That is absolutely the final straw for this title bid'

Speaking on Sky Sports News, Craig Slater said: "We're still awaiting official confirmation from Mercedes that Russell will have to have this engine change, but we understand it's almost an inevitability.

"This is not the place where you want to take a grid penalty because it is difficult to overtake in Singapore, so the reality is if Russell has to start at the back of the grid for the Grand Prix itself, he is going to find it very difficult to get anywhere near double-digit points in the race itself. It will be hard for him to get into the top five.

"Eighty-four points back, that is absolutely the final straw for this title bid. Key for Russell is finishing with a run of victories if he can somehow regain the upper-hand because that would send the signal for 2027 that he remains a viable contender and someone who can defeat young Kimi Antonelli. Russell needs to end this year on a strong note to give himself belief he can maybe win the Championship next year."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater explains why George Russell's Singapore GP grid penalty could end his chances of a world title this season

Why did Mercedes suffer 'worst weekend of the season'

Mercedes brought a major aerodynamic upgrade to Malaysia, their biggest since May's Canadian Grand Prix, but were comfortably beaten by Red Bull's Max Verstappen who converted pole position into victory.

Toto Wolff described it as Mercedes' "worst weekend of the season", mainly due to Russell's retirement which he stated was "not acceptable".

But, in terms of outright pace, Mercedes were surprisingly outperformed by Red Bull and Lord puts it down to multiple factors.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the Sepang International Circuit

"The combination potentially of updates, track temperature and track surface caused an interaction and a set of behaviours that meant the car was not in its usual happy state, that the drivers were having to turn the car on the throttle in the slow corners," he explained.

"That was further exacerbating the challenges with tyre temperatures.

"That's not an easy thing to unpick. It's a bit of a 3D problem that we need to work through and then figure out exactly what steps we take going forward to make sure that we've got the base understanding that we need to understand that the update is working well and that we're heading in the right direction in our development, not just for this year's car but for next year as well.

"That's work that's going on at the moment back at the factory and also in Singapore in order to establish exactly what the plan is for the coming days and the race weekend in Singapore."
