Sports.title: Lifeline for LIV Golf with potential $300m investment
Sports.content:
LIV Golf has secured a potential $300m windfall from BC Partners Credit as it looks to continue into 2027.

Sky Sports News understands LIV has officially entered into an RSA - a Restricted Stock Award - with BC Partners and the league is confident it can move ahead with LIV 2.0.

The league lost its multi-billion-dollar funding from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) following the end of the 2026 campaign and filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States.

LIV hopes a court-supervised "restructuring process" can be completed early next year.

This new agreement includes a commitment from BC Partners to provide funding, subject to court approval, with a hearing scheduled on October 14 to approve the deal.

The arrangement secures an extension for the league to discuss terms with its players, with talks now open until October 25.

Image: LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil says BC Partner Credit's investment can help the league become 'truly global'

BC Partners Credit keen to put LIV on 'sound financial footing'

Sky Sports News understands there is no obligation on players, who are owed millions of pounds, to stick with LIV, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts.

Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, said in a statement: "Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf's emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season."

BC Partners Credit will support the next stage of LIV, under which players would become equity owners of the league and its teams.

Major winners Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau, Cameron Smith and Dustin Johnson are among the players who signed with LIV following its creation in 2021 having been lured over from the PGA Tour.

Those golfers are some of the creditors listed with unsecured claims - Rahm heads that with 7.5m (£5.5m).

Image: Jon Rahm is one of the plyers owed millions of pounds

England's Tyrrell Hatton (£2.5m) is among the creditors, as is five-time major winner Brooks Koepka (£1.25m), who quit LIV to re-join the PGA Tour earlier this year.

LIV CEO: We believe ‌deeply in the future of this league'

LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil said: "This investment is an important ‌step forward for LIV Golf, and I want to thank Ted Goldthorpe and the entire BC Partners team for their conviction in what we're building.

"We believe ‌deeply in the future of this league and in the opportunity to build something distinctive alongside our players.

"We're delivering on our major milestones, and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers."

The league said the funding would enable it to move from the planning stage to operational execution.

Sports.title: White's Dorking have new co-owners - and ambitions to become 'the world's local club'
Sports.content:
Football needs charismatic characters - and Marc White is certainly one of those.

It is more than likely you will have seen one of his rants go viral on social media. In that respect, he is one of a kind.

But he also has no equal in the way that he set up Dorking Wanderers with a group of friends in 1999 - and is still there, 27 years on. The chairman, the manager, the face of the club.

After a recent FA Cup second qualifying round win over Southall FC, he posted from the club's X account: "Thanks for tonight to all of our loyal supporters & never forget we were in Crawley & District Division 5. Step 17."

It has been a long, long journey. One that has cost millions and taken in an incredible 12 promotions.

Dorking finished 16th in the National League in 2022/23 - their best ever finish and the closest they have come to the EFL, which is the stated goal. At this point, why would it not be?

Currently, they are back in the National League South - but now White has significant additional backing.

US entrepreneur Frank Villares had first become involved in Dorking in 2024, through the 'Rise With Us' campaign, which allowed the public to buy shares in the club to help them achieve their goals. A £180,013 target was set, with £333,180 the actual figure raised by 746 investors.

In the summer, he and his wife Debra Tucker were announced as co-owners and growth investors.

"Frank and Debra are massive English football fans and there's this huge enthusiasm for the English pyramid in the US as that's the one thing the US money can't buy," says White, speaking to Sky Sports in a room overlooking the club's Meadowbank home.

"They were actually looking around for a bigger interest in a club. They wanted to be more involved and I was actually helping them with that, telling them what to watch out for.

"They'd gone to four or five clubs and a deal fell through last minute so I just said: 'Don't forget, there's always Dorking Wanderers!' It just felt like everything had gone wrong for a positive reason. Then they were like, 'You know what, we've already said to ourselves we love Dorking, why are we even doing this?!'

Image: White (centre) with co-owners and growth investors Frank Villares and Debra Tucker

"They are both 40 plus VAT and they're in a position now in life where they want to really enjoy and have a project and they want to win - Frank has even put a picture of the team at Wembley, an AI job, on his vision board!

"They're perfect because they trust us to run it, but they want to be involved as well. This is just the beginning."

In addition to Villares and Tucker, a consortium led by former professional ice hockey player James Sixsmith acquired a shareholding in the summer.

"We want to surround this club with people that want to succeed and want to win and James is very similar," adds White.

"We're really lucky. James and Daryl [Cumberland] from his consortium are part of that mechanism behind it all. As we go up the divisions and as we find more success, their involvement will become greater and greater.

"I want to say to the people involved: 'Listen, here's the thing. If we put in another X million, we could actually get to the Championship or we can build a stadium and we can do X, Y and Z. We've got big players in our setup that are going to enable us, not just financially, but also in terms of decision-making and having the right mindset towards growth.

"The legacy of Dorking Wanderers is to find a way to progress. What people love about the club is the underdog story of coming from nowhere to somewhere. We have to find a way for that to continue."

Image: Dorking have climbed from step 17 of the non-League pyramid to step 2 (Image: Dorking Wanderers)

What does that look like in practice?

"The investment has made things easier. But in football, everything you do, whether it's on or off the field, costs a lot of money. We're by no means set for life, not in a million years. We're just in a position where we can add some things, largely off the field.

"But that kind of off-field investment can generate more income, which we can invest on the field, hopefully. That's where the success cycle comes; win more games, more fans, promotion, more fans.

"There's not one football club in the world that really profits. You might get the odd one but, in general, someone somewhere is putting time, effort and money into a football club. Off the field is the largest part of the football club.

"You're in the entertainment business and you've only got one show a week normally. The rest is all hard work."

Speaking of, White is, naturally, one of the central figures on the YouTube channel Bunch of Amateurs, which documents all the behind-the-scenes goings-on at Dorking.

The channel currently has more than 200,000 subscribers and a global audience.

"We had half a billion unique views last year of the club. Half a billion. Ten times the average Premier League club. My thing is to part capitalise on that, but part deliver. Imagine what happens to that with more promotions?

"As a result, every single match there's someone from Australia, New Zealand or America. They'd be the three top places every game.

"I went down to Costa one morning to get a coffee. It opened at 7am and I looked like I'd just been f*****g dug up. Two people came in with these Dorking Wanderers shirts on. They were American and had just got off a flight and they couldn't believe they'd seen me.

"It's a bit surreal like that, but it's all positive. I like the recognition I get. I don't really get any bad words about me from anyone that knows the game. I quite like the recognition of the hard work that's gone into it because it would be easy just to think I just swear at refs. Obviously, there's a lot more to me!"

Throughout the interview, White keeps coming back to V2 - the next version of the club.

"V1 took us from the park fields to where we are today," he says. "Everything is teeing up this club to have a V2. We're better equipped now.

"I think we need to get promoted again really soon. Next year or two minimum. We then need to try and do a bit of a double and then try and break into the Football League.

"I think breaking into the Football League genuinely will make us one of the world's greatest sporting successes. As big as that sounds. I don't know f*****g any others!"

One potential obstacle is that, while White has been so successful at Dorking, he does not hold the coaching badges necessary to manage in the EFL.

"We'll take care of that, that's fine," he says. "The dream really is to be in there. I'd love it."

Image: Dorking's finished 16th in the National League 2022/23 - their highest finish to date (Image: Dorking Wanderers)

But the ambitions extend far beyond the EFL.

"I feel like we really want to be the whole world's local club," White says.

"We believe we're the pioneers of like real, relatable content with a local football team. It's given us this global stage and that trying to capitalise on that and people feeling like they belong to a local community, even if they live in Mississippi.

"Frank tells me he can't believe how many times he gets stopped in America - even in Texas, someone said to him 'I love Dorking!'.

"We want to just like continue to put the club on a global reach - and we identify with the fact that winning will be a part of that. So we have to find a way to win."

As for this season, Dorking are currently eighth in the National League South, three points behind leaders Maidstone United. A trip to Dover Athletic - a point and a place above them - beckons on Saturday.

"Standard stuff, really. Stressful. We've done alright. Loads of injuries, all that s**t. Standard modern football," says White as he picks up his bag, ready to dart to a podcast record.

"Dorking are always in the mix, so we'll be there again."

There is no time for sentimentality - only the next challenge.

Sports.title: Football Daily | South Korea’s golden boys and a brouhaha over military service
Sports.content:
FINAL DRAFT

In his 1965 song Draft Dodger Rag, Phil Ochs detailed the occasionally ludicrous lengths some young American men went to avoid conscription to the military. While he listed ruptured spleens, poor eyesight and flat feet as more mundane ailments, mentions of bone spurs (Donald J Trump), conscientious objecting (Muhammad Ali) and 30-day hygiene protests (Ted Nugent) were all conspicuous by their absence from the protest singer’s lyrics. Ochs almost certainly had no idea that the best way to avoid the draft in South Korea is to be really good at sport.

Monday’s Football Daily revealed that mere seconds after captaining his country to gold at the Asian Games, Lee Gi-hyuk was overcome with an ill-advised urge to publicly brag how victory meant he could not be drafted for military service. The South Korea skipper was joined in his tone-deaf celebrations by teammates Yang Min-hyuk (of Tottenham) and Park Seung-soo (of Newcastle). Their exemption came on the back of a government promise offering any podium-toppers from South Korea a free pass from their 18 to 21 months of obligatory service to be conducted before they turn 35. The subsequent public outcry was deafening, no doubt prompted by the vast majority of able-bodied South Koreans who don’t get so lucky, as well as South Koreans who view conscription as a duty to be honoured, rather than a hardship to avoid at any cost.

“I got caught up in the happiness, adrenaline and excitement of the moment,” simpered Lee in his subsequent apology. “I am deeply sorry to the fans who are currently fulfilling their military duty, as well as to all those who sincerely supported us.” While the defender promised to reflect on his behaviour, it has now emerged he may also be forced to ponder the notion that he has potentially kiboshed future opportunities for other athletes to take advantage of an exemption that has been in place for more than 50 years. It seems South Korea’s Ministry of National Defence was already reviewing plans to completely abolish special sports exemptions and his post-match braying is likely to accelerate the process, making him as popular as a rattlesnake buried in a game of lucky dip.

“Ultimately, we have plans to cut back or scrap the supplementary service, including one designed for artists and athletes, and reflect it in the basic outline for defence reforms,” droned a military suit. “From the perspective of the defence ministry, we are deeply sorry for the remarks made by some people in the sports industry.” Despite their victory, South Korea’s gold medallists will still have to complete three weeks of basic training and 544 hours of community service for their country. Given their high profiles and ill-advised boasting, Football Daily suspects these recruits can look forward to no end of barked orders, miles of marching on the drill square and an unnaturally high allocation of cleaning duties in the latrine.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi has completed football and can bid Argentina farewell with pride
Sports.content:
Not for the first time, Lionel Messi is returning to the Argentina national team. This occasion, however, will be accompanied by a sense of completion and celebration rather than obligation, as the country bids farewell to probably the greatest footballer ever. Messi will wear the Argentina shirt one last time this week for a friendly in Buenos Aires against Benin (who else?!) after he was invited back for a celebratory runout following his decision to retire from international football after the World Cup final.

He has retired before. In 2016, having suffered heartbreak in a major international final for the third year in a row, Messi was seemingly done. “This is tough and a difficult time,” he said after the Copa América Centenario final defeat to Chile. “The end has come for me and our team. It has been four finals – it just wasn’t for me unfortunately. I looked for it and wanted it so badly, but it didn’t happen. This is best for everyone – for me and for a lot of people that wish this. The team has ended for me, a decision made. I tried many times and I leave without being able to obtain it.”

Fortunately, about six weeks later after a national campaign urging him to change his mind, Messi confirmed he wasn’t quitting. Another 10 years with the national team would follow, and what a time it proved to be. Having finally won the World Cup – as well as earning more caps (208 after Tuesday’s game) and scoring more goals (125) for Argentina than anyone – Messi no longer has anything to prove to anyone.

Given what Argentina have achieved in the last five years, the 16 barren years of Messi’s international career feel like something from an alternate reality. They lost Copa América finals in 2007, 2015 and 2016, as well as the World Cup final to Germany in 2014.

And it wasn’t as if there was a huge amount of promise for Argentina immediately following Messi’s 2016 U-turn. Argentina’s participation at the 2018 World Cup was a debacle. They were poor in qualifying – reports of a player mutiny stirred after a 3-0 defeat to Croatia in the group stage – and then they were dumped out by France in the last 16 (admittedly, they did run the eventual champions close in an instant classic in Kazan).

Messi took time away once again after Russia 2018. It was a difficult period for Argentina, who parted ways with Jorge Sampaoli as coach and appointed his assistant in his place. It was an unpopular decision that Diego Maradona slammed in his characteristically earnest manner. “He’s a great guy, but he can’t even direct traffic,” said Maradona. “How can we give the Argentina team to him? Are we all crazy?”

He was, of course, talking about Lionel Scaloni, who quite plausibly doesn’t know how to direct traffic, and it’s highly likely he never has. But you know what he’s done a pretty good job of directing? The Argentina team.

Scaloni – and Pablo Aimar – seemingly did enough to convince Messi his absence need not be permanent, and what a curious quirk of fate this turned out to be, given Scaloni reportedly only got the job because he was an easy and cheap option. Seven years on, he’s the only Argentina coach to have won the World Cup and multiple Copa América titles – and Messi has been essential to all those successes.

Scaloni is also the Argentina coach Messi has played for the most (79 caps), and that feels symbolic. Scaloni has excelled in creating a team that maximises Messi’s influence at the top end of the pitch without needing him to muck in defensively.

Other players pick up the slack by working that bit harder, but they seem to relish doing his dirty work as if it is an honour to help Messi focus on what he does best. Those famous images of the players walking out to warm up at the 2026 World Cup, looking like Messi was leading his own personal militia, supports the idea they were all in on it.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi leads out the Argentina team before their match against Algeria at the World Cup in 2026. Photograph: Maja Hitij/Fifa/Getty Images

And why wouldn’t they be? After consecutive Copa América wins either side of glory at Qatar 2022 – their first World Cup triumph since 1986 – and a run to the final at this summer’s World Cup, Argentina have enjoyed the kind of success they had not seen for a generation.

While no player has played in more men’s World Cup matches than Messi (34) and he shares the record for most editions played in (six), much of his legacy in the tournament will be linked inextricably to the last two. Of his 33 World Cup goal involvements, a tournament record, 22 came in the 2022 and 2026 campaigns. His 10 goal involvements in Qatar four years ago was the joint most at the tournament; and only Kylian Mbappé (14) bettered his 12 in North America.

Linked to that, Messi did briefly break the record for most World Cup goals in tournament history when he reached 18 with a double against Austria this year to move past Miroslav Klose – though his final total of 21 was one short of Mbappé’s 22.

Messi’s output this summer was also helped by him scoring in nine successive World Cup matches, a run stretching back to the successful 2022 campaign in Qatar and a tournament record. He set another record by becoming the first player to start three men’s World Cup finals (2014, 2022 and 2026), with Cafu the only other player to even feature in three.

Qatar 2022 was obviously the most significant. This success robbed his critics of the only stick they could beat him with. When Copa América success in 2021 wasn’t quite enough to satisfy certain people – who would point to the fact that Pelé and Maradona had won the World Cup – Messi eventually got there in 2022 and played the role of Argentina’s inspiration. That was his final frontier, and while it may not have made the 2026 failure any easier to take, it ensured a bulletproof legacy.

The significance of Scaloni’s impact should not be understated. A host of Argentina coaches had tried and failed to win international titles with Messi – and some of them had more individual talent in the squad.

View image in fullscreen Fans in Rosario, Messi’s home town, celebrate his international career. Photograph: Marcelo Manera/AFP/Getty Images

With that in mind, Tuesday’s game will serve as a reminder that Argentina are entering a new era, one slightly clouded by the uncertainty of what they can achieve without Messi. Their talisman remained their best player until his final match. So, will they adapt without his creative ingenuity and decisiveness, or can the collective work ethic and unity they have cultivated sustain them?

We shall see. For now, though, it’s time for Argentina to celebrate what they have achieved with Messi because there is no guarantee it will ever be as good as this again. Argentina had already won the lottery once before with Maradona; it’ll surely be a while before they strike gold a third time. Luckily, Messi provided them with memories to last a lifetime.

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: Uefa investigating allegation Israel player spat at Ireland coach
Sports.content:
Uefa has launched an investigation into claims a member of the Republic of Ireland coaching staff was spat at during the heated Nations League encounter with Israel on Sunday.

The European governing body has confirmed that post-match reports submitted by match officials “contained an allegation of an incident in or around the tunnel at half-time” and that it will be the subject of a disciplinary investigation “regarding potential misconducts from player(s)”.

Witnesses at the match, held in the Serbian town of Backa Topola, reported hearing a member of the Irish staff – understood to be the fitness coach Damian Doyle – claim he had been spat on by an Israeli player as the teams went down the tunnel at half-time.

A spokesperson for the Israeli Football Association denied the reports, saying “no one had spat towards the coach”.

After the match Ireland’s coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, said his team had been subject to a number of apparent provocations in the buildup and sought to defuse the incident.

“There have been a lot of those ‘accidents’ and we were clever enough to avoid it before it went too far,” Hallgrimsson said. “I felt it was their intention to intimidate us and make us do something stupid. I give big credit to how the players handled their emotions.”

The investigation will probably extend the rancour that turned this double-header between Ireland and Israel into a geopolitical flashpoint. Ireland had been under intense pressure from supporters at home to boycott the matches and conducted a vote over whether to fulfil the opening fixture in Hungary.

Quick Guide How do I 

The second match, nominally an Ireland home fixture, was held in Backa Topola after the Football Association of Ireland said “operational challenges” would prevent it from staging it safely in Dublin.

The buildup involved increasingly heated accusations made by both parties, and two Israeli journalists were banned from attending Ireland’s post-match press conference after Uefa found they had brought “football into disrepute by using a press conference for politically motivated purposes” and displayed “improper behaviour” during and after a pre-match press conference.

Hallgrímsson has asked that Uefa keep Ireland and Israel separate from each other in future draws. A Uefa spokesperson said: “Decisions to avoid certain teams being drawn against each other are made taking into consideration several factors, especially conditions between the two countries leading to structural risks for security. Uefa handles every situation very carefully on its own merits and monitors all facts and developments.”

Sports.title: Union Berlin’s Marie-Louise Eta: ‘I wanted to impress through my work, not because I am a woman’
Sports.content:
In April Marie-Louise Eta became the first woman to lead a men’s top-flight team in one of Europe’s big five leagues, stepping in as interim head coach of Union Berlin following the dismissal of Steffen Baumgart. Her job was to keep Union in the Bundesliga and she did just that with two wins, a draw and two losses in her five games. They finished 11th.

It was not the first time the trailblazer had made history. Three years earlier she had become the first woman to serve as an assistant coach in the men’s Bundesliga and in 2024 she led the Union men’s team in one game. The Bayern Munich manager, Vincent Kompany, described her appointment as something that could open doors for younger women who want to become coaches.

This season Eta is in charge of the Union women’s side and, trying to take stock of a momentous 12 months, the 35-year-old tells Moving the Goalposts: “For me, it was never about being the first. It quickly became clear that it wasn’t about making history, but about supporting a team and achieving success together once again.”

There was a lot of media attention on her gender and she says her first matches were not “just about football at that time, but also very much about the issue of women in the game”. It was, she admits, very intense. Union lost their first two games, against Wolfsburg and RB Leipzig, but then came a draw against Cologne and a 3-1 victory at Mainz. At full time, Eta punched the air and joined her players in applauding Union’s fans. She ended her spell with a 4-0 victory over Augsburg.

“I wanted to impress through my work, my performance and my approach as a manager, not because I’m a woman or because I’m supposed to represent or embody something special,” she says. “I wanted to be judged by the same standards as my male colleagues.”

When she was appointed there was sexist and derogatory abuse on social media, which the club publicly condemned and described as “embarrassing and insane”. There was also a lot of positivity, however, and Eta says women and girls messaged her to say that her journey had encouraged them.

View image in fullscreen Eta received a huge amount of attention during her five-game stint, both good and bad. Photograph: Alex Grimm/Getty Images

“My hope is that my journey will encourage young girls to believe in their own potential and to pursue their goals,” she says. “If I can play even a small part in opening further doors, I’ll be very pleased. Ultimately, however, it shouldn’t be gender that decides, but performance and the quality of the work.”

What did she learn? “It is important to stay true to yourself and remain clear-headed. As a coach, it’s not just about tactics and football, but above all about bringing people along with you, giving them confidence and solutions, and helping them develop.”

The plan was always that she would take charge of the women’s team for this season and she wants “to build a team that plays football with courage, energy and intensity” and to “dictate games and be dominant”. She adds: “It isn’t just about results and league positions. It’s just as important to me that the players continue to develop, that we improve as a team, and that we play a style of football we can identify with.”

Union had a difficult start to the season with Bayern Munich first up. They lost 4-1 and failed to pick up a point in their first four games but have since beaten RB Leipzig , Stuttgart and, in the cup, Magdeburg.

The tactical changes have reflected that search for an identity. Eta began with a 4-4-2 but then switched to a 4-3-3. The formation changed but the ambition did not. Eta has never thought about legacy. “For me, it’s always been about football and working with people to achieve success together as a team.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Eta may have no interest in defining herself as a symbol. But she cannot control what other people see when they look at her. For the young girls who wrote to her, she is proof that the boundaries of football have moved.

Sports.title: ‘Brighton are the world’s most forward-thinking club’: Jason McCarthy on retiring at 29 to coach
Sports.content:
“You blow your whistle and then, all of a sudden, voom, you have 20, 30 people standing to attention,” says Jason McCarthy, discussing his transition into coaching after retiring from playing aged 29. He put on his first sessions while a defender at Wycombe, taking the club foundation’s under-16s. “I was so flustered. I learned very quickly: if I’m going to do this in front of men – hopefully, eventually – then I need to practise.”

He accepted the role of Brighton’s under-21s assistant at the start of last year and recently returned to the role after two months in interim charge this summer, while the head coach, Shannon Ruth, supported Fabian Hürzeler’s first-team staff. McCarthy has huge admiration for Hürzeler, Brighton’s impressive 33-year-old head coach who at 31 became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history and was part of his interview process.

“It was the first interview I ever went for,” recalls McCarthy. “He asked me a lot of questions: ‘How do I see the game? What sort of teams do I watch? When did I realise that I wanted to be a coach?’ He retired at 23, so he was really empathetic: ‘It’s scary, it’s daunting, people will tell you to keep on playing, but trust the feeling you have.’”

Brighton, third in the top flight before visiting Sunderland on Saturday after a flying start, are frequently referenced as a model club. McCarthy chuckles as a moment that speaks to Hürzeler’s “incredible growth mindset” crosses his mind. “I saw him running around the training ground, holding a piece of paper and reading. I think he read somewhere that taking on information while exercising can help you remember it. He’s constantly trying to improve himself. How can you not be inspired by that?”

View image in fullscreen Jason McCarthy finds Fabian Hürzeler’s approach to training inspirational. Photograph: Paul Hazlewood/BHAFC

Across an hour in McCarthy’s company, his passion for the role and joy at helping others prosper becomes apparent, as does his gratitude to Brighton for giving him the opportunity to express himself as a coach. Before he joined, their approach fascinated him from afar. “I thought: ‘These guys think differently. They don’t just go tried and tested. They might listen to a 29-year-old who’s potentially retiring.’ Brighton, in my opinion, are the most forward-thinking club in the world.”

He cites Mauricio Pochettino, whose work he saw first-hand at Southampton, as another source of inspiration. McCarthy made 301 career appearances for clubsu across the top four divisions, one of those coming in the Premier League when Ronald Koeman handed him his Southampton debut as an 87th-minute substitute at Crystal Palace on Boxing Day in 2014. “The quickest bib-to-shirt change you’ve ever seen. I was on the right with [Sadio] Mané … crazy. Koeman was a lot colder than Pochettino, but a very good coach. He’d make me feel terrible; he liked joining in drills – he was in his 50s but he’d never lose the ball and here I was, couldn’t trap a bag of cement. Even at that age I was curious about coaching and management styles.”

McCarthy, 31 next month, tells a lovely story about Pochettino at Southampton. He was 17 and cleaning José Fonte’s boots when he felt an arm on his shoulder. “It was the gaffer. He said: ‘I watched your game for the under-21s. I thought you did this well, you could have done this better, so, next week, you’ll train with us and we’ll work on some of those things.’ I went out for training on the Monday, I was right-back in an 11 v 11 and the manager is stood right behind me. They would’ve just had a big Premier League game but he was talking me through what he wanted. I felt like he knew me inside out, and I was just a scholar; he made me feel 10ft tall.”

View image in fullscreen Jason McCarthy debuted for Southampton off the bench against Crystal Palace in 2014. Photograph: Michael Zemanek/BPI/Shutterstock

It was McCarthy’s friend Tobi Sho-Silva, a former Charlton trainee now of Hampton & Richmond Borough, who encouraged him to get the ball rolling on his coaching badges. McCarthy was 26 and, until that conversation, he had other ideas. “I’m a man of faith, so I thought maybe I’ll end up being a pastor or working within the church. But then I did my [Uefa] B licence and I knew after about a week that I was way more suited to coaching than I was playing. It snowballed from there.”

McCarthy began putting his thoughts on paper and studying peers. He completed a diploma in psychology and a course in data analytics. He observed games live and remotely, regularly pausing matches to record interesting nuggets. He explains his intrigue in watching Barcelona under Hansi Flick, Michael Carrick’s work at Middlesbrough and Jim McNulty’s in non-league with Rochdale. “There’s a link between them – possession – but they do it in different ways. I always wanted to play in a team that played good football but I wasn’t ever good enough, to be honest. I worked under some coaches who would say: ‘This is how we want to play.’ And then in the week we would do nothing geared towards it and just expect it to show up on a Saturday.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Coincidentally, one of McCarthy’s final appearances came against Brighton under-21s in the EFL Trophy, against players he now coaches. His last game was in the same competition in December 2024. By then, he long felt he was making a bigger impact coaching than playing. How quickly did that dawn on him? “I was probably about 27. I had a quite serious chat with my wife and my mum and dad. I said: ‘I feel bad because I know a lot of people would love to be in my position. Do I need to park coaching and come back to it?’ I had teammates and coaches telling me: ‘Relax, you’ve got a playing career to finish.’ But it’s one of the best decisions I’ve made.”

McCarthy reflects on his playing days with pride – they took him to Wembley three times and he walked out as captain with his kids there – but is determined to take further strides on the sidelines. He plans to apply for his pro licence next year. “I want to challenge myself at the elite level – I’d love to do that one day. I’m very fortunate I’m at an elite club, so I get to see elite behaviour, standards, traits, players and staff, daily. What I did as a player … can I be even better as a coach?”

View image in fullscreen Jason McCarthy: ‘I always wanted to play in a team that played good football but I wasn’t ever good enough.’ Photograph: Peter Flude/The Guardian

Brighton’s under-21s, who last month overcame Paris Saint-Germain, were Premier League 2 champions for the first time last season. “I was incredibly proud to be part of a side that created history for the academy,” McCarthy says. “I believe winning and development come hand in hand so to help create that winning mentality within the group is something all of the staff can be really proud of. Hopefully it is just the start.” Stepping up to lead the team, he says, “has lit the fire for me to keep pushing and progressing within my coaching career”.

His faith keeps him grounded. “It’s part of my identity,” McCarthy says. “I pray before games, I read the Bible daily. I wouldn’t be where I am today without God. A big reason I’m so excited about the future is my faith, because when I started on my coaching journey, did I think that in my first interview, I’d be standing across from Fabian Hürzeler? No … how is that even possible?”

Sports.title: Schooled for success: how English lessons power Midtjylland’s talent factory
Sports.content:
If there is a secret to Midtjylland’s success in the transfer market then it starts in the classroom. Before this summer the Danish club renowned for an innovative approach had banked more than €200m (£170m) in sales since 2018, and they have just enjoyed the most profitable window in their short history.

The departure of the Guinea-Bissau striker Franculino Djú for Trabzonspor and the Chile forward Darío Osorio’s move to Crystal Palace on loan with an obligation to buy will potentially bring in €62m (£53.2m), with both deals completed in 48 hours at the end of the window. That followed the departures of the homegrown winger Aral Simsir and South Korean defender Lee Han-beom for Club Brugge for another €25m. The next batch of recruits included David Martínez, a 20-year-old Venezuela international from the MLS side LAFC. “I think hectic will be a good word,” says the technical director, Kristian Kjær, of the past couple of months.

What those sold have in common is that they were schooled for success by Midtjylland’s methodical approach that includes mandatory English lessons at least three times a week. “They are as important for them as it is to train,” Kjær says. “Because if they cannot understand English within six months, they cannot communicate with the coach. So it’s quite important for our common success.”

In a squad that has 17 nationalities from five continents, communication is key. Midtjylland employ coaches from all over the world to help new arrivals settle in. “We’re not running Midtjylland as a Danish club; we are an international club,” says Kjær, who describes Djú and Osorio as “poster boys for what we are trying to do”.

The fee for Osorio, whose move was confirmed almost two hours after the Premier League deadline had passed, is in line to become the most expensive Danish top-flight sale, with Palace having an obligation to pay £22.3m next summer and up to another £3.4m in bonuses. The 22-year-old made his first Palace start in their 3-0 Carabao Cup win against Middlesbrough after coming on against Fulham a few days earlier in the Premier League. He was spotted by Midtjylland’s scouts playing for Universidad de Chile and the club saw off competition from RB Leipzig, Milan and Atalanta to sign him in August 2023 – the month the Brentford owner, Matthew Benham, sold his controlling stake to the Danish businessman Anders Holch Povlsen.

“Darío prioritised the importance for him to start in a club and environment in Europe that could help him grow so one day he could go to the Premier League, which has been his dream since he was a small boy,” Kjær says. “His integration off the pitch was most important. Chilean football is not, and I don’t try to sound disrespectful, the most professional setup when it comes to nutrition and habits outside the pitch. Darío used to eat a lot of white bread for dinner and he couldn’t understand why he was not fully energised in the morning. That was one of the first things we did: look into his nutrition plan.”

View image in fullscreen Franculino Djú left for Trabzonspor in the final hours of the transfer window. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

Osorio, a predominantly left-footed forward who prefers playing as an inverted right-winger but can also fill the No 10 role, hit the ground running in Denmark and ended his first season with eight league goals.

“Since then, we have seen him putting on layers and layers,” Kjær says. “Darío has been outgrowing the league for some time and he was by far, in my opinion, the best player by a distance. We are very happy to see him making the step and believe he has the quality to be competitive in the Premier League, not as a sub but as a starting lineup player.”

There were a few nervous moments on deadline day as Palace pursued Malick Fofana before pivoting back to Osorio at the last minute when the Lyon forward picked Sunderland.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We prepared both the agent and the player that everything can easily end up being in the last days of the window because English clubs are not that brave to bring in players from outside England, especially not from the not top five leagues,” Kjær says. “It was a bit stressful, especially for Darío. But at the same time, mentally, he was also a bit prepared for that: ‘OK, I have to perform in the beginning of the season to keep myself in the shop window.’”

Midtjylland are hoping that the arrival of the 20-year-old Martínez for €7.3m, a Danish record, will help to fill the void left by Osorio and Djú, their top scorer last season with 17 goals. Thanks to the club’s FC Ebedei academy in Nigeria, which was established in 2004 and has helped to produce players such as Coventry’s Frank Onyeka, Midtjylland’s squad has also been boosted by the addition of the promising teenagers Olashile Musa Lawal and Ikenna Udechukwu as they attempt to win the title for the first time since 2024. They were runners-up last season to the surprise package AGF.

“We are just standing on the shoulders of the work we have done earlier,” says Kjær. “But, to sound a bit boring because it takes so much work, it’s also a bit according to strategy. This is what we hoped for, but also what we have worked for. That is why it makes us proud. It’s not just pure luck.”

Sports.title: How did some City fans become aggressive defenders of a nation state’s regime? | Sean Ingle
Sports.content:
A video of Liam Gallagher playing in a 1996 charity football match resurfaced on social media recently. Dressed in Manchester City blue and a bucket hat, in truth he appears to be in a fug of cigarettes and alcohol. But then, out of nowhere, he hits a shot into the top corner. Since last week, though, the Oasis singer has preferred to defend the honour of his club with his studs up.

As the fallout from the biggest scandal in British football history headed into a second week, Gallagher was asked what he made of rival fans wanting City to lose all their trophies after being found guilty of all the serious charges against them. “There all NEUROTIC little GIMPS,” came the reply on social media. It was one of dozens of sweary, punchy, and often amusing responses, all built on a solitary article of faith: that City will somehow find a way to wriggle free.

But Gallagher is hardly standing alone. Over at Bluemoon, the biggest City forum, the tone has been just as defiant – albeit with a sprinkle of gallows humour. “Have we been blamed for the Titanic hitting the iceberg yet?” asked one user. “Manchester City shot JFK,” wrote another. “This isn’t just a fight between the PL & City. It’s a fight for the heart, soul & future of football,” reckoned a third.

Staggeringly, the forum now has over 192,000 posts since the initial charges against City, dating back to 2023. Naturally the Premier League, jealous rivals and the media all come under heavy fire. Yet there remains a curious reluctance among fans to accept wrongdoing – or to criticise the club’s owners.

How might we explain that? I am not sure it is down to pure tribalism, or a determination among City fans to wait for the club’s appeal to play out. It’s more complicated, and more interesting, than that.

Let us try to get into the head of the most vociferous City fan since last Tuesday. For decades they were in United’s shadow, then everything changed. Their city did too, given how much Abu Dhabi United Group pumped into it. You can forgive them, then, for not wanting to believe that it was all built on sand during the legal process.

But now? Now there is no excuse. So what might explain the reluctance to accept what the independent commission report lays out in great detail? According to the Irish academic Colm Kearns, one reason is because the United Arab Emirates has not only brought unprecedented success and forged emotional bonds with City fans “but have also co-opted elements of the club’s fanbase as aggressive defenders of their regime”.

In 2023 Kearns and his colleagues analysed huge numbers of posts from City fans, going back years, and found that some of them would not only “overlook ethical violations by the Group, but decry and – in some cases – attack the Group’s critics.”

In other words the club’s owners had successfully leveraged the tribal loyalty of City fans into being Manchurian Candidates – or, rather, Manchesterism Candidates.

Kearns tells me that some sports journalists had even self-censored because of the impact of online abuse from City fans. “We had people talking about how fans would go online and try to find their troll through their personal social feeds, and it sent that on to their editor to get them in trouble,” he says.

There is another massive factor here: social media, and the way we now consume sport and communicate with other fans. Thirty years ago, most City fans would live near Manchester and see fans from other clubs at work and in the pub. Nowadays, they can dwell in an online space made up entirely of people who support their own club.

View image in fullscreen Social media has created tribal online spaces for sports fans. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

“I think it makes fans perhaps more tribally myopic than they would have been before and less likely to look outside of their own club’s perspective,” says Kearns.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Academics also talk of “sports fandom circles”, in which supporters across the globe increasingly mobilise and fiercely defend athletes or their teams. That phenomenon, which came out of east Asia with popular culture and music, leads supporters to be laser-focused on their own tribe. But it hardly encourages lighthearted banter, common ground, or compromise.

In City’s case, Kearns suspects that some fans are putting the club above the wider game, citing a Reddit post that said: “I am a City fan first and a football fan second.” Although, as he concedes, it is impossible to know how many online posters do not live in Manchester, or go to games, and therefore feel the need to prove their bona fide credentials by sticking up for the club at all costs.

Either way, where we could go next is interesting. If you were a far-right tech billionaire, why wouldn’t you want to buy a successful sports team – especially if you knew there was an army of potential defenders of your reputation among your new fanbase?

Over the weekend I went through the fan forums of other clubs to see what their supporters made of the guilty verdict against City. The overwhelming majority welcomed it, of course, even if some questioned whether City would really get properly punished for their crimes, given the relationship with Abu Dhabi and the British government.

“Once you lose faith that the rules apply equally, football becomes something else,” one wrote. “Every title, every match, carries a question mark. I feel cheated. I’m one of the victims. And for that, I hate Manchester City.”

Some will agree with that sentiment. Others will raise their eyebrows. I do wonder, though, would that poster feel the same way if the boot was on the other foot, and their club was in the line of fire?

Sports.title: Man City wanted Bayern Munich star before wild spending spree – but star said no
Sports.content:
Man City wanted Bayern Munich star before wild spending spree – but star said no

Bayern Munich midfielder Aleksandar Pavlovic reportedly rejected a summer switch to Manchester City.

The Germany international has become a regular under boss Vincent Kompany following an extended run of form.

3 Pavlovic remained loyal to Bayern this summer despite interest from Man City Credit: Getty

Pavlovic, a product of Bayern’s academy, has gone on to make 106 appearances for the club.

The midfielder has registered 12 goals overall for the reigning Bundesliga champions and in doing so, has caught the eye of Manchester City.

According to prominent German journalist Florian Plettenberg, the Premier League club were rebuffed in their efforts to lure Pavlovic to the Etihad Stadium this summer.

Thanks, but no thanks

"Manchester City had been pushing to sign Aleksandar Pavlovic since March. There were concrete talks,” Plettenberg confirmed on X.

"FC Bayern were informed that #MCFC were prepared to pay up to €100m (approximately £84.8m) - long before they signed Ayyoub Bouaddi/Enzo Fernandez.

"Pavlovic felt honoured by the interest and thought about it. But ultimately, he said NO. No negotiations with Bayern took place."

The 22-year-old’s importance at Bayern has been mirrored at international level with new Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp already making the midfielder a key component of his side.

He started last week’s 2-0 win over Serbia and followed it up with another solid display in Sunday’s goalless draw against Greece.

His swashbuckling style appears to have gone down well with Klopp who paid tribute to the star after Sunday’s match in Thessaloniki.

“What a game by Pavlovic. He was everywhere!” Klopp told reporters after the match.

3 Germany boss Jurgen Klopp has immediately taken a shine to Pavlovic Credit: Getty

Manchester City’s interest came amid a huge midfield overhaul following the arrival of Enzo Maresca as Pep Guardiola's successor.

In total, they shelled out a whopping £450million on new signings with £327m of that amount spent on midfield trio Fernandez, Elliot Anderson and Bouaddi.

City’s need to revamp their midfield even saw them break their own transfer record twice.

There were further arrivals at the Etihad with Iliman Ndiaye joining from Everton for £65m and Allan from Palmeiras for £34m.

Teen prospect Jeremy Monga joined from Leicester City in a £12.5m deal while goalkeeper Geronimo Rulli swapped Marseille for Manchester for £1.7m.

City were recently found guilty of 115 breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules.

3 Enzo Fernandez became Man City's record signing this summer, eclipsing Elliot Anderson who was signed just weeks earlier Credit: Getty

The club appealed the verdict last Thursday evening and are now awaiting the outcome from the appeal panel who have 30 days following the hearing's conclusion to deliver a final decision.

If the appeal fails, points deductions, relegation, or expulsion from the Premier League are all possibilities.

Sports.title: Where to watch Liverpool v Man City as Enzo Maresca eyes record held by Pep Guardiola amid guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Where to watch Liverpool v Man City as Enzo Maresca eyes record held by Pep Guardiola amid guilty verdict

Manchester City will face an 'absolute bear pit' at Anfield this weekend following the news that the club were found guilty of all charges by the Premier League.

After the 40-page statement was released, it was found that the Manchester-based outfit inflated their financial position by over £900million between the period of 2009 to 2018.



3 Manchester City have started the season with a 100 per cent record in all competitions Credit: Getty

The eight-time champions of the league continue to protest their innocence and have stressed they will be taking the necessary legal requirements.

Now Enzo Maresca's men will travel to Anfield to face Liverpool in their first game since the guilty verdict was revealed.

Andoni Iraola has made an unbeaten start to his life as Liverpool boss but he has only won two out of his first five games.



Additionally, Chris Kavanagh has been selected to referee the highly anticipated meeting on Sunday.

It will be the first Liverpool match the 41-year-old referee has took charge of since the 4-2 defeat at Aston Villa on May 15 while he also officiated Liverpool's 3-0 loss at the Etihad last season.



Maresca is hoping to win his sixth match in a row this season for the Citizens.

He could become the fourth manager to complete this feat alongside Carlo Ancelotti with Chelsea, Pep Guardiola with Man City and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer with Manchester United.



3 Man City owners and executives have continued to plea their innocence Credit: Getty

Where to watch Liverpool v Man City?

The highly anticipated fixture will take place on Sunday, October 11

The game at Anfield will kick off at 4:30pm.

It will be shown live on Sky Sports Premier League and Sky Sports Main Event from 4pm following their coverage of Crystal Palace v Nottingham Forest and Hull v Everton, respectively.

talkSPORT will have coverage on GameDay Live with Sam Matterface, Darren Ambrose and Perry Groves from 1:30pm.

Listen talkSPORT through the website or find us on DAB digital radio through your smart speaker and on 1089 or 1053 AM.



Download and listen to all our live commentaries via the talkSPORT app, whilst talkSPORT is also available to watch on Samsung TV Plus.

Subscribe to the talkSPORT YouTube channel for news, views and analysis plus our regular goals show and for more, 

For the latest odds and bet boosts for every big event, visit talkSPORT BET.

3 Man City were dominant against the Reds in their title defending season Credit: Getty



What's been said?

On talkSPORT's Sports Bar, Jason Cundy said: "Manchester City against Liverpool at Anfield... it's going to be an absolute bear pit.

"Of all the games City could have had that weekend, baring in mind Liverpool will be feeling aggrieved after they fell second and there was that amazing tussle between Pep and Klopp.

"I think in the modern game, that was one of the best leagues we've ever watched."

Dean Saunders responded: "I think at Anfield on the weekend, Liverpool will represent the whole of Great Britain and they will probably let Man City know, it will be a 'this is from all of us, take this.'



Cundy added: "Well there is a chance they go into the game without Erling Haaland and it would not surprise me one little bit if City got a result there... and by that I mean win."

Norway superstar Haaland was substituted in the 67th minute in his side's 2-1 defeat away at Portugal on Sunday night.

The striker was the one who signalled he needed to come off.

Haaland's Norway teammate Leo Ostigard said of his substitution: "It's clear that you want him on the field as long as possible.

"But he plays an incredible number of games, and he's a human being too."

Sports.title: Wrexham set for further boost to capacity in major Racecourse stadium update
Sports.content:
Wrexham set for further boost to capacity in major Racecourse stadium update

Wrexham has confirmed council-approved plans for the installation of 2,250 extra seats in their new Kop Stand.

Construction on the Kop began in December after a proposal for the addition of 5,500 new seats was given the green light by the Wrexham County Borough Council Planning Committee.

2 Wrexham have announced that the Kop End will have a total capacity of 7,750 with the addition of 2,250 new seats Credit: Getty

However, the total capacity of the reconstructed stand on the south-east side of the ground is now set to increase to 7,750.

Championship side Wrexham say the 2,250 new seats will sit in the second tier, and the overall capacity at the Racecourse Ground will grow over 18,000.

"The increase in seating capacity in the new Kop Stand will allow the club to cater for the strong demand for tickets for home matches from local fans, as well as the many international fans that visit both the club and the City of Wrexham bringing with them much needed revenue for the local community," a statement read.

"A key part of the club’s submission was an updated Travel Plan that included a commitment to the strong promotion across all club channels for the continued use of public transport on match days.

"These include the use of both bus and rail, with a close liaison with bus operators and Transport for Wales, and the continuation of the existing park and ride schemes plus the free parking option available exclusively on matchdays at Eagles Meadow."

Looking to the future

Hollywood owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney have looked to redevelop the Racecourse Ground since completing their takeover in February 2021.

The club then purchased the freehold 16 months later for a reported £2million from Wrexham Glyndwr University.

Wrexham were controversially given an £18m grant in public money to help support the ground's redevelopment.

Former Welsh Minister for Culture, Skills and Social Partnership, Jack Sargeant, defended the decision to award the funding.

"It's a really big development in the heart of Wrexham, it's the whole city, it's the gateway project," he claimed.

2 The Racecourse Ground will have a total capacity of over 18,000 once all the work has been completed Credit: Getty

Wrexham's plans to upgrade the Racecourse Ground mark their continued intentions of earning promotion to the Premier League.

They were promoted across three consecutive seasons from 2022/23 to 2024/25, rising from the National League to the Championship.

However, they finished seventh in the league last season and missed out on the play-offs by two points.

Wrexham are 14th with two wins from eight in the current campaign but are only three points adrift of eighth, which is one of two added play-off spots.

An away clash at Derby County is their first test after the three-week international break on Saturday.

Wrexham then host West Brom three days later, with the Kop Stand set to remain unfinished in the background.

Sports.title: Liverpool signing is already one of the best in Europe and ‘enormous’ upgrade
Sports.content:
Liverpool signing is already one of the best in Europe and ‘enormous’ upgrade

Jeremy Jacquet will be one of Europe's top five centre-backs if he maintains his trajectory, says European football expert Andy Brassell.

The French star has seamlessly adapted to life as a Premier League player following his £55million move to Liverpool, with the club conceding just four goals from five league games.



3 Jacquet had just 56 senior appearances under his belt prior to joining Liverpool

In contrast, Chelsea, who backed out of a deal to sign Jacquet in January, have shipped a league-leading 12 goals in the same span.

Jacquet's bright start at Anfield prompted new France boss Zinedine Zidane to hand the defender his first international call-up.

The 21-year-old went on to keep a clean sheet in his senior debut as France beat Belgium 1-0 and reprised his role for a 1-1 draw with Italy.



Even though Jacquet's international sample size is just 180 minutes, Brassell believes he's shown more than enough to prove he belongs at the elite level.

Andy Brassell's verdict on Jeremy Jacquet

"What's clear is that even at this early stage in his international career, he feels an enormous upgrade on the players around him," Brassell told talkSPORT.com.



"Ibrahima Konate has not had his best year, both with Liverpool and Real Madrid, where he's not exactly hit the ground runing. Dayot Upamecano is a great centre-back, but he has his moments where he switches off.

"I think people are absolutely blown away by how he (Jacquet) stepped up. He was good for Rennes but I don't think you can realistically expect a central defender of more experience than him to come into the Premier League and boss it like that straight away.



"So, for someone of his age to do it is absolutely remarkable."

Zidane placing his faith in Jacquet is notable in itself.

A former Ballon d'Or winner who went on to enjoy significant managerial success in charge of Real Madrid, Zidane knows all the qualities required to be considered a world class player.

3 Zidane may view Jacquet as a first-choice centre-back going forward Credit: Getty

As brilliant as Jacquet's defensive abilities may be, Brassell pointed out that it's an entirely different element to his game that Zidane may be particularly enamoured with.

Why Zinedine Zidane 'loves' Jeremy Jacquet

"He's everything that Zidane loves," Brassell said.

"He's physical, he's composed on the ball, he's a good leader.

"And think of the players that Zidane has hung his hat on throughout his coaching career and the players that he's been able to at Real Madrid. It's not naive players by any stretch of the imagination. He expects a level of maturity more than most coaches do. And Jacquet has been able to meet that.



"So if we're talking about him as one of the best 5-10 centre-backs in Europe already, never mind just young players. I think if he continues like this, this season, he's there, definitely. There's no doubt about it."

Unfortunately Jacquet's international break has not ended as planned, with the defender rested for France's 4-1 win over Belgium on Monday due to a hamstring strain.

3 Jacquet's move to Liverpool was agreed before Iraola joined, but he's already warmed to the defender Credit: Getty

Jacquet's potential injury comes ahead of Liverpool's crunch clash against Manchester City at Anfield on Sunday.



Should the centre-back miss out, Joe Gomez looms as an option to slot in alongside Virgil van Dijk.

Sports.title: ‘Corrupted his thinking’ – Paul Scholes questioned for demanding 12th Premier League medal amid Manchester City fallout
Sports.content:
Simon Jordan fears Paul Scholes' stint as Oldham boss transformed him into a mouthpiece for controversy.

Prior to his stint in charge of Oldham, which lasted seven games in 2019, Jordan felt Scholes was 'a very balanced individual that made very sensible points.'



2 Scholes retired from playing in 2013 and launched his podcast in 2025 Credit: Getty

But in the following years, Scholes' measured opinions have seemingly made way for divisive opinions on all the big talking points, many of which are shared on his podcast alongside fellow Manchester United great Nicky Butt.

Scholes' latest gripe centered around Manchester City being found guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules from 2009 to 2018.

Significant punishments are expected to be handed down, with some suspecting City could be stripped of the three Premier League titles they won in that period.



And Scholes, who was at United when City won their first of the three league titles, wants to benefit from any retrospective action.

"I want my medal," Scholes wrote on Instagram.

Simon Jordan questions Paul Scholes' medal demand

However, Jordan felt the Red Devils great should not stoop as low as demanding silverware via social media.



"Maybe his experience of management at Oldham has corrupted his thinking, because all of a sudden, what he's got is a podcast and he feels that he and Nicky have got to say controversial things," Jordan said.

"I think he's a bit better than that, really."

Conversely, Arsenal hero Martin Keown understood Scholes' frustration, but he felt the titles won by City should go unclaimed rather than being gifted to the teams who finished second.



Martin Keown calls for Manchester City's titles to be declared void

"I can't tell him how to behave, how to think," Keown said.

2 City won seven major trophies between 2009 to 2018 Credit: Getty

"If I was involved, I'd be angry.

"For me, I think it just should be void. I think if we're going to take away Manchester City's trophies through that period, it should be made void and they should just leave it as it was."

How many Premier League titles has Paul Scholes won?

Luckily for Scholes, he already has a significant number of Premier League winners' medals in his trophy cabinet.

The midfielder has won the competition an absurd 11 times, beginning in 1996.



Scholes' last Premier League medal was in 2013, which was Sir Alex Ferguson's final season in charge of United.

Despite Scholes' gargantuan haul of Premier League titles, he does not boast the most among all players.

Instead, that honour belongs to fellow Red Devils legend Ryan Giggs, who has won the league a record 13 times.

Sports.title: Where to watch Manchester United v Tottenham as Red Devils have fitness concerns over 10 players
Sports.content:
Where to watch Manchester United v Tottenham as Red Devils have fitness concerns over 10 players

Manchester United and Tottenham have been hit by multiple injury issues as Premier League action returns in a must-win game for both managers.

United have just five points from five games this season, as Roberto De Zerbi's bottom-of-the-table Spurs are searching for their first three points of the season.



3 Michael Carrick will be sweating on the fitness of Bruno Fernandes Credit: Getty

The Lilywhites are winless in their first five matches, and have failed to score in four of them as their two solitary points so far have come from 0-0 draws.

Additionally, both sides have experienced numerous players withdrawing from their respective nation team's camps during the international break.

For the Red Devils, Kobbie Mainoo withdrew from international duty after coming off 10 minutes from the end of the draw with Fulham but Carrick said it was a tactical decision at the time.



Portugal manager Jorge Jesus also revealed that Bruno Fernandes had been playing with an injury at United for the past three games.

Rashford picked up a hip injury in the World Cup and the pain has become progressively worse during his return for United before the international break.



United will also be likely without Benjamin Sesko, Amad, Manuel Ugarte, Patrick Dorgu, Matthijs de Ligt, Noussair Mazraoui, and Tom Heaton.

Spurs have been hampered by a number of fresh injury issues too as first-choice centre-backs Micky Van de Ven and Jan Paul van Hecke both picked up problems while on international duty with the Netherlands.



The Tottenham captain had Luka Jovic land awkwardly on his arm after a challenge, with the Oranje coach Xavi Hernandez adding that the player 'felt dizzy because he suffered [pain] in the finger, [but] it's not a big injury'.

Right-back Pedro Porro is likely to miss Saturday’s match due to the hamstring injury he sustained during the 3-2 defeat to Aston Villa immediately before the international break.

Other players expected to miss out on the clash include Dejan Kulusevski, Mykhaylo Mudryk, Wilson Odobert, and Xavi Simons.

3 Pedro Porro missed the international break due to a hamstring injury Credit: Getty



Where to watch Manchester United v Tottenham

Spurs head north to Old Trafford on Saturday, October 10.

Kick off is set for 5:30pm, as the Premier League enters Gameweek 6.

The match will be shown live on Sky Sports Premier League and Sky Sports Main Event from 5pm.

talkSPORT's Game-Day Phone-In with Jamie O'Hara and Jason Cundy will have all the latest from the game too.

Listen talkSPORT through the website or find us on DAB digital radio through your smart speaker and on 1089 or 1053 AM.

Download and listen to all our live commentaries via the talkSPORT app, whilst talkSPORT is also available to watch on Samsung TV Plus.



Subscribe to the talkSPORT YouTube channel for news, views and analysis plus our regular goals show and for more, 

For the latest odds and bet boosts for every big event, visit talkSPORT BET.

3 Carrick has only won one league game this season and Man United are sitting 12th in the table Credit: Getty

Manchester United v Tottenham: What's been said?

On talkSPORT's Hawksbee & Jacobs, former Spurs defender Anthony Gardner said: "We have a decent record against United. Our start of the season is down to so many changes over the summer.



"I think it's all down to manager. They've given him the trust and the leeway to bring in what he wanted to bring in and it seems as though it's still a transitional stage.

"It will probably be disappointing for the fans because they would want to see the team hit the the ground running, so then a lot of pressure come in and talking.

"You can see that the players are under pressure at the moment, and their struggling to find any top form and the manager has to restore the confidence in them.

"I feel it's a collective thing where they have to pull together, it's going to take time but they might not have enough time with the fans being so anxious for the club to do well. The club is huge. Brilliant fans and they deserve better.



"They've had their moments winning the Europa League, but the fans want more!"

Sports.title: Simon Jordan: Premier League needs to be disbanded, Man City scandal proves its rules aren’t fit for purpose
Sports.content:
Simon Jordan: Premier League needs to be disbanded, Man City scandal proves its rules aren’t fit for purpose

Disbanding the Premier League would be the nuclear option in the wake of Manchester City's financial scandal.

But Simon Jordan believes the drastic action is exactly what's required as City's significant breaches proved the competition's rules are out of date.



3 City are at risk of receiving a historical set of sanctions from the Premier League Credit: Getty

The Premier League was founded in 1992 but its current iteration is light years away, especially when it comes to ownership and finances.

Only four clubs in the top flight boast a majority ownership that is either an English individual or group while two, including City, are state-owned.

The competition also penned a four-year domestic broadcast deal beginning from the 2025/26 campaign worth an eye-watering £6.7billion.



Owing to the riches on offer in the Premier League, clubs flexed their financial muscles this summer as the combined transfer spending reached £3.5b.

Why does Simon Jordan believe the Premier League needs disbanding?

Despite the dizzying figures being bandied around regarding transfers, TV deals and sponsorships, Jordan believes the Premier League's rules remain rooted in the past, so much so he is unconvinced they can be brought up to accurately reflect the modern state of the game.



"My overriding argument is, you have made this league so fabulously successful, you've made it the most investable league in the world, you've made that success off the back of that, and you've turned the tap off," the former Crystal Palace owner said on talkSPORT's White and Jordan.

"And you've turned it off, for what reason? Because there's this mythical idea that everyone is going to go bust unless you control it.



"Now, if you want to control things, you can do redistributions.

"Really, the only way to evolve this game is to disband the Premier League, recreate it with a whole new set of rules that are fit for purpose rather than tacking on rules that have existed for 125 years and keep trying to finesse them to meet ownership models that are so much more sophisticated now."

Jordan added that the current rules aren't written to reflect nation-state ownerships or billionaires who 'suddenly decide they don't want the rules'.

3 The Abu Dhabi United Group owns an 82 per cent stake in City Credit: AFP

The ex-Palace owner also felt City could have had their verdict overturned and simultaneously expedited a reform of the Premier League's rules had they gone to a European court.



"They'd have overturned the fit and proper person test because that's nonsense, they'd have overturned the SCR and FFP rules because they're anti-competitive and anti-trust," Jordan said.

He added: "It's (fit and proper person test) a restricted practice because people can arbitrarily decide who is a fit and proper person."

How could Manchester City be punished for the financial breaches?

That same test could be used again should City's current ownership, led by United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour, decide to sell in the wake of the club being found guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.

The ownership group has been at the helm since 2008 and helped establish City as a European powerhouse via significant investment, some of which is alleged to have been illegal.



A raft of possible sanctions have been discussed, including a transfer ban, hefty fines and points deductions which may result in relegation.

3 Under Mansour's ownership, City have won 20 major trophies Credit: Getty

Some have even questioned whether City could be stripped of the three league titles they won between 2009 to 2018, which is the period they are alleged to have committed the financial breaches.

But Jordan does not believe that type of punishment benefits anyone.

Simon Jordan's verdict on stripping Manchester City of their league titles

When asked for his thoughts on whether City could be stripped, Jordan responded: "Just out of curiosity, what does that achieve? They've been slaughtered.



"Do you think the idea that Abu Dhabi's sole focus in life to own an English, beautiful, shiny football club that's now been built into a wonderful machine in the City Football Group, has now been diminished and damaged beyond all reparations?

"And you look at it and say Abu Dhabi are going to come away from this with any currency, even if they buy the Premier League out and turn around and say, 'We'll give you £1billion in compensation and every club can have a double dip of £50m each.

"They're never going to get out from underneath."

Jordan added: "I don't think it's pointless. I just don't know what it achieves.

"It's about what we do now going forward."

Sports.title: James McClean update after club attempted to terminate contract: ‘I will decide when I retire’
Sports.content:
James McClean has revealed that he is undergoing 'one of the most difficult periods of his life' as a dispute with Derry City continues.

The 37-year-old rejoined Derry in January this year, but the club have been trying to terminate his contract since the summer.



3 McClean hasn't played for Derry since July Credit: Getty

In a statement from PFA Ireland on behalf of McClean, they revealed that the winger has been suffering with an injury.

He has been left out of the squad without any sufficient reason being given, and he was told in the summer that the club wanted to rip up his contract.

They had informed him that they didn't believe he had the physical capacity to perform anymore.



And now, the PFA Ireland have released a statement.

It read: "As has been widely reported, we are representing James McClean in a dispute with Derry City FC over the terms of his contract.

"There has been a lot of conjecture and misinformation about the situation pertaining to James’ medical status and we would like to take this opportunity to clarify matters.



"In short, James has had a hip injury which had been causing intermittent issues for him. This has caused him to miss some games and occasional training sessions. He has sought medical treatment for this and is currently fit and well.

"He has trained fully for the last nine weeks and has made himself available for selection. He recently played in an internal match arranged by the club. He believes he can help the team and has not been provided with a satisfactory reason for being left out of the squad.



"He believes that the reason for this is a dispute which first arose in early August when the chairman of the club stated that his contract had been terminated. As a result of this, he contacted this association and has been provided with legal advice from PFA Ireland’s solicitor, Stuart Gilhooly SC.

"The upshot of this advice has been protracted correspondence between Mr Gilhooly and the club. Instead of terminating the contract as alleged, it transpires that they had in fact set about invoking Section 18 of the Standard Players Contract which states that if a player is deemed to have a permanent incapacity as determined by an agreed and independent physician, then the club is entitled to terminate the contract with six months notice.

3 McClean made 108 appearances as a Wrexham player, winning League One before heading back to where it all started Credit: Getty

"To date, no physician, either independent or agreed, has reached such a conclusion. Indeed, an Orthopaedic Surgeon, Mr Desmond Gibson, who saw him at the request of the club as recently as 21 September said he believes he can continue to play football as long as he is not in severe pain. He is not in severe pain and is willing, able and anxious to return to playing for Derry City.



"The club has a duty of care to James, who they signed without conducting a medical. He is much loved native of Derry and highly regarded Irish international centurion. We would hope that this matter can be resolved in an amicable and sensible manner and in such a way that would allow James to play again for the club he loves."

What did McClean say?

McClean added his own words to the statement as well in which he made it clear he wouldn't be forced into retiring.

He said: "This has been one of the most difficult periods of my life, both personally and professionally. When I agreed to come home from Wrexham, I did so in good faith, based on commitments made to me both playing wise and regarding my future after football. I uprooted my family midway through the school year because I believed in the vision presented to me, both for the short term and the long term.

"I accept that some of my actions over the past few months were misjudged, and my frustrations should have remained in-house. I take responsibility for that - and I apologise. Derry City is my club, and I respect everyone who cares about it as much as I do.



"I was asked to help drive standards, to speak up, and to use my experience to further professionalise my hometown club. From the start of the season, I tried to do this to the best of my ability, but I felt when I did my opinions were not well received.

3 McClean isn't giving up his contract without a fight Credit: Getty

"While I’m happy to hold myself accountable when I am wrong and when my performances have not been to the levels I expect of myself, I cannot understand or accept that I have been treated this way over the past few months.

"For any club to feel it is ok to attempt to terminate a player's contract without any due process or just cause is incomprehensible, and it sets a dangerous precedent for every player in this league.



"I was approaching 37 years old when I signed for Derry City. It is well accepted that any player of that age will have occasional injury issues. I have been open about what my body now faces, and that has not been easy to come to terms with.

"But I am not permanently incapacitated, or anything even remotely close to that. I am capable of contributing and doing well in the League of Ireland. I train as hard and give as much as anyone.

"I will decide when I retire. Nobody else will make that decision for me. When that time comes, my body will tell me. This is my life and my career. I deserve the same duty of care and fairness given to the majority of other players at Derry City FC.

"I am ready to play when called upon."

What has happened with McClean and Derry?

McClean played ten of the first 11 League of Ireland games he could before suffering injury.



The hip problem kept him out of action for five games.

He returned but started four of the next seven with his final league match being 56 minutes in a 4-2 defeat at the start of July.

The former Republic of Ireland international hasn't appeared since, and McClean has been very vocal about his situation.

He has cited broken promises, and he is back in training with his deal due to expire in November, and it remains to be seen if he gets to represent his boyhood club again.
