Sports.title: Welcome to the Premier League's most dangerous road: After TWO Hull City stars crash on their way to training in a matter of weeks, Daily Mail Sport's man takes a trip down quiet residential road himself
Sports.content:
Welcome to the Premier League’s most dangerous road. That might sound like the intro to a Channel 5 documentary, but it is where we are: Millhouse Woods Lane, a stone’s throw from Hull City’s training ground, where two players have flipped their cars and somehow walked away without a scratch – to their bodies at least. In the space of a month, Sorba Thomas and Lucas Gourna-Douath have ended up head over heels in the same spot in their expensive sports cars. Can that be a coincidence? I made the three-hour journey to Cottingham, the pleasant suburb of Hull, to find out. Honesty hour: I questioned whether a 272-mile round trip to look at a road would be worth it. Spoiler alert: it was! So here I am, standing on a quiet road about a 15-minute drive from the MKM Stadium and the city of Hull, getting dirty looks from the locals who are all wondering the same thing: 'Who is this idiot with a selfie stick?'. Immediately after turning on to the road, I couldn't help but chuckle. Surely this can’t be the place where two cars have been flipped on their side, can it? After all, this is an A-road lined with parked cars down one side, meaning drivers heading towards the training ground must give way or venture into the wrong lane with caution. The speed limit was 30mph but, as my driving instructor used to say, it is an absolute maximum, not a word of advice on how fast to travel. Heeding those words of wisdom, we travelled down at approximately 8mph, which felt about right given the lack of space and the ominous, hefty kerb on the right-hand side. Such caution was appropriate even despite the fact the car we used for this assignment could probably be bought at least ten times over for the money Hull’s players had splurged on their fancy 4x4 vehicles. Sorba Thomas and Lucas Gourna-Douath both flipped their cars outside Hull's training ground Gourna-Douath's car is seen after the crash close to the Premier League club's training ground My working theory on the cause of the mystery incidents is this: drivers are forced to pull into the right-hand lane but don't realise how little space they have and end up clipping the kerb. Doing this at any kind of significant speed could easily lead to the car ending up on its back and the drivers’ feet facing the sky. This is a deceptively dangerous road where you wouldn't want to exceed 20mph. After our driving test, I decided to retrace the players’ movements on foot, dodging a supermarket delivery driver who was forced to mount the kerb. Another reminder this road is not exactly designed for the larger vehicles. It really is easy to see how these incidents happened. Lib Dem Councillor Phil Redshaw agrees with our theory that the 30mph speed limit is excessive. ‘Whatever the cause, given the fact that both vehicles overturned on to the pavement, a reduction of the speed limit to 10mph would not appear unreasonable,’ he told Daily Mail Sport. Redshaw has requested an urgent safety review of the road and added: ‘We can’t just write it off as two unfortunate incidents.’ Though our investigation was somewhat light-hearted, there is undoubtedly a serious matter at hand here. Thomas and Gourna-Douath are both incredibly fortunate to emerge unscathed, even if the latter did post a picture of his flipped car on Instagram with the joke: ‘Can’t park there mate’.

Your browser does not support iframes.

Three weeks ago Thomas was involved in a crash that saw his car flip onto its roof Players are being educated on the matter. Shaun Whiter, a former non-league player, has just been invited to go into the 72 English Football League clubs to give talks on how to be safe behind the wheel. Whiter had both legs amputated following a road traffic accident. ‘I was a non-league footballer, the night before pre-season I was involved in a road traffic accident in which the driver fled the scene,’ Whiter explains. ‘I lost six pints of blood but was saved by the ambulance team that helped me come back round. I was meant to be in a coma for a week but came out in four hours, as you can imagine you look down at a bedsheet with half of you missing. ‘You think you’re going to kick a football around the next day but all of a sudden that all is taken away from you. It was hard to get over that physically but of course mentally. There is a potential spiral of drink, drugs and suicide from the impact of this. ‘I now have prosthetics at a cost of about £250,000. That is the ripple effect of what these accidents could cause. I started seeing headlines of “footballer…”, “footballer…”, “footballer…”. Football rallied round me but I would see the ripple effect of what it can cause.’ Gourna-Douath poses for a photograph with the same car he later crashed Luckily, both incidents in Cottingham ended with more damage to the cars than the players – although one local told Daily Mail Sport that a dark blue Mini Cooper had also been damaged in one of the incidents. ‘The lads are clearly in a rush to get to training which speaks volumes,’ said local Terry Pearson. ‘However, as a local road user I'd say they should leave the flipping for opponents in games.’ Perhaps that will be the message from manager Sergej Jakirovic when his team safely reconvene after the international break.

Sports.title: From sneaking into Edinburgh pubs at 15 to WrestleMania: WWE star Joe Hendry reveals his incredible rise to the top... and explains why he wants Logan Paul FIRED
Sports.content:
Joe Hendry can still remember being 15 years old and sneaking into an Edinburgh pub to perform at its open mic night.

Under-age and armed with the musical ambitions that would consume the next decade of his life, the Scot was learning how to command an audience long before tens of thousands of wrestling fans were chanting his name.

More than 20 years later, Hendry has travelled an extraordinary path from the pubs and music venues of the Scottish capital to the biggest stage in professional wrestling.

After initially believing he was too small to become a wrestler, the 38-year-old eventually took the plunge and last year found himself facing WWE legend Randy Orton at WrestleMania.

Now signed to WWE, he has also gone back to his musical roots with the release of his album Beyond Belief, which is already a top album in the charts and trending No1 in the iTunes soundtrack chart.

And if the relentlessly self-promotional lyrics are anything to go by, success has certainly not damaged his confidence.

'Basically, all the songs are singing about how great I am,' Hendry told the Daily Mail. 'So if you're a Joe Hendry fan, this is the one for you.'

Joe Hendry has enjoyed a remarkable rise in his wrestling - and music - career

One song in particular has attracted attention: Fire Logan Paul.

And Hendry makes no attempt to disguise his message towards his fellow WWE star.

'I think every so often, as a wrestler and a musician, you've got to take some time to do something right, use your platform for good,' he said.

'And I can't think of anything better than firing Logan Paul.'

Asked whether his WWE colleagues might privately listen to the song, Hendry joked: 'I have no idea whether any of my colleagues have ever just one day decided to spin Fire Logan Paul, but it wouldn't surprise me.'

It is a typically mischievous answer from a man who has managed to turn music into a central part of his wrestling persona.

But long before wrestling took him around the world, Hendry was a fixture on Edinburgh's live music circuit.

'I used to play in Cabaret Voltaire,' he said. 'I think I've played in Cabaret Voltaire more than any other person. I've probably played there 40 to 50 times.

'I played in Studio 24 before it shut down. I played in Whistle Binkies.

'Every week there was a bar called Acanthus... I used to play there doing live music and open mic night when I was 15.

'You're supposed to be 18 to be in that pub, but I was 15, just learning how to play in front of an audience.

'We then sold out the Liquid Rooms. I got 1,000 people into the Picture House before that closed down. So yeah, I've got a long history with Edinburgh venues.'

Music was in the family.

Hendry's father was a DJ with an obsessive love of music and encouraged his son's creative ambitions, introducing him to Apple's GarageBand software at 15.

For the next decade, Hendry played music and wrote songs.

But another ambition was refusing to disappear.

'I knew in my heart pro wrestling was number one and it was never going to go away,' he said. 'I had to do it.'

The inspiration had originally come from The Rock.

Hendry says he did not become a serious wrestling fan until he was around 14, when the future Hollywood superstar captured his imagination.

Yet despite his enthusiasm, Hendry initially convinced himself that a wrestling career was not realistic.

'I thought in my mind I wasn't big enough to be a wrestler,' he admitted.

'Then I got on the independent scene and I was the bigger guy in nine out of 10 matches, and I was like, "Oh, I don't know what I was worried about here".

'That's the thing I love about wrestling. It doesn't matter what size you are because everybody can have a role in professional wrestling.'

Hendry took on wrestling legend Randy Orton at WrestleMania 41

The turning point arrived at New Year as 2012 became 2013.

Hendry was unhappy with the direction his life was taking and decided that instead of celebrating Hogmanay, he would make himself a promise.

'This has not been a good year,' he remembers thinking. 'This is not going well. I have nothing to my name, nothing to show for all this work.

'But as of tomorrow, I am a professional wrestler.'

It was not an overnight transformation.

Hendry says there were jobs to take and bills to pay. He started a business and endured moments when achieving his wrestling ambition appeared almost impossible.

He simply refused to abandon it.

'I just kept believing in myself, kept moving forward, and I worked my way up over 13 years to face Randy Orton at WrestleMania in front of 80,000 people,' he said.

'And now here I am, signed to WWE.

'So my message is: if anyone's got a dream, it's never too late. Go out there and do it.'

Music, meanwhile, has proved crucial to Hendry's wrestling success rather than becoming the abandoned first act of his career

His self-penned entrance theme I Believe in Joe Hendry went viral, helping transform his name and his trademark 'believe' catchphrase into an international wrestling phenomenon.

The song also presents Hendry with an unusual problem.

Other wrestlers want him to write entrance themes for them.

He refuses.

'Absolutely. Hell no, it's not happening,' he said.

'Writing that song, I Believe in Joe Hendry, took me like two and a half weeks full-time.

'So to do that for somebody else, I don't know, man. I've got to focus on Joe Hendry here. Come on.'

Nor would he exchange his own theme for that of another wrestler.

'Hell no. I've got the best entrance theme in the game,' he insisted.

'No one has a better entrance theme than mine.'

His musical influences are rather less bombastic.

Hendry names American rock band Weezer as his favourite group of all time and credits them with inspiring his songwriting.

And when Britpop's great battle was being fought between Oasis and Blur, Hendry belonged firmly in the latter camp.

'I was never an Oasis fan until probably a year or two ago,' he admitted.

'I didn't really appreciate their music. It just wasn't my thing. I was more of a Blur guy when they were doing the Oasis-Blur thing.

'But now, in retrospect, it's hard to deny they've got the thing.'

Hendry names Weezer as his favourite group of all time and credits them with inspiring his songwriting

Perhaps inevitably, Hendry now judges Liam and Noel Gallagher partly through the eyes of a professional wrestler.

'With music and art, it's about style and substance, and they have both style and substance,' he said.

'They have amazing songs, they have a look about them, they have an attitude.

'And if wrestling's the same way, if I look at Oasis as a wrestler, they've got all the tools to be the top guy. They've got a swagger about them.'

For all the miles Hendry has travelled since those teenage Edinburgh gigs, however, one ambition is much closer to home.

He wants the opportunity to wrestle in front of a Scottish WWE crowd.

And Hendry believes the supporters who helped propel his career can make it happen.

'It comes down to the fan support,' he said.

'If the fans are loud enough, if they say his name and he appears...

'If enough fans demand for Joe Hendry to be at the Hydro, then chances are he's going to be at the Hydro.

'But I can't guarantee it. I'm hoping the fans are loud enough. They're saying my name.

'And if enough people say my name, I hope that we hear my music that night.'

For the teenager who once sneaked into Edinburgh pubs simply to get the chance to perform, hearing that music booming around a packed Scottish arena would be quite a homecoming.

Sports.title: Riot police rush to stop mass brawl after Nations League clash descends into chaos - as Suriname make racism accusation and urge FIFA to take action
Sports.content:
Riot police rush to stop mass brawl after Nations League clash descends into chaos - as Suriname make racism accusation and urge FIFA to take action

Riot police were forced to intervene after a bad-tempered Nations League clash between Guatemala and Suriname descended into chaos on Monday.

In what was a crunch encounter in the competition, Guatemala triumphed 1-0 thanks to a 96th-minute winner from Matthew Evans.

The result didn't tell the story though, with Suriname reduced to ten men after Richonell Margaret was sent off in the second half following an incident with home supporters.

It was later revealed that Margaret had been the subject of alleged racist abuse, with referee Joe Dickerson seen making the X gesture, FIFA's no-racism sign.

Following a delay of around ten minutes, Dickerson was seen in conversation with Suriname captain Myenty Abena, who ultimately decided to continue the match after discussions with team-mates.

Nevertheless, the red card sparked a flashpoint with both benches up in arms after Margaret's dismissal before things escalated again at full-time.

#FanáticosPlus | 🚨 BATALLA CAMPAL EN GUATEMALA 🇬🇹



Jugadores y cuerpo técnico de Guatemala y Surinam se fueron a los golpes tras el partido por la Liga de Naciones de Concacaf. pic.twitter.com/CTGekJnqvD — Fanáticos + (@FanaticosGMV) October 6, 2026

Riot police were forced to intervene after Guatemala vs Suriname descended into chaos

Guatemala won the game 1-0 but the encounter was marred by allegations of racist abuse

Players and officials from both sides found themselves involved in a chaotic brawl, with videos showing them trading blows as supporters screamed down from the stands.

Things became so heated that riot police were forced to intervene, and videos showed officers running onto the pitch and attempting to separate the teams.

After the game, Suriname skipper Abena then shared a lengthy and emotional Instagram post about what had gone on and urged the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) and FIFA to act.

He wrote: 'A call for action to @concacaf and @fifa. There are moments when football becomes about much more than just the game.

'During our match against Guatemala, we were subjected to racist abuse from the stands throughout the game. At one point, emotions took over and one of our players reacted.

'Because behind every shirt is still a human being - with emotions and with limits. The referee decided to show him a red card, changing the entire course of the match.'

Abena added: 'As captain, I was faced with a difficult decision: Do we walk off the pitch and accept the consequences, or do we continue with 10 men and refuse to let racism drive us away from the game we love?

'With around 20 minutes left, we chose to continue. Not because what happened was acceptable. Not because it didn't affect us. But because of our love for football, our country, and each other.'

Margaret later shared several racist comments and images that had been sent to him on social media before he posted an Instagram story aimed at the governing bodies.

He wrote: 'The entire stadium is making monkey noises at me and my teammates. Do we always have to accept this? @concacaf @concacafnationsleague @fifa.'

Suriname urged FIFA and CONCACAF to take action following the bad-tempered encounter

This is not the first time Suriname have faced alleged racism, with a similar incident happening during a World Cup qualifier in El Salvador last year.

Their general manager Brian Tevreden was on the touchline for both matches and hit out at what had gone on.

'This is scandalous, and it simply cannot go on like this,' he said. 'We are the ones being punished: the entire match was turned upside down.

'And beyond tonight, it's already the second time this has happened to us in Central America. It's disgraceful.

'I am seriously considering no longer traveling with my team to places where this is allowed to happen. CONCACAF and FIFA really have to take action now.'

Abena added: 'Now, I call on FIFA and CONCACAF to take responsibility and act. As players, we made the decision to stay on the pitch and finish the game under extremely difficult circumstances. We did our part.

'After our experience in El Salvador we continued with nothing but love for the game. Now experiencing this in Guatemala, we can no longer stay silent.

'If we truly want racism out of football, words and campaigns are not enough. There must be action and accountability when it happens.'

The 1-0 victory sealed Guatemala's place in the CONCACAF Nations League quarter-finals at the expense of their opponents.

Sports.title: How Liam Rosenior is rebuilding his career under the watchful eye of France's RICHEST man - and the blueprint he is offering young English coaches after Chelsea catastrophe
Sports.content:
Every so often, a cluster of appointments hint at a trend forming - young British managers moving abroad to follow pathfinding young players in search of an alternative route to the top.

The Premier League is a tough nut to crack for a new generation of homegrown coaches unable to satisfy the demands for top-flight experience or the tactical fashions currently leaning towards those from Spain or Germany.

Increasingly, young coaches are telling their agents they want to go abroad to forge careers, but those opportunities are exceedingly rare and rarer still in Europe’s elite leagues.

In Paris, however, Liam Rosenior is quietly reconstructing a reputation shredded by a torrid 106 days in charge of Chelsea.

Quietly at least until the flashpoint which followed the 2-1 victory against his former club Strasbourg before the international break, when his post-match fist-pumping celebrations riled fans in the away end and sparked a confrontation on the pitch between rival players.

Perhaps he can be forgiven for letting off steam. Rosenior has kept a respectable silence in five months since his exit from Stamford Bridge and has tried to let his work do the talking since landing a top job at one of the most exciting projects in European football.

Paris FC is a club owned since November 2024 by the family of Bernard Arnault, France’s richest man and founder of the luxury goods conglomerate LVMH, which owns world famous brands including Dior, Louis Vuitton and Moet & Chandon.

Liam Rosenior celebrated exuberantly after Paris FC's win over his old club Strasbourg

... a confrontation between the sides followed with fans upset by Rosenior's celebration

Paris FC sit third in Ligue 1 and remain unbeaten after five games under Rosenior

The Arnault family are worth an estimated £113billion, a fortune which dwarfs most of the individual owners in the Premier League and appear determined to sink some of it into their football venture.

Red Bull have bought a stake in Paris and Pierre Ferracci, the club’s president since 2006, has agreed to stay on to impart continuity and his experience of the football industry.

The ambition is clear and gathering momentum. Paris won promotion to France’s top-flight in 2025 to end an absence of 46 years, and installed Marco Neppe, formerly with 10 years in recruitment roles at Bayern Munich, as their sporting director.

They have a net spend near £130million across the last three transfer windows.

The bulk of it spent on young players with scope to develop. And that is where head coach Rosenior comes in having performed so well on a similar brief during 18 months at Strasbourg, Chelsea’s sister club where he finished seventh in his only complete season.

Paris are nicely poised in third in Ligue 1, unbeaten in the first five games and currently three points and three places ahead of Qatari-owned neighbours and back-to-back European champions Paris Saint-Germain.

Paris FC are owned by Bernard Arnault, pictured with his wife Helene

Paris FC sit third in Ligue 1 after an unbeaten start to the season

On the doorstep they have one of the richest talent beds in football.

Rosenior’s stock may have taken a hit in English football from the ridicule he suffered at Chelsea, initially for his fondness for corporate jargon in front of the TV cameras and later for results, but in France there are plenty who admire his talent.

Like Graham Potter, he has returned to a league where he feels appreciated and where he can mature as a coach in a calmer, less judgmental and more stable environment.

Potter took his time. He took almost two years out after his own bitter Chelsea experience followed by nine months at West Ham, before returning to Sweden where he built his career with seven successful years at Ostersunds.

As Sweden boss, he has proved an instant hit. First, he rescued their World Cup campaign and qualified for the summer tournament via the play-offs and now has won three and drawn one of his four Nations League games in this international break.

For ambitious coaches looking for alternatives, they lights the way.

Potter and Rosenior both stepped beyond the comfort zone of English football, embraced different cultures and been rewarded.

Another is Ian Cathro, also in France and top of the second tier with St Etienne after finishing eighth and 10th with Estoril in Portugal.

Sweden are flying high under Graham Potter, and Monday's 1-0 win over Romania - with a goal from Arsenal's Viktor Gyokeres - gave them 10 points from four Nations League games

Cathro, a 40-year-old Scot sacked after seven months as Hearts boss in 2017, fell back into the backroom team of Nuno Espirito Santo with whom he first cut his coaching teeth at Rio Ave in Portugal in 2012.

These breaks usually come from network connections. St Etienne are owned since 2024 by Canadians Kilmer Sports Ventures and have ex-Arsenal pair Ivan Gazidis and Huss Fahmy in key executive roles. Nevertheless, the breaks must be maximised.

Cathro is fluent in Portuguese and now holding press conferences in French at St Etienne.

The linguistic skills matter. It is evidence of commitment as well as vital for the communication which is key to success. Potter can speak in Swedish and he told Daily Mail Sport in an interview before the World Cup finals how there are times when he feels Swedish.

Although doing most of his public speaking in English, Rosenior’s French is good enough to converse with his players and staff and understand insults thrown his way by the Strasbourg fans.

Other British coaches who can be found plying their trades in Europe include the Belgium-born Still brothers, Will at Auxerre in France and Ed at La Louviere in Belgium.

Former Hearts boss Ian Cathro is thriving at St Etienne after a positive spell at Estoril

Also in Belgium’s Pro League, Lee Johnson is at Lommel and Mick Beale is at Zulte Waregem.

Beyond this, the Brits abroad can be found in the usual places. There is a healthy contingent in the United States, most prominently Dean Smith at Charlotte and Matt Wells at Colorado.

And those enticed to the Middle East, such as Brendan Rodgers at Al-Qadsiah and Des Buckingham at Al-Kholood in Saudi Arabia. Jonjo Shelvey is coaching in the second tier of UAE football.

Smith and Rodgers are post Premier League and probably enjoying a relatively stress-free life whereas former Oxford boss Buckingham and former Tottenham assistant manager Wells are still early in their careers.

It will be interesting to see where it takes them and whether Wilfried Nancy’s 33-day ordeal at Celtic deters British clubs from recruiting out of Major League Soccer.

Dean Smith has been head coach at Charlotte FC in MLS since 2023

There are veterans of world coaching still out there doing their thing. Stuart Baxter, 73, is in his second spell at Halmstad in Sweden, the latest port of call on a 22-stop coaching career spanning eight different countries across three continents.

Stephen Constantine, 63 with six different national teams and six clubs, five of them in Cyprus, during his 27-year coaching journey, is at Rwanda for a second time.

British coaches are scattered around the world. They can be found in minor leagues and with minor nations and yet chances remain slim across Europe’s top five leagues.

There are four British coaches in the Premier League. Frank Lampard and Gary O’Neil fighting to beat the odds with promoted clubs, David Moyes at Everton and Michael Carrick seldom far from questions about his future at Manchester United.

Rosenior is not in such a bad place at all. Watch this space.

Sports.title: Poppy-protest footballer James McClean, 37, hits out at Derry City after hometown club claimed he was 'permanently incapacitated' in failed bid to tear up his contract
Sports.content:
Poppy protest footballer James McClean has hit out at his hometown club Derry City after they tried to rip up his contract.

McClean, 37, branded it 'incomprehensible' and a 'dangerous precedent' for the club to try and terminate his deal due to his physical issues.

Derry attempted to bin off McClean in August – despite signing him in January on a multi-year deal – reportedly claiming he is unable to fulfil his contract's terms because he is not fit enough to play or train.

Interim manager Mark Connolly has left McClean - who refused to wear a poppy while representing English and Welsh clubs at the height of his career, out of his squad, but the former Wrexham man insists he is ready to feature when called upon in a defiant statement.

'This has been one of the most difficult periods of my life, both personally and professionally,' McClean said in a statement on the PFA Ireland website.

'When I agreed to come home from Wrexham, I did so in good faith, based on commitments made to me both playing wise and regarding my future after football. I uprooted my family midway through the school year because I believed in the vision presented to me, both for the short term and the long term.

James McClean has hit out at his club Derry City for trying to terminate his contract

'I accept that some of my actions over the past few months were misjudged, and my frustrations should have remained in-house. I take responsibility for that - and I apologise. Derry City is my club, and I respect everyone who cares about it as much as I do.

'I was asked to help drive standards, to speak up, and to use my experience to further professionalise my hometown club. From the start of the season, I tried to do this to the best of my ability, but I felt when I did my opinions were not well received.

'While I'm happy to hold myself accountable when I am wrong and when my performances have not been to the levels I expect of myself, I cannot understand or accept that I have been treated this way over the past few months.

'For any club to feel it is OK to attempt to terminate a player's contract without any due process or just cause is incomprehensible, and it sets a dangerous precedent for every player in this league.

'I was approaching 37 years old when I signed for Derry City. It is well accepted that any player of that age will have occasional injury issues. I have been open about what my body now faces, and that has not been easy to come to terms with.

'But I am not permanently incapacitated, or anything even remotely close to that. I am capable of contributing and doing well in the League of Ireland. I train as hard and give as much as anyone.

'I will decide when I retire. Nobody else will make that decision for me. When that time comes, my body will tell me. This is my life and my career. I deserve the same duty of care and fairness given to the majority of other players at Derry City FC. I am ready to play when called upon.'

McClean signed for his hometown club at the start of the 2026 season and has two years left on his deal. The star has regularly made headlines for his refusal to take part in Remembrance Day commemorations.

James McClean turned up for Derry City training despite them reportedly trying to rip up his contract

Derry sit fourth out of ten teams in the League of Ireland Premier Division, a disappointing campaign after finishing runners-up in 2023 and 2025.

In June, McClean hinted at his unhappiness following his return home after a 15-year spell in English football.

'Family (are) enjoying being home – probably not so much myself, if I’m being honest,' McClean said during a punditry appearance on RTE.

'You know, you have a lot of conversations on the phone, and then you come home and you quickly realise that what you hear on the phone is not what you see in reality.

'There’s a lot of factors that’s contributed to that, but we’ll leave them for another day.'

McClean has previously spoken out about his reasons for not wearing the poppy, a decision he first made while playing for Sunderland in 2012. He maintained that stance throughout his career in England, despite being regularly targeted with abuse.

'The poppy which originally stood for World War 1 and 2 has now been adopted into honouring and remembering British soldiers that have served in all conflicts throughout the world including those who opened fire and murdered 14 innocent civilians on Bloody Sunday Jan 1972, in my home city, as well as many other brutal crimes throughout Ireland,' McClean said in 2024.

'That is why I never have and never will wear a poppy. If the poppy’s sole purpose was to honour World War 1 and 2 then I would have no issue wearing it, but that’s not the case.

McClean has regularly made headlines throughout his career for his refusal to take part in Remembrance Day commemorations

'I respect those who do as I am fully aware we have different beliefs and upbringings, I would never force my beliefs on others, I’m not naive or stupid enough to expect the matter to be reciprocated, especially as the poppy is forced now on everyone in the UK and god forbid someone doesn’t wear it, the abuse they have to endure. The irony of all of this is that the poppy originally stood to honour those who fought for the right of freedom in both World Wars.

'Some people, no matter what, will not educate themselves or want to educate themselves, so to those who throw abuse about (matters they know nothing about), with insults like ‘hates our country’ – well I don’t. Some of my best relationships I’ve made through the years are with people born and raised in England and have completely different beliefs to me ... One thing I never have and never will do, is bend the knee to compromise my convictions.'

McClean, who has won 103 caps for the Republic of Ireland since choosing to play for them rather than Northern Ireland whom he represented in the Under 21s, said he had received 'death threats' for his stance over the poppy.

Last October, speaking during an episode of Virgin Media's Living with Lucy, he told presenter Lucy Kennedy how his family feared he would be shot while away on international duty after he first refused to wear a poppy on his shirt in 2012.

'I was getting death threats, people were saying I should be shot,' he said. 'I was getting bullets in the post, bullets sent to the club.

'That night, I met up with Ireland. The club had received threats that basically I was going to be shot. The game was on TV. I was going to be shot, this and that. (My wife, Erin) is back up in Newcastle, she’s panicking, she’s s*****g herself. They had to put security outside my hotel room door the whole night.

'Then, obviously, we’re playing the game, Erin’s watching the game, she’s panicking, she’s thinking, "He’s going to be shot on TV". Thankfully, nothing happened or nothing ever has happened.'

He added: 'I was getting death threats, people were saying he should be shot and dragged across the Cenotaph.

McClean, who has won 103 caps for the Republic of Ireland since choosing to play for them rather than Northern Ireland, said he has received 'death threats' for his poppy stance

'I could have easily just said, "I'll wear a poppy", and sold myself out and be known for my football or "I'll not wear a poppy" and be known as that but I've stayed true to myself.

'Six or seven people from the Creggan estate (where he grew up) died on Bloody Sunday that day so for me to wear a poppy in support of the people who carried out those atrocities...

'It frustrates me how people can’t see that. How is it even a debate of why I should wear the poppy?'

Sports.title: MAN CITY, WHAT HAPPENS NEXT: When will they be punished? Can Premier League look at post-2018 accounts? Is anyone criminally liable? How much can rivals sue for? And what now for ex-City chief Omar Berrada? MIKE KEEGAN reveals all
Sports.content:
Eight years on from the start of the biggest scandal in recent British sporting memory, we finally have a verdict. But we don't yet have all the answers.

While the football world is reeling from the bombshell news that Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges against them, the Premier League dropped the other shoe on Tuesday night – revealing in full, excoriating detail the scale of the cheating.

The club remain insistent they are innocent, and that they intend to appeal, despite the League presenting such overwhelming evidence that City cooked the books to the tune of £900million in a nine-year period from 2009 to 2018.

So what happens now? And when will it all finally end?

Here, Chief Sports Reporter MIKE KEEGAN answers the big questions that remain after the most explosive week in the history of the Premier League.

Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of charges against them by the Premier League

Pep Guardiola won six league titles across 10 seasons at City

What is the timeline now - what information is still to come out and when?

The first landmark date is this Friday, which is the deadline for City to submit an appeal. An appeal was always viewed as an inevitability given the club continue to protest their innocence and chief executive Ferran Soriano has now confirmed one will be forthcoming.

The Premier League handbook goes into great detail about the time constraints surrounding appeals as part of an attempt to expedite the process. For example, any hearing can only last for five days, should be concluded within 12 weeks of the initial verdict and witness and expert statements should run to no more than 30 pages.

However, the first hurdle will be the make-up of a new panel. The chair of the existing panel should ‘as soon as reasonably practicable’ inform the parties involved of the identities of the proposed individuals.

Objections should then be made within two working days. Given how this has played out so far, this could be the first stage that suffers a delay. With so much riding on the choice of the panel, and so much at stake, an objection may well be forthcoming should either side have misgivings over a proposed individual.

Legal experts believe it is unlikely there will be a conclusion this season and that the case may well fall under exceptional circumstances, with those timelines not applying. With regards to a sanction, the Premier League are refusing to comment on whether that will come before the appeal is finished. However, it would appear there is a desire within the League to speed things along.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters now faces the prospect of kicking out the most successful team in his league for the last 15 years

What will happen to the witnesses judged to have given dishonest evidence?

Good question. Section 29(b) of the released judgment said that 'certain... factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest'. The identity of these people, who gave evidence on behalf of City, has not been revealed.

It would appear the Premier League are pushing for redactions to be removed, with a clue given at the bottom of their bombshell statement on Tuesday.

It stated that while the League were ‘only permitted to publish a redacted version of the summary of the Commission’s "core findings"’ that ‘the process remains ongoing and any further information related to the proceedings that has not been published by the Premier League remains confidential’. They also vowed that, ‘unless legally prevented from doing so’ they would ‘publish the full decision’.

One to watch.

Why were the panel members not named?

If you were asked to rule on such a hugely-emotive case as this, would you want the public to know your identity?

As the Premier League have noted, the process is ongoing and there is a hope that more material will be released. The exact reason for the panel not being named is unclear at the moment, but that may change further down the line, depending on legal arguments.

Are there any grounds for criminal prosecution?

That remains to be seen. The priority for both parties right now will be the appeal.

The difficulty here is that there is not really a precedent in this country. In Italy, suspended sentences were handed out to former Juventus executives, including ex-chairman Andrea Agnelli, with regards to a false accounting case.

Agnelli got 20 months, while ex-sporting director Fabio Paratici – by then managing director of football at Tottenham – was handed 14 months.

There are few parallels for criminal punishment - in Italy, Juventus chairman Andrea Agnelli (second left) and sporting director Fabio Paratici (right) were handed suspended sentences

How will the compensation claims work?

Four of City's Premier League rivals – Arsenal, Manchester United, Tottenham Hotspur and Liverpool – lodged legal claims ensuring that they would not be ‘out of time’ in the event that City were found guilty.

Each will already have an idea how much they are going to claim for. The most obvious avenue is the argument that City cost them European qualification and it would appear that, in that area, Spurs have the strongest case. Between 2009 and 2018, they finished one place outside the Champions League spots, with City ahead of them, on four occasions.

The irony here is that a process instigated by former Arsenal chief executive Tim Lewis could net their north London rivals a huge windfall, with £200million mentioned.

It is not just, however, failure to qualify for Europe. Knock-on effects, such as an inability to sign a certain level of player, could also be considered.

The likelihood is that an independent arbitration panel would sit and decide on level of payout, as was the case when Burnley won a £35m payout from Everton in June over the Toffees' PSR breach.

For time purposes, it could be that all four cases would he heard at the same time, although each club may want their own situations to be dealt with individually.

Arsenal are one of four clubs who have reserved the right to seek compensation against City

Tottenham can feel most aggrieved - City denied them Champions League qualification four times in the nine-year period being investigated

Would compensation payments count towards future financial calculations?

It is highly unlikely, given that it would run the risk of creating a vicious circle in which City breach year after year, and be viewed as a double punishment.

Are there any grounds for UEFA to revisit their own City case?

UEFA will wait to see the result of the hearing in full before making a decision. But Daily Mail Sport understands it is highly unlikely they will revisit the case, despite the Premier League stating City were 'significantly in breach' of both their and UEFA's rules.

The verdict obtained by City at the Court of Arbitration for Sport when they overturned their two-season Champions League ban in 2020 would be incredibly difficult to reverse given it upheld some of UEFA’s findings but not others, which it found were ‘time-barred’. City instead received a fine of €10m and had their ban rescinded.

Could the Premier League look at transactions post-2018 now?

They could. Whether they would want to, given the expense and effort that went into this case, is another issue.

At the moment, the feeling within Premier League Towers is one of vindication, and that will linger should City’s appeal fail. Would they want a second leg having won the first so convincingly?

How could City being put into the EFL work in practice? Would EFL clubs have a vote or just be told this is happening?

The EFL have declined to comment. However, there is a rule (11.6.2) that seems to exist for such situations.

Should City be given a points deduction that only sees them relegated to the Championship, then it is simple. They will be relegated. If, however, the sanction relegates them to League Two, it gets a little complicated.

First, they would need to apply to the FA to re-enter the pyramid. If that were successful, their absence would mean one more team would need to be promoted from each of the EFL divisions next season, to make up for the gap in the Premier League.

City could be kicked all the way back down to League Two - but would first have to apply to re-enter the pyramid

Could City’s auditors face any action?

BDO have audited City's accounts for years, and still do. But the Premier League found City 'filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of their finances from their auditors and football regulators'.

When contacted by Daily Mail Sport, BDO said they ‘remain bound by confidentiality so cannot comment on this occasion’.

Some would view the prospect of action against the firm as incredibly harsh, although we understand BDO could still face an investigation by the Financial Reporting Council (FRC). Sources say the regulator is 'aware' of the situation and 'looking into it to see if there is anything that falls under its remit'.

The FRC refused to comment.

BDO could argue they only acted on information they were given and point out that had it not been for the hacker Rui Pinto (rather than the Premier League’s compliance team) none of these details would have come to light.

What does this all mean for Omar Berrada?

The Manchester United chief executive joined them in 2024 from City, where he held a number of executive roles from 2011 including chief operating officer.

United have declined to comment. That said, it would be hard to imagine a world in which club officials did not carry out the relevant due diligence when Berrada was appointed in 2024 – almost a year after the City charges were made public.

Sports.title: The man staking his reputation - and £100m - on taking down Man City: Richard Masters has faced down mutiny, a pandemic and the Premier League owners club. Now insiders reveal how he'll fight the biggest scandal in British sport
Sports.content:
The man staking his reputation - and £100m - on taking down Man City: Richard Masters has faced down mutiny, a pandemic and the Premier League owners club. Now insiders reveal how he'll fight the biggest scandal in British sport

A couple of days after Manchester City were found guilty of cheating, the former chairman of a Premier League club attempted to describe the challenge of imposing law and order on British football.

He had a little think and then offered this soundbite to Daily Mail Sport: 'It can be a bit like managing a creche.'

That view was then relayed to an executive at one of the current 20 clubs comprising our top-flight. He made a slight update to the assessment: 'It's more like a difficult high school now - the kids have grown up and in some cases become delinquent.'

They were both joking around a serious point, but played to the common sentiment that few jobs in sport exist with the same complications as those faced by Richard Masters.

Since his appointment as CEO of the Premier League in December 2019, Masters has been confronted with a global pandemic, the Project Big Picture manoeuvrings from Manchester United and Liverpool, the mutinous intentions behind a Super League, an acceleration in foreign and state ownership and, of course, the era-defining trial of Manchester City.

To cite one of Masters' former colleagues and a close friend: 'Taking those areas as a whole, it's a f****** tough hand to be dealt.'

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters' reign will be defined by the eventual outcome to their legal case against Manchester City

Masters would strongly reject any notion of a crusade against Man City, highlighting that guilt was reached by an independent commission and that his job is to administer rules set by clubs

Daily Mail Sport has consulted a dozen sources who know Masters and have worked around him to better understand the highest-ranking individual on the side of the establishment.

Most are quick to agree on three details. One: Masters is nothing like his long-time predecessor, the charismatic Richard Scudamore, an arch-politician who found it easier to charm or coerce the room during a reign of constant financial growth. Two: The landscapes in which they worked have changed dramatically. Three: Masters would strongly reject any notion of a crusade against Manchester City, highlighting that guilt was reached by an independent commission and that his job, in the most reductionist terms, is to administer rules the clubs themselves had voted to play by.

But, on the latter, there is an observation worth making – the appetite to commit an estimated £100million in legal resources to the City battle has challenged the perennial accusation of judicial bias in favour of the big clubs. British football has never known a confrontation of such stakes.

Irrespective of whether Masters finds the personalisation of this fight inaccurate, his reign will be defined by its eventual outcome, as will a somewhat bigger issue – the integrity of the past two decades of the Premier League.

It is a far cry from Masters' arrival in the role, which occurred in highly unusual circumstances, because he was only fourth choice to replace Scudamore. A shambolic recruitment process that stretched 18 months had seen Susanna Dinnage named as successor, but she declined after her appointment had been announced and the current BBC director general Tim Davie also turned it down. Completing a chaotic hat-trick, David Pemsel was given the job but resigned before starting because of allegations about his private life. All of which opened a sliding door to Masters.

As a sales and marketing man, with long stints at the England and Wales Cricket Board, the EFL and the Premier League, his perception as an accidental candidate didn't help in the hornet's nest of football politics.

'Richard wouldn't have been human if there wasn't a little bit of imposter syndrome in the initial months in the job,' said one former colleague well acquainted with the machinations of a Premier League stakeholder meeting. Another source adds that there were individuals in those meetings, typically attended by two representatives per club and a further dozen Premier League staff, who felt Scudamore's replacement wasn't up to it.

Much of that derives from comparisons between very different men. One Premier League executive describes Scudamore as routinely making phone calls beyond midnight to corral the 20 clubs on big issues across his 20-year reign. 'A chief whip in another life', said the source.

Masters is viewed as being nothing like his predecessor Richard Scudamore, an arch-politician who found it easier to charm or coerce the room during a reign of constant financial growth

Masters is more corporate in style and less charismatic in nature, but his approach has slowly been viewed as a strength as football landscape has required a different kind of diplomacy

The depiction is of a CEO in Scudamore who never knowingly entered a vote without being reasonably sure of the outcome. 'Didactic' and 'controlling' were words used with some affection by a former staffer, with Scudamore's sharpest achievement rated as his ability to 'keep the peace' between 20 separate entities with conflicting agendas. By consensus, that was a more impressive feat than overseeing the consistent rise in television revenues.

Masters, an Aston Villa fan who turned 60 in June, is more corporate in style, more process-driven, far less charismatic in nature. For a time, that was interpreted as worse. But within Premier League circles it has slowly been viewed as a strength after a seven-year period in which the football landscape has required a different kind of diplomacy.

'There are still one or two in the room that are not convinced by him,' said a prominent source at a Premier League club.

There is no denying that Masters has had questionable moments – his reference to Everton and Nottingham Forest as 'small clubs' during their Profitability and Sustainability Rules skirmishes in 2024 was easy fodder for some of those who have detected two-tier justice in how the Premier League apply its rules.

A bigger matter was the takeover of Newcastle United by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. The Premier League claimed they have 'legally binding assurances' that the Saudi state would not control Newcastle, which has long struggled with the smell test for one fact above others – the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman is also the chair of the Public Investment Fund.

Some will see such decisions as flawed and acts of willing delusion; another would say that football's world has changed beyond recognition and there are not enough tiny violins to play notes of sympathy for those trying to control it. Masters' record within it is not without blemishes, especially in the balancing between financial regulation and the stifling of ambition. But there is an acknowledgement that he has overseen a uniquely challenging time, starting with Covid just months after taking office and extending to the City debacle.

'There was a perception that the Masters regime was worse than the Scudamore regime but that has softened quite a bit,' said an executive at a Premier League club.

'Scudamore had great abilities to do certain things. He was a master politician and a superb negotiator. He was a brilliant anticipator of problems and would get ahead of them. If Richard Masters could do anything better, it might be for him and Alison (Brittain, the Premier League chair) to get ahead of the problems quicker. They aren't as skilled politically, don't have the same nous, but he is very strong at working through a problem.

The takeover of Newcastle United by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund has been among the key challenges faced by Masters during his time as Premier League chief executive

'The stuff Masters has had to contend with is more extreme than his predecessors. He has done a very decent job of it in very, very choppy water. Covid was a huge thing to deal with – almost overnight, the revenue streams were being stopped and he was the man on a Zoom call having to answer 40 faces on a screen about when football could resume.'

A different source cites the threat of a Super League as the biggest crisis and City merely the messiest. 'It helps that he is a very calm guy,' said a club source. 'Whatever people think of how the Premier League works under him, he is a decent man with decent values and he is mostly applying the rules we as clubs have voted for.

'I have never seen him lose his temper in the meetings and there have been times when the criticism has been personal.

'He can be blamed for anything and everything. If there is a bad refereeing decision, he will get a call. If the economy in Singapore affects revenue, he will get blame. But again, he is very calm in the way he works through the role, very good at compartmentalising an issue, and I think he has done a solid job on balance.'

In a room of Premier League clubs, 'solid' and 'decent' can pass for a compliment.

Those meetings, of which there are around five per year, can be feisty. Some can spend hours arguing about the seemingly trivial. According to a source, one recent debate saw multiple changes to the draft of a rule about which side of the dugouts should be used for substitutes warming up mid-match.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the meetings around the Covid protocols or the Super League breakaway are understood to have been the most heated. Discussions around Manchester City have not reached those levels. Presumably, too much popcorn was being consumed in the creche to kick up a fuss.

Sports.title: Manchester City's punishment should last up to FIVE YEARS so they are forced to sell stars, says Jamie Carragher
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher believes Manchester City's punishment for financial misconduct should last five years – and that their owners should be forced to sell the club. The Liverpool legend wants to see the club hit with penalties for half a decade so that their highly paid stars are encouraged to move on. Manchester City were blasted by the Premier League last month for making 'sham' agreements to manipulate their financial accounts to the tune of £900million over a nine-season period which saw them win eight trophies. City insist they are innocent and are appealing the verdict, which found them guilty of 114 of 115 charges. Carragher told The Overlap Fan Debate: 'People talk about 80 points or 100 points, but that's just over one season that gets you relegated and then you come back again. 'And I think a few players would leave, but I think some of them would say, "I could put up with that for a year". It also builds a connection with the supporters, it'll be seen in a great light. Jamie Carragher says Manchester City should be punished for five years so that their players are less likely to stick around The Premier League have confirmed that Manchester City are guilty of the most serious financial rule breaches 'But I think because this has gone on for so long, I do think the punishment should be over a number of years, three to five years and then players would move on. 'But then you've got the financial aspect of how can they afford the wages of those players if they haven't got Premier League money? If they're having to pay all this money out and you can only spend the money that you're bringing in. They'll have to abide by it now.' He added: 'These owners, I said that straight away [that the owners should leave the club if found guilty], so I didn't know how the owners could continue. How can you ever trust them if they're found guilty of this? And the problem being is my worry for it is it won't be a case of, if they lose the appeal, 'Okay, yeah, we'll get on, we'll take our punishment.' 'I think because of where they're from, the power they have, the finances they have, they'll never admit they were wrong in this, and they would always say we were wronged. This was a sham, the Premier League as such, or different people. And I think they'll [the Manchester City owners] keep just dragging it on and I think it'll just drag the game into the gutter. 'And it almost needs sorting out for the game, but also for Manchester City, their support to move on from it. And I don't think they'd ever be able to move on from it with those people.' In 2022, Pep Guardiola said he would quit the club if he felt the club's hierarchy had ever lied to him. The next year, he said he would not walk out on his deal, even if he was relegated to League One. Guardiola always insisted he was 'fully convinced' that the club is innocent and said in May: 'I trust them, I trust them. Because I spoke with them and I trust how they behave and how they did.' But Carragher called into question whether Guardiola could ever have really believed his bosses, saying: 'Pep, he's involved in the commercial deals, but the fact that he's involved with those people sort of four or five times a day, daily, I just struggle to think, would he really believe them fully, 100%, what they're saying? Premier League CEO Richard Masters claimed that the commission's verdict had 'vindicated' the league's decision to pursue the charges

Your browser does not support iframes.

'After what comes out about Mancini and different things? I just didn't know if that changed it.' In September, Daily Mail Sport reported how City had been found guilty of 114 of 115 charges against them. In a lengthy statement, the Premier League say City arranged 'sham contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on "sham" agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs'. It also says the club falsely altered the financial picture at the Etihad to the tune of £900m. The club had agreed exorbitant sponsorship deals with a number of companies, but those sponsors only paid part of the fee. The rest was propped up by the Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club. As the Premier League note, this allowed City to 'artificially inflate the club’s revenues' and therefore spend more under Premier League rules. The higher the revenue a club records, the more they are permitted to spend. Moreover, further 'sham' deals, funded by ADUG, allowed the club to 'record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred'. The Premier League say that revenues were inflated and costs reduced to the tune of £900m in an attempt to comply with spending rules. The result was that the club 'filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators'. Roy Keane has claimed he would throw away his medals if he was a Manchester City player It added that the club was 'significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits' during the time period in question, 2009-2018 when it won eight major trophies. Had City reported accurately 'it would have been in breach of both the League's and UEFA's spending limits by a very substantial amount'. The panel also found that City committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and good faith in that it failed to assist the Premier League's four-year investigation, triggered by the emergence of club emails obtained by a hacker. Indeed, City had 'made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation'. Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League, said: 'The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade. 'It also vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently. 'It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously. 'This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission's decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans.' Manchester City have insisted on their innocence throughout the saga (Pep Guardiola pictured with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak) In a statement released a short time later, City said it was ‘disappointed and surprised’ and referred to the ‘opinion of the Premier League Commission’. It added: ‘The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums. ‘The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe. ‘The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence. ‘The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete.’ City have until Friday to appeal. Man City were first charged with the 115 breaches in February 2023. While that totemic number stuck, the figure – as they subsequently corrected – was actually 130. Of those, 54 were charges of ‘failure to provide accurate and up-to-date financial information’ while there were 14 charges of ‘failure to provide accurate financial reports for player and manager compensation’. Both sets related to alleged offences between 2009 and 2018 (2009-2018), an eight-year period which saw the club win four Premier League titles, the FA Cup, and three League Cup competitions. There were also five charges of ‘failure to comply with UEFA’s regulations, including Financial Fair Play Regulations’ and seven charges of breaching the Premier League’s profit and sustainability regulations between 2015 and 2018. There were also 35 counts of failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations between 2018 and 2023. The hearing into the 130 breaches began last September at London’s International Dispute Resolution Centre, with the Premier League sparing no expense and enlisting KCs Adam Lewis and Andrew Hunter to take its case.
