World.title: Liberia: A Government Assessment Shows Liberia Is 69 Percent Ready for Ebola. Frontline Health Workers Say the Missing 31 Percent Matters
World.content:
Dr. Sia Wata Camanor, National Public Health Institute of Liberia’s acting director general, spoke at the Ministry of Information press briefing this month, where she released the findings of the Institute’s Ebola preparedness assessment.

Summary:

• A nationwide Ebola preparedness assessment found Liberia 69 percent ready overall, while logistics scored only 47 percent, leaving major gaps in equipment, supplies, isolation facilities and training.

• Frontline health workers say those logistics gaps can mean the difference between safely isolating a suspected patient and exposing staff, other patients and communities.



• Health authorities say they are tightening procedures at major points of entry, but the next steps, funding and timetable for closing the gaps remain unclear.

By Augusta S. Lafalay, senior reporter with New Narratives

Liberia has stronger disease surveillance and laboratory systems than it did during the 2014 Ebola crisis, but the country is still only 69 percent prepared to respond to another outbreak, according to a nationwide Ebola preparedness assessment by the National Public Health Institute of Liberia. The weakest area was logistics, which scored just 47 percent.

At a September press conference to release the findings of the assessment, Dr. Sia Wata Camanor, acting Public Health Institute director general, said the country was in the “medium” preparedness range. “We don’t have the tools. We don’t have the materials,” she said. Though the risk remains low, she warned against complacency.

Health experts welcomed the government’s transparency, but they said that the number is more than a technical score. It points to shortages and weaknesses in the things health workers would need first if a suspected Ebola patient arrived at a clinic or hospital: personal protective equipment, functioning isolation space, transport, laboratory supplies, ambulances, trained staff, and a system able to move those resources quickly.

“When we say there is a lack of logistics, it can sound like we are simply talking about supplies. But for a health worker, it is much bigger than that,” said Lela Dolo, executive director of Help a Mother and Newborn in Liberia and a medical student training to become a doctor. “Do I have the personal protective equipment I need? Can a suspected patient be safely isolated and referred? Can a specimen be transported quickly? Is there an ambulance or vehicle available? Can the response team reach the community?”

The question is foremost in the minds of the country’s healthcare workers who bore the brunt of the disease in 2014. If an Ebola case reaches the country, gaps could put frontline workers at risk, slow the response and increase the chance that an infection spreads beyond a health facility and into communities.

The National Public Health Institute of Liberia’s assessment, conducted across all 15 counties, examined surveillance, points of entry, emergency operations centers, laboratories, isolation facilities, county health teams and rapid response structures. Health authorities have said surveillance officers and rapid response teams are operating nationwide, while laboratory testing and specimen transport have improved. But officials also identified the need to replenish protective equipment, maintain isolation facilities, run more simulation exercises and continue training newly deployed health workers.

For Liberia, the warning carries a painful history. During the 2014-2015 epidemic, 378 health care workers in Liberia had confirmed Ebola and 192 died, according to a U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention review . Weak infection-prevention systems left health facilities vulnerable, with many lacking triage and isolation protocols, protective gear, or running water early in the crisis.

The toll weakened a health system that was already short of skilled workers. The infected health workers represented about 12 percent of Liberia’s confirmed Ebola cases, even though health workers made up only a small share of the population. Early in the epidemic, many facilities closed after transmission occurred among staff. Health workers who did not feel protected, walked away.

Dolo said the Liberian health system has learned from the last epidemic and has stronger surveillance and response systems. Her concern is whether those systems are backed by the practical resources needed when an emergency begins.

“You can train health workers to recognize Ebola and follow the right protocols, but knowledge alone cannot protect them,” she said. “They also need the tools and systems to safely do what they have been trained to do.”

Joseph Somwarbi, a pharmacologist and former head of the Legislature’s health committee, said logistics failures can quickly become safety failures. He said all parts of the chain must work together.

A shortage in one part of that chain can put frontline staff in a dangerous position. If protective gear is insufficient health workers may have to delay care or risk exposure. If laboratory agents or specimen transport are unavailable, confirmation can take longer. If supplies are concentrated in Monrovia, rural facilities can lose valuable time waiting for materials to arrive.

“Delay in procurement, delay in transportation means no access,” Somwarbi said. “No access means not available. Not available means you’re not prepared.”

Those weaknesses become especially serious in an Ebola outbreak, he said, because the first response begins before laboratory confirmation. A patient with symptoms and a relevant exposure history must be identified, separated from other patients, reported to surveillance teams, safely assessed and tested, while health workers use infection-prevention measures. Contacts may then need to be identified and monitored.

“When the system is not prepared, even 24 hours is too much of a time for disease to spread,” Somwarbi said.

The threat of Ebola remains constant. The latest outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (the country’s 17th outbreak) has reached 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths, according to the World Health Organization , making it the second largest outbreak after the 2014 outbreak in West Africa. Experts said cuts to international aid, especially by the United States, have dramatically reduced the capacity to contain the virus. That same outcome would likely play out in Liberia, which relied heavily on U.S. help to stamp out the 2014 outbreak, were the virus to reach the country.

Liberia has responded to the DRC’s outbreak by increasing screening and surveillance at airports, seaports and land crossings. Travelers are required to cooperate with screening and reporting procedures. Procedures, health experts said, are in place to make clear who screens travelers, what happens when someone meets a suspected-case definition, how referral and transport should work, and how information moves from border health staff to surveillance and response teams.

But the country has struggled with capacities at points of entry. A 2024 peer-reviewed evaluation of eight designated Liberian points of entry found gaps in areas including quarantine, communication, water, electricity, transport, and trained personnel.

Experts said the importance of clear procedures was underlined in May, when health authorities monitored 16 travelers arriving from countries of concern. None developed Ebola symptoms during the required 21-day follow-up, according to the Institute. But a WhatsApp voice message circulated claiming suspected Ebola patients had been taken to John F. Kennedy Medical Center, sparking fear and mistrust in the community.

Experts said the incident highlighted a basic communication challenge: officials needed to clearly communicate to the people what they were doing to increase trust. Dr. Camanor’s press conference and transparency about the assessment were a sign the government has learned from the May experience.

From here, Camanor said the assessment findings would be shared with the Ministry of Health, World Health Organization and other partners, and that the National Public Health Institute planned to take the findings to the Ministry of Finance, Cabinet and Legislature to seek support for closing the gaps.

In May, Dr. Louise Kpoto, the health minister, told lawmakers that the Ebola preparedness budget was $US4.2 million.

FrontPage Africa/New Narratives contacted Dr. Kpoto and National Public Health Institute leadership by telephone and email seeking answers on what the government will do next, whether any of the $US4.2 million has been approved or released, a timetable for addressing the gaps, and how progress will be measured. Neither responded by the publication deadline.

Somwarbi said a follow-up assessment would be one way to show whether new spending improves preparedness. That would allow the public and health workers to compare the current weaknesses with what has been fixed, rather than relying only on promises or budget figures.

For Dolo, the practical test is simpler. “If the first suspected Ebola patient walks into a health facility tomorrow, does the health worker who meets that patient have everything they need to recognize the risk, protect themselves, protect other patients and activate the response system immediately?” she asked. “If the answer is not yet a confident yes, then there is still work to do.”

World.title: EFLA Accuses Boakai-Koung Administration of ‘Systemic Disregard’ for Liberians in Europe
World.content:
MONROVIA — The European Federation of Liberian Associations (EFLA) has accused the Boakai-Koung administration of systematically sidelining Liberians living in Europe from its flagship diaspora engagement initiatives, sharply criticizing the government’s annual diaspora conference as a platform that fails to represent the broader Liberian diaspora.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

In a statement issued on October 4, 2026, EFLA President Francis M. Mensah said the organization was taking exception to the manner in which the government has organized its annual diaspora conferences, arguing that the events have increasingly centered on Liberians in the United States while excluding communities in Europe.



The criticism comes as the Joseph Boakai-Koung administration has made diaspora engagement a major component of its domestic policy, holding two annual diaspora conferences in the United States since 2025.

EFLA, which describes itself as the umbrella organization for Liberian associations across Europe, said it expected the conference to bring together Liberians from across the world to discuss issues affecting the diaspora and Liberia.

Instead, the organization alleged that the conferences have become heavily U.S.-focused.

“The Annual Diaspora Conference, by its goals and objectives, should bring together all Liberians in the diaspora to assemble, network, and discuss issues affecting the wider Liberian Diaspora community, as well as the issues the government of Liberia faces,” EFLA said.

“Unfortunately, the past two diaspora conferences have been turned into a spectacle of prom and pageantry,” the organization alleged, claiming that senior government officials and their associates have traveled to Washington, D.C., at government expense.

EFLA said Europe was not represented at this year’s conference, arguing that such an omission undermines the stated objective of creating a global platform for Liberians abroad.

‘Systemic Neglect’

The European group said its concerns predate the current administration, noting that it has repeatedly attempted to engage successive Liberian governments over what it described as the “systemic neglect” of Liberians residing in Europe.

The concerns, according to EFLA, range from consular challenges in the Nordic countries to the limited participation of European-based Liberians in government-sponsored diaspora initiatives.

The organization also pointed to the financial contribution of Liberians in Europe through remittances and businesses in Liberia.

“So, we must not be taken for granted!” EFLA said.

The organization further accused conference organizers of being insufficiently intentional about involving Liberians from Europe, alleging that panel discussions and other side events are often structured to accommodate government allies, friends and family members.

“The sad truth is that the organizers have never been intentional about getting Liberians in the European Diaspora involved, but continue to pretend to include diaspora Liberians from Europe,” the statement said.

Government’s Diaspora Push

President Boakai’s diaspora initiative was launched from a commitment made in late 2024 to establish a structured global platform for Liberians living abroad.

The government has said the initiative is intended to move beyond the traditional focus on remittances and encourage the more than 500,000 Liberians living abroad to contribute to Liberia through entrepreneurship, investment, technology transfer and professional expertise.

The inaugural Liberia Annual Diaspora Conference was held in Washington, D.C., from September 26–28, 2025, under the theme “Building the Future Together.” The gathering brought together hundreds of delegates physically and more than 1,300 virtual participants, according to organizers.

The 2026 conference, held September 25–27 at the Hilton Alexandria Mark Center in Virginia, was organized under the theme “From Dialogue to Delivery: Diaspora Capital, Innovation, and the Next Liberia.”

The second conference sought to move discussions toward practical economic initiatives, including investment, agribusiness, innovation and youth empowerment.

EFLA, however, argues that the geographic concentration of the initiative contradicts its stated global character.

Europe Threatens Wider Pushback

EFLA said it would no longer participate in what it characterized as poorly organized diaspora activities conducted by government functionaries.

“Going forward, Liberians in Europe will not be involved in any haphazard activities organized by government functionaries,” the organization declared.

The group also warned that it could seek engagement with European institutions over what it described as the Liberian government’s failure to include Liberians residing in the European Union in its diaspora activities.

“Europe hosts some of Liberia’s development partners, and we, as Liberian taxpayers in Europe, can engage the European Union Parliament about the Liberian government’s flagrant disregard for including Liberians residing in the EU in diaspora activities it organizes,” EFLA said.

The group stressed that no segment of the Liberian diaspora should be treated as more important than another.

“No one group of diaspora Liberians is better than the others,” EFLA said, demanding that Liberians in Europe receive the same level of respect and opportunities afforded to their compatriots in the United States.

EFLA said it has been involved in advocacy and humanitarian initiatives benefiting both Liberians in Europe and communities in Liberia. It also cited its role, alongside partners including ALCOD, in advocacy that contributed to the passage of Liberia’s Dual Citizenship Act and its ongoing efforts to promote voting rights for Liberians abroad.

The organization said it remains committed to contributing to Liberia’s development but wants the government to recognize the European diaspora as an equal partner.

“In Union Strong, Success Is Assured!” the statement concluded.

World.title: Liberian Entrepreneur LeAnn Knowlden Honored in Zimbabwe, Tanzania and Ghana
World.content:
Founder of Top Agency, who started a school newspaper at 14, picks up three continental recognitions in 2026

MONROVIA – Liberian entrepreneur and media personality LeAnn Knowlden has earned recognition in three African countries this year, adding continental attention to a career that began with a student newspaper she launched as a teenager.

Knowlden, founder and CEO of Monrovia-based Top Agency, was named among Africa’s Top 100 Female Leaders 2026 by the SOWA Awards in Zimbabwe. In Tanzania, Iconic Africa named her Iconic Woman of the Year 2026 in the Business Leadership and Social Impact category. In Ghana, she was listed among the 100 Most Influential Africans in Infrastructure 2026.

The three honors cover different areas: women’s leadership, business and social impact, and infrastructure.



Early start in media

Knowlden’s interest in media dates to her school days. At about 14, she founded The Jaguar’s Journal, a student newspaper at her school in Liberia.

She has recalled that the paper’s success earned her a chance to meet then-Vice President Joseph Nyuma Boakai. She had hoped to meet the President that day, but met Boakai instead and sold him two copies of the paper.

Boakai, who served as Vice President from 2006 to 2018, was elected President in 2023.

Zimbabwe and ‘Africa by Africans’

Knowlden’s trip to Zimbabwe for the SOWA Awards also advanced Africa by Africans, a cultural storytelling project she leads. The visit produced her first hospitality partnership in Southern Africa, with Victoria Falls Safari Lodge.

The project promotes the idea that Africans should travel the continent, support African businesses and tell African stories themselves rather than relying on outside accounts.

Social impact in focus

The Tanzania recognition highlighted her social impact work. Knowlden helped promote a fundraising campaign for Tilnette Woods, a young Liberian woman who needed hip surgery. The campaign met its goal, and Woods has since had the surgery and is recovering, according to Knowlden’s office.

A broader view of infrastructure

On the Ghana recognition, Knowlden has described infrastructure as more than roads and buildings, extending to the systems, partnerships, platforms and businesses that open access to economic opportunity.

Through Top Agency, she has worked in communications, events, brand strategy, cultural programming and entrepreneurship. She also hosts television programming and runs Planet LeAnn, a cultural storytelling platform.

Knowlden describes her work across business, tourism, media and community building as parts of one goal: connecting people, brands and opportunities across Africa.

World.title: Liberia: Monrovia Celebrates as Temi Nkem Claims Victory in Big Brother Naija Season 11
World.content:
MONROVIA — Reality TV fans across Liberia joined the rest of the continent over the weekend to celebrate as Temi Nkem officially emerged as the winner of Big Brother Naija Season 11, tagged “Show Ya Sef.” Her triumph marks a historic moment in the reality franchise, making her the fifth female winner to take home the coveted crown.

The finale concluded an intense 10-week journey that captivated viewers throughout West Africa, including a massive following here in Liberia, where fans frequently gathered at local view centers and tuned in via DStv

to root for their favorite housemates.

After millions of votes were tallied across Africa, Temi Nkem secured the top spot by pulling 25.87% of the total votes. She narrowly edged out first runner-up Aikou, who garnered 23.68%, while Sheba finished as the second runner-up with 9.80%.



As the Season 11 champion, Temi Nkem walks away with a grand prize package featuring a brand-new SUV and 90 million Naira in cash.

The remaining 10 million Naira from the grand 100 million Naira cash pool was set aside for the season’s Most Influential Player of the Week (MIPOW) prize fund.

This season proved to be one of the most unpredictable and dramatic in BBNaija history. A total of 24 housemates competed through grueling Head of House games, weekly nominations, and game-changing twists like the “Gambit play” and revolving veto powers.

It also set a show record by recording two disqualifications and a voluntary exit—marking the first time all three events occurred in a single season.

Speaking on the successful run of the show, Atinuke Babatunde, Executive Head of Content and Channels, West Africa at MultiChoice, expressed gratitude to the loyal fanbase across the region.

“Season 11 has been another exciting chapter for Big Brother Naija,” Babatunde stated. “We saw 24 housemates bring their personalities, perspectives, and individual approaches to the game, and we are pleased to have shared their journey with our viewers.

We thank everyone who watched, voted, and joined the conversation throughout the season, as well as our sponsors and partners for their continued support.”

Big Brother Naija continues to solidify its position as Africa’s most-watched reality television platform. For Liberian youth and pop culture enthusiasts, the show remains a cultural touchstone and a vital launching pad for continental stars in media, fashion, music, and film.

World.title: Liberia: LMDC Pushes Tighter Regulation of Traditional Medicine, Warns Against ‘Cure-All’ Claims
World.content:
SANNIQUELLIE, Nimba County — The Liberia Medical and Dental Council (LMDC) is calling for stronger regulatory, research and monitoring frameworks to govern traditional medicine and ensure its safe integration into Liberia’s healthcare system.

The call was made by LMDC Registrar General Dr. Augustus Garlet Quiah on behalf of Council Chairperson Dr. Ayun K. Cassell III and members of the Council during the 24th African Traditional Medicine Day celebration in Sanniquellie, Nimba County.

Held under the theme, “Reflection on Research and Development Efforts of Traditional Medicine towards Achieving Universal Health Coverage in Liberia,” the event brought together traditional and conventional healthcare practitioners, government institutions, researchers, community stakeholders and health-related organizations.



Dr. Quiah said sustained investment in research, policy development, capacity building, monitoring and regulation is necessary to ensure that traditional medicine practices are safe, responsible and appropriately incorporated into Liberia’s broader healthcare system.

“There is a need for clear policy and regulatory frameworks that will guide and monitor traditional healthcare practices, including establishing appropriate treatment limits and ensuring that practitioners do not make blanket claims that their remedies can cure all diseases and medical conditions,” Dr. Quiah said.

He said effective regulation would also create opportunities for stronger collaboration among government institutions, academic and scientific researchers, conventional healthcare providers and traditional medicine practitioners.

“Through collaboration, research and effective regulation, Liberia can create a more inclusive and resilient healthcare system that responds to the needs of every citizen, while ensuring that public safety remains a priority,” he added.

Traditional Medicine’s Role

The LMDC Registrar General acknowledged the significant role traditional medicine continues to play in Liberia, particularly in rural and underserved communities where access to conventional healthcare services remains limited.

While stressing that conventional medicine remains an essential component of Liberia’s national health system, Dr. Quiah said the potential contribution of traditional medicine to achieving Universal Health Coverage should also be recognized.

However, he cautioned that efforts to promote traditional medicine must be accompanied by scientific research, evidence-based practices, professional capacity building, monitoring and appropriate regulation to protect patients and the wider public.

The celebration was organized by the Ministry of Health through its Division of Traditional, Complementary and Alternative Medicines.

Participants included representatives of the Liberia Intellectual Property Office (LIPO), Liberia Medicines and Health Products Regulatory Authority (LMHRA), West African Health Organization (WAHO), LMDC, Ministry of Local Government, Traditional Medicine Association of Nimba, Liberia Traditional Medicine Federation (LIMEF) and the Nimba County Health Team.

The Office of Nimba County Superintendent Kou Meapeh Gono also participated, with the Superintendent represented by her Special Assistant, Prince Yeah, who served as keynote speaker.

Medicinal Plants Garden Launched

As part of the celebration, organizers officially launched the Nimba Medicinal Plants Garden, an initiative intended to highlight the importance of medicinal plants and preserve traditional healthcare knowledge.

Traditional healthcare providers were also certificated in recognition of their contributions to healthcare delivery through traditional medicine.

Meanwhile, local authorities have pledged to strengthen monitoring of traditional medicine practitioners, particularly those who use radio stations and other public platforms to advertise remedies while claiming that their products can cure all diseases and medical conditions.

The LMDC said such claims require closer scrutiny as part of efforts to protect the public from unsafe practices and misleading medical information.

Registration, Licensing Urged

Traditional and complementary medicine practitioners were encouraged to formally pursue registration and licensing in line with Ministry of Health and World Health Organization guidelines.

According to the LMDC, practitioners should begin by expressing their interest through the Ministry of Local Government, followed by engagement with the County Health Team before proceeding to the Complementary Medicines Unit at the Ministry of Health.

Final licensing or certification is to be handled by the Liberia Medical and Dental Council.

The Council said it remains committed to working with the Government of Liberia, health professionals, healthcare institutions, development partners, communities and other stakeholders to strengthen health regulation and promote a safe, accountable and quality healthcare system for Liberians.

World.title: Liberia: Gandhi’s Legacy of Compassion Lives On as India Donates Medicines to Liberia’s Group of 77 Disabled Center
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Embassy of India in Liberia has marked the 157th birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi with a call for peace, nonviolence, dialogue and compassion, while strengthening its humanitarian engagement with Liberia through a donation of medicines to the Group of 77 Disabled Center.

By Patience M. Jones, [email protected]

The celebration, held Friday at the Indian Embassy in Mamba Point, brought together members of the Indian community, government officials, disability advocates, educators, students and other invited guests, including a delegation of Liberian legislators led by Hon. Ellen A. Attoh-Wreh, Chairperson of the Women Legislative Caucus of Liberia (WLCL).



A major highlight of the commemoration was the unveiling of a newly installed bust of Mahatma Gandhi on the lawn of the Embassy’s Chancery.

The Embassy said the bust is intended to serve as a lasting reminder of Gandhi’s philosophy and his call for humanity to choose peace over violence, love over hatred, dialogue over confrontation, compassion over indifference and service over self-interest.

Gandhi Jayanti, observed annually in India as the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, is also commemorated by the United Nations as the International Day of Non-Violence.

Speaking at the ceremony, Indian Ambassador to Liberia Manoj Bihari Verma welcomed the Liberian lawmakers and other guests, describing their participation as a reflection of the growing partnership between India and Liberia.

Ambassador Verma also recalled Gandhi’s famous Talisman, which urges decision-makers to consider how their actions affect the poorest and most vulnerable members of society.

He said Gandhi’s philosophy remains relevant beyond India, emphasizing that his message belongs to humanity as a whole.

For Liberia’s disability community, however, the commemoration carried a more direct humanitarian significance.

As part of the celebration, medicines were donated to the clinic of the Group of 77 Disabled Center by members of the Indian pharmaceutical and business community in Liberia.

The contributions came from Abeer Pharmaceuticals, Lucky Pharmaceuticals, Bunty Pharmaceuticals and other members of the Indian community.

The donation was formally received on behalf of the Group of 77 Disabled Center by Senior Administrator Raymond Kolubah Zarbay Sr. and Deputy Health Services Director Fatu Sirleaf.

Zarbay, speaking on behalf of Madam Synleseh Stephenie Dahn Koung-Second Lady of Liberia and Executive Director of the Group of 77 Disabled Center, expressed appreciation to the Embassy of India, Ambassador Verma and the Indian business community for their support.

He said the donation followed engagements between the Center and the Embassy in November 2025 and September 2026, during which the needs of persons with disabilities and possible areas of cooperation were discussed.

According to him, the medicines will strengthen the Center’s capacity to provide healthcare services to persons with disabilities and surrounding communities.

He also reaffirmed the Center’s commitment to ensuring accountability and responsible distribution of the donated medical supplies.

The medicine donation, the Center said, represents more than material assistance, describing it as a demonstration of solidarity and friendship between the Indian and Liberian peoples.

The humanitarian gesture came as the Embassy concluded Seva Pakhwada, a fortnight-long service campaign observed from September 17 to October 2 by India and Indian diplomatic missions abroad.

During the campaign, Embassy officials participated in a Swachhata Pledge, beach-cleaning activities and the planting of coconut saplings under the Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam initiative.

The Embassy said the campaign reflects the spirit of seva, or selfless service, which was central to Gandhi’s philosophy.

At the Gandhi Jayanti celebration, the connection between the philosophy of service and community action was further underscored through cultural performances by schoolchildren, including traditional dances and Gandhi’s favorite devotional songs, known as bhajans.

The program also featured reflections on Gandhi’s life and values and the singing of Vande Mataram.

Meanwhile, WLCL Chairperson Ellen A. Attoh-Wreh highlighted the continued relevance of Gandhi’s principles of peace, nonviolence, service, dialogue and reconciliation.

She said the values are particularly relevant to the work of legislators as they seek to promote inclusion, dialogue and peaceful resolution of differences.

The Liberian legislators’ participation also followed their recent South-South Peer Learning Mission to India from August 10–15, 2026, under an IBSA Fund-supported project titled “Women Legislators in Liberia: Promoting Voice, Leadership and Gender-Responsive Governance for Sustainable Development.”

The project is supported by the governments of India, Brazil and South Africa.

The Embassy of India also praised the Indian community in Liberia for its continued contribution to Liberia’s social and economic development and for helping strengthen the longstanding bonds between the two countries.

For the Group of 77 Disabled Center, the partnership signals an opportunity to deepen cooperation in healthcare, disability inclusion and community development.

The Center said it looks forward to strengthening its engagement with the Embassy of India and members of the Indian business community, particularly in addressing the healthcare and inclusion needs of persons with disabilities.

As Gandhi’s bust now stands at the Indian Embassy in Monrovia, the occasion served not only as a commemoration of his life, but also as a practical demonstration of one of the values associated with his legacy: service to humanity.

World.title: 28-year-old man dies mysteriously in Nakonde
World.content:
A 28-year-old man of Katozi Village in Chieftainess Waitwika’s Chiefdom in Nakonde District has died under unclear circumstances at a liquor store where he used to work from.

Muchinga Province Police Commissioner, Lubinda Mayamba confirmed the incident in a press statement made to the media.

Mr Mayamba identified the deceased as Cletus Bwalya.

He said brief facts are that, the now deceased was employed by his elder brother, Chrispine Mulenga, owner and operator of a liquor store at Katozi Village.

He added that the deceased had been working at the said liquor store since 10th June, 2026 and had been sleeping there.

“The deceased used to sleep at the liquor Shop due to the fact that he usually knocked off late and feared being attacked while returning home,” he said

The Police Commissioner alleged that on 4th October, 2026 at around 17:00 hours, liquor store owner Chrispine Mulenga checked on the deceased at the liquor store and found him selling beer and appearing to be in good health, saying the deceased did not complain of any illness or discomfort.

Mr Mayamba disclosed that the incident occurred between 4th October, 2026 at around 17:00 hours and 5th October, 2026 at around 06:00 hours, at Katozi Village in Nakonde district.

However, on 5th October, 2026 at around 06:00 hours, Chrispine Mulenga went to the liquor store to conduct a stock taking exercise with his younger brother, the now deceased, upon arrival, he found the door to the liquor store widely open, with music still playing inside.

Mr Mayamba said upon checking the premises, he found his younger brother lying motionless on the floor and subsequently discovered that he was dead.

The matter was then reported at Nakonde Police Station.

Acting on the report, Mr Mayamba said officers rushed to the scene, and it was established that the body of the deceased was found lying on the floor inside the liquor store, facing upwards, near the counter.

Mr Mayamba stated that after conducting a physical inspection of the body no visible physical injuries were observed.

He further said the body of the deceased is currently in Nakonde Urban Health Centre Mortuary awaiting a post-mortem examination to ascertain the actual cause of death.

An inquiry file has since been opened, and investigations are underway.

World.title: Eastern Province steps up world food day preparations
World.content:
Eastern Province has heightened preparations for the 2026 World Food Day commemoration slated for 16th October.

This year’s provincial commemoration will be held at Chipata Trades Training Institute, under the coordination of the Eastern Province Administration.

Provincial Food and Nutrition Coordinator, Norman Siame, confirmed the development in an interview with the media in Chipata.

Mr Siame said the province has partnered with the Provincial Nutrition Coordinating Committee (PNCC), Ministry of Health, German Corporation for International Cooperation (GIZ), Food and Agriculture (FAO), World Food Programme (WFP) and other stakeholders.

He said the commemoration aims to promote good nutrition, dietary diversity and sustainable food systems in the region where stunting still stands at 32 percent.

“The stakeholders are eager to promote nutrition in the province. We want to move from just food availability to nutritious food,” Mr Siame said.

He disclosed that a number of activities have been lined up to mark the day, including exhibition and cooking demonstrations of local nutritious foods such as orange maize, beans, groundnuts, soyabeans, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, and traditional vegetables.

Mr Siame said agricultural field visits will also be conducted in Chipata District to showcase climate-smart farming and bio fortified crops supported by GIZ and the Ministry of Agriculture.

He added that school activities have been included, with learners from selected primary and secondary schools expected to present poems, songs and drama performances on nutrition and food security.

According to Mr Siame, the Ministry of Health will take centre stage during the commemoration to conduct educational sessions on healthy diets, infant and young child feeding, and prevention of non-communicable diseases.

This year’s commemoration will be held under the theme “Innovate today, Nourish Tomorrow” which emphasises science-based innovations and inclusive approaches to build resilient and sustainable food systems.

Mr Siame said as the day draws closer, more stakeholders and cooperating partners have come on board and pledged full mobilisation and logistical support to ensure the event is a success.

World.title: Mwanakampwe commends FSP for reducing poverty
World.content:
Central Province Permanent Secretary, Milner Mwanakampwe is impressed with the milestones the Food Security Pack (FSP) Programme is recording in poverty alleviation among vulnerable households in the region.

Dr Mwanakampwe says the FSP programme has continued transforming the lives through distribution of agricultural inputs to vulnerable but viable farmers across the province.

He was speaking when a delegation from the Ministry of Community Development and Social Service paid a courtesy call on him in Kabwe.

He said the programme, which is implemented by the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services, has done wonders in all the districts but particularly in Chitambo, Mkushi and Chisamba.

Dr Mwanakampwe says the department of community development in some districts has used part of the recoveries from the beneficiaries to build offices and skills development centres, which are impacting local communities.

He has urged the World Food Programme (WFP) and other cooperating partners to continue supporting the programme for the benefit of the vulnerable in society.

And Ministry of Community Development and Social Services, Chief Community Development Officer, Martin Mwansa, says the government remains committed to implementing social protection programmes to alleviate poverty at community level.

World.title: Clergy calls for sustaining Zambia’s development gains
World.content:
As Zambia prepares to celebrate its 62nd Independence anniversary, Lusaka-based clergyman, Brighton Matoka says the country has made significant strides that should be sustained.

Pastor Matoka of Christian Community Church in Lusaka’s Woodlands said Zambia had grown beyond political independence to make progress in economic development, while remaining a beacon of peace and hope on the continent.

He was speaking in an interview with the media during a recent visit to Chief Kakoma’s Chiefdom in Mwinilunga District, North-Western Province for the Lubanji Lwa Kulema Nzambi traditional ceremony.

Pastor Matoka, who is also a nephew of Zambia’s first Information Minister and freedom fighter, the late Peter Matoka said the Church had also played a critical role in the country’s growth and development agenda since independence.

He said the Church had contributed to education, healthcare, national food security and employment creation, in addition to providing spiritual guidance to national leaders and citizens.

Commenting on this year’s Independence theme, “Zambia at 62: Our Journey, Our Growth, Our Future,” Pastor Matoka described it as timely saying it provided an opportunity for citizens to reflect on the country’s past challenges and build on the progress made.

He said Zambia’s future remained bright and urged citizens to harness the country’s potential while preserving its reputation as a beacon of peace and hope.

Meanwhile, Pastor Matoka commended the Government for its efforts to recognize and support freedom fighters, but called for more meaningful interventions beyond the awarding of medals of honour.

He proposed that the Government consider empowering families of surviving freedom fighters through improved housing and scholarships for their children.

“The freedom fighters are the architects of the democracy and freedom we are enjoying today as a nation. It is because of their sweat that we are here today. Some of them died and bled as they struggled to bring independence,” he said.

Pastor Matoka also called for increased investment in North-Western Province, saying the region remained behind in infrastructure development despite being one of the country’s major contributors to copper and other mineral production.

He said the province needed improved infrastructure, including hospitals, universities and road networks to unlock its economic potential.

“North-Western Province is potentially the richest province in the country today. It is a bedrock of minerals, has good rainfall patterns, forests for timber and rivers that do not run dry among other things, hence, the need to invest back in that land,” he said.

World.title: Zambia, Zimbabwe draft bi-national commission rules
World.content:
Ministry of Defence Permanent Secretary Maambo Hamaundu, has called on defence and security experts from Zambia and Zimbabwe to be frank, candid and thorough in formulating rules of procedure that will guide the Defence and Security Cluster of the Zambia-Zimbabwe Binational Commission.

The Permanent Secretary says the government is delighted to officiate at the gathering of experts drawn from the defence and security wings of the two countries, convened to develop a durable framework for engagement.

Speaking when he officially opened the Central Defence and Security Committee Meeting of the Zambia-Zimbabwe Binational Commission in Lusaka today, the PS commended the initiative, saying it was critical to ensure continuity and progress in maintaining peace and security.

He said the objective of the meeting is to ensure that the defence and security cluster does not lose track of the milestones and progressive measures already put in place for the maintenance of peace and security along the common border, which stretches approximately 800 kilometers.

“We must not lose track of the milestones that we achieved, of the plans that we have made, of the progress that we had initiated, despite this change,” he said.

PS recalled that the two countries had made a number of resolutions and decisions under the Joint Permanent Commission on Defence and Security, saying following the elevation of the engagement to a Binational Commission, it was important not to lose focus but to build on past achievements.

He said the elevation gives more impetus to continue with the co-mandate of the defence and security wings, whom he described as the first and last line of defence for both countries.

The Permanent Secretary urged delegates to ensure their deliberations are thorough and exhaustive in order to come up with rules of procedure that will stand the test of time.

“Let us be critical in our analysis. Let us interrogate the documents thoroughly. There is no need for us to hold back,” he said.

He said the meeting brings together various professionals including lawyers, military experts and civilians, and called on all minds to converge and develop the rules of procedure.

The PS assured delegates of government’s unwavering support for the meeting and for future engagements under the Binational Commission, stating that the government will not allow the peace and security obtained in the two countries to be disturbed.

He described the experts gathered as unsung heroes and anchors of peace and security for both nations, whose work often goes unnoticed by the public.

He expressed confidence that given their rich experience in managing the Joint Permanent Commission on Defence and Security, the experts will execute the task ably and produce a document that will shape future engagement on national defence and security.

“The document that you come up with here has an indication of what the future will look like and I am very confident that with this team here, the future is definitely bright,” he said.

World.title: Zambia to sign US health funding agreement
World.content:
Zambia is expected to sign a major health funding agreement with the United States this week, following months of negotiations over contentious provisions in the proposed deal.

Minister of Health Roma Chilengi says the government is now fully aligned with the United States on the Health Compact Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), which is expected to support Zambia’s health sector over the next five years.

Professor Chilengi was speaking during a media briefing in Lusaka today.

And Professor Chilengi stated that the agreement has undergone extensive negotiations after the government raised concerns over several clauses in the initial draft.

He said the government engaged with the United States in a series of discussions, to ensure the agreement is aligned with Zambia’s national interests, resulting in revisions that both parties are now comfortable with.

“Government is hopeful that the agreement will be signed this week on Thursday, paving way for continued cooperation between Zambia and the United States in strengthening the country’s health sector,” he said.

World.title: IBA tours New Apostolic Church 28 TV
World.content:
The Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA) has underscored the importance of continued sustainability for media institutions, saying the authority will continue engaging with them in its role as a regulator.

Speaking before touring New Apostolic Church 28 TV, IBA Director General Webster Malido highlighted the need for media institutions and the regulator to work collaboratively on compliance.

Mr Malido said the church plays an integral role in the broadcasting sector, emphasising that Zambia is a Christian nation.

He also commended NAC 28 TV for its positive compliance record.

Director General who is on a farmiliarisation tour of media institutions stated that NAC 28 TV is one of the standard bearers in broadcasting infrastructure.

Earlier, NAC 28 TV Board Chairperson Philimon Songolo welcomed the IBA’s visit to the station and highlighted the important role the regulator plays in the TV station’s success.

Bishop Songolo noted that the station is currently developing various components and working on content that aligns with the values of the New Apostolic Church.

Bishop Songolo emphasised that these engagements by the IBA will help the station’s operations, adding that once the station is ready and equipped to produce news, it will begin broadcasting news.

“NAC is known for its music, which is largely what we do, but we can do much more,” he said.

The Bishop said the station remains compliant and intends to maintain that standard even as it has the potential to expand its income generating activities.

World.title: Isoka man arrested over suspected murder
World.content:
Police in Isoka District have arrested a 36-year-old man in connection with the suspected murder of his 85-year-old father at Senye Village in Chief Katyetye’s Chiefdom.

‎Muchinga Province Police Commanding Officer, Lubinda Mayamba, revealed in a statement that the incident occurred between 18:00 hours on October 4th, and 07:00 hours on October 5, 2026.

‎Mr Mayamba said the deceased, Eliot Mutambo, was found dead inside a grass-thatched house after sustaining a suspected fractured skull.

‎He said police visited the scene following a report made at Isoka Police Station on October 5, 2026, and recovered a stone suspected to have been used in the commission of the offence.

‎Mr Mayamba said the body was later taken to Isoka District Hospital Mortuary, where it is awaiting postmortem examination to establish the cause of death.

‎He said the deceased had travelled to Senye Village on October 2, 2026, to visit his son, Lucky Mutambo.

‎The Police Commanding Officer said preliminary investigations indicate that the deceased and his son were drinking traditional beer known as involo on October 4 before the deceased retired to bed.

‎Mr Mayamba said Lucky Mutambo was later detained in police custody to assist with investigations, while the motive is suspected to be linked to allegations of witchcraft.

‎He said a docket of the case has been opened and the suspect will appear in court soon.

World.title: Kenya: Young People Must Shape Their Own SRHR Future, Says Kenyan Activist
World.content:
Adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) in Eastern and Southern Africa continue to face a disproportionate burden of HIV, early and unintended pregnancy, and poor sexual and reproductive health outcomesâparticularly during key life transitions such as leaving school, early pregnancy, migration, or exposure to violence.

Across Africa, young people are being told that their sexual and reproductive health and rights matter. But for many, accessing those rights remains a daily struggle.

Progress on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) has been made by governments and health systems, but this progress is not equal. Many adolescents, particularly girls and young women, still face obstacles to accessing the information, services, and legal protection they need to make informed choices regarding their bodies and futures. Fear of being stigmatized and concerns about confidentiality and who to go to for help can also be reasons why young people are not able to access sexual and reproductive health information and services when they need them.

Millions are still being affected by preventable risks, such as new HIV infections, early pregnancies, child marriage, gender-based violence, and period poverty. The gap between the rights that are promised on paper and the rights that are experienced in everyday life is further exacerbated by the fact that access to contraception, HIV prevention, comprehensive sexuality education, and youth-friendly health services remains a challenge for many.

Young people are increasingly demanding that this gap be taken seriously. They are calling for better access to sexual and reproductive health services and for comprehensive sexual and reproductive education in schools and health centres, free of stigma and shame.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Kenyan HIV and SRHR activist Jerop Limo said that closing that gap means moving beyond simply talking about young people and giving them a meaningful role in designing, implementing and holding health systems accountable.

"The reality is that we have made progress, but that progress is not being experienced equally by young people," Limo said. "We have more knowledge, more HIV prevention options, more conversations around SRHR, and stronger recognition of young people's leadership. But for many adolescent girls and young women, especially those living in poverty or in underserved communities, the ability to actually benefit from these advances remains a dream."

She said the biggest gap lies between what exists on paper and what young people experience in their everyday lives. She said policies, guidelines and new technologies mean little if a young woman cannot get accurate information, afford transport to a facility, or find a service in stock, or if she encounters stigma from a provider or fears being judged.

Limo warned against treating young people as a single group.

Their realities, she said, are shaped by where they live, their economic circumstances, disability, gender, HIV status, relationships, and many other factors. She added that the response has to be much more community-centered and responsive to those different realities.

Limo's own experience with HIV shaped her path into adolescent health advocacy. She began working in the HIV response eight years ago as a facility peer educator. As a young person living with HIV, she quickly discovered that access to treatment was only one part of what young people needed. Young people were also grappling with adherence, disclosure, fear, grief, relationships and self-worth, and with the question of what life could look like beyond an HIV diagnosis.

Her work has since taken her beyond Kenya and onto the global stage.

In 2025, Limo was recognised by the Gates Foundation's Goalkeepers community for her leadership in HIV and youth reproductive health. But she said the recognition is not hers alone. It belongs to the young people who have shared their experiences with her and the peer educators working in health centres every day.

The platform, she said, allows her to carry their everyday priorities directly to global decision-makers.

One of the biggest lessons she has learnt is that young people do not need adults to constantly tell them what their problems are or what solutions they need. They need people and systems that are willing to listen, trust them and create space for them to shape those solutions.

Today, Limo is Executive Director of the Ambassador for Youth and Adolescent Reproductive Health Program (AYARHEP), a youth-led organisation working on adolescent HIV and SRHR in Kenya.

A central part of Limo's advocacy is changing how institutions understand youth participation.

"Youth leadership, for me, is not simply putting a young person on a panel or giving young people a speaking slot," she said. "It is about young people having actual influence over decisions, programmes and resources."

At AYARHEP, she said, young people are not only beneficiaries but also peer educators, advocates, community mobilisers, programme designers and accountability actors. Limo said that peer connection is one of the strongest tools youth-led groups have.

"There is something very powerful about a young person sitting with another young person and saying, 'I understand what you are going through,'" she said. That peer connection, she said, can open conversations that may not happen in a formal institution.

Youth-led organisations also tend to sit closer to the realities of communities, she added. They hear first when a service is failing, when a product is unavailable, when a young person is too afraid to visit a facility, or when a national policy is failing to translate into meaningful change at community level. However, Limo said that youth-led organisations cannot be expected to carry the responsibility alone. Governments, donors and larger institutions need to recognise young people's expertise and provide the resources needed for youth-led organisations to lead at scale.

Misinformation is a growing concern too.

The challenge is particularly acute in an environment where misinformation and opposition to SRHR continue to shape what young people hear and believe. Young people need information that is accurate, understandable, relevant to their realities and delivered through channels they actually use and trust.

AYARHEP uses peer engagement, community dialogues, social media and youth-friendly spaces to allow young people to ask questions without fear of judgement. The organisation also engages caregivers, teachers, health workers, community leaders and other gatekeepers because young people's SRHR needs cannot be separated from the communities around them. Creating an enabling environment is essential, said Limo.

Limo said misinformation must be countered without shaming those who believe it. "If we want young people to trust us, we have to create spaces where they can say, 'I heard this, is it true?' and receive a respectful answer," she said.

Digital platforms have become increasingly important in the HIV and SRHR response, but Limo believes that young people should not only consume information online. They should also have the skills to identify misinformation and make informed decisions.

Limo said that stigma remains one of the biggest barriers preventing young people from accessing care. It surrounds HIV, sexuality, contraception, pregnancy and abortion, and extends to young people simply wanting to make decisions about their own bodies.

She said practical challenges, including services that are not youth-friendly, inconvenient operating hours, stock-outs, transport costs, lack of confidentiality and judgmental providers, can further discourage young people from seeking care.

Limo also said another major challenge is the information gap.

Young people today can reach enormous amounts of information, she said, but not all of it is accurate."Access to information has to mean access to trusted, evidence-based and understandable information," she said.

For Limo, one of the most urgent issues is ensuring that the incredible progress we are seeing in HIV prevention science actually reaches the people who need it. She cited lenacapavir, an injection that protects against HIV for six months and is given twice a year. Kenya became the first country in East Africa to roll it out in February. Limo said clinical studies show it can be up to 96% effective.

For many young women, she said, taking a pill every single day is hard to keep up, so an option they need only twice a year gives them real choice and more control over their own protection.

The rollout has begun in 15 high-burden counties, with plans to expand to all 47.

"Making the injection free at public health facilities isn't enough," Limo said. The next hurdle is ensuring that adolescent girls and young women know about the injection, can obtain it locally, and feel safe asking for it without judgment.

Young people as decision-makers

Limo said meaningful participation means far more than consultation. Young people, she argued, should be involved at every stage: identifying the problem, designing the response, implementing it, monitoring it, and holding institutions accountable.

"Young people are experts in their own lived realities," she said.

Even a team of highly experienced technical experts can produce an excellent programme on paper, she said, but if young people are not part of designing it, they can still miss important realities about how it will work in someone's life.

At AYARHEP, she said, the value of this approach has been clear through community scorecards, peer-led programming, youth support groups and community dialogues. Young people can tell you not only whether a programme is reaching them, but whether it is actually working for them.

Limo believes the question should therefore change. "We need to move from asking, 'How can we involve young people?' to asking, 'What decisions should young people have power over?'" she said.

What frustrates Limo most is when young people's participation stops at the conversation.

She said conferences and policy dialogues matter, and that she values every opportunity to be in those rooms. They are where community realities reach decision-makers directly, and many of the partnership discussions most important to her work begin there.

"My frustration is when young people speak, our quotes go into a report, and we are not included in the discussions and decisions on the next steps," she said.

Young people are often described as the leaders of tomorrow, Limo said, but they are already leading today. They are implementing programmes, mobilising communities, collecting evidence, shaping policies and creating solutions.

Sustained youth leadership, she added, needs sustained investment. Partners and funders can work with advocates who keep showing up and delivering results when they invest in young leaders.

"The opportunity now is to move from youth visibility to youth investment by bringing young people in early and keeping them in the process, from design through to accountability," she said.

Funding under strain

The push for meaningful youth leadership comes at a difficult time for HIV and SRHR programmes, as funding pressures affect community-based organisations across Africa.

Funding pressure is being felt most directly at the community level, she said. When funding shrinks, it is not just an organisational budget that changes.

"We have seen fewer community activities, fewer peer educators, reduced outreach, fewer spaces for young people to access psychosocial support and less capacity for youth-led organisations to hold systems accountable," she said.

Limo said there is a contradiction in asking communities to take greater ownership of the HIV and SRHR response while the organisations rooted in those communities struggle to survive.

"We need to stop seeing youth-led and community-based organisations as temporary project implementers," she said. "They are part of the infrastructure of the response. Communities built the response."

Close 

Sustaining that infrastructure, she said, will require longer-term and more flexible funding, investment in organisational capacity, and genuine recognition that communities hold expertise that cannot simply be replaced.

"We also need to protect the gains we have made. We cannot keep rebuilding community systems every time a funding cycle changes," said Limo.

A call to policymakers and funders

For policymakers and funders, Limo said, is to listen differently.

She said that young people need more than programmes designed for them. They need the opportunities, resources and decision-making power to help design and lead those programmes themselves.

She urged decision-makers to recognise that young people's priorities do not always fit neatly into programme categories. HIV, mental health, education, economic empowerment, relationships, violence, SRHR and digital safety are interconnected in a young person's life, she explained, and responses need to reflect that.

She also urged decision-makers to invest in choice.

She pointed to the exciting scientific developments in HIV prevention, but said innovation only becomes meaningful when communities can access it, understand their options, and make informed choices about what works for them.

Limo asked funders not to stop at paying for activities.

"Invest in the people and organisations that make the activity possible, the young leaders, peer educators, community organisations and networks that remain in communities long after a particular project has ended," she said.

What gives Limo hope, she said, is young people themselves.

She has watched young people who were once afraid to speak in meetings grow into peer educators, advocates and leaders, she said. She has seen young people living with HIV move from simply trying to survive their diagnosis to becoming powerful voices in the response, and young women challenge systems, ask difficult questions and create solutions for their communities. "I am one of them," she said.

"That is the future I am working towards," Limo said, "one where young people are not spoken about only as vulnerable populations and beneficiaries, but recognized as people with agency, expertise and the ability to shape their own futures."

Through AYARHEP, she wants to keep building spaces where young people can access information, services, support and opportunities, and where they can also influence the systems around them. Ultimately, she said, she wants a future where a young person does not have to fight the system to access basic healthcare, accurate information, or dignity.

"And perhaps most importantly, I want young people to believe that their lives can be bigger than the challenges they were born into," said Limo.

World.title: Somalia: All 7 Surviving Pakistani Crew Members Rescued After Somalia Pirate Hijacking
World.content:
Islamabad — All seven Pakistani crew members who survived a pirate attack off Somalia's coast have been rescued, Pakistan's foreign minister said Monday.

The Palau-flagged oil tanker, MT Honour, was hijacked by Somali pirates in late April, around 30 nautical miles off Somalia's coast while sailing to Mogadishu. Ten of the 17 crew members aboard were Pakistani nationals.

The last three Pakistani survivors have been rescued and flown to Addis Ababa, accompanied by a team from the Pakistani Embassy in Djibouti, Ishaq Dar said on US social media company X.

They are expected to leave the Ethiopian capital for Karachi on the first available Ethiopian Airlines flight on Wednesday, he added.

Four other Pakistani crew members were rescued in late September, more than five months after the hijacking.

They arrived in Karachi on Sunday aboard an Ethiopian Airlines flight from Addis Ababa.

Three Pakistani crew members were killed during the incident, and their remains have also been repatriated to Pakistan.

World.title: Ghana: Cabinet Approves Establishment of Ghana Space Agency - Minister
World.content:
THE government is advancing plans to transform the Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute (GSSTI) into a fully-fledged Ghana Space Agency to strengthen the country's participation in the emerging global space economy.

The proposed agency is expected to provide a stronger institutional framework for coordinating Ghana's space activities, developing national space programmes, promoting research and innovation, facilitating public-private partnerships and strengthening international cooperation.

It will also support the development of space infrastructure and related technologies.

Speaking at a press conference in Accra yesterday, the Minister of Environment, Science and Technology, Dr Zanetor Agyemang-Rawlings, said the initiative formed part of her First 100 Days Public Engagement Agenda, aimed at moving Ghana's space science and technology agenda from aspiration to implementation.
