She said processes were already underway to draft a Bill for the establishment of the agency following Cabinet's approval.

Dr Agyemang-Rawlings said the transformation would provide the country with the appropriate legal, institutional, technical and operational framework to coordinate its space activities. Read More

World.title: Ethiopia: Four African Countries Call for De-Escalation of Tension in Ethiopia
World.content:
This call comes amid the growing tension between Ethiopia's federal government and authorities in the northern Tigray region.

Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan have called for a de-escalation of the conflicts across their region, including Sudan's civil war and the crisis in Ethiopia.

In a joint statement issued Sunday at the end of a meeting in New Alamein City, Egypt, the countries called for dialogue and a peaceful resolution of the conflicts.

The statement was signed by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Mohamud and Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, according to Al Jazeera.



The countries declared that cross-border challenges required "a dialogue, not confrontation."

They also demanded that the coastal states retain control of the Red Sea; a stance that appears to respond to Ethiopia's pursuit of sovereign access to the sea and a naval presence.

This call comes amid the growing tension between Ethiopia's federal government and authorities in the northern Tigray region; a situation that has many in the country fearing that it could tip back into the kind of war that devastated it a few years ago.

PREMIUM TIMES reported renewed armed clashes in the northern Tigray region between the Ethiopian government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) two weeks ago.

The rebel forces also seized control of Mekelle and the Alula Aba Nega Airport.

Government and allied forces, however, retook the city of Mekelle on Sunday after the TPLF said it "temporarily moved out of" Tigray's regional capital to "operate from somewhere else."

According to local media, Tigray interim leader Abraham Belay accused the government of preparing a new temporary administration for the region and said it hopes to hold regional elections within months.

Meanwhile, Ethiopia has accused neighbouring Eritrea of directly backing the rebel alliance during Ethiopia's 2022 civil war. It also accused Egypt and Sudan of backing the armed alliance in the recent confrontation.

Sudan, which has been at war since April 2023, has accused Ethiopia of interfering in its crisis.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Confirms First Ebola Case as Patient Returns From DRC
World.content:
Kenya has confirmed its first case of Ebola virus disease in Nairobi, ending months of heightened surveillance and preparedness following the spread of the deadly Bundibugyo strain in the Democratic Republic of Congo and neighbouring Uganda.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale confirmed the imported case on Tuesday, saying the patient had travelled from the DRC through Uganda before entering Kenya.

Duale said the patient, who had lived in the DRC for about seven years, developed illness approximately a month ago and sought treatment at several health facilities in the country before beginning his journey back to Kenya.

The patient travelled by road from the DRC into Uganda before boarding a flight to Nairobi, where he arrived at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) on Saturday, October 3, at about 1:10pm.



According to Duale, the flight was carrying 23 passengers.

WHO declares Uganda Ebola-free

The patient underwent routine public health screening at JKIA before proceeding to the immigration desk, raising questions over how the infection was detected and the measures now being taken to identify and monitor people who may have been exposed during his journey.

“The Ministry of Health wishes to inform members of the public that it has confirmed the first imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease,” Duale said.

The confirmation marks a significant development for Kenya, which had remained free of confirmed Ebola infections despite mounting regional concerns.



The government had been preparing for the possibility of an imported case for several months as Ebola spread across the DRC and was reported in Uganda.

In June, Duale told Parliament that Kenya had activated its National Ebola Incident Management System and intensified screening at airports and land border crossings. More than 71,000 travellers had been screened at the time, while 22 suspected Ebola alerts reported in nine counties had all tested negative.

The Ministry of Health had also stepped up surveillance at the Malaba border because of the movement of people between Kenya and Uganda. By early June, authorities said 59 suspected Ebola cases tested in Kenya had returned negative results.

A national Ebola preparedness and response taskforce was subsequently established to coordinate surveillance, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, case management, risk communication and cross-border response.

The taskforce brings together national and county governments, health agencies, security authorities, development partners and technical experts.

Kenya’s first imported case comes as the Ebola outbreak in the DRC continues to grow.

The World Health Organisation said on September 25 that the outbreak had spread to 63 health zones across seven provinces, including Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, Bas-Uélé and Sud-Ubangi.

By September 23, the DRC had recorded 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 48.1 per cent. WHO warned that the geographical expansion of the outbreak was increasing the risk of cross-border transmission.

More recent figures reported by Congolese authorities showed the outbreak had surpassed 8,000 confirmed cases. On October 2 the DRC had recorded 8,300 confirmed cases and 4,018 deaths across seven provinces, making the current outbreak the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history.

The outbreak is being driven by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, a strain for which there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment. WHO says insecurity, population movement and cross-border trade have complicated efforts to contain transmission.

The scale of the outbreak has also prompted experimental treatment efforts. More than 250 people exposed to the virus in Ituri are participating in a trial of obeldesivir, an experimental drug being studied as post-exposure protection against infection.

The patient’s movement through Uganda is particularly significant because the country had also experienced an outbreak of the same Bundibugyo strain after infections crossed its border from the DRC.

Close 

Uganda recorded 20 confirmed cases during its 2026 outbreak, including imported and locally acquired infections. The country was declared Ebola-free on July 28 after completing the required 42-day period without a new confirmed case.

However, WHO has continued to warn that Uganda remains vulnerable to reintroduction because Ebola transmission has persisted in neighbouring DRC and people continue to cross the border.

Kenya’s confirmation therefore highlights the difficulty of containing the disease in a region characterised by extensive movement of people, goods and vehicles across borders.

The Ministry of Health had repeatedly cautioned that Kenya’s geographical position and extensive regional connectivity left it exposed to imported infections.

In May, the ministry announced heightened surveillance, laboratory testing, border screening and public awareness measures after WHO and Africa CDC classified the regional Ebola outbreak as a major public health threat.

World.title: Kenya: 3,6 Million Prepare For 2026 Exams
World.content:
Nairobi — The Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) will deploy 342,005 contracted professionals to oversee national examinations and assessments involving 3,634,846 candidates between October 16 and November 20.

KNEC Chief Executive Officer David Njengere announced the figures on Monday during the launch of the 2026 National Examination and Assessment Season, saying extensive preparations had been put in place to ensure the exercise is conducted smoothly and with the required integrity.

"The Council will administer assessments and examination to a total of 3,634,846 candidates between 16th October and 20th November 2026. KNEC will engage a total of 342,005 contracted professionals to facilitate the conduct and management of the field administration process," Njengere said.

The 2026 exercise will cover the Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE), Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA) and Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA).



The total candidature represents a 6.13 per cent increase from the 3,424,836 candidates registered for national examinations and assessments in 2025.

According to figures released during the launch, 1,380,463 learners have registered for KPSEA, while 1,206,028 will sit KJSEA. The KCSE candidature stands at 1,048,355, making 2026 the first year the number of KCSE candidates has crossed the one-million mark.

The KCSE examination season will begin with rehearsals on October 16, followed by papers with low candidature from October 19 to 30. Papers involving large numbers of candidates will then be administered from November 2 to 20.

The KPSEA and KJSEA assessments will run from October 26 to 30.

Tougher measures

KNEC has announced tighter security measures for this year's examination season, including the use of smart padlocks on all examination storage containers.

The technology was piloted in 250 containers last year and will now be rolled out across the country. The locks will be monitored from KNEC headquarters and will record access to the containers, helping the council detect unauthorised opening or tampering.

The containers will be opened only at designated times. KPSEA and KJSEA papers will be accessed from 6am, while KCSE centre managers will collect examination papers at 7am and 12.30pm for the morning and afternoon sessions respectively.

KNEC will also separate morning and afternoon KCSE papers in specially marked cartons to minimise the risk of mix-ups and unauthorised access.

The council has further personalised examination papers with candidates' details, although the identifying information will be removed before scripts are released to examiners for marking.

Njengere warned candidates and parents against paying individuals who claim they can provide examination papers before the scheduled dates.

He said candidates would see the actual papers for the first time when they sit the examinations, urging parents not to lose money to fraudsters promising advance access to examination materials.

Mobile phones have also been identified as a major threat to examination integrity. KNEC has warned that candidates and examination officials will not be allowed to have phones at examination centres during examination sessions, with violations treated as examination malpractice.

For KCSE alone, KNEC will deploy 10,765 centre managers, 12,274 supervisors, 57,432 invigilators and 21,388 security officers. At least two police officers will be assigned to each KCSE examination centre, with additional security provided at centres with larger candidate populations.

Heavy rains

Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba also warned that heavy rains could disrupt the examination process and said the government had activated contingency measures to ensure candidates are not disadvantaged.

The Kenya Meteorological Department has forecast above-average rainfall associated with the El Niño phenomenon, prompting authorities to prepare for possible flooding, damaged roads and other challenges that could affect access to examination centres and movement of examination materials.

Ogamba said relevant government agencies would work together to respond to any disruptions during the examination period.

The government has also expanded storage capacity for examination materials, with 48 additional containers installed in sub-counties, bringing the total number of containers to 701.

Close 

Education officials have also raised concern over the growing use of artificial intelligence and digital technologies to facilitate examination malpractice.

Basic Education Principal Secretary John Ololtuaa urged examination officials to remain vigilant and ensure emerging technologies are not used to compromise the credibility of the assessments.

Education officials have warned that examination malpractice could undermine public confidence in the country's education system and said those found violating examination regulations would face disciplinary or legal action.

The 2026 examination season comes as Kenya continues its transition to the Competency-Based Education system, with KPSEA and KJSEA forming part of the new assessment framework.

Notably, 2026 will also be the second-last KCSE examination for the 8-4-4 cohort, with the final 8-4-4 class expected to sit the examination in 2027.

KNEC has said it will operate a 24-hour call centre throughout the examination period to allow candidates, officials and members of the public to report incidents and seek assistance.

World.title: Kenya: Govt Identifies 109 Criminal Gangs, Warns Against Political Violence Ahead of 2027 Polls
World.content:
Nairobi — The government has intensified its crackdown on criminal gangs and organised violence, identifying 109 organised criminal gangs and groups operating across the country as Kenya prepares for the 2027 General Election.

Internal Security Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo said the government was particularly concerned about the use of organised youth groups for political intimidation, attacks and harassment.

He warned that the growing involvement of criminal groups in violence could undermine the rule of law, erode public confidence in state institutions and pose a serious security threat ahead of the elections.

The 109 groups identified by the government are an increase from the 89 criminal groups declared illegal in 2016 through Gazette Notice No. 10427.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to the government, 38 of the groups are based in Western Kenya, 22 in the Rift Valley, 20 in Nairobi, 12 in Nyanza, 11 at the Coast, three in Eastern, two in North Eastern and one in Central Kenya.

Omollo said security agencies arrested and arraigned 1,827 suspects for offences linked to goonism and organised criminal activity between January 1 and August 31, 2026.

Trans Nzoia recorded the highest number of arrests at 491.

During the same period, courts secured 729 convictions, with the Rift Valley accounting for 36.5 per cent of all convictions.

A further 716 cases remain before the courts, according to the government.

Omollo said the figures demonstrate that the government's response extends beyond arrests to investigations, prosecution and convictions.

The government said security agencies have shifted their focus from individual offenders to the wider networks that facilitate and sustain organised criminal activity.

Through intelligence-led policing, investigators are targeting gang leaders, recruiters and financiers, while linking cases and investigating connections between seemingly unrelated incidents.

Financial investigations are also being pursued where evidence exists to trace proceeds linked to extortion, robbery, illegal businesses and other organised criminal activities.

However, the government acknowledged that the fight against organised gangs has become more difficult because of increasingly decentralised structures and the proliferation of small arms and light weapons, particularly along vulnerable border areas.

Authorities said they are strengthening multi-agency cooperation, community-based intelligence and collaboration with neighbouring countries to tackle criminal activities that cross borders.

The government said security agencies would remain alert to attempts to mobilise criminal gangs or organised youth groups for political intimidation, disruption or violence ahead of the 2027 General Election.

Omollo stressed that the Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to participate in political life but warned that violence and intimidation have no place in the electoral process.

Security agencies will maintain visibility during political activities and take lawful action against criminal conduct, regardless of those involved, he said.

Those who recruit, finance or direct criminal groups will be held accountable alongside individuals who carry out acts of violence.

The Inspector-General of Police has directed regional police commanders to take firm, decisive and lawful action against criminal gangs and organised violence within their areas of command.

The government also warned that police officers found, through due process, to have facilitated criminal activities or failed to take appropriate action would face administrative or disciplinary measures.

The government acknowledged that enforcement alone cannot permanently eliminate organised criminality, particularly where former offenders return to the same environments and networks that initially drew them into crime.

Omollo said the government would therefore combine arrests and prosecutions with prevention, rehabilitation and reintegration programmes.

The initiatives will involve the Probation and Aftercare Service, Kenya Prisons Service, county governments, faith-based organisations and community leaders to help former members of criminal groups rebuild their lives and reintegrate into their communities.

The government also urged young people to take advantage of legitimate employment and enterprise opportunities available through programmes including the NYOTA Programme and Hustler Fund.

Close 

Omollo said some young people are recruited into criminal groups through promises of quick money, while others are coerced or exploited by individuals who finance and direct violence.

He said limited economic opportunities can leave young people vulnerable to such exploitation, although this does not excuse criminal conduct.

The government has called on parents, guardians, teachers, religious leaders and community leaders to work with security agencies to prevent young people from being recruited into criminal groups.

Members of the public have also been urged to report suspected criminal activity through credible channels.

The government cited the Fichua kwa DCI initiative, which can be reached through the toll-free number 0800 722 203, as one of the channels available for reporting suspected crime.

Omollo said the government would continue to strengthen intelligence-led policing, investigations and prosecutions while taking action to protect lives, property and communities.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 6, 2026
World.content:
press review

Nigeria Orders Probe into Tragic Ondo Military Plane Crash

Nigerian authorities are investigating the crash of a Nigerian Air Force ATR-42 aircraft near a naval base in Igbokoda, Ondo State, which had 25 passengers and seven crew members on board. The aircraft was travelling from Benin to Lagos on a routine mission when it crashed into a swampy area. President Bola Tinubu ordered a thorough investigation and declared three days of national mourning, with flags to fly at half-mast. The Nigerian Air Force said search and rescue operations were immediately activated. The Ministry of Aviation, Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau and Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority offered technical support. Ondo State Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa also deployed emergency, health and security agencies to assist. Local officials and eyewitnesses reported finding wreckage, human remains and personal belongings at the difficult-to-access crash site, with early accounts indicating there may have been no survivors.

Abiy Ahmed Sworn In for Second Term as Ethiopia's Prime Minister



Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has been sworn in for a second five-year term as the country formally begins a new parliamentary term amid renewed conflict in Tigray and worsening tensions with neighbouring Eritrea. Abiy took the oath during the inaugural session of the seventh House of Peoples' Representatives, with the new administration described as the "Medemer Government", reflecting his political philosophy of cooperation and national unity. The inauguration comes as federal forces and their allies consolidate control of Mekelle after the Tigray People's Liberation Front withdrew from the city. Fighting has continued elsewhere in the region, including reported airstrikes and artillery attacks. The renewed violence has raised fears of a return to the devastating 2020–2022 Tigray war. Ethiopia has also accused Eritrea of supporting a new rebel alliance, a claim Asmara denies, further straining regional relations and raising concerns about a wider Horn of Africa conflict.

Ugandan President Questions Progress on Appeal of Death-Row Daycare Killer

Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni has questioned the handling of the appeal of Christopher Okello Onyum, who was sentenced to death after being convicted of murdering four toddlers at a daycare centre in Ggaba, Kampala. Speaking to the NRM Caucus, Museveni said the case appeared to have "disappeared" after the appeal was filed and questioned whether appellate proceedings could be held in the same community where the original trial took place. Onyum was convicted by the High Court in April following a mobile trial at Ggaba Community Church. The victims were Gideon Eteku, Keisha Agenorwoth Otim, Ignatius Sseruyange and Ryan Odeke, who were killed at the Ggaba Early Childhood Development Centre on April 2. Onyum has appealed both his conviction and sentence, arguing that the evidence was not properly evaluated and that his mental state was not adequately considered. The Court of Appeal remains responsible for determining the merits of the case.

Malawi Proposal Seeks Major Changes to Vice-Presidency

A Lilongwe resident, Boldwin Bickiel Dzuwalatsoka, has submitted a draft Constitutional Amendment Bill proposing major changes to Malawi's Vice-Presidency. The proposal would end the automatic succession of a Vice-President to the presidency, make the position appointive rather than elected on a joint presidential ticket, and allow the President to dismiss the Vice-President at any time without impeachment proceedings. The Vice-President would also have a largely ceremonial role, with executive powers delegated by the President. Under the proposal, if the presidency became vacant, the Speaker of Parliament would become interim President within 24 hours and organise a fresh presidential election within 90 days of the deceased President's burial. Dzuwalatsoka argued that the current system has contributed to political tensions and power struggles between presidents and their deputies. The proposal has not yet been tabled in Parliament and would require constitutional scrutiny and the necessary parliamentary support before it could take effect.

Close 

U.S. Supreme Court Ruling May Resume Deportation Flights to Liberia

The US Supreme Court's decision to allow the Trump administration to continue deporting migrants to third countries temporarily could lead to the resumption of deportation flights to Liberia. At least 20 people have already been deported to the West African nation, some of whom had never had any connection to Liberia. The policy has referenced the nation's long and complicated relationship with the United States, dating back to the early 19th century when the American Colonization Society advocated sending free Black Americans to Africa. Those settlers established Liberia, which became Africa's first independent republic in 1847. Thousands of Black Americans and others were transported there during the 19th century, although many died from disease and others faced severe hardship. The latest deportations are different in circumstances, but critics and historians have noted parallels with earlier US efforts to remove nonwhite people viewed as unwanted from American society. The Supreme Court is expected to consider the broader legality of the current third-country deportation policy.

World.title: France explodes again as students riot over education
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Violent scenes are emerging from France Tuesday as tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets to demand education reform, forcing the reported closure of more than half of the country's high schools.

France's interior ministry said 6,100 people have been taken into custody since the protests began in September, while at least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Reuters.

Video taken in cities including Paris, Lyon and Strasbourg showed demonstrators facing off with police, lighting fires and dodging tear gas. In other areas such as Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs with messages like, "The state has killed national education," Reuters reported.

The Interior Ministry estimated that 86,000 people took part in demonstrations outside Paris on Tuesday morning. More were gathering in the capital for a protest scheduled for the afternoon.

"What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social.

TEEN'S HAND BLOWN OFF BY POLICE GRENADE DURING FRENCH STUDENT PROTESTS: REPORT

Authorities began shutting schools last week to try to diffuse tensions after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry. The High School Students Union also told Reuters that over half of France's high schools were closed or blockaded Tuesday.

Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats.

Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students’ compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.

"We want more money for the national educational system so that high schools are renovated," Roberta, a recent high school graduate in Paris, told Reuters.

FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE

In one of the recent demonstrations on Monday, a 15-year-old had picked up a police dispersal grenade that detonated in the town of Lens, losing his hand and part of his lower arm, officials said.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has asked ministers in France to address student demands including repairs to aging buildings, a call for longer lunch breaks and a review of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day, according to Reuters.

Felix Barney, a university student, told The Associated Press that the police response as disproportionate.

"It doesn’t have any sense to hit minors," he said.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Tuesday defended policing methods used against high schoolers, saying the police response has been proportionate in "almost all cases."

Fox News Digital's Louis Casiano and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

FIRST ON FOX: A blue city in one of the country's hottest battleground states is accused of being a potential hotbed of foreign worker visa fraud, according to the House lawmaker who represents the area.

Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., is writing to the Trump administration on Tuesday asking for an investigation into alleged abuse of the H-1B work visa program in his own district. He warned in the letter that his district is a "suspected hotspot of this fraud" and offered himself as "an interlocutor to help enable cooperation with state-level agencies and law enforcement."

Georgia's 7th Congressional District, which McCormick represents, encompasses part of the Atlanta metro area including the city's northern suburbs. That includes part of Fulton County, whose top prosecutor, Fani Willis, has been under heavy scrutiny by Republicans in recent years.

FEDERAL JUDGE STRIKES DOWN TRUMP’S $100K H-1B VISA FEE, RULING IT AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL TAX

"Established by the Immigration Act of 1990, the purpose of the H-1B program is to allow American businesses to temporarily bring in foreign citizens to fill key, high-skill employment positions when the domestic workforce demonstrably cannot provide the necessary labor," McCormick wrote.

"Unfortunately, the H-1B program has become the subject of rampant fraud and abuse for the nefarious purposes of obtaining labor that bad actors can exploit below-market-rate wages and abusive work conditions given H-1B holders’ dependence on retaining their employment in order to avoid removal back to their country of origin."

FURY ERUPTS AS US BRAND FIRES 1,600 EMPLOYEES AFTER SECURING THOUSANDS OF FOREIGN WORKER VISAS

He said the alleged fraud is sowing uncertainty in the U.S. labor market by undercutting wages and unfairly increasing competition for American workers, particularly those fresh out of college.

"Bad actors have developed illicit methods for meeting the requirements for obtaining H-1B visas and the necessary work authorizations, and they employ these methods at scale to enrich themselves through fraud and exploitation via the most threadbare compliance with the letter of the law," McCormick wrote.

VICE PRESIDENT VANCE SAYS MIGRANT COMMUNITIES SHOW 'CLEAR PATTERN' IN FEDERAL FRAUD AS INVESTIGATIONS WIDEN

The Georgia Republican said his suspicions were raised by "stakeholder engagement, reports from my constituents, and recent federal investigation and enforcement activity targeting entities in and around GA-07."

And while he did not name specific businesses or people he believes are associated with such fraud, McCormick argued, "Metro Atlanta’s recent economic growth and international airport unfortunately make it a logical area of concentration for these bad actors."

EXCLUSIVE: ‘PHANTOM EMPLOYEES' SCANDAL SPURS GOP CRACKDOWN ON $36B INCENTIVE FOR COMPANIES TO BYPASS AMERICANS

The Trump administration launched an investigation into suspected H-1B visa fraud in July.

H-1B visas have become the subject of fierce debate on the right, with prominent critics like Vice President JD Vance calling it a "broken" system while calling to eliminate it altogether.

Supporters of H-1B visas, like Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy, have argued it's critical for attracting global talent in fields like technology and engineering that are key to keeping the U.S. at the forefront of global innovation.

World.title: Coco Gauff calls out 'insane' racist comments after 16-year-old opponent gets emotional following controversy
World.content:
Coco Gauff found herself in some controversy in her match at the China Open against 16-year-old Sun Xinran, who was playing on home soil.

Gauff stopped a rally after electronic advertising boards lining the court flickered during a point late in the first set of her 7-5, 6-1 third-round victory over Xinran, a 16-year-old who recently won the U.S. Open junior title.

Sun appeared about to win the point when Gauff stopped playing, but the chair umpire then ordered the point to be replayed.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Gauff explained what occurred in the moment, but not before replying to a post on X calling her a racial slur.

"hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist. the amount of racist comments/dms I’ve received in the last few hours is insane," Gauff said, adding that she is "not a cheater or a thief."

Gauff has called out racism in the past, saying she received similar comments from gamblers earlier this year.

Gauff then said that she saw a light "flicker" early on in the point "but was not sure if that is what I actually saw."

"We are told before the matches we are allowed to continue to finish play so KEEP IT (sic) MIND i am thinking about all of this while i’m playing the point. anything can be challenged after the point is over... If I would’ve lost the point my opponent is also free to do the same thing and ask for a replay and she would’ve have been completely in her right to do so," Gauff explained.

Gauff said she saw the light flicker again and raised her hands.

PATRICK MCENROE ON U.S. OPEN WEED SMELL, TRANS ATHLETES, FOREIGN RECRUITS RESHAPING COLLEGE TENNIS

"It was an unfortunate situation but it is out of my control, the think pieces and calling me an unfair is ridiculous when those are the rules. I did not make them, I think it’s weird i’m getting hate for following the rules," Gauff said.

"Xinran is incredible talent and player, I apologized for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood."

Sun, who was given a wild-card entry by tournament organizers and was making her WTA Tour debut, appeared distraught after the loss. Gauff, who reached the fourth round of Wimbledon as a 15-year-old in 2019, sympathized with Sun.

"I did not like to see her so emotional as I’ve been there and I really understand what it is like but this is just the beginning of an incredible career. It was an honor to share the court in front of her home crowd."



Gauff will now play in the round of 16 on Wednesday against Elise Mertens.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Yoshinobu Yamamoto vs Chris Sale in pivotal NLDS Game 3 as Dodgers and Braves meet tied 1-1

That is the situation facing the Dodgers and Braves today. The Los Angeles Dodgers have been one of the best teams in baseball for years. A season after winning the World Series for the second straight year, they went out and signed the best closer available — a weakness for the team — and the best hitter available. World.title: DNA testing confirms body of flight attendant who was killed and thrown from bridge
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Authorities announced that DNA testing identified a body found in a Texas creek as a missing flight attendant whose roommate has been charged with killing her and dumping her remains off a bridge.

Rana Nofal Soluri, 47, was found on June 13 by a fisherman on the bank of Brushy Creek under a bridge in Montague County, about 70 miles northwest of Fort Worth, according to police and local reports. The remains were taken to the University of North Texas Health’s Center for Human Identification, where DNA testing recently confirmed the identity as Soluri, a Fort Worth Police Department spokesperson told NBC News.

Soluri worked for Envoy Air, a regional carrier owned by American Airlines, and had been missing since March 2025. She had taken time off for a minor operation and was expected to return to work on March 31, 2025, but a co-worker reported her missing months later, on June 11, 2025, after she failed to return and could not be reached, police said.

TERROR CELLS INSIDE FOREIGN AIRLINES 'CERTAINLY A POSSIBILITY,' RETIRED PILOT WARNS

Dennis Day, 67, Soluri’s former roommate and longtime friend, was arrested in June 2025 and charged with murder. Police said Day admitted he "snapped" during a dispute with Soluri before he "began to strangle her with his bare hands," according to an arrest warrant cited by reports.

Day allegedly told investigators he strangled Soluri on the kitchen floor, dragged her body into the backyard, loaded her "head first" into a large black trash bin and transported her body roughly 70 miles away before dumping it over a bridge, according to court documents.

Investigators said home surveillance video from Day’s Fort Worth house showed him dragging "what appears to be a lifeless body from the home into the backyard" on March 21, 2025. Police also said an "inadvertent call" and message on another woman’s phone captured a panicked Day asking for help moving Soluri’s body.

FLORIDA JUDGE RIPS INTO MOM ACCUSED OF LEAVING 4 CHILDREN AT HOME TO GO ON 3-DAY CRUISE

That woman, identified as Joni Thomas, also known as Joanne Walters, 63, was charged with tampering with evidence with intent to impair a human corpse. Police allege that she helped Day dispose of Soluri’s body. Both cases remain pending.

Before the DNA confirmation, prosecutors said Day had bragged to people in jail that he could not be convicted if authorities never found Soluri’s body, according to a notice filed by the Tarrant County Criminal District Attorney’s Office and cited by the Fort Worth Star-Telegram.

A GoFundMe page set up for Soluri’s daughter, Lulu Soluri, said American Airlines helped fly her mother’s remains to Seattle for a Muslim burial, which took place on Sept. 29. The fundraiser said Lulu also plans to travel to Texas for a future court date, where she is expected to deliver a statement.

"Lulu is a very private person, so this is a huge feat for her to face the person accused of killing her mother," the GoFundMe read. "Lulu thanks everyone for their support. She is always overwhelmed knowing how many people have helped her during this process."

World.title: Russia says no plague found in contacts of Siberian lab worker who died
World.content:
Plague had not been detected among close contacts of a worker in an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia who died last week, with 60% of the identified group tested so far, officials in Russia said Tuesday.

News from Russia’s consumer and health watchdog on Sunday that a female staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East had died from a “pneumonia of undetermined” origin last week has raised public health fears worldwide.

“Laboratory testing identified two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection,” watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said in a statement, referring to the virus that causes the common cold. “No other infectious disease pathogens were detected among the contacts,” the statement said, without mentioning the word “plague.”

Regional and national Russian authorities have not confirmed that plague was involved in the woman’s death. But American officials have urged more transparency from Moscow, with a State Department spokesperson saying Monday there had been “reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague” in Irkutsk oblast.

Lab workers at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East, in an undated photo. via AP

The World Health Organization, which oversees global public health matters, said Tuesday that Russian health officials had informed the agency in response to its request on the lab worker’s death that no case of plague has been recorded in Irkutsk.

“According to the authorities, the woman’s illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection,” it said.

No case of plague or other high threat pathogen has reportedly been found among the woman’s close contacts, the WHO said, quoting the response from the Russian officials, adding that it’s awaiting confirmation from the Russian side about “what pneumonia-causing pathogen had led to the individual’s death.”

On Friday, Maksim Modin, mayor of the Shelekhov municipal district near the border with Mongolia, said that the inpatient facility where the worker is said to have been treated had been closed for quarantine. Russian media cited officials saying that nearly 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under precautionary medical observation.

Russian media outlets have named the woman and identified her as being 28 years old. These details have not been announced by officials.

Irkutsk’s governor, Igor Kobsev, said Monday that no “microorganisms linked to the employee’s professional activities were detected” in her body.

The Irkutsk regional branch of Rospotrebnadzor on Tuesday denied what it called “fake” reports circulating online that an “enhanced sanitary-epidemiological regime” and strict restrictions have been imposed in the region.

“No such decisions have been made at this time,” it said in a statement, saying the situation in the region remains stable.

The headquarters of Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, in Moscow on Monday. Igor Ivanko / AFP via Getty

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that even though there is “very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia,” if “something like that gets out, it could quickly spread.”

President Donald Trump told reporters Monday the United States would do what it could to help Russia.

“I hate to see them having it,” Trump said. “It’s a rough disease.”

Meanwhile, some of Russia’s neighbors have been stepping up preventive measures and quarantine controls at border crossings.

The Kremlin has called for those concerned to heed official statements.

“Rospotrebnadzor provides comprehensive information,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said when reporters pressed him about rumors spreading amid sparse official statements.

Peskov also deferred to Rospotrebnadzor when asked if the worker’s lab results would be released or if an autopsy has been conducted.

On its website, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East says it was founded in 1934 “as a scientific and operational body for combating plague,” but over the years, its scope of responsibility expanded to include “other highly dangerous diseases,” including cholera and anthrax.

The institute says it’s a “multidisciplinary research and anti-epidemic facility” that helps ensure epidemic safety in the region.

World.title: California officials condemn Trump for saying Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
World.content:
California officials denounced President Donald Trump for saying at a campaign rally in Nebraska on Monday that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego, calling his remarks “deranged” and “irresponsible.”

In an apparent reference to the effect of the Iran war on U.S. prices, Trump said, “Remember, with the war, it’s just artificial. It’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.”

“They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego,” Trump said, drawing cheers from the crowd.

California and the state’s leaders are a frequent target of Trump’s ire, particularly Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat who is widely viewed as potential 2028 presidential contender. In his comments at the rally, Trump appeared to be making light of the potential for Iran to attack major American cities.

00:42 Trump draws backlash for saying Iran could 'take out' L.A. 00:00 00:00

In response to the backlash, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said in a post on X that the controversy “is not rooted in reality.”

“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped,” Cheung said. “America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”

State and local officials rebuked the president over his comments.

“After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” Newsom said in a post to X. “He is deranged and dangerous.”

The mayors of Los Angeles and San Diego also quickly responded to the president’s remarks. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat, wrote on X that Trump’s “statements against our city are dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety.”

“The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” Bass wrote. “In the face of irresponsible threats, as Angelenos, we know how to stand together and protect our city.”

San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria, also a Democrat, said in a post to X that his city “is not collateral damage.”

“We are not expendable,” Gloria added. “And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”

In his remarks, Trump also said the war would be over “very soon,” something he has suggested dozens of times over the past several months. The president has argued that the war was necessary to ensure Iran could not develop a nuclear weapon.

California’s Democratic senators also condemned the president’s comments.

In a post on X, Sen. Alex Padilla accused Trump of “inviting an attack on U.S. soil, putting millions of Americans and hundreds of thousands of our servicemembers at risk while trying to get Americans to cheer for an attack on our own country.”

“What kind of Commander in Chief does that?” Padilla added.

Sen. Adam Schiff hit back at Trump’s remark that the war would end soon.

“How many times have we heard that promise?” Schiff wrote on X. “And if it means attacks on two major American cities in the process, he is not troubled by the cost.”

California is considered a solidly blue state and its voters supported Trump’s Democratic opponents in all three presidential elections.

World.title: Flydubai pilot planned 9/11-style attack, source tells NBC News
World.content:
TEL AVIV — The pilot who allegedly tried to bring down an Israel-bound flight had been planning a 9/11-style attack by crashing into the country’s main airport in Tel Aviv, a Middle Eastern official has told NBC News.

The pilot, identified by NBC News as Hamman al-Hamammi, told investigators Monday that he wanted to evade Israel’s defenses and crash into the Ben Gurion Airport or another building, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the person was not authorized to speak publicly.

An Omani citizen, multiple sources from three agencies briefed on the investigation and a diplomat in the Middle East identified al-Hammami. Authorities have not officially released the identity.

He is currently being questioned by investigators in the United Arab Emirates after he was transferred from Saudi Arabia. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to an airport in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely, after last week’s dramatic midair incident.

Emirati authorities said Saturday that the pilot attacked his fellow pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls.

Omani pilot Hamman al-Hamammi. Obtained by NBC News

The jet which was carrying 174 mostly Israeli passengers then plummeted 14,000 feet in just 29 seconds, according to data from the aviation tracking service Flightradar24, causing panic onboard.

Machchhar, an Indian national and a veteran pilot of 17 years, said in a call Friday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that his fellow pilot told him he was going to pray, something he didn’t consider unusual as observant Muslims pray five times a day.

A few minutes later, he said he felt a strong blow to the head. “Because of his initial blows, my vision was almost like nothing, and I was completely blurred out,” he added. “The next feeling that I had was that the aircraft was sharply going down.”

A video of the call was released by Netanyahu’s office.

Initially, Machchhar said, he thought there was “catastrophic damage to the aircraft,” but once the blows kept coming he “realized that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”

In a separate call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, also Friday, Machchhar said he managed to open the cockpit’s door on the second attempt, despite the blows raining down.

“I gave everything that I had, and just went for the door and opened the door. And thankfully, people were waiting to pounce back,” he said.

Focus has shifted onto the missed security signals ahead of the flight.

Citing sources familiar with the matter, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday that al-Hammami had “previously been banned from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views.”

Passengers from a Flydubai flight. Jamal Awad / Xinhua via Getty

It is unclear how a citizen of Oman, an Arab country with no diplomatic relations with Israel, was allowed to fly the plane carrying Israelis to Tel Aviv.

According to Israeli law, airlines must provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, up to 48 hours before a flight.

Israeli investigators are leaning towards the assessment that the pilot was acting as a lone wolf, according to an Israeli official and a source familiar with the matter, although they said there is still more to learn about what led to his radicalization.

In the meantime, Netanyahu has called on the head of the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to review “all security aspects” of Israel’s civil aviation in the aftermath of the incident.

Elsewhere, Vice President JD Vance underlined the concerns potential security failures.

“That person should not have been flying an airline, and so we’re certainly looking at our procedures within the United States to make sure that people who are obviously flight risks are not getting behind the wheel of an airplane,” he told a reporter at Joint Base Andrews on Monday.

World.title: Here are the finalists for the 2026 National Book Awards
World.content:
Here are the finalists for the 2026 National Book Awards

NPR

Does "the third time's the charm" apply to prestigious literary awards? Edwidge Danticat will have the opportunity to find out. She's now a three-time finalist for a National Book Award, which were announced Tuesday morning. Danticat's novel, Dèy, is about a woman who witnesses a violent gun attack in a Miami mall. Danticat's short story collection Krik? Krak! was a finalist for the prize in 1995, and her book Brother, I'm Dying, was a non-fiction finalist in 2007.

The other writers up for the 2026 fiction prize include Hannah Lillith Assadi, Julián Delgado Lopera, Valeria Luiselli, and debut novelist Morgan Thomas, whose book Mad Eden is a form-bending story following a patient navigator at a center providing gender-affirming care.

Sponsor Message

Similarly blending forms in the nonfiction category is Camonghne Felix. Her book Let the Poets Govern: A Declaration of Freedom is both a memoir and a call-to-action, drawing on Felix's background as a communications strategist. Felix is up against Colin Asher, Sara Nović, Joseph Osmundson, and Abdelrahman ElGendy, whose memoir, Huna, explores his time in an Egyptian prison.

The winners of the National Book Awards will be announced Nov. 18, 2026.

World.title: What to know about nationwide protests in India over voter list changes
World.content:
What to know about nationwide protests in India over voter list changes

toggle caption i Rafiq Maqbool/AP

NEW DELHI — Protests have spread across India in the past week as opposition parties and civil society groups demand the resignation of the country's election chief over alleged manipulation of voter lists.

The campaign has been led in part by India's "Cockroach" youth movement, which previously organized street protests that forced the education minister to resign in July.

Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the poll body's ongoing revision of voter lists. They accuse the revision could disenfranchise millions of voters and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP. The commission and government deny any wrongdoing.

Sponsor Message

Here's what to know:

Voter list changes fueling the protests

India is the world's largest democracy with hundreds of millions of people voting in national and state elections. The Election Commission plays a central role in determining voter eligibility and administering elections, making changes to electoral lists politically significant.

The dispute centers on a nationwide voter list revision known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR. It began last year in the eastern state of Bihar ahead of local elections and has since expanded to most of India's states and federally administered territories.

Under the process, voters are required to provide documents showing they are eligible to remain on the lists.

The Election Commission says the exercise is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible entries and ensure legitimate voters remain registered. Critics say it could instead exclude legitimate voters, particularly poorer and other vulnerable communities.

They also say the requirements are confusing and difficult for many people to provide, particularly those who lack older government records or other documents.

Critics say the changes could benefit Modi's party

India's Election Commission is an independent constitutional body overseeing elections and maintaining voter lists, but opposition parties accuse the commission of favoring Modi's party. They allege the changes could remove people more likely to support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters who favor the BJP.

Sponsor Message

The BJP and the Election Commission reject the allegations and say the revision has no political motive. Modi's party says the list is being updated to weed out what they call "infiltrators."

The issue was prominent in West Bengal's crucial state elections earlier this year after a voter list revision removed about 9 million names, or roughly 12% of the electorate. The deletions left millions of eligible voters unable to cast ballots. Modi's party won the state for the first time.

toggle caption i Rafiq Maqbool/AP

Politics can impact commission rulings

Indian law requires a majority vote of commission members to enact changes making disagreements among its members potentially significant.

The Indian Express newspaper reported in September that two of the three election commissioners had formally objected to several decisions involving voter list revisions, registration procedures and the commission's digital systems.

The newspaper reported Kumar, the election chief, rejected those objections.

The Election Commission said the report reflected "differing views and deliberations" rather than formal written objections.

Protesters seek end to changes that could reshape elections

The "Cockroach" movement, opposition parties and civil society groups have called for Kumar to resign or be removed and for an inquiry into his conduct, including possible criminal proceedings. They want the current revision halted and the previous electoral lists used for future elections.

They also demand a more independent and transparent process for appointing election commissioners.

Election Commission data indicates voter lists in some regions could shrink by as much as 30%, fueling concerns among opposition parties and protest groups over potential exclusions.

The dispute is likely to intensify as the changes resulting from the revision expand throughout India, which is facing a series of state elections early next year.

World.title: Vietnamese police arrest 12 suspected of prowling city streets at night, snatching cats for meat
World.content:
Vietnamese police arrest 12 suspected of prowling city streets at night, snatching cats for meat

toggle caption i Humane World for Animals/AP

HANOI, Vietnam — Police in Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City arrested 12 men suspected of operating a citywide ring that stole and resold about 2,700 cats for meat, Vietnamese state media said.

Police identified 39-year-old Luu Thanh Binh as the alleged leader of the network. He and 11 others were being investigated for theft, state media said Monday.

Investigators said Binh bought stolen cats, kept them at a facility in the city's north and resold them for meat. He worked with suppliers who recruited others to ride motorcycles through residential neighborhoods between 11 p.m. and 4 a.m., hunting for cats and trapping four to 10 cats each night.

Sponsor Message

Eating dog and cat meat is not unique to Vietnam and has been practiced in parts of Asia, though it is not common practice. In Vietnam, cat meat traditionally is more commonly consumed in the north, among older generations.

The practice has declined with growing pet ownership and urbanization, and younger Vietnamese are more likely to regard dogs and cats as companion animals.

In 2024, more than 250,000 people signed a petition calling for an end to Vietnam's dog and cat meat trade. The city of Hoi An also pledged in 2021 to end the sale and consumption of dog and cat meat.

Some believe eating cat meat brings good luck, though there is no scientific evidence for such claims.

Police raided the network on July 8 and found about 50 cats and dozens of traps, state media reported.

The suspects told investigators they had stolen and sold about 2,700 cats, the reports said. Police did not say how long the operation had been running.

Police returned 13 of the cats confiscated in the raid to their owners. A nonprofit animal rights group was caring for the others while authorities sought to identify their owners.

Under Vietnamese law, dogs and cats are considered private property, and stealing them is considered theft. Criminal prosecution generally applies when the value of the stolen property exceeds 2 million dong ($77).

Sponsor Message

In a separate raid in June, police reported they had rescued more than 400 cats. At least 40 were reunited with their owners, but dozens of dead cats were found packed in ice.

World.title: Ex-spy chief is arrested in Germany on suspicion of trading state secrets and treason
World.content:
Ex-spy chief is arrested in Germany on suspicion of trading state secrets and treason

toggle caption i Michael Kappeler/DPA via AP

BERLIN — A former head of Germany 's foreign intelligence service was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion that he had passed state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the federal prosecutor's office said.

August Hanning, who led the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005, is "strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage," the federal prosecutor's office said in a statement.

Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. A former aide, identified as Manfred D., was also arrested Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany and has been charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.

Sponsor Message

The statement did not reveal who the two men were suspected of spying for.

The premises of both men were searched Tuesday.

Former aide allegedly supplied Hanning with BND documents

The prosecutor's office said Manfred D. worked as Hanning's chief of staff and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026.

"In his role, he had access to confidential information," the prosecutor's office said.

Both suspects are believed to have agreed in 2010 to have Manfred D. continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the BND to Hanning in exchange for payment, the statement said.

"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings," the statement said.

Hanning used the information in private consulting work, and on one occasion "used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service."

Manfred D., who in line with German privacy rules cannot be identified by his full name, provided Hanning with classified information for several years, the statement said, but it was not immediately clear if the collaboration continued until their arrests on Tuesday.

Sponsor Message

The office did not say which country the foreign agent worked for and said "it has yet to be determined if the material reached the intended recipient."

The statement added that "Hanning was in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D., for several years."

Hanning is suspected of involvement in a prominent child abduction case

Hanning came under scrutiny in a separate investigation into the abduction of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block's children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a custody battle that had been going on for several years.

The investigation into that case led to Tuesday's arrests.

The current proceedings stem from evidence found during a search of Hanning's residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor's office stated.

Hanning and a retired official from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office are suspected of having accepted a contract from Block in 2022 to abduct her children while serving as executives of a security firm, the public prosecutor's office announced in the fall of 2025, according to German news agency dpa.

The Blocks are a prominent Hamburg family best known for their popular national steakhouse chain Block House. The custody trial has received a lot of attention in the country, with German tabloids offering heavy coverage from the court.

A message to the BND for comment was not immediately returned.

German opposition lawmaker calls for a quick probe

German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz expressed shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation.

"This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story," said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services.

"We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations leveled against former BND chief Hanning," von Notz told Spiegel Online.

Sponsor Message

"We have been criticizing the dubious and wide-ranging lobbying activities of former top officials and those with the highest security clearances in the Germany for years," he said and called for banning former officials with security clearances from engaging in private consulting work after leaving office, Spiegel Online reported.

World.title: Dems have edge in midterms, poll shows. And, Paramount-Warner Bros. merger to close
World.content:
Dems have edge in midterms, poll shows. And, Paramount-Warner Bros. merger to close

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

In four weeks, Election Day will be here, and a series of new polls show Democrats have a decided advantage in the midterms. They are favored to win the House with a narrow majority. Democrats need 218 seats for a majority, and the Cook Political Report forecasts a net gain of five to 15 seats, which would give them between 220 and 230 seats in January. The Senate has shifted more dramatically. Six seats have moved toward the Democrats' direction since June, according to Cook's ratings. Initially seen as a long shot for Democrats, the Senate is now within reach. These projections come as President Trump's approval rating is low.

A new era in Hollywood is set to arrive today as David Ellison's long-anticipated $111 billion merger with Paramount-Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery is expected to close. Despite facing months of public protests, the deal has cleared legal and regulatory challenges in the U.S. and Europe. The media conglomerate Skydance unites two film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, both more than 100 years old.



🎧 Ellison defended the merger against critics concerned about him having too much media power, NPR's Mandalit del Barco says. As part of a settlement to move the deal forward, Ellison agreed to produce 30 films a year with the combined studios, but critics remain skeptical. Concerns also linger about CNN's future, given that Ellison is an ally of Trump. To address these worries, Ellison promised to establish an independent oversight board to protect CNN from political interference. People who don't agree with the deal predict that viewers may soon see an increase in cost for streaming services and they could have fewer choices, according to del Barco.

Catherine Sweeney from NPR network station WPLN was one of seven media witnesses to observe Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike, the first woman to face the death penalty in the state in nearly 200 years. Each witness sensed that the lethal injection might not proceed smoothly. Pike's attorneys had requested the Tennessee Supreme Court to allow hanging instead due to concerns that her platelet disorder and small veins would make the injection painful and ineffective. Sweeney describes what she saw and heard throughout that day.

Sponsor Message

Russian authorities are urging people to remain calm after a worker at an infectious diseases institute in Siberia died from a mysterious illness, raising speculation about a potential plague outbreak. Last Tuesday, a 28-year-old female lab worker at the anti-plague Research Institute in Irkutsk fell ill and died two days later. Questions remain over the cause of her death. Here's what we do and don't know.

On the road to the midterms

by Majd Al-Waheidi , Morning Edition and Up First digital editor

NPR

Four weeks from now, the midterm election will help decide the balance of power in Congress. And ahead of Election Day, Morning Edition will be traveling to six states with some of the most competitive races to hear what voters say is shaping their decisions.

Steve Inskeep is reporting from North Carolina and Georgia. Michel Martin is headed to Ohio and Michigan. Leila Fadel is reporting from Maine. And A Martínez is heading to Texas.

Across the political divide, one concern keeps rising to the top: the cost of living and what it means for people's economic futures.

But voters are weighing more than their bills. Immigration and the rapid growth of massive data centers are also part of the conversation. So is the voting process itself, including new restrictions that are raising questions about how ballots will be cast, secured and counted.

Over the next four weeks, Morning Edition will report from different races and electorates across the country, asking many of the same questions: What matters to voters now, what has changed and where is the country headed next?

So what will our hosts be listening for when Morning Edition hits the road? We asked them. Here are four things on their minds:

Steve Inskeep: "I am watching and listening for people who feel this election is personal. By which I mean that, beyond their general opinion of the state of the country, they feel they were directly affected by the events of the past two years — the Trump administration's dramatic moves to reshape immigration, government, education, science, research, the military, emergency management, taxes, foreign policy and the economy at large.

Sponsor Message

Michel Martin: "Ohio is also a key location for the Trump administration's mass deportation campaign, as well as a leading industrial and logistics hub, a place where we should be able to see how the administration's economic policies are playing out. Trump isn't on the ballot, but his policies are. So let's see how that's going.

"Michigan was once considered a big part of the Democrats' 'Blue Wall,' but in recent years has chosen both Democrats and Republicans in key races. And the Democratic base has had beef with the national party. So what's driving voters? Are they mad? Sad? Or just exhausted? We hope to find out."

Leila Fadel: "The path to controlling the Senate in part runs through Maine, and that's why we're reporting in the state before the midterm elections. I want to know what drives voters, and how much party loyalty still plays a role. Are their votes up for grabs? Or are they locked in along party lines?"

"This is a state that's seen some of the worst of the immigration crackdown; a man was killed by ICE. It has one of the longest borders with Canada, and so the trade war hits differently. The Democratic candidate Troy Jackson is facing incumbent Susan Collins, who has won her state five times before. So, we'll be asking what people want from their candidate and if it matters which party that resonating message comes from."

A Martínez: "Texas Republicans gerrymandered five congressional districts to favor the GOP in the upcoming midterms. In three of them, the new maps created more Latino voters."

"What's behind the Texas GOP's big bet on Latino voters, and will it help Republicans keep control of the U.S. Senate?"

Follow the reporting: Maine coverage airs today. Texas is up next on Oct. 13, followed by reporting from North Carolina and Georgia, and Ohio and Michigan. You can follow along on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in the Up First newsletter.

A new NPR series is taking readers and listeners to breakfast tables around the world. In Munich, Germany, a Bavarian breakfast typically consists of boiled veal sausage, sweet mustard and a giant pretzel, all washed down with beer. Demetrios Kyriakides, who spent a year researching Bavarian breakfast joints in Munich, says the ambiance of Gemütlichkeit, which describes conviviality, is just as important as the food. A meal is often accompanied by brass oom-pah-pah music. This feast is usually finished before the church bells ring at midday, signaling that all good things must come to an end. World.title: What voters in 6 key states could tell us about the 2026 midterms
World.content:
What voters in 6 key states could tell us about the 2026 midterms

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/Getty Images

A version of this essay first appeared in the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get the news you need to start your day — plus a little fun — every weekday and Sunday.

Four weeks from now, the midterm elections will help decide the balance of power in Congress. And ahead of Election Day, Morning Edition will be traveling to six states with some of the most competitive races to hear what voters say is shaping their decisions.

We already have some clues about where voters stand. The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll found registered voters favor Democrats for Congress over Republicans by 12 percentage points. President Trump is also very much on voters' minds, with 45% saying their vote for Congress is a vote against him, compared with about a quarter who say they are voting to support him.

Sponsor Message

Across the political divide, one concern keeps rising to the top: the cost of living and what it means for people's economic futures.

But this year, some of the forces driving those costs are coming from far beyond voters' own communities. The war with Iran is affecting prices at the gas pump. Tariffs imposed in Washington are reaching the checkout counter. Foreign policy, economic policy and household costs are becoming harder to separate.

Republicans and Democrats are both campaigning on promises to make everyday life more affordable. But voters are weighing more than their bills. Immigration and the rapid growth of massive data centers are also part of the conversation. So is the voting process itself, including new restrictions that are raising questions about how ballots will be cast, secured and counted.

And in several of these states, another question hangs over the races: What do voters want from their own parties, and do old political loyalties still hold? Those are some of the questions that Morning Edition will take on the road, using the six states as a window into an electorate that is changing.

Steve Inskeep is reporting from North Carolina and Georgia, two closely watched Southern states. North Carolina has an open Senate seat and newly redrawn congressional districts. Georgia has competitive races for Senate and governor after several elections in which voters have backed candidates from both parties.

Sponsor Message

"I am watching and listening for people who feel this election is personal," Inskeep said.

He wants to hear from people who feel directly affected by the Trump administration's changes to immigration, government, education, taxes, foreign policy and the economy.

"Trump is not on the ballot but has urged voters to act as if he is, and given the consequential acts of his administration, voters are likely to respond as if he is," Inskeep said.

Michel Martin is headed to Ohio and Michigan, where some of the biggest questions are about political change in the Midwest. Ohio has competitive races for governor and Senate against a backdrop of economic anxiety. In Springfield, Martin will also look at how the end of temporary protected status for Haitians is affecting a community where Haitian immigrants make up a significant share of the population — and whether disagreements over immigration are changing how voters see their own parties.

Michigan offers a different set of tests. Trump won the state narrowly in 2024, when anger over the Biden administration's handling of the war in Gaza was a major issue for some voters, particularly in Michigan's Arab American communities. The state also saw a sharp increase in young-voter turnout. This year, an open Senate seat and a governor's race offer another chance to see whether those shifts are carrying into the midterms — and what role younger and Black voters are playing in the Democratic coalition.

Martin calls Ohio and Michigan "two big consequential states that have always told us a lot about where the rest of the country is, and is going."

In Michigan, she will be asking what is driving voters after the state has chosen both Democrats and Republicans in key races.

"Are they mad? Sad? Or just exhausted? We hope to find out," Martin said.

Sponsor Message

Leila Fadel is reporting from Maine, where a Senate race could help determine control of the chamber. Republican Sen. Susan Collins is seeking another term against Democrat Troy Jackson. Immigration and trade are also part of the political conversation there.

"I want to know what drives voters and how much party loyalty still plays a role," Fadel said. "Are their votes up for grabs? Or are they locked in along party lines?"

Maine's long border with Canada also gives the trade war a different dimension, as tariffs and tensions over cross-border trade affect businesses and communities with close economic ties to Canada. The state has also been affected by the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. Fadel said she will be asking voters what they want from their candidates — and whether the party delivering that message matters.

A Martínez is heading to Texas, where Republicans are testing whether recent gains among Latino voters will hold. The state's U.S. Senate race has also put Texas in the national fight over control of the chamber.

Republicans redrew five congressional districts to favor the Republican Party in the midterms, including three with more Latino voters. Martínez said that this makes the party's strategy around Latino voters one of the questions he wants to examine.

"What's behind the Texas GOP's big bet on Latino voters, and will it help Republicans keep control of the U.S. Senate?"

Over the next four weeks, Morning Edition will report from races and electorates across the U.S., asking many of the same questions: What matters to voters now, what has changed and where is the country headed next?

Follow the reporting: Maine coverage airs today, Oct. 6. Texas is up next on Oct. 13, followed by reporting from North Carolina and Georgia and then Ohio and Michigan. You can follow along on Morning Edition and NPR.org, as well as in the NPR app and the Up First newsletter.
