World.title: A history of presidents naming things after themselves (It's short. They rarely do)
World.content:
A history of presidents naming things after themselves (It's short. They rarely do)

toggle caption i Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images

President Trump recently underscored his desire to have his name appear on the facade of the Kennedy Center with a threat. "Frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," Trump told reporters. "It'll end up being ripped down."

Trump or his supporters have called for the president's name to appear on everything from naval battleships to airports. It's pretty rare for sitting presidents to stamp their identities on infrastructure, currency and other public assets — though history shows there are a few exceptions.

George Washington "didn't want a lot of fuss"

Discussions regarding this issue go all the way back to the first presidential administration.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Victoria Arocho/AP

"They were trying to figure out what was the right balance between the prestige required to give this new office respect, but also recognizing that they were not trying to re-create a monarchy," said Lindsay Chervinsky, executive director of the George Washington Presidential Library and author of The Cabinet: George Washington and the Creation of an American Institution.

Chervinsky said the issue first came up at the federal level during Washington's presidency around the Coinage Act of 1792. Congress was figuring out what to put on the inaugural American coins, given the habit in Great Britain and other nations of plastering the reigning monarch all over theirs.

"The House of Representatives said that the president should not be on currency because of this monarchical tie," Chervinsky said.

Chervinsky said Washington shared their concerns. The president usually shied away from ostentatious self-celebration. "He didn't want a lot of fuss," she said.

But sometimes, Washington didn't seem to mind it. "They did name the federal city Washington to honor him while he was still in office," Chervinsky said.

But what about the Hoover Dam?

Most administrations have generally kept the names and faces of sitting presidents off public assets since then, viewing it as unseemly.

On the few occasions when a sitting president's name has appeared — such as on dams named for Teddy Roosevelt, Calvin Coolidge and Woodrow Wilson — it tended not to be the man in office pushing for it himself. "Usually it is political supporters," Chervinsky said. And the history around the naming process can be fraught.

The most prominent example of this is the Hoover Dam.

toggle caption i Keystone/Hulton Archives/Getty Images

The massive public works project located near the Boulder Canyon on the Arizona-Nevada border had been known in the early stages of its development as the Boulder Dam. Hoover's secretary of the interior, Ray Lyman Wilbur, suggested rechristening the project in 1930 as the Hoover Dam, owing to the lead role Hoover had played in its planning. "Hoover negotiated the deal among the states known as the Colorado River Compact that allocated the river's water among seven states," said Kenneth Whyte, author of Hoover: An Extraordinary Life in Extraordinary Times. "So it was generally agreed that it was deserved."

Sponsor Message

Apparently, the president thought so too. "Hoover, I think, was pleased about it," said Whyte. "But he did not talk a lot about it at the time. He didn't want to be seen to be doing self-aggrandizing things."

But the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration was having none of it. After Roosevelt took office in 1933, his secretary of the interior, Harold Ickes, called for the dam to revert to its original moniker.

"Ickes based this argument on the fact that the original legislation that authorized Congress to fund the project was called the Boulder Canyon Project Act," said Marist University's David Woolner, a senior fellow and resident historian at the Roosevelt Institute, and the author of several books about the 32nd U.S. president. "And he did not like the politics of Herbert Hoover."

Woolner said Roosevelt did not object to the change. He kept his political rival's name out of his 1935 dedication speech, consistently referring to it as "Boulder Dam."

The naming coup was short-lived.

Although there was some initial opposition from Democrats, in 1947, Congress voted unanimously to change the name back. Woolner said this happened "in recognition of Hoover's early support for the project, and after the former president gained praise for his humanitarian work during and after the First and Second World Wars."

There's always the presidential library ... or "library"

Roosevelt, for his part, wasn't "particularly anxious to have things named after him," Woolner said.

But that didn't stop Roosevelt from lending his name to one major project during his presidency — the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum — "which of course he initiated," said Woolner.

toggle caption i Craig Ruttle/AP

In keeping with this tradition, President Trump told reporters at a press briefing earlier this year he is planning to build himself a presidential library in Miami.

Except it probably won't be a library. And presidential libraries are, technically speaking, public-private assets.

Sponsor Message

"I don't believe in building libraries or museums," Trump said. "But it's most likely going to be a hotel with a beautiful building underneath and a 747 Air Force One in the lobby."

One thing that seems certain, judging by a video rendering on the president's social media channel promoting the project: Trump's name will be prominently displayed on its facade.

World.title: Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in physics for work on high-energy neutrinos from space
World.content:
Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in physics for work on high-energy neutrinos from space

toggle caption i Angela Weiss/Pool AFP via AP

STOCKHOLM — Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in physics on Tuesday for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and his discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.

"Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument. His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy," Mark Pearce, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics, said in a news release.

Halzen spoke to the committee by phone from Italy on Tuesday.

"It was a great surprise and I obviously didn't expect it," he said.

Sponsor Message

Halzen said it was predicted before that he would win the Nobel Prize but the announcement still made him feel "strange."

Born in Belgium, the 82-year-old scientist is affiliated with the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the U.S. Efforts by The Associated Press to reach him were not immediately successful.

The IceCube Neutrino Observatory is a research facility located at the South Pole in Antarctica, according to its website, and the University of Wisconsin–Madison is its lead institution.

Neutrinos are tiny cosmic particles with a mind-bogglingly small mass. Yet they are everywhere: they spew from stars like the sun and trillions zip through our bodies every second.

Scientists can't glimpse the mysterious ghost particles zooming around on their own. Instead, they measure what happens when the tiny particles collide with other bits of matter, producing flashes of light or charged particles.

Halzen studied a rare gang of neutrinos that scientists consider messengers from the cosmos, offering clues to how the universe evolved.

His research into capturing neutrinos at the South Pole dates back to the 1980s.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the award in Stockholm.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.

Sponsor Message

Last year, three scientists won the Nobel Prize in physics for research on the strange behavior of subatomic particles called quantum tunneling that enabled the ultra-sensitive measurements achieved by MRI machines and laid the groundwork for better cellphones and faster computers.

The announcements of this year's prizes began Monday with the Nobel Prize in medicine being awarded to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.

This week's awards continue Wednesday with the chemistry prize and literature on Thursday. After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.

World.title: Ottawa gives Stelco's U.S. owner 5 days to share plan to keep jobs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ottawa has given the U.S. owner of Stelco five business days to share a plan to maintain jobs at the Hamilton steelmaker or face potential legal action.

Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs said last week it plans to lay off as many as 500 workers as it idles certain steel production at Stelco, which the federal government says violates "binding commitments" made when it bought the company in 2024.

In a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon on Monday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Ottawa is prepared to seek a court ruling to enforce the agreement under the Investment Canada Act.

"The Government of Canada takes compliance with undertakings seriously," Joly wrote in the letter, obtained by CBC News on Tuesday.

"Where an investor fails to comply with an undertaking, the Act provides remedies for breaches, including an application to the superior court for orders that may include directing compliance, divestiture, or monetary penalties.

"I trust that such steps will not be necessary."

Cleveland-Cliffs acquired Stelco in a $3.4-billion cash-and-stock deal that, according to a news release at the time, kept " national interests at the forefront" and recognized the "importance of the workforce."

According to Joly's letter, this includes " undertakings to continue to employ at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees as were employed when the transaction was announced."

Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves has said the cuts are necessary and justified by the Canada-U.S. trade war, arguing that Stelco's ability to sell steel to the U.S. was an "underlying condition" of the deal.

Joly said the company's commitments "do not cease to apply simply because business strategy or market conditions have changed."

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week Ottawa will "use all powers that we have" against Cleveland-Cliffs as it pursues the Ohio-based company to the "fullest extent of the law."

CBC News reached out to Cleveland-Cliffs for comment on Tuesday.

Funding from Ontario

Meanwhile, Ontario’s government on Tuesday pledged to invest more than $200,000 with Ottawa through the Canada-Ontario Workforce Tariff Response to help protect steel and manufacturing workers in the Hamilton area.

The funding will help 75 workers and jobseekers upgrade their skills and transition to in-demand careers, according to the province's minister of labour, immigration, training and skills development.

"Ontario is fighting back against President Trump's attacks on our economy by helping our workers retrain, upskill, and stay competitive," Trevor Jones said in a statement.

Goncalves has expressed support for Trump's Section 232 measures, which put up to 50 per cent tariffs on steel and aluminum imports from Canada.

Goncalves has said he supports Canadian steel workers, and that "America first is not America only."

Last Monday, amid news of the Stelco layoffs, Trump touted a $15-billion US investment plan by Minnesota-based steelmaker Mesabi Metallics to build a massive plant in Iowa as evidence that his administration's tariffs on imported steel are working as intended.

World.title: CAQ fatigue key to sovereignist PQ's historic victory
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebecers have elected a sovereignist government, even though most of them aren't in favour of a separatist vote.

But this is different from 2014.

When Pauline Marois’s version of the Parti Québécois (PQ) was pegged to form a minority government, there was no clear timeline on a potential referendum.

The current leader and soon-to-be premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has insisted for years that a referendum should be held within the first four years of a PQ term.

Yet, three decades after the 1995 sovereignty referendum, Quebec's historic political cleavage — and the PQ's raison d’être — did not prevent the party from forming a minority government.

In his victory speech, St-Pierre Plamondon said that "francophones’ struggle in America" will find meaning once Quebecers get a country and the recognition that comes with that.

"We deserve it just as much as all other peoples who have their own country and democracy," he told a crowd at the PQ headquarters in Montreal. "It is a matter of justice and equity, but it is also a matter of survival."

Voters chose change — even if they don't want referendum

Last December, about a month before announcing his resignation, former premier François Legault predicted that the Quebec general election would result in a battle between the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ), the party he co-founded, and the Quebec Liberal Party (PLQ).

"Everyone will understand that [PQ Leader Paul] St-Pierre Plamondon equals a referendum we don’t want," Legault told Radio-Canada host Patrice Roy. "He’ll go down in the polls."

But Legault was wrong. The thirst for change after eight years of the CAQ in government seemed to overpower concerns about a referendum.

Throughout the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon often posed the rhetorical question, “Do we really want 12 years of the CAQ?”

Voters resolutely decided they didn’t.

The end result: the CAQ was obliterated, left with no seats in the National Assembly. And despite the best efforts from CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette and PLQ Leader Charles Milliard, sovereignty did not act as an effective wedge issue in this campaign.

Polls have consistently shown that sovereignty is a low priority of Quebecers, with one Léger poll showing that 70 per cent of Quebecers would not support separating from Canada.

But the electoral math told a different story.

In a remarkable feat made possible by the first-past-the-post electoral system, the PQ formed a minority government with as little as 28 per cent of the popular vote — the lowest voter share to achieve that in Quebec's history, and one that is certain to add fuel to the debate about electoral reform.

WATCH | St-Plamondon tells English speakers 'we're in the same boat': Parti Québécois leader addresses English-speaking Quebecers in victory speech | Duration closed caption 0:33 Paul St-Pierre Plamondon took a moment to speak to anglophones in the province, saying that all Quebecers face the same challenges, and that he looks forward to solving problems together.

Given the sovereignty project's timeline — with a vote pushed to 2029 or 2030, after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office — a referendum seems distant, if not entirely unlikely given the government's fragility.

What is certain, though, is that Quebecers gave St-Pierre Plamondon a short leash, forcing him to work alongside other parties, namely the Liberals and the PCQ, who would block any legislation opening the door to a referendum.

The PQ’s costed platform estimates that a sovereignty referendum would cost $130 million.

All parties benefit from CAQ’s collapse

Fréchette was the only leader not to have won their riding, signalling the CAQ's freefall.

At CAQ headquarters in Trois-Rivières, Que., Fréchette — who spent much of the campaign attempting to distance herself from Legault, even omitting the CAQ logo from her posters — spent part of her 10-minute concession speech thanking him.

WATCH | Fréchette makes concession speech: CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette takes ownership of party’s fall in concession speech | Duration closed caption 0:48 At party headquarters in Trois-Rivières, Que., Fréchette thanked her National Assembly colleagues. She said the party’s fall was her responsibility alone, and that being premier was the greatest honour of her life.

Taking over from the CAQ’s founder, especially after the party’s popularity had waned, was an expected uphill battle.

Compounding the challenge, Fréchette had previously served as a prominent CAQ cabinet member leading the ministries of immigration, francisation, and economy — portfolios that cast a shadow over any image of renewal she tried to project for a declining party.

Fréchette also attempted to position herself as best equipped to defend Quebec against Trump, whom she called her "main opponent." However, as premier, her ability to face the U.S. president head-on is inherently limited. Claims of foreign interference, drummed up by members of Fréchette’s team weeks before the election, did little to help her credibility either.

The CAQ’s losses were to the benefit of opposition parties, particularly the Conservatives, who experienced a historic breakthrough achieved through targeted campaigns in the Quebec City area.

WATCH | Duhaime celebrates Bellechasse riding victory: Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime projected to win seat in Bellechasse riding | Duration closed caption 0:12 This was Duhaime’s third attempt to win a seat in the National Assembly with the Conservatives. During this provincial election, Duhaime focused his party's campaign around Quebec City and Chaudière-Appalaches regions.

The Conservatives won 19 ridings — the party’s first elected seats in 90 years. It was a celebratory moment for PCQ Leader Éric Duhaime, who on his third attempt as leader managed to capture a seat in the Chaudière-Appalaches region.

It remains to be seen whether St-Pierre Plamondon, like so many leaders before him — including Legault — will keep his promise to reform the electoral system that led him to power.

World.title: Giant underwater Kelvin wave could 'pack a punch' for B.C. in mid-October
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A giant underwater wave of water connected to this year's El Niño weather pattern is moving up the west coast of the Americas, raising alarm bells among scientists about how climate change is magnifying the impacts of the naturally occurring phenomenon.

The so-called Kelvin wave is not unexpected. But like El Niño as a whole, it is happening on top of human-caused climate change that has already warmed the oceans and atmosphere.

A smaller wave already reached B.C. earlier this summer, and the next one is expected to arrive within one to two weeks, according to Bill Merryfield, a research scientist at Environment and Climate Change Canada.

"We actually did already see over 30 centimetres in some locations in June. And so the coming wave looks like it'll be a stronger one," Merryfield said.

What causes it?

The Kelvin wave is a naturally occurring weather phenomenon, just like El Niño itself. In normal years, winds blow from east to west along the equator in the Pacific Ocean, generally pushing water from South America toward Asia.

During El Niño years, however, those east-to-west winds weaken or can reverse direction, allowing water to move east instead.

"When these Kelvin waves reach the coast of South America, there's nowhere further east for this pile up of water to go. And so it splits and starts running up and down the coasts of the Americas" and eventually all the way up to Canada, Merryfield said.

Sea-level monitoring data collected at Tofino, on Vancouver Island's Pacific coast, shows the impact of the earlier Kelvin wave in June.

Rather than a giant tsunami-like wave, the Kelvin wave temporarily raises sea levels.

"You can think of it more like a very broad, hundreds of miles wide, but very shallow bulge in the height of the ocean surface, so by maybe a foot or so," University of California climate scientist Daniel Swain told CBS News last month .

What will it do to the West Coast?

Merryfield said the impacts are most pronounced during king tides, particularly high tides that happen when the gravitational pull of the sun and moon combine to produce higher-than-normal tides.

"So if you put that 30 centimetres of sea level rise on top of a king tide, and then maybe you add a winter storm to that, which causes a storm surge, that's when you really start to get into trouble," he said.

"This extra foot or so of sea level rise due to El Niño can pack a punch."

WATCH | El Niño's grim forecast: El Niño-fuelled heat could kill half a million people by February: study | Duration closed caption 1:51 The record global heat brought by this year's powerful El Niño could lead to nearly half a million more deaths worldwide by the end of February, according to a report that also highlights the impact of climate change on extreme heat.

Those surges could be intensified by another effect of El Niño, further raising sea levels along the B.C coast. El Niño can strengthen northward winds along the coast, pushing even more water toward shore.

These compounding effects — the Kelvin wave, stronger northward winds and winter storms, on top of climate change already raising sea levels and intensifying extreme weather — could worsen flooding and erosion along the coast. Strong El Niños in the past have caused widespread erosion on California's beaches.

Local authorities there are placing emergency sand on beaches and expect the Kelvin wave to raise water levels six to 12 inches, the Associated Press reports .

Exceptionally high king tides and powerful waves damaged protective sand and wooden berms in Long Beach, Calif. in June. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

The impacts of the Kelvin wave — and El Niño more broadly — could extend far beyond this season, Merryfield warned.

The oceans absorb much of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases, moderating global warming as humans continue to burn fossil fuels. During El Niños, however, some of that stored heat is released from the ocean into the atmosphere.

World.title: Canada's trade surplus widens to more than 4-year high in August, as front-loading ramps up
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's trade surplus widened substantially in August to $4.2 billion, data showed on Tuesday, as exporters rushed to increase shipments to the U.S. before President Donald Trump's new tariffs took effect.

Analysts polled by Reuters had forecast the trade surplus would expand to $1.55 billion, from an upwardly revised $787 million.

As exporters shipped more to ​the U.S. to beat the looming 50 per cent tariffs, Canada's exports stateside surged 8.1 per cent in August, while imports from the U.S. were down 2.5 per cent, Statistics Canada reported.

This change helped Canada post a trade surplus with the ​U.S. of $11.2 billion, a 19-month high, lifting its share of exports to its biggest ⁠trading partner to almost ⁠70 per cent for the first time since September 2025.

Trump's new ‌tariffs, which cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports to the U.S., came into effect on Aug. 22.

Economists have said that September would show a more accurate impact of the new tariffs, which apply to a variety of items, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods ⁠and hockey equipment.

September will also show the impact of Canadian counter-tariffs on U.S. imports and Trump's ban on some goods imports from Canada.

Canada's overall exports increased by 2.5 per cent in August to $77.91 billion, after falling by 2.6 per cent ‌in the previous month.

Exports of energy products — refined petroleum products and crude oil — posted the biggest overall gain, increasing by 4.7 per cent to $19.03 billion. A stronger Canadian dollar also affected the value of exports.

Consumer goods, machinery exports up

Excluding energy products, exports were up 1.8 per cent. In volume terms, total exports rose 2.5 per cent, StatsCan ​said.

Exports of consumer goods were up 6.6 per cent, industrial machinery, equipment and parts were up 10.1 per cent and electronic and electrical equipment and parts increased 11 per cent ⁠in August, the statistics agency said.

Imports were down two per cent to $73.71 billion, with imports of motor vehicles and ⁠parts posting the largest decline in August.

As Canada negotiated waves of tariffs across some crucial sectors ⁠such ⁠as steel, aluminum, autos and lumber for ​almost 18 months, its export dependence on the U.S. had shrunk, while exports to the rest of the world ​rose, as it sought to ⁠diversify its trade partners.

After increasing 8.2 per cent in July, exports to countries other than the U.S. fell 8.5 per cent in August, and imports decreased. Its trade deficit with countries other than the U.S. widened to $7 billion in August from $5.3 billion in July, StatsCan said.

The Canadian dollar strengthened after the trade data, with the currency trading up 0.05 per cent ⁠to $1.4250 to the U.S. dollar, or ‌70.18 U.S. cents.

World.title: Works by Canadian authors Margaret Atwood and Ryan North among books banned in U.S. schools
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nearly 12,000 bans took place in American public schools over the past year, according to a new study from PEN America.

This is the highest total since the free expression organization began tracking removals five years ago.

The report arrives during the international Banned Books Week, which runs from Oct. 4 to Oct. 10. This year’s theme is "Let Books Be. Protect the Freedom to Read", during which events at U.S.-based schools and libraries and other locations call attention to censorship efforts.

While Canada marks its dedicated intellectual freedom campaign in February, some Canadian libraries and bookstores engage in global outreach and displays during this October window.

For the second straight year, American author Stephen King was the author most likely to have his work withdrawn. King’s books were pulled 312 times, with The Shining and The Green Mile among those impacted.

Also among the banned novels in American schools is Canadian author Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale, the classic dystopian novel about a totalitarian society in what used to be part of the United States.

The most banned individual title was Patrick McCormick’s novel about a girl sold into sexual slavery in India, Sold, for which PEN found 25 removals.

Other books commonly targeted include Laurie Halse Anderson’s Speak, her prize-winning novel about a teenager who falls silent after being raped; Ellen Hopkins’ novel about drug addiction, Crank.

(Riverhead Books)

Several titles appear in PEN America’s Index of School Book Bans for the first time during the 2025-2026 school year, including classic novels, gamebook adaptations, popular fiction and coming-of-age young adult stories, manga, and an anthology on feminism.

Among these titles is Romeo and/or Juliet: A Chooseable Path Adventure, a 2016 graphic novel by Ottawa-born webcomic and comic book writer Ryan North.

Many of the bans took place in Florida and Texas, where restrictive laws have been passed and both politicians and conservative activists have pushed for removals. PEN has also found that school district administrators rely increasingly on AI to determine which books should be pulled.

Themes of race, racism, sexuality and gender identity remain the most common reasons books are challenged.

“School libraries make knowledge and ideas available, ensure books remain available for all regardless of personal or political ideologies, and open gateways to stories that inform, challenge, and reflect the realities of the world back to readers,” the PEN report, titled Banned in the USA, reads in part.

“Book bans impede the freedom to read, cutting students’ access to a diversity of views, voices, perspectives, and literature they deserve to encounter.”

In all, PEN found 11,982 cases of bans, affecting 7,370 individual works. Over 4,500 were on the list for the first time, ranging from the 19th century classic Jane Eyre to Sui Ishida’s Tokyo Ghoul manga series.

PEN America and the American Library Association have both reported historic surges in bans since the early 2020s, although their methodologies differ. PEN counts books removed even for a short time as a ban, while the ALA only includes books that have been permanently pulled.

According to the library association’s most recent report, published in April, some 5,600 instances of bans took place during the previous year.

- with files from CBC Books

World.title: Direct spending on Canadian military could reach more than $163B by 2035: budget watchdog
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Direct spending on the Canadian military could reach $163.6 billion by 2035 under the Liberal government's proposal to meet NATO's benchmark target of five per cent of GDP, the Parliamentary Budget Office said Tuesday.

However, a lot of unknowns remain that could affect government finances down the road, the fiscal watchdog said in a new report.

"Meeting Canada's defence commitments will require substantial increases in government expenditure and investment, with important implications for economic activity, industrial capacity and the composition of production in Canada," said the report penned by PBO researchers.

Since the federal government uses an accrual method when counting defence expenditures — basically recording money when it is earned, and paying bills when they are owed, not when cash actually changes hands — the impact "would increase the budgetary deficit by $63.7 billion, or 1.4 per cent of GDP," the PBO said.

What the fiscal pain might be will depend on how Prime Minister Mark Carney's government manages the increase. The PBO presents two scenarios: one where there's a gradual, steady increase in the buying of new equipment and the other where purchases are postponed.

Under both the Liberal government of Justin Trudeau and the Conservative government of Stephen Harper, it became routine to postpone big-ticket equipment purchases. Money from some of those items was reprofiled to later years; in other cases, the funds lapsed and were returned to the federal treasury.

In a previous report, the PBO tracked more than $18 billion set aside for military spending that lapsed under the Trudeau government.

Carney ordered the injection of $9 billion into defence last year in order for Canada to meet the old NATO spending benchmark of two per cent of gross domestic product. The new target of five per cent of GDP — 3.5 per cent on direct military spending and 1.5 per cent on defence infrastructure — is to be phased in gradually over the next decade.

Carney has said the plan is for Canada to hit a four per cent target on defence spending — 2.5 per cent and 1.5 per cent — by 2030.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan appears at the Commons committee on government operations and estimates on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on June 16. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Annette Ryan, who took over as parliamentary budget officer in the spring, told the House of Commons defence committee on Monday that the government's plan to reach the new target after 2030 is still a work in progress.

"It'll take some time before we can actually see the effect of all of these investments," she told committee MPs.

Ryan said the PBO has begun work to model what sort of economic impact the drastic increase in defence spending will have on federal finances and the Canadian economy.

"This is a very rapid increase," Ryan said in French, noting there are procurement risks.

"I think that Canada's industrial capacity may not be able to meet the need, which is a risk.… And we might ask, what are we getting back from all of these industrial and technological purchases? That's another source of risk," she said. "So yes, there are a number of risks associated with these very significant sums of money."

World.title: 18-year-old from Yorkton, Sask., faces terrorism-related charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An 18-year-old resident of Yorkton, Sask., is facing terrorism charges for allegedly posting videos as a member of 764, a listed terrorist entity in Canada.

The person was arrested in Alberta on Sept. 24 by the RCMP federal policing northwest region's Integrated National Security Enforcement Team (INSET), and RCMP announced the charges in a news release on Tuesday.

The individual was a youth (under the age of 18) at the time of the alleged crimes, so their identity is protected under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

"Following a report of concerning online activity, INSET began an investigation into a Telegram user who allegedly posted a series of videos depicting real-world activity as a 764 member," the RCMP news release says.

"Investigators found the user was also referenced in numerous 764-related chatrooms on Discord and Telegram."

764 is "a transnational online ecosystem of violent online predators who coerce youth to participate in acts involving child sexual abuse and exploitation, self-harm and the torture of animals," the RCMP says.

Parts of the 764 network have extreme ideological views and victimize children, the news release says.

764 was listed as a terrorist entity in December 2025.

The 18-year-old is charged with participating in the activity of a terrorist group, facilitating terrorist activity and two counts of committing an offence for a terrorist group.

The individual is scheduled to appear in Yorkton provincial court on Tuesday afternoon for a bail hearing.

World.title: Why are 3 trees planted upside down at Fredericton Botanic Garden?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At the Fredericton Botanic Garden, visitors may expect to find trees planted firmly in the ground.

Instead, three ash trees are standing upside down.

The unusual installation, known as the Stumpery, has become one of the garden’s most popular spots for photos and selfies, despite starting as little more than a joke.

The trees were among 14 ash trees the garden at the west end of Odell Park had to remove after they were infected by the emerald ash borer, an invasive insect that attacks trees.

The garden wanted to make sure the trees were not simply wasted, said Linda Stephenson, executive director of the Fredericton Botanic Garden.

WATCH | 'It means different things to different people,' garden director says : Turning damaged trees upside down | Duration closed caption 1:58 Residents find unintended meaning in Fredericton Botanic Garden’s new installation, which features upside-down trees damaged by the emerald ash borer.

“Some of the trees were cut up into firewood that was given to people that could benefit from it,” Stephenson said. “Some have gone to a mill to be planed to make benches in the park.”

Three of the trees, each about 14 feet tall, were turned into the Stumpery.

Stephenson said volunteers Eldon Toner and Matt Forlot had heard about stumperies before and decided to create one at the garden.

Then Toner suggested taking the idea a step further.

He turned the trees upside down.

“Why did we turn it upside down? I have no idea,” Toner said. “We just did it for a joke.”

The joke has attracted considerably more attention than Toner expected.

Stephenson said people have stopped at the garden’s resource centre to talk about the installation, while photos of it have circulated on social media.

“It’s become the selfie site in the garden,” she said.

Not just for pictures

Some visitors see more than just an unusual photo opportunity.

Liam Jackson, a Fredericton resident who visited the Stumpery, said he liked the idea of giving the diseased trees a second purpose.

“If these were sick trees, now they’ve got a second life,” he said.

Stephenson said people have also interpreted the installation as an art piece, although she said there is no single meaning behind it.

“Since none of us really know what the meaning of it is, I think that’s sort of neat, that it means something different to different people,” she said.

For Toner, the artistic interpretation was not part of the original plan.

He said he was working nearby when he overheard visitors discussing the upside-down trees and suggesting the garden had an artist in residence.

A serious tree disease

“They noticed me and they just asked me a few questions about it and who thought of this,” he said. “And I said, well, you’re looking at him.”

While the Stumpery is playful, the problem that created it is serious.

The emerald ash borer has killed millions of trees across Canada since its arrival in the country was confirmed almost 25 years ago.

Toner estimates there are between 500 and 600 ash trees on the 56-acre garden property. He expects many could eventually have to be removed because of the beetle, which was first detected in the city in 2021.

“In the next 10 years, they’re either going to be falling down in the woods or cut down for safety reasons,” he said.

Stephenson said the garden is already seeing more ash trees affected by the insect and expects managing them to be a continuing challenge.

The garden plans to give the Stumpery another transformation next spring, adding flowers and vines around the trees.

Stephenson encourages people to visit the garden and see the installation for themselves.

The garden is open until dusk and there is no admission charge.

World.title: Design trends: Comfortably contemporary
World.content:
Article content

But the real star in this part of the house is the staircase. As is so often true of staircases, often the simplest forms conceal the most highly complex engineering. Jessica points out that, to keep the look as clean and pure as possible, there’s virtually no millwork, casings or extraneous materials within which to hide joinery; all you see is the waterfall-style treads flush against white walls. World.title: Israel’s referendum on October 7, Benjamin Netanyahu and much more
World.content:
Article content

He had been planning to propose to his girlfriend Ziv Abud before the October 7 massacre. They were both there at the Nova music festival. They hid inside a roadside bunker. He was abducted, and she was under a pile of bloodied bodies. And for 505 days in captivity, he was sure that she was dead. He had sat awake for her. He had sat shiva. He had convinced himself that she was dead, and he was going to have to move on without her — while she was publicly campaigning for his release. And they recently got married, and they’ve just published a book of their own about what it is to rebuild your life and to rebuild a relationship after you’ve already mourned it and assumed that it was gone.
