World.title: Elecciones generales del 29-N, en directo | Puigdemont celebra la “derrota” de los poderes públicos que “han impedido y retrasado” la aplicación de la amnistía
World.content:
El ‘expresident’ celebra la “derrota” de los poderes públicos que “han impedido y retrasado” la aplicación de la amnistía | Feijóo: “Nada puede borrar que la amnistía es otro engaño más de Sánchez” | El PNV garantiza la convalidación del decreto principal de vivienda aprobado de nuevo por el Gobierno

El expresident de la Generalitat Carles Puigdemont no ha desvelado cuándo regresará a España en su comparecencia de este martes en Waterloo (Bélgica), pese a que el juez Pablo Llarena ha levantado la orden nacional de detención que pesaba sobre él tras la sentencia del Tribunal Constitucional que ordena al Supremo amnistiar la malversación del procés. Puigdemont ha celebrado la decisión, que a su juicio “supone la derrota de los diversos poderes públicos españoles que han impedido y retrasado la aplicación de la ley de amnistía”, aunque ha advertido de que la amnistía “no es en sí misma la solución” al conflicto entre Cataluña y España. “Decidimos ir al exilio a hacer política y no hemos parado hasta asegurar que el regreso también tenga un sentido político”, ha afirmado. El líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, ha afirmado que “respeta” el criterio del tribunal de garantías, pero ha cargado contra la medida de gracia: “Nada puede borrar que la amnistía es otro engaño más de Sánchez”. Mientras, el Consejo de Ministros ha aprobado de nuevo los decretos de vivienda, y el PNV ha anunciado que volverá a apoyar el principal, lo que garantiza su convalidación en la Diputación Permanente. Por otro lado, la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, ha insistido en sus sospechas de que el Gobierno puede hacer “trampas” en las elecciones generales y ha vuelto a recomendar votar en las urnas en lugar de por correo, pese a que el portavoz del PP, Borja Sémper, había defendido que el sistema “es garantista”.

EL PAÍS ofrece de forma gratuita la última hora de la protesta por la vivienda. Si quieres apoyar nuestro periodismo, suscríbete.

World.title: “Si un alumno no entrena la capacidad de frustración, entre lo bueno y lo fácil elegirá lo fácil”
World.content:
Horizontes laborales en un futuro dominado por la IA. Conversaciones sobre la educación que queremos | Pensemos el mañana (Episodio 5)

Miguel Antón, profesor del IESE Business School, y su alumna Ana Jara charlan sobre qué habilidades deben desarrollar las futuras generaciones tras la irrupción de la IA en el mundo laboral: dominar la comunicación oral y el trabajo en equipo, preservar la capacidad de concentración y desarrollar el pensamiento crítico

Miguel Antón PROFESOR DE FINANZAS Y DIRECTOR DEL MIM Y DEL MIF EN IESE BUSINESS SCHOOL Es licenciado y máster en Economía por la Universidad de Navarra y doctor en Finanzas por la London School of Economics. En el IESE Business School su misión es guiar y formar a aquellos jóvenes que quieren convertirse en los ejecutivos del mañana en grandes compañías Ana Jara ALUMNA DEL MÁSTER EN MANAGEMENT EN IESE BUSINESS SCHOOL Después de estudiar Humanidades se matriculó en una escuela de negocios para dar un giro a su carrera y buscar mejores salidas laborales. Su objetivo al finalizar esta formación es incursionar en el universo de las grandes consultoras

¿Qué vamos a hacer cuando las máquinas hagan nuestro trabajo? La pregunta que abre esta nueva entrega de Pensemos el mañana, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja y EL PAÍS para responder a los desafíos que presenta la educación, es la que articula la conversación entre dos perfiles muy concernidos, cada uno a su manera, por el futuro del mundo del trabajo: por un lado, el profesor del IESE Miguel Antón, cuya misión es analizar en profundidad los cambios en el mercado para ofrecer a los futuros ejecutivos las herramientas con las que puedan hacerse un hueco en una gran compañía; y por otro Ana Jara, una de sus alumnas, que observa con cierta inquietud cómo la irrupción de la inteligencia artificial (IA) puede cambiar por completo la estructura de las empresas.

“¿Un consejo para los jóvenes que quieran ser exitosos en el trabajo? Que comuniquen bien”

En este entorno volátil, Antón ofrece una receta en la que destacan varios pilares: dominar a la perfección la comunicación oral y saber trabajar en equipo; preservar la capacidad de concentración en un mundo inundado de estímulos; desarrollar el pensamiento crítico para manejar y cuestionar grandes volúmenes de información; entrenar la capacidad de frustración y buscar conocerse a uno mismo: las fortalezas, los deseos y los sueños más profundos, pero también las debilidades.

“Los alumnos tenemos miedo porque todo está evolucionando tan rápido que no sabemos si en dos años vamos a tener trabajo”

Un consejo, este último, que lleva al profesor a vaticinar que las nuevas generaciones, representadas en alumnos como Ana, deberán volver a plantearse a aquellas preguntas esenciales que en la Antigua Grecia dieron origen a la Filosofía, no solo para encontrar su sitio no solo en el mercado de trabajo sino en el mundo: ¿Quiénes somos?, ¿de dónde venimos?, ¿hacia dónde vamos?

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

World.title: Por la cuenca del Ruhr, en El Dorado del sueño alemán que vive una segunda vida
World.content:
El carbón y la industria siderúrgica convirtieron el Ruhrgebiet en una región próspera y destino de inmigrantes en busca de trabajo en Alemania. Hoy los vestigios de su arqueología industrial son escenario de una ambiciosa apuesta verde

Hay una ciudad, en el corazón de Alemania, donde en los años cincuenta y sesenta del pasado siglo los transportes públicos ponían carteles en español. Lo hacían para que pudieran orientarse los muchos inmigrantes españoles que habían ido allí a buscarse un futuro, no a delinquir —qué pronto se nos olvidan las cosas—. Duisburgo, en la cuenca del Ruhr (Ruhrgebiet), era ya desde finales del XIX un emporio industrial, donde el carbón de las minas regionales era transmutado en coque, más calorífico, con el que alimentar los altos hornos, obtener arrabio o hierro crudo y convertirlo luego en acero. El Ruhrgebiet se vería de noche desde el espacio como una mancha de luz tan potente como Londres o París.

Había allí pozos mineros, almacenes de carbón, coquerías, altos hornos, gasómetros para contener el gas residual de la conversión de la hulla en coque. Hasta veinte minas alimentaban en los años treinta a las instalaciones siderúrgicas. El carbón, motor del “milagro alemán”, llegó a duplicar su producción entre 1945 y 1959. Escarmentados por las carnicerías de las dos guerras mundiales —a las que tanto habían contribuido las fábricas del Ruhr—, seis países centroeuropeos firmaron, en 1951, el Tratado de París, que ponía en pie una Comunidad Europea del Carbón y del Acero. La que luego se ampliaría como Comunidad Económica Europea (1957) y, finalmente, como Unión Europea. Pasear hoy entre los esqueletos oxidados de esa arqueología industrial produce la misma sensación acre que vagar entre templos y mármoles griegos o romanos. Ruinas modernas de una distopía consumida, reducida al recuerdo y la melancolía.

Duisburgo, en el hormiguero anfibio donde el Ruhr confluye con el padre Rin, es un estimulante ejemplo del paso feliz de la distopía a la realidad, del sudor de los talleres al disfrute vital. La ciudad, que había sido almacén de carbón y coque para la elaboración de hierro y acero, fue también conocida como “el capacho del pan” de toda la cuenca del Ruhr, por los muchos molinos que convertían el grano llegado de todo el mundo en el sustento necesario para una población que no paraba de crecer.

Vista del puerto de la ciudad alemana de Duisburgo. Jochen Tack ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Aquel trajín comercial fue posible gracias al que presume de ser el mayor puerto interior del mundo. Su pulso se detuvo tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial, pero el arquitecto Norman Foster se encargó de elaborar un plan general para el puerto (1988-1998). Los viejos graneros, molinos y almacenes se fueron rehabilitando para convertirse en oficinas, museos, hoteles y restaurantes. Y los muelles y su cinta de ribera, pegados a la antigua muralla medieval, se convirtieron en espacios de ocio y esparcimiento.

Exterior del Museo Küppersmühle, un centro de arte moderno y contemporáneo con sede en el puerto interior de Duisburgo. tichr ( GETTY IMAGES )

Uno de los primeros edificios recuperados fue el MKM, Museo Küppersmühle de Arte Moderno, convertido por la reconocida pareja de arquitectos suizos Herzog & De Meuron en centro de vanguardia —los mismos arquitectos repetirían, años después, idéntica fórmula en el CaixaForum de Madrid—. Aquí se puede ver hasta el próximo 1 de noviembre una muestra dedicada al escultor español Jaume Plensa.

Otro de los museos articulados con diseño vanguardista sobre viejos ladrillos es el vecino Kultur- und Stadthistorisches Museum, museo de historia de la ciudad, que incluye una “Cámara de Mercator” dedicada a su más ilustre hijo adoptivo. Porque Gerard Kremer (latinizado como Gerardus Mercator) fue un flamenco que servía para todo: geógrafo, matemático, filósofo, teólogo, profesor, dibujante y grabador, inventor… En 1544, cuando contaba 32 años, se instaló en Duisburgo, donde abrió un taller de cartografía. Fue el primero en llamar “atlas” a su colección de mapas. Su aportación más perenne fue la llamada “proyección de Mercator”, es decir, la representación de un mapamundi (orientado a la navegación marítima) donde se respetan las formas de los continentes, pero queda alterado su tamaño. Justamente en septiembre de este año, a propuesta de Togo y la Unión Africana, la ONU aprobó una resolución para abandonar la proyección de Mercator y corregir el mapamundi actual, dando a África, por ejemplo, un tamaño mayor y más ajustado.

'Tiger and Turtle – Magic Mountain', una instalación artística diseñada en 2011 por Ulrich Genth y Heike Mutter en Duisburgo. Rupert Oberhauser ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Mercator no llegó a acabar los tres tomos de su atlas (fue su hijo Rumold quien lo hizo). El cartógrafo murió en esta ciudad en 1594, y está enterrado en la iglesia del Salvador, junto al Ayuntamiento y una fuente monumental en su honor. Tanto la iglesia como el Ayuntamiento quedaron muy dañados por las bombas de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, como era de esperar en semejante objetivo industrial. La iglesia, de porte catedralicio y hechuras góticas, ofrece el contraste de unos vitrales modernos, muy hermosos, acoplados a una sillería ennegrecida más por la humedad que por el curso del tiempo.

La fachada del Ayuntamiento de Duisburgo. Marek SLUSARCZYK ( GETTY IMAGES )

Es poco lo que en torno a este núcleo ha conservado la ciudad de su pasado, por la guerra. Calles amplias y espacios arbolados se animan con un trajín urbano cosmopolita. Restaurantes y bazares reflejan de manera silente la antigua diversidad de lenguas, sabores y ambiciones. Aquí siguen conviviendo vecinos de más de 170 nacionalidades, hijos o nietos algunos de la marea humana que llegó en pos del “sueño alemán”.

Pero donde más brilla la efervescencia del ocio es un poco al norte de la ciudad, en el Landschaftspark (“parque paisajístico”), que ocupa los amplios terrenos del antiguo complejo industrial. Se llega fácilmente con la línea 903 del tranvía que parte de la Hauptbanhof o estación central. En 1901, August Thyssen, patriarca de la saga familiar, hizo construir las fábricas de hierro y acero que en la Primera Guerra Mundial (y luego en la Segunda) surtirían de armas y munición al ejército alemán —una visión impactante del efecto desastroso del nazismo en una familia de magnates industriales es la de Luchino Visconti en su película La caída de los dioses (1969)—.

Landschaftspark ocupa los amplios terrenos del antiguo complejo industria a las afueras de la ciudad alemana. Peter Eitel ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Tras una azarosa historia, que a punto estuvo de llegar a su completa demolición en 1944, la planta cesó su actividad con la crisis del acero de 1985. En la década de los noventa, sin embargo, se convirtió en uno de los más importantes proyectos de reconversión. Ahora el parque es un pulmón verde enorme, con numerosos paseos para ciclistas y senderistas, donde todas las viejas instalaciones están bien aprovechadas. En el alto horno nº5 existe una plataforma elevada para abarcar el conjunto, accesible día y noche gracias a la instalación lumínica del artista Jonathan Park, que imprime al laberinto metálico un aura espectral y misteriosa.

Los antiguos almacenes son ahora auditorios, salas de exposición, teatro o cine. Hay áreas para juegos infantiles o deportes, muros de hormigón para la escalada, una granja escuela, incluso un centro de buceo en el gasómetro, inundado en parte. Sin duda, este es uno de los parques más exitosos del medio centenar de enclaves similares que se reparte por el antiguo mapa industrial.

A solo 16 kilómetros de Duisburgo, en Oberhausen, se encuentra Gasometer Oberhausen, un imponente gasómetro que acoge exposiciones que requieren un espacio extraordinario. Algo más lejos, en Essen (a 28 kilómetros), el Zollverein es un complejo singular, designado patrimonio mundial por la Unesco en el año 2001, con minas, acerías e imponentes edificios de estilo Bauhaus convertidos en espacios culturales, centro de danza o museos —como el Ruhrmuseum, acondicionado por el arquitecto Rem Koolhaas, o el Dot Design Museum, cuyo origen está en las colecciones de objetos de la familia Krupp—. Un complejo excepcional tanto por la antigua osamenta como por su actual vitalidad.

La efervescencia cultural del Ruhrgebiet no desfallece; al contrario, ya se están ultimando estructuras para otro gran proyecto que irá de abril a octubre de 2027: el IGA (Internationale Gartenausstellung), una exposición de jardinería con vocación de apuesta de futuro al verde, y de convertir a esta región industrial alemana en la más ecológica del mundo. Habrá que ocuparse de ello.

World.title: Shepherds turn to dogs to defend sheep from wolves on the Veluwe
World.content:
Shepherds in the Veluwe region have come up with a novel solution to deter wolf attacks by hiring Italian mountain dogs to guard their sheep.

Stichting Schapedrift Ermelo, a volunteer organisation that tends a herd of sheep on the heathlands in Gelderland, acquired two Maremmano-Abruzzese sheepdogs this summer to protect the herd from prowling wolves.

The forested Veluwe region has the biggest concentration of wolves in the Netherlands, with seven packs living in an area of 1,000 square kilometres, since the predators returned in 2019.

The organisation has put up eight-foot electrocuted fences around its sheep enclosure to keep wolves out, but the animals are still vulnerable when they are being herded across the heath.

“We see an increasing threat from wolves,” shepherd Marion Derks told Omroep Gelderland. “And there are a few walking round here that were interested in the sheep.”

The two white-haired dogs have been used for centuries to defend sheep. They are valued for their non-aggressive nature and alertness, Derks said.

“As soon as they see danger, you see their attitude change and they go into defensive mode,” she explained. “They make themselves bigger and more imposing and start barking.”

She said the dogs were not expected to confront or attack wolves. “Their presence is meant to stop the wolves approaching,” Derks explained. “Wolves will take easy prey but if they think it’s going to be too difficult, they’ll look for something else.”

World.title: Dutch woman causes a stir by winning world porridge-making title
World.content:
When Gina Saarberg started cooking porridge as a student to save money on food, she could never have guessed that it would take her all the way to a world title.

The 28-year-old from Zutphen won the Golden Spurtle at the weekend, the prestigious trophy awarded to the winner of the annual porridge making championships in Carrbridge, Scotland.

Saarberg put her success down to the ingredients she used, including pinhead oats from Noord-Brabant company De Halm and water from her home city in Gelderland. “It’s very soft and I think the mineral content may have something to do with it,” she told BBC Scotland.

A panel of judges headed by former Gleneagles chef Neil Mugg named Saarberg as the best of 30 competitors from 14 countries, including Norway and Australia. She qualified for the event by winning the Dutch national championships in June.

“I started eating porridge in my student days, but I used rolled oats,” she said. “When I switched to oatmeal I found that it made a much creamier porridge – it reminded me of rice pudding.”

The contest, now in its 33rd year, only allows competitors to use oats, water and salt to make traditional porridge, although there is a speciality category where oatmeal can be combined with more exotic ingredients.

Saarberg said: “I only started adding salt to my porridge for the competition and quickly realised that it really brings out the nuances and different aromas, and makes it taste much better.”

The speciality award was won by Australian porridge champion Rob Reid with his porridge cannoli, a fusion of Sicilian and Scottish cuisine based on his own heritage.

“My dad’s Scottish and my mum’s Sicilian, so when I was thinking about what I could do, the idea came to me,” he said. “Then I had to work out how I could possibly make it in 30 minutes.”

World.title: Forbion raises €2.3bn, now Europe’s top biotech investor
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Naarden-based venture capital firm Forbion, which specialises in life sciences companies, has raised €2.3 billion for 2 new biotech funds, its largest fundraising to date.

The firm says it is one of the biggest life sciences venture capital fundraisings in the past 5 years. It takes Forbion’s assets to around €7.5 billion, which it says makes it Europe’s largest specialist life sciences investor, citing data from research firm Preqin.

The funds will finance around 30 companies, ranging from early-stage firms to those already testing drugs on patients.

Forbion says some of the money will go to companies in North America as well as Europe.

Investors include Dutch pension money managers MN and PGGM, as well as US drugmaker Eli Lilly.

The cabinet named life sciences and biotechnology as one of 4 sectors in which it wants to recruit highly skilled foreign workers, under a national talent strategy agreed in July.

World.title: Booking goes to court to force staff to go to the office
World.content:
Website Booking.com has asked a court to order its employees to work at least two days a week in the office to settle a long-running internal dispute.

The company’s works council has refused to sign off on a change to its working conditions that would require its 7,000 staff at its head office in Amsterdam to travel in to the capital twice a week.

Booking.com issued guidance at the end of the coronavirus lockdowns in 2022 advising its staff to spend 40% of their working time in the office, but some workers still work almost entirely from home, a spokesman told the Financieele Dagblad.

Any change to working locations needs to be approved by the company’s works council (Ondernemingsraad) under Dutch law, but the council refused to endorse the plan, forcing Booking.com to take the case to court.

The company argues that homeworking is bad for teambuilding and productivity, while staff surveys indicate that most workers find it easier to collaborate with their colleagues when they are in the office.

The new rules would allow staff to choose which days they come in to work: one day to be agreed within members of a team and the other on an individual basis.

The works council has said there is no business case for compelling employees to be present in the office two days a week.

World.title: Cinemas pause Naza screenings ahead of October 7 anniversary
World.content:
Cinema screenings of the Israeli documentary Naza, which investigates the war on Gaza, is being suspended from most Dutch cinemas from Tuesday until the weekend so that they do not coincide with the commemoration of the October 7 Hamas attacks.

This is in line with the wishes of the film’s makers, two Israeli documentarians, who fear that their safety – and that of their families, who are still in Israel – will be further threatened if the film is shown around the date.

The Dutch film distributor Cherry Pickers, which is responsible for the film in the Netherlands, has said it will heed their wishes. The duo have not yet returned to Israel since the film’s release, but their families have been harassed and the government is moving to strip them of their nationality.

Naza is composed of interviews with 24 anonymous Israeli intelligence and military personnel involved in military campaign on Gaza since October 7, 2023. They describe how civilians were routinely killed, often hundreds at a time, to target single militants.

They also describe how surveillance was used to track suspects and wait until they were at home with their families before bombing them, as well as using special AI systems to select and kill targets. Israeli officials have disputed many of the claims.

A screening of the film in Delft last week on the opening day was interrupted by an Israeli group, one of whom took a microphone and began telling the audience how her family was murdered by Hamas. Another tried to project footage of the attacks onto the cinema screen.

World.title: Patients fear shortage of medicinal cannabis when rules change
World.content:
Patients who rely on medicinal cannabis are worried about supplies running out when the government ends its contract with the only Dutch licensed grower next year.

The health ministry is not renewing the contract between the Bureau for Medicinal Cannabis (BMC) and Bedrocan from 2027 as part of a plan to liberalise the supply chain by letting suppliers sell directly to pharmacies.

But the rule changes have been delayed, meaning that Bedrocan, based in Emmeloord, will be unable to sell its products at all from next year.

The government says it will import medicinal cannabis from abroad to ensure patients are not denied treatment. The BMC has ordered in extra stocks for the start of next year, but these medicines will go out of date in mid-2027.

Around 7,000 people in the Netherlands are prescribed cannabis for conditions such as MS and epilepsy, or as a form of palliative care.

The MS Vereniging, which represents people with multiple sclerosis, warned that using a different variant of the medicine would be less effective for some patients.

Specific variety

In a letter to health minister Sophie Hermans, the MS association said some patients who had been prescribed cannabis long-term were dependent on a “specific variety” of the drug and switching to an alternative version would affect the quality of their treatment.

The ministry disputed this in its reply, saying there was “no scientific evidence that different varieties have different therapeutic effects”.

But Renger Witkamp, professor of pharmacology at Wageningen University, said different varieties of cannabis were known to work differently. “Cannabis is different from synthetic medicines,” he told the Volkskrant. “The plant contains dozens of chemicals that collectively determine the effect.

“The relationship between those chemicals is determined by the plant variety, but also by the conditions in which it is grown, such as light, soil and fertiliser.”

World.title: Heinen struggling to hit deadline for capital gains tax reform
World.content:
Finance minister Eelco Heinen is in a race against time to introduce a new capital gains tax system by his promised deadline of 2028, financial institutions have warned.

Heinen is under pressure from right-wing opposition parties JA21 and SGP to replace the current income tax regime as quickly as possible as part of the deal to pass next year’s budget.

The minister also needs to plug a €7 billion hole in the finances after left-wing parties Pro and Volt forced the government to drop its planned cuts to social security as the price for their support. The minority government needs the votes of at least two opposition parties in parliament to pass legislation.

Heinen said 2028 could be achieved with “the maximum stretch from everyone”. But banks and the Council of State, which advises the cabinet on the legal implications of its bills, cast doubt on his timetable when asked by NOS.

The Council of State said it was “impossible” to have its analysis ready by next Monday, October 12, so that parliament can debate the bill next week. A spokesman said October 19 was the earliest realistic date.

The Dutch banking association NVB said its members need time to adapt their IT systems so they can pass the relevant details of their customers’ income to the tax office.

Risk of fraud

If customers have to provide the information themselves it increases the risk of delays, inaccuracies and fraud, the banks have warned.

The tax office is also under pressure to update its systems to deal with other reforms, such as the introduction of compulsory work incapacity insurance for people who are self-employed.

Changing the income tax method at the same time would be likely to delay the insurance plan by a year, civil servants told NOS.

Every year that the cabinet delays the overhaul of the income tax system is costing the government an estimated €3.5 billion in lost revenue.

Assumed gains

Heinen’s latest draft does not explain how he plans to compensate for the income lost during the transition to capital gains tax, which will only raise tax on assets and investments when they are sold.

The current “box 3” method charges taxpayers on their assumed gains from their assets every year, but the Supreme Court struck out this system in 2021 because it was unfair on savers whose wealth was held in low-interest accounts.

Heinen included a proposal to lower the thresholds for the “box 3” wealth tax as a stopgap measure in his submission to the Council of State, but parliament has already indicated it does not support this reform.

World.title: Unhealthy food outlets dominate Dutch cities, say researchers
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The food in 10 major Dutch cities has become less healthy over the past decade, according to new research by Amsterdam UMC.

Health executives from the 10 cities have written to health minister Sophie Hermans urging her to speed up a promised food law that would let councils limit unhealthy outlets, Het Parool reported on Tuesday.

The researchers scored 31 types of food outlet, from greengrocers to fast-food chains. The scores combined expert ratings with checks of more than 83,000 products against the “Wheel of Five” (Schijf van Vijf), the official Dutch healthy eating guidelines.

Each neighbourhood was then given a score from -500 (extremely unhealthy) to +500 (extremely healthy), based on the type, number and proximity of nearby outlets.

All 10 cities scored negative in both 2014 and 2024, ranging from -252 in Groningen to -327 in Leiden. Amsterdam fell from -287 to -301. Across the cities, 77% of neighbourhoods scored lower in 2024 than 10 years earlier.

In Amsterdam, 96% of food outlets fall into categories the researchers rate as unhealthy. Some 87 of the city’s 90 secondary schools and vocational colleges are in what the report calls a “very unhealthy” food environment.

The councils say they currently lack a clear legal basis to refuse outlets selling unhealthy food.

“That more than nine in 10 secondary schools and vocational colleges are in an unhealthy food environment means young people are surrounded every day by an offer that makes choosing healthily harder,” Amsterdam health executive Alexander Scholtes told Het Parool. “I am not willing to resign myself to that.”

World.title: Poland detains senior managers from state oil giant Orlen over pre-election fuel price cuts
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained and charged five current and former senior managers at state energy giant Orlen as part of an investigation into allegations that the company artificially lowered fuel prices in the run-up to the 2023 parliamentary election. At the time, many experts and the then-opposition – which won that election and is now in power – accused Orlen of cutting prices to help the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party’s re-election campaign. Prosecutors say that the decisions made by the executives constituted “a gross violation of procedures” and caused “over 4.1 billion zloty” (€938 million) of financial damage to the company. If found guilty, the accused could face up to 25 years in prison. Prokurator przedstawił pięciu menadżerom Orlen S.A. zarzuty wyrządzenia spółce szkody w wysokości ponad 4,1 mld zł w związku z nierynkowym kształtowaniem cen paliw w 2023 r. ⬇️https://t.co/yjiaX0ehHu — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) October 6, 2026 At the end of August 2023, just over a month before the elections, Orlen, which controls around 60% of Poland’s fuel market, began sharply cutting its wholesale petrol prices as well as the prices at the large network of petrol stations it runs. By early October, the wholesale price of unleaded petrol had fallen by nearly 12.7%, while average prices at petrol stations had dropped by about 10%. The price cuts, however, puzzled experts because oil prices on international markets were rising and the zloty was weakening, both of which would normally push fuel prices higher. The relatively low prices in Poland encouraged some motorists from neighbouring countries to travel to Poland to tank up, while some Polish drivers began stockpiling fuel. Just days after the election, held on 15 October, fuel prices began to rise. State oil firm Orlen's wholesale petrol prices have risen this week after falling in the leadup to Sunday’s elections Some had accused Orlen of artificially lowering prices to help the ruling party’s election campaign and warned they would rise afterwards https://t.co/FLUs1n8EA9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 19, 2023 Figures from the then-opposition accused Orlen of lowering prices to win popularity for the government ahead of the elections. Under the leadership of its then-CEO, Daniel Obajtek, the company had regularly carried out actions seen as beneficial for the ruling PiS party. Obajtek is now a PiS MEP. In October 2023, Krzysztof Brejza, a lawmaker from the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) – which was then in opposition and is now Poland’s main ruling party – notified prosecutors of a potential crime. He claimed that strategic fuel reserves had been emptied as part of Orlen’s price-cutting move. Now, after a lengthy investigation, prosecutors have announced that five current and former managers have been detained. One, named only as Michał R. under Polish privacy law, served as a member of Orlen’s board from 2018 to 2024. The others are identified as an executive director, two office directors, and the head of a department responsible for pricing. The National Prosecutor’s Office said that all five had been charged with causing large-scale economic damage, which carries a prison sentence of between five and 25 years. “The charges concern abuse of power and failure to fulfil managerial duties, causing damage to Orlen in the amount of over 4.1 billion złoty in connection with the implemented pricing policy,” wrote prosecutors. They said that the main aim of that pricing policy was to keep the price of fuels below the psychological threshold of 6 zloty per litre, and that this was carried out “in a manner detached from market realities…in gross violation of numerous formal and informal procedures applicable to the managerial staff at Orlen”. Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that Poland has been “disgraced in front of the entire world” by a new @FT report on how state energy firm Orlen lost $230 million through a botched effort to buy Venezuelan oil under the former government https://t.co/LlGcgXOvGG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2026 Speaking anonymously to broadcaster TVN, one of the prosecutors involved in the case said that the executives’ actions had implications not only for Orlen’s finances, but also Poland’s national security, given that strategic reserves are meant to be saved for emergency situation. “State security was jeopardised for the sake of politics,” they said. “These reserves are intended, at a time of war, to ensure there is fuel for tanks, to put it simply.” Meanwhile, justice minister Waldemar Żurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, wrote on social media that Orlen and Obajtek had, by “manually controlling prices”, “acted to the detriment of national assets in order to save the party’s [grip on] power”. Na polecenie łódzkiego wydziału ds. Przestępczości Zorganizowanej Prokuratury Krajowej funkcjonariusze ABW zatrzymali wczoraj 5 byłych i obecnych menadżerów Orlen S.A., w tym byłego członka zarządu spółki z lat 2018-2024. Jesienią 2023 roku Daniel „wszystko mogę” Obajtek ręcznie… https://t.co/qV9qroeBu0 — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 6, 2026 Obajtek today rejected the allegations and defended Orlen’s actions under his leadership. He accused the current government of acting to distract from its own failure to keep fuel prices under control. “They couldn’t cope with rising fuel prices so – for show and without any substantive justification – they’re detaining experienced managers thanks to whom fuel cost less than 6 zloty [per litre] in the summer and autumn of 2023,” he wrote on social media. “If I have to answer for the fact that Poles paid little for fuel, then I would be honoured,” he added. However, speaking at a press conference, Żurek declared that, “in a state governed by law there are proper procedures for lowering prices”. Instead, under PiS, there was “a state of lawlessness, a state run like a private fiefdom”. Nie potrafili poradzić sobie z rosnącymi cenami paliw, więc – na pokaz, bez żadnego merytorycznego uzasadnienia – zatrzymują doświadczonych managerów, dzięki którym paliwo latem i jesienią 2023 roku kosztowało poniżej 6 złotych, gdy baryłka ropy była po 100 dolarów, a dolar 4,20… — Daniel Obajtek (@DanielObajtek) October 5, 2026 In a separate case, the European Parliament last year stripped Obajtek of legal immunity to face charges for allegedly using Orlen’s funds to serve his own private interests. Polish prosecutors are also pursuing him for allegedly violating Poland’s press law and falsely reporting his income in a tax return. Last month, the Financial Times reported on how, under Obajtek’s leadership, Orlen lost $230 million (856 million zloty) trying to buy Venezuelan oil through intermediaries, unsecured payments and cryptocurrency transfers. Obajtek, however, argued that he managed to turn Orlen into one of Europe’s largest companies, including diversifying it away from its traditional focus on oil and towards other forms of energy, including gas, hydrogen and renewables. World.title: Poland and Lithuania prepare to evacuate one million Baltic residents to Poland in event of war
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland and Lithuania are jointly preparing plans for the evacuation of one million or more residents of the Baltic states into Poland in the event of a war or other major crisis, amid growing concern in the region over potential Russian aggression. On Monday, the two countries’ interior ministers met to discuss the issue following a recent large-scale Lithuanian mobilisation exercise that also involved Polish officials. The pair also addressed their joint response to the migration crisis on the borders orchestrated by Russia’s ally Belarus. “In crisis situations, it is best to cooperate. It is best to prepare such plans through mutual understanding, thus attempting to address potential situations,” said Lithuanian interior minister Martynas Katelynas, speaking alongside his Polish counterpart, Marcin Kierwiński, at the Budzisko-Kalvarija border crossing. “As for this crossing here, this place that connects us with Poland, this plan foresees approximately one million, and perhaps even more, refugees who will be able to be evacuated from our countries in the event of war,” he added. The three Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – are seen as a primary potential target for Russian aggression. NATO states, including Poland, have in recent months warned of the growing possibility of Moscow conducting some form of “provocation” against the alliance’s eastern members. Lithuania last week finished a major exercise testing its national mobilisation system in the event of war or other crises. For the first time, it included elements relating to cross-border evacuation of civilians from the Baltic states to Poland. Alongside thousands of Lithuanian officials, a 20-person Polish team, led by representatives of the interior ministry, took part in the exercise. This has allowed Poland to develop “an agenda and action plan for what must be adjusted very quickly: cross-border evacuation plans, infrastructure and alternative border crossings in an emergency, as well as reception points”, said Kierwiński, adding that “we will begin intensive work” on implementation. Poland already has extensive recent experience in receiving civilians fleeing conflict. In 2022, it became the primary destination for the millions of refugees fleeing Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion. Poland’s government and civil society quickly implemented measures to support the refugees, almost one million of whom remain in the country. Almost 80% of Poles say they would want Poland to come to the aid of the Baltic states if they were attacked by Russia The poll follows controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure casting doubt as to whether Poland should come to their defence https://t.co/l3dj02ETZ5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 10, 2026 The two ministers also used their meeting to discuss their joint response to illegal migration. Both countries have been the target of a crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus, which has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross into Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. In response, Poland last year introduced checks on its borders with Lithuania and Germany. Those measures have been repeatedly extended, including last week, when Poland announced that they would remain in force until at least March 2027. “Border controls with Germany and Lithuania allow us to catch people illegally crossing the border from the Baltic states,” said Kierwiński on Monday. “As soon as there are grounds to end these controls, we will discontinue them. But for now, we have decided that they will remain in place for at least another six months.” Poland is reintroducing controls on its borders with Germany and Lithuania to prevent the “uncontrolled flow of migrants”, in particular those returned by Germany after entering illegally "Poland’s patience is running out," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/Pttd3FvpHA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2025 Katelynas emphasised that “Lithuania and Poland share a common goal: to ensure the protection of our borders and effectively prevent irregular migrants from moving through our countries and across the Schengen area”. He also noted that an agreement between the two countries on cooperation between police, border guard and customs services is currently being finalised. “Poland and Lithuania are like brothers and sisters who support each other and will continue to do so,” said Katelynas. Kierwiński likewise expressed his satisfaction that the two countries “speak with one voice…because this part of Europe, the eastern flank of NATO and the EU, must speak with one voice to address and counter the threats posed by Russian imperialism and the difficult situation beyond our eastern border”. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. She emphasised the “urgency” of protecting the EU’s frontier from the “predator” Vladimir Putin https://t.co/O9bhmLha44 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2025 Last month, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Poland has already recently suffered airspace violations by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter. It has also been the primary target for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. In response, the Polish government has moved to expand the network of warning sirens along the Ukrainian border, launched a campaign informing the public how to respond to aerial threats, and started more clearly marking bomb shelters. The Polish-Lithuanian border area, which sits between Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and is known as the Suwałki Gap, is seen as a potential target for Russia in the event of war. Poland and Lithuania held joint military exercises there in 2024 to test their defensive capabilities. World.title: Reports claim Trump tried to change Poland’s government. What do we know?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Media reports claim that US President Donald Trump, during a previously unreported meeting earlier this year with Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, suggested that he leave Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition and form a new government with the right-wing opposition. Kosiniak-Kamysz has confirmed that the meeting took place, but has not commented on what was discussed. Meanwhile, Tusk himself has said that, while he wants to “maintain discretion”, the information he received from Kosiniak-Kamysz indicates that Trump was interested in discussing the “internal situation in Poland”. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has even more bluntly suggested that the meeting may have served as “an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics”. Below, we outline how the controversy unfolded, what we know so far, and how senior political figures have commented on the issue. The context Poland’s government is a broad coalition that ranges from left to centre right. Although Tusk’s centrist Civic Platform (KO) dominates, it would not have the parliamentary majority necessary to rule if it lost any of its junior coalition partners. One of those partners is the Polish People’s Party (PSL), which is the most conservative element of the coalition. It has clashed with its partners over issues such as abortion and LGBT+ rights. PSL is led by Kosiniak-Kamysz, who serves as both deputy prime minister and defence minister. Some elements of the right-wing opposition have suggested that PSL could break with Tusk to form an alternative government, perhaps even with Kosiniak-Kamysz as prime minister. Last year, PSL controversially polled its members on whether they would want to do so. However, PSL and its leader have repeatedly insisted that they remain loyal to Tusk’s coalition. The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026 Meanwhile, the government is in constant conflict with President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition. Nawrocki is also a close ally of Trump, who endorsed him during last year’s presidential election. By contrast, Tusk and his government have clashed with the Trump administration, though they also seek to maintain close relations with the US as Poland’s most important security partner. The meeting The news that Kosiniak-Kamysz had met with Trump in March this year came to light in a rather roundabout way. On 21 September, Poland’s defence ministry announced that a planned meeting at the Pentagon between Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, planned for 23 September, had been cancelled “at the urgent request of the American side”. The official reason for the change of plans was Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US at the same time. However, some commentators in Poland claimed that Hegseth had actually cancelled the meeting at the behest of figures close to Nawrocki. In an effort to debunk those claims, Adam Bielan, a senior PiS figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, claimed that he and Nikodem Rachoń, a presidential advisor, had helped to arrange a meeting earlier this year between Kosiniak-Kamysz and a US figure “much more important than Hegseth”. Rachoń later confirmed this, but said that the meeting had been secret and he was unable to reveal the identity of the US official. He urged Kosiniak-Kamysz to do so. The defence minister obliged, confirming that the meeting had been with Trump himself and had taken place at the White House on 2 March, alongside a ceremony at which a US army officer, Michael Ollis, was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honour for giving his own life to save that of a Polish officer, Karol Cierpica, in Afghanistan. “I had the opportunity to talk to President Trump for a moment, for which I am very grateful,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz, who noted the role of Nawrocki’s office in arranging the conversation. What did Trump say to Kosiniak-Kamysz? Neither Rachoń nor Kosiniak-Kamysz indicated what had been discussed at the meeting. However, last Friday, Dominika Wielowieyska, a leading Polish journalist, claimed that her conversations with various sources, who she did not name, had indicated that Trump used the meeting to encourage Kosiniak-Kamysz to split with Tusk and form a new government with the right-wing opposition. “Trump suggested to Kosiniak-Kamysz that it would be best if he formed a coalition with the right, and that then they would have 100% support from the United States and the presidential administration, and the door would essentially be open to achieving great success for many Poles,” said Wielowieyska, who writes for Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading liberal daily that is hostile towards Nawrocki and sympathetic towards Tusk. She added that Kosiniak-Kamysz had immediately shared information about the meeting with the government but that Rachoń had failed to submit a note about it to the foreign ministry, despite that being normal practice and despite a request for a note from foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. Today, Republika, a right-wing broadcaster with close ties to Nawrocki and the opposition, likewise reported, based on unnamed sources, that, “during the conversation with Kosiniak-Kamysz, there were indications that the Americans were interested in a change of prime minister in Poland”. What has Poland’s government said? On Friday, Sikorski took to social media to respond to a claim by Bielan that the Trump-Kosiniak-Kamysz meeting was intended to “unblock” negotiations regarding Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base. “In the case of such an important conversation, the organiser [Rachoń] had an obligation to prepare a note,” wrote Sikorski, adding that such a document never reached the foreign ministry. “Could that be because the meeting also served as an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics?” Z tak ważnej rozmowy organizator miał obowiązek sporządzić notatkę. Do @MSZ_RP ona nie dotarła. Czyżby dlatego, że spotkanie służyło też próbie zaangażowania obcego państwa w naszą wewnętrzną politykę? https://t.co/0wL0QZBxPv — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 2, 2026 On Monday, Tusk himself told broadcaster TVN that Kosiniak-Kamysz had informed him about his meeting with Trump immediately after it took place. He added that the subject of the meeting “is too interesting to talk about publicly”, but that military “bases were not the topic of the conversation”. “The conversation was of a confidential nature, and therefore I feel obliged to maintain discretion. It was more about the internal situation in Poland, that’s how I would put it most delicately,” said Tusk. Kosiniak-Kamysz himself also confirmed on Monday that the question of a permanent US base in Poland had not been discussed at the meeting. He noted that, in March, that issue was not even seriously on the table, because it was only two months later that Trump announced he intended to send additional troops to Poland The defence minister did not give any further details about the content of the meeting, which he described as “informal”. Rozmowa miała dyskrecjonalny charakter i dlatego czuję się zobowiązany do dyskrecji – powiedział w poniedziałek premier Donald Tusk reporterce @tvn24 @WojcikowskaMaja, pytany o spotkanie ministra obrony Władysława Kosiniaka-Kamysza z prezydentem USA Donaldem Trumpem. World.title: Thousands of protesters trap Polish bishop in church amid anger over dismissal of local priest
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Thousands of protesters blockaded a bishop inside a church in a Polish village on Sunday – and some even physically attacked him – amid anger over the dismissal of a popular long-serving local Catholic priest. As a result, police were called in and, after efforts by negotiators to calm the crowd failed, officers escorted the bishop away from the premises after midnight. „Kościół w Grojcu otoczyło kilka tysięcy osób, parafian i uczęszczających do grojeckiej świątyni. #Aktualnie Okrzyki „jesteśmy z Tobą” dla księdza Józefa Zborka." Materiał od @FaktyOswiecim pic.twitter.com/3zaqlBCDF6 — Sebastian Kościelnik (@S_Koscielnik) October 4, 2026 The incident took place in the village of Grojec, near the city of Oświęcim in southern Poland. The municipality has an official population of around 3,200, but local media – including the Gazeta Krakowska newspaper and Fakty Oświęcim website – report that around 3,000 people gathered on Sunday evening to protest. They were angered by the decision to remove local priest Józef Zborek, who has served in the parish for almost 30 years, from his position. The diocese of Bielsko-Żywiec says the priest was found in church proceedings to have been guilty of “serious and proven irregularities in the performance of his duties”. However, the actual nature of his offences has not been publicly revealed, with the church noting that, under canon law, only Zborek himself can do so. The case against him was initially reported in 2024. The priest repeatedly appealed against the decision, taking the case to the Vatican. However, the decision to remove him was upheld, with Zborek removed from his position on Saturday. On Sunday, Roman Pindel, the bishop of Bielsko-Żywiec, visited Grojec to meet with the parish council and discuss the situation. Afterwards, he proceeded to the local church to attend the Eucharist. However, before his arrival, thousands of people had gathered around the church, holding signs saying “Don’t take away our parish priest”. Some burst inside and disrupted the ceremony. Asked about the reasons for Zborek’s popularity, one woman told Gazeta Krakowska that he had accepted children who had been turned away by other priests for first communion and had “no problem baptising illegitimate children”. News website Onet reports that one local theory is that the priest was removed from his position because he had not charged parishioners for sacraments. Churches in Poland generally expect people to make payments in return for sacraments such as baptism, confirmation and marriage. 🔴Sceny pod kościołem. Biskup w eskorcie policji. Jest nagranie Nocna interwencja policji przed kościołem w Grojcu w Małopolsce. Biskup bielsko-żywiecki Roman Pindel wraz z towarzyszącymi mu księżmi został wyprowadzony ze świątyni pod eskortą funkcjonariuszy. Wszystko po… pic.twitter.com/XEXU3LOMXm — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 5, 2026 After the church service had been disrupted, Pindel and several other priests retreated to the sacristy. Social media videos show protesters shouting angrily at the bishop. Some even physically assailed him and had to be pulled away. Once inside, the bishop faced continued verbal aggression. Shortly afterwards, the police arrived, including specialist negotiators. Pindel spoke to the crowd, explaining that the decision to dismiss Zborek had been confirmed by the Vatican and was final. The bishop reiterated that only Zborek himself was authorised to disclose the reasons for his dismissal. But, with a large, angry crowd still gathered outside and blocking all exits, the bishop was evacuated under the protection of officers at around 1 a.m. Hundreds of people have protested in Kraków’s Kazimierz district against plans to evict residents and businesses – including some of the area's famous bars and galleries – from historic church-owned buildings that will be redeveloped into a luxury hotel https://t.co/Xo3SmkWc9g — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 24, 2026 Subsequently, the Bielsko-Żywiec diocese issued a statement saying that the “aggressive crowd” had “threatened the health and lives of the priests”. It also noted that Zborek had been dismissed after a full canon law process in which he had been able to defend himself and appeal. “We know that many people, especially his parishioners, are experiencing this pain,” they wrote. “However, we ask that you accept this decision in a spirit of faith and in unity with the church.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland updates nuclear strategy with delays to launch of first two plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government has updated Poland’s nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new document acknowledging that the country’s first-ever nuclear plant will go online in 2036, three years later than previously planned, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule. The delays were widely anticipated, as Poland is already behind the schedule set out in the previous nuclear programme, adopted under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government in 2020. However, the current administration says the country is still on track for nuclear to become a major part of a more diversified energy mix, providing around 15-16% of electricity generation by 2040. “This is not just a plan to develop new capacity, but also to build a strong Polish nuclear industry,” energy minister Miłosz Motyka wrote on social media. “We are building a nuclear sector that will drive the Polish economy and serve our security for decades to come.” Rząd przyjął aktualizację Programu polskiej energetyki jądrowej 🇵🇱 To nie tylko plan rozwoju nowych mocy, ale także budowy silnego polskiego przemysłu jądrowego ⚡️ ✅ W sumie do 9 GWe nowych mocy jądrowych; ✅ coraz większy udział polskich firm – docelowo nawet 70 proc. przy… pic.twitter.com/8DorRLUWUj — Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) September 29, 2026 Under the updated Polish Nuclear Power Programme (PPEJ), Poland plans to develop two nuclear power plants with a combined capacity of around 6 GW to 9 GW, using large-scale Generation III+ reactors. The first plant, which will have a total capacity of about 3.75 GW, is being built in partnership with an American consortium made up of Westinghouse and Bechtel in the municipality of Choczewo on the Baltic coast. Preparatory work at the site is already underway. The European Commission last year approved Polish state aid for the project, which is set to receive 60.2 billion zloty (€13.8 billion) in public support between 2025 and 2030 In March 2026, the investor submitted an application to the president of the National Atomic Energy Agency for a permit to construct the plant, with the pouring of the first nuclear concrete scheduled for 2028. The first reactor is now expected to enter commercial operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Construction of Poland’s first nuclear power plant is now set to begin after the @EU_Commission approved Warsaw’s request to allocate 60 billion zloty (€14.2 billion) in state aid for the project https://t.co/Z7BJpRRKnq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 9, 2025 Plans are already underway for a second nuclear power plant, with construction scheduled to begin in 2032 and the first unit expected to come online around 2040, one year later than previously planned. Bełchatów and Konin in central Poland remain the preferred locations for that plant, with both areas offering existing energy infrastructure and extensive experience in electricity generation. Companies from the United States, France and Canada are currently competing to supply the technology and build it, with Poland to choose its partner next year. Alongside expanding nuclear capacity, the programme aims to increase the role of Polish companies in the sector. Domestic firms are expected to account for about 40% of the value of the first reactor project, according to the government. That share could rise to as much as 70% for subsequent units as Polish companies build up expertise, experience and the necessary certifications. The government also plans to develop the broader skills base needed to support the nuclear industry, involving universities, research institutes, technical schools and businesses. A group of prominent Polish businesspeople – including @RBrzoska of @InPostPL and @mati Staniszewski of @ElevenLabs – are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by Poland's richest man, Michał Sołowow https://t.co/NFoCh9JmYz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 1, 2026 The expansion of nuclear power is part of a broader effort to reduce Poland’s traditional reliance on coal, which currently generates around half of the country’s electricity. That is by far the highest figure in the EU. Poland has already been diversifying its energy mix. Coal has declined from supplying 87% of power a decade ago. Meanwhile, the share of renewables has risen from 9% to 29% over the same period. Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 As well as traditional large-scale nuclear power plants, Poland is also pursuing small modular reactor (SMR) projects. SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed onsite, are much smaller than traditional reactors, and proponents say they provide a faster and more cost-effective way of adding nuclear capacity. World.title: Remains of 115 Polish WWII soldiers exhumed in Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of over 100 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending the city of Lviv – which is now in Ukraine but was then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of World War Two. The work continues recent moves towards reconciliation over the issue of exhuming victims of the war, which has long been a point of contention between the two countries. ℹ Komunikat o zakończeniu prac ekshumacyjnych na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie ⚠️ Zakończyły się prace ekshumacyjne na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie, znajdującej się obecnie w granicach administracyjnych Lwowa. Działania… pic.twitter.com/w9rSHuLeua — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) September 28, 2026 During the work on a 260-square-metre area at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv, which began in August, experts found 133 burials. They were identified as 115 soldiers from the Polish army and 18 from the German Wehrmacht. They died during the Battle of Lwów in September 1939, when Poland sought to defend the city from Nazi Germany, which had invaded from the west on 1 September, and the Soviet Union, which invaded from the east on 17 September. On 22 September, the Polish forces surrendered and the city came under Soviet control, as Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had decided when secretly agreeing to divide up Poland in the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact earlier that year. Efforts are now focused on identifying the remains. Experts have taken bone samples for DNA testing, which will be compared with samples from possible relatives. Another part of the puzzle will be the roughly 2,900 objects – including identification tags, bayonets, helmets and religious items – discovered at the site alongside the remains. “For us, the identification of the remains is the most important stage of the work, because it is important to return these people their names,” said Dominika Siemińska, a researcher from Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), in a statement published by Lviv city council. “Currently we have a list of 76 [potential] names,” she added. However, because “so many years have passed, it will be difficult to find their relatives”. Siemińska also expressed her gratitude to the authorities in Lviv “for providing us with protection, support and the opportunity to work peacefully”. She said that “cooperation with the Ukrainian side is going very well”. The final stage of the work will be the burial of the recovered remains of Polish soldiers at the Polish cemetery in the Ukrainian city of Mostyska. The date of the ceremony has not yet been announced. The German remains are being handed over to the Volksbund organisation, which specialises in searching for and reburying German soldiers, said the IPN. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 Last year, Ukraine also granted permission for the exhumation of Polish soldiers in Lviv. Researchers subsequently found the remains of 31 people, as well as possible remains of dozens more that were difficult to identify due to them having been reburied and the manner of their death in artillery fire. They were also reburied in Mostyska, at a ceremony attended by prominent officials from both Poland and Ukraine. Previously, from 2017 to 2024, Ukraine had banned searches for Polish victims of World War Two on its territory in response to the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist partisan formation that fought against the Soviets but also led the massacre of ethnic Poles. However, in a major diplomatic breakthrough last year, Ukraine allowed exhumations to resume, including both the Polish soldiers in Lviv as well as victims of the UPA-led massacres, tens of thousands of whom are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Researchers have subsequently uncovered the remains of dozens of victims of the massacres, who have also been reburied in ceremonies attended by both Polish and Ukrainian officials. However, such steps towards reconciliation have been hindered this year by a dispute sparked by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision to name a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest state honour. Since then, both sides have moved to calm tensions, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan to resolve the dispute, including issuing “a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. World.title: Polish coal mining giant JSW to shed 4,200 jobs – 21% of its workforce – this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state-owned mining firm Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa (JSW), which is the EU’s largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland’s biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year. The plans come as JSW seeks to turn around its finances after years of large losses, as well as a broader shift in Poland away from reliance on coal. Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa do końca 2026 r. zwolni ponad 4,2 tys. osób. – Musimy kierować się interesem spółki – mówił na konferencji prasowej prezes JSW. Więcej: https://t.co/7Sxrhuuaja pic.twitter.com/evJoQal0c3 — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) October 1, 2026 On Wednesday, JSW’s management board announced that it expected the size of its workforce to decline by 4,248 by the end of this year, bringing it below 16,000, down from 20,135 at the end of March. “We anticipate that approximately 2,200 people will leave in the third quarter, and about 1,400 in the fourth quarter,” adding to those who have already left, said the firm’s CEO, Bogusław Oleksy, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Last year, Poland introduced a new law making it easier for coal companies to close mines and reduce their workforce. It provides for large severance payments and other measures intended to soften the blow for those who lose their jobs. News service Strefa Inwestorów says that, on this basis, more than 3,000 JSW employees have the option to take so-called mining or mineral-processing leave while just under 1,200 can opt for one-off severance payments. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill that makes it easier to close down coal mines and provides severance pay of 170,000 zloty to miners. The measures are seen as a key part of Poland’s transition towards cleaner forms of energy https://t.co/vH6MU4nBsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 The workforce reduction is part of JSW’s recovery plan for 2026-2035, announced this week. Other key objectives include cutting costs and investment without decreasing production while increasing the share of coking coal in output. When asked how the workforce reduction would affect production, Oleksy said the company would optimise its operations to make more efficient use of employees and equipment. He noted that most of the losses would be administrative positions rather than staff directly involved in production. In February this year, the company reached an agreement with unions to reduce labour costs in order to help stabilise the company’s financial position. JSW employees almost unanimously supported the agreement, reported broadcaster TVN. The initial results of the cost-cutting measures are beginning to show. In the first half of 2026, the cost of extraction per tonne fell to 609 zloty (€139) from 778 zloty a year earlier. JSW’s long-term goal is to bring the cost down to around 560 zloty per tonne. The company is still posting heavy losses, though those have also fallen this year. JSW posted a net loss of just over 1.0 billion zloty in the first half of 2026, around half the 2.1 billion zloty figure from the same period a year earlier. For the full year 2025, the company recorded a loss of 6.3 billion zloty, which was down from a record figure of 7.3 billion zloty in 2024. Polish state-owned mining giant JSW, the EU's largest producer of coking coal, has reported a record annual loss of 7.3bn zloty. It attributed the results to falling coal prices, lower production volumes, and the impact of a one-off write-off https://t.co/vrSgRu630b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 11, 2025 JSW’s announcement comes just as some officials and industry representatives are warning that the energy crisis caused by conflict in the Middle East could increase demand in Poland for coal, which is still used to generate around half of electricity and to heat almost a fifth of homes. Polish coal is among the most expensive in the world to extract, and the industry survives largely due to heavy public subsidies. In 2026, the state is expected to spend 5.5 billion zloty propping up the sector, after an outlay of 9 billion zloty last year. Successive governments have been seeking to move away from coal, which went from producing 87% of Poland’s electricity in 2015 to 52.2% in 2025. Meanwhile, between 2015 and 2024, the proportion of households using hard coal for heating fell from 40% to 17%, while those using natural gas doubled from 10% to 21%. However, the energy crisis prompted by US and Israeli attacks on Iran this year has resulted in natural gas prices soaring. As a result, Poland’s state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, said last month that the geopolitical situation meant coal’s role this year would be “larger than we anticipated”. “We are currently increasing output at coal companies and are aware of the energy sector’s demand for coal as a stabilising factor,” he said, quoted by news service Money.pl. World.title: Polish president backs down and approves government’s windfall tax on fuel companies
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has reversed course and signed into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits that he had previously blocked. The government had been pushing the president to approve the measures amid soaring fuel prices. In announcing his decision on Thursday, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, insisted that he now expected the government to move to lower fuel prices for consumers. A few hours later, the government confirmed that it would do so, and on Friday morning it announced cuts in VAT and excise duty on fuels. Nie pozwolę rządowi dłużej odsuwać od siebie odpowiedzialności za tę trudną sytuację. Podpisałem ustawę dotyczącą nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych i zakończę proces ustawiania Polaków w roli politycznych zakładników. To rząd ponosi pełną odpowiedzialność za ceny paliw -… pic.twitter.com/7AX8v4a9Q0 — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) October 1, 2026 The windfall tax will levy a one-off charge of 60% of excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. It is expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€914 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset some of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by cutting VAT and excise duty and introducing a maximum daily price. Those measures were initially in place from March to June. However, in July, Nawrocki announced that he would not sign the windfall tax into law. He instead sent it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment. That process can take years, effectively killing off the bill. The president argued that the proposed measures “raised serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that the tax would be retroactive, applying to revenue earned from the beginning of March. Since then, he and the government have been locked in a dispute over the issue, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk arguing that measures to reduce fuel prices, which were briefly reintroduced in the last two weeks of August, can only be restored if Nawrocki signs the windfall tax. Nawrocki’s office, however, has argued that fuel companies would pass the costs of the tax onto consumers, therefore actually increasing prices. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In September, the government’s majority in parliament passed the windfall tax bill a second time. And Nawrocki has now backed down, announcing in a recorded speech on Thursday evening that he would sign the bill into law. However, he has still asked the TK to assess its constitutionality. Nawrocki declared that he was seeking to call the government’s bluff. He claimed that they were actually hoping the windfall tax would fail so that the treasury could continue obtaining normal tax revenue from high fuel prices, as well as dividends from state oil giant Orlen. By signing the bill, the president said he was “ending the process of holding Poles hostage”. He now expected the government to “immediately” reintroduce measures to bring down prices at petrol stations, as well as the cost of fuel for farmers. To nie ja wygrałem. Wygrali Polacy, którzy już w weekend zapłacą mniej za paliwa. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 1, 2026 In response, government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVN that they were ready to make the necessary decisions to reduced prices on Friday and that the measures could be in force already by the weekend. “It’s good that the president has stopped blocking this,” he said. On Friday morning, the government announced that it would reduce VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and cut excise duty – both measures it also used earlier this year. The new policies will be in place until 31 December. Energy minister Miłosz Motyka told Polskie Radio that maximum daily prices would also be reintroduced. Earlier, on Thursday evening, finance minister Andrzej Domański announced on social media that he estimated fuel costs would be reduced by 1.2-1.3 zloty per litre once the subsidies were reintroduced. According to price monitoring service ePetrol, diesel prices are currently averaging around 9.14 zloty per litre while PB95 petrol is at 8.19 zloty. Those are both record highs. Ustawa o podatku od nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych właśnie wpłynęła do RCL. Jeszcze dziś będzie ogłoszona. Oznacza to, że już w weekend ceny na stacjach paliwowych będą niższe. Szacunkowo o około 1,2-1,3 zł na litrze. I po co były te gierki, Panie Prezydencie? — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 1, 2026 The dispute over financing fuel price cuts comes at a time of growing concern over Poland’s public finances, something Nawrocki referred to in his address on Thursday. Poland has been running one of the EU’s highest deficits, despite the government committing to bringing it down after being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time this year. Last month, Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The last time the country was at A3 level was in 2002.
