World.title: Famous Dancing House Photo Spot in Prague Is Set for a Major Makeover
World.content:
Jiráskovo Square in Prague is set for a major redesign that will change one of the city’s best-known photo spots near the Dancing House.

The project, estimated to cost around CZK 35 million, will replace part of the damaged lawn with paving, restore a historic fountain and move the monument to writer Alois Jirásek.



The Prague 2 district plans to carry out the transformation over the next two years. The redesign is based on a 2022 study prepared by archiF studio.

The square’s lawn has long been a problem. Its location directly opposite the Dancing House makes it a popular stopping point for tourists, many of whom step onto the grass to take photographs with the distinctive building in the background.

One of the most common poses involves visitors appearing to support the Dancing House with their foot or kick it. The repeated foot traffic has left the grass heavily damaged, despite attempts to restore it.

Under the new plans, part of the lawn will be replaced with a paved surface. This will create a more durable area for visitors to take photographs while reducing pressure on the remaining greenery.

Historic fountain to return to operation

The redesign will also restore the Cubist fountain created by architect Vlastislav Hofman. The area around the fountain will be repaved, while the fountain itself will be returned to its original appearance and function.

Water is expected to flow through the fountain again after decades.

Architect Soňa Formanová, one of the project’s authors, said the team was able to locate Hofman’s original documentation, including plans covering the fountain and the approaches to the nearby bridge.

The project will also introduce a raised edge around the lawn that can be used for seating. New flowerbeds and trees are planned for the northern part of the square, while existing shrubs considered unsuitable for the area will be removed.

The monument to Alois Jirásek, the Czech writer after whom the square is named, will be relocated to the center of the small park.

World.title: Queer Arts Festival PINKBUS Returns With New Performances and International Guests
World.content:
The PINKBUS Festival will return to Prague on November 3-14 with several days of theatre, dance, drag, music, visual art and performance.

This year’s edition, titled Forward March!, will focus on the need to keep moving forward amid an uncertain social and political climate.

Organised by the PINKBUS queer arts platform, the festival aims to create a space for artists and audiences to meet, experiment and share experiences. The programme combines established artists with new projects and will also mark the beginning of a new season for the platform.



One of the highlights of this year’s festival will be the premiere of two original works developed through the PINKBUS open call First Ride.

Richard Eliáš, an Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague (AVU) student, will present the interdisciplinary drag fantasy I Guess It’s Kind of My Fault, or What?. The second project, by the performative art collective Izbová teplota & Alejandra, is Štúrovci Went to Devín and Had Some Fun, offering a new and unconventional take on the group of Slovak national revival figures known as the Štúrovci.

The festival will also feature international guests. French artists Nicolas Poggi and Giselle Hauscarriaga will present SUDOR (Sweat), a Czech premiere performed with a local cast. The post-performative work explores physical exhaustion, sweat and the limits of the body.

Another premiere, Lipsync Her Name… Because It’s Precious, is being created in collaboration with the Italian festival RAINBOW.IT and Slovak organisation DRAMA QUEER. The performance focuses on three figures from European LGBTQIA+ history: Lucy Salani, Romina Cecconi and Ota Tasinata.

Directed by Tomáš “Grófka” Procházka, the production combines three monodramatic sketches exploring identity and the determination to remain true to oneself. The cast includes Italian actor Antonello Foddis and his drag alter ego La Trave Nell’Okkio, as well as Czech performer Venice, also known as Martin Talaga.

The programme will also include the PINKPANEL discussion series. This year’s edition, titled (The Tinsmith’s) Hammer Against Queerness, will examine the potential impact of current cultural policy on LGBTQIA+ artistic production and discuss possible forms of resistance.

The festival will conclude with a special BEST OF edition of the PINKBUS variety show, featuring Venice, Just Karen, La Cuntessa, Tonic Garbáge, Helena Araujo and other performers, alongside special guests.

World.title: Roger Waters Brings New Pink Floyd Show to Prague in June 2027
World.content:
Roger Waters will bring a new Pink Floyd concert production to Prague next year, with LEGACY – A Pink Floyd Show scheduled for June 8, 2027, at O2 universum.

The new production has been created under Waters’ direction and will feature a ten-piece band led by his son, Harry Waters. The Prague show will focus on music from what is widely regarded as Pink Floyd’s most influential period, spanning 1971 to 1979.



The setlist will draw from four of the band’s best-known albums: The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

The music will be accompanied by a new visual production featuring high-resolution LED screens and imagery inspired by Pink Floyd’s original artwork and stage concepts.

Harry Waters will serve as the show’s musical director, performing on Hammond B3 organ and piano while also contributing vocals. He has a long history with the band’s music and spent more than 15 years performing alongside his father on major tours, including The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall.

His connection to Pink Floyd goes back even further. As a child, Harry’s voice appeared on “Goodbye Blue Sky” from The Wall. He also saw the original The Wall concert production at a young age.

The band includes drummer Graham Broad, guitarist Edo Scordo, bassist and backing vocalist Dahniel Knight, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Ryan Saranich, keyboardist Matt Riddle, lead vocalist Clifton David Broadbridge and backing vocalists Eva Avila and Genevieve Little.

Roger Waters co-founded Pink Floyd in 1965 and became the band’s principal lyricist and conceptual leader following Syd Barrett’s departure. He played a central role in the creation of albums including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

Ticket prices start at 1,600 CZK

Live Nation Club and O2 presale starts October 8, 2026, at 10:00 AM

Tickets on sale via Ticketmaster and Ticketportal starting October 9, 2026, at 10:00 AM

World.title: GALLERY: Vltava Philharmonic Reveals Its Interiors for the First Time
World.content:
Prague’s planned Vltava Philharmonic has offered the first detailed look inside the building, releasing visualizations of its main foyer and the spaces serving its three principal concert halls.

The interior design will combine wood, glass and stone, with flowing shapes inspired by the Vltava River and the building’s distinctive sloping roof. The plans also emphasize open public spaces designed to connect the concert halls with the rest of the building.



The main foyer will be dominated by a large glass wall extending across several floors. Its curved geometry is intended to echo the movement of the Vltava and will separate the open foyer from other areas of the building.

Light-colored solid wood panels will cover the ceilings, following the contours of the roof above. Stone elements will be used in areas connecting the public foyer with the foyer of the main concert hall, including spaces designed for both seating and standing around bar counters.

´

The project has become significantly more expensive

The cost of the Vltava Philharmonic has increased sharply since the project was first estimated.

In 2021, the projected construction cost was CZK 6.1 billion. After the Danish architecture studio Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) won the international competition in 2022, the estimate rose to CZK 9.4 billion.

A more detailed architectural study completed in 2024 put the figure at CZK 11.65 billion. The latest estimate is CZK 11.98 billion for the building itself.

Once improvements to the surrounding area are included, the overall project is expected to cost almost CZK 17 billion.

Construction could begin in 2028

The city expects to obtain the permit in the first quarter of 2027. A general contractor would then be selected, with construction currently scheduled to start in the first quarter of 2028.

Trial operations are planned to begin in 2033.

The Vltava Philharmonic will occupy three underground and six above-ground floors. In addition to five concert halls, the complex will include facilities for the Czech Philharmonic and the Prague Symphony Orchestra (FOK), a music department operated by the Municipal Library of Prague, a creative hub, a restaurant and publicly accessible terraces.

The building is being designed by Bjarke Ingels Group, whose proposal was selected in the international architectural competition in 2022.

World.title: Up to 80 Startups to Pitch Investors at Prague’s Engaged Investments Conference
World.content:
The international Engaged Investments conference, taking place on October 21 and 22, 2026, is significantly expanding its scope this year.

The event, which brings hundreds of startup investors from all over Europe to Prague, is now fully opening its doors to tech founders and the broader innovation ecosystem.



Alongside the main program, the two-day event will feature two specialized industry tracks focusing on fintech and defense, pitches from up to 80 startups, and an extended accompanying program.

Real defense instead of geopolitical theories

The defense track is being organized in collaboration with the Invest in Bravery initiative, which is deeply involved in the Ukrainian ecosystem, alongside the European EUDIS Matchmaking program for defense and Cassini Matchmaking for space technologies.

A special guest will be Senior Lieutenant Mykyta Puz, Defense Industry Liaison Officer of the Azov Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine. He previously worked in business and AI product management before volunteering for the front lines in 2024.

He will shed light on what a modern army truly and urgently needs from the defense industry. Alongside him, speakers will include Erin Hallock, Managing Partner of the NATO Innovation Fund, a representative of the renowned Ukrainian fund Brave1, and others.

Fintech that solves business, not theory

The UnBundled Fintech track, which will run throughout the second day of the conference, is being prepared by The FinTechers in collaboration with Mastercard. The goal is to connect the traditional banking sector with technology companies and investors. The program will focus on stablecoins and tokenization, operational resilience of banks, liability for fraudulent payments, and the deployment of artificial intelligence in financial services.

In addition to new technologies, it will address what European companies need to grow into global players without relying on American capital and infrastructure.

Speakers will include Michal Vodrážka, Director of the Payment Systems Regulation Division at the Czech National Bank. In a debate with Jiří Raška, Chief Technology Officer of Partners Banka, he’ll raise the question of who takes the hit when a payment ends up in a fraudster’s hands. It’s a timely topic, with mandatory payee verification coming in 2027.

The block dedicated to stablecoins and new financial infrastructure will be opened by Dorothea Ysenburg, Vice President of Global Partnerships for Digital Assets and Blockchain at Mastercard. Maryna Muntian from J.P. Morgan will also present, discussing why Central European banks and investors still lack mutual trust when looking at the same deals.

A place where startups find real investors

Closing investments is one of the core components of the conference, which last year attracted investors from more than 20 countries. Up to 80 selected startups, ranging from early-stage to Series A, will have the opportunity to pitch their companies in three minutes to investors actively investing in their respective segments. This year will introduce new dedicated pitching blocks for startups in the fields of financial technology, defense, and space.

On October 22, the best fintech projects from the two-day “Coding the Future of Finance” hackathon—organized on October 19 and 20 by The FinTechers together with Deloitte, AWS, and other partners—will also be presented to investors.

World.title: Designblok 2026 to Take Over Six Prague Venues This Week
World.content:
The 28th edition of Designblok, Prague’s international design festival, will take place from October 6 to 11, 2026, across six locations in the city.

The professional program and conference begin on Tuesday, October 6, while the main festival opens to the public on Wednesday, October 7. This year’s theme is “Light,” with exhibitions and installations exploring both the practical and symbolic role of light in design.



The program will look at design as a tool for addressing social and economic challenges and examine its role in everyday life. Curated exhibitions, exhibitor installations, discussions on the Designblok Stage and the Designblok Talks conference will explore themes including knowledge, truth, hope and sustainability.

The Trade Fair Palace (Veletržní palác) will serve as the festival’s main venue. It will bring together hundreds of presentations by designers, brands, schools and emerging talents, alongside curated exhibitions, lectures and workshops. The venue will also host activities for children and adults.

At the Prague Castle Riding School, Designblok will present two curated exhibitions connecting contemporary design and craftsmanship with Czech cultural history.

The Museum of Decorative Arts in Prague will host one of the festival’s main exhibitions, as well as dozens of design presentations and a special project marking the 100th anniversary of the creation of the popular Czech puppet character Hurvínek.

The Industrial Palace will host much of the festival’s conference and social program, including Designblok Talks, a live edition of the Czech quiz show AZ-kvíz focused on design, and the Designblok Awards Gala. The venue is reopening following its recent reconstruction.

Saturday will also bring fashion shows featuring finalists from the international Diploma Selection competition, which highlights emerging designers from around the world.

Other Designblok venues include the Chapel of the Holy Cross in the Second Courtyard of Prague Castle and the UMPRUM Technology Centre on Mikulandská Street. The latter provides facilities for student projects and workshops.

World.title: Bollywood and Beyond: Prague Indian Film Festival Returns for Its 23rd Edition
World.content:
The Prague Indian Film Festival will return for its 23rd edition from October 8 to 10, bringing a selection of recent Indian films to Kino Světozor.

The festival will open with a historical drama and feature Bollywood, arthouse cinema, a Sundance-winning film and a vampire comedy.

The festival opens on Thursday, October 8, in the presence of the Ambassador of India with Main Vaapas Aaunga, directed by Imtiaz Ali.

Set against the Partition of British India in 1947, the film follows a young Sikh man and his Muslim girlfriend whose lives are transformed by the political upheaval of the period.



Friday’s program will offer two very different takes on contemporary Indian cinema. Bollywood fans can see Cocktail 2, a romantic comedy about a love triangle starring Shahid Kapoor, Kriti Sanon and Rashmika Mandanna. The film follows the successful 2012 movie Cocktail.

The festival will also screen Cactus Pears, an arthouse drama set in a remote village in Maharashtra. The story follows a man who returns home after his father’s death and, while observing traditional mourning rituals, reconnects with a childhood friend.

The film won the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival, where it drew attention for its portrayal of a relationship that goes beyond friendship.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Prague Indian Film Festival 🎥🇮🇳 (@pragueindianfilmfestival)

Saturday afternoon will once again be dedicated to popular Indian films from the 1990s and 2000s. This year’s selection is Rang De Basanti, the 2006 film starring Aamir Khan.

The film has also gained renewed attention in India in connection with recent student protests. Festival art director Radim Špaček said he followed the demonstrations online and saw Rang De Basanti become one of the films associated with the movement.

Saturday evening will take a turn toward horror with Thamma, which combines comedy, horror and vampire folklore. The film stars Ayushmann Khurrana and Rashmika Mandanna, who also appears in Cocktail 2. It is directed by Aditya Sarpotdar.

Dance will also be a major part of the festival program. The accompanying Indian Dance Festival will feature workshops and masterclasses with instructors from around the world, culminating in the Bollywood Fiesta dance gala at Prague’s Rokoko Theatre on Sunday, October 11.

The festival will also feature Indian food, cinema decorations by Sanu Babu and a Bollywood dance party on Saturday night. DJ Dance Sandeep will perform at Theatro Music Club at the Karlín Music Theatre.

World.title: Prague’s Oldest Nightclub Lávka is Closing After 36 years
World.content:
One of Prague’s best-known nightlife venues is closing after more than three decades beside the Charles Bridge.

Lávka, which opened in 1990 on the banks of the Vltava, held its final farewell party on September 30. The club will leave its historic premises by October 8 as the City of Prague prepares to renovate the building.



For 36 years, Lávka was more than a nightclub. Its programme included concerts, theater, exhibitions, fashion shows and other cultural events. Its visitors included former president Václav Havel, politician Karel Schwarzenberg and singer Karel Gott.

The venue also hosted Czech acts including Lucie and Lunetic, as well as international performers such as Supertramp and R.E.M.

The first version of the venue was modest. It began as a theater bar in the Bedřich Smetana Museum, replacing the building’s cloakroom. With little money available, co-founder Boris Gaydečka and his partners constructed the bar themselves using scaffolding and wooden boards found on the site.

Advertising on the newly launched Radio Evropa 2 helped attract customers, and the business soon outgrew its original space.

Over the years, Lávka became a regular stop for performers from very different parts of Prague’s cultural scene. Its stage hosted the avant-garde Opera Mozart, the Semafor theater and the Spejbl and Hurvínek Theatre.

During the catastrophic floods of 2002, water eventually reached the ceiling despite efforts to protect the premises.

The damage was extensive. Seating was destroyed, a piano borrowed from the museum was swept away and doors were torn from their hinges.

The building is now being cleared

The end of Lávka’s original premises is linked to a wider renovation of the historic building.

The former Old Town Waterworks building belongs to the City of Prague and has been associated with the Bedřich Smetana Museum since 1936. The museum will also leave the building as part of the planned renovation.

Lávka will continue operating a canteen and café in the neighboring building owned by the Czech Association of Scientific and Technical Societies.

World.title: Hungary officially enters race to host 2036 Olympics – Budapest named as main venue
World.content:
Hungary is officially among the countries in the running to host the 2036 Summer Olympics and Paralympics, with Budapest named as the central location for the proposed Games.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) confirmed that Hungary is one of seven interested parties currently in continuous dialogue over the 2036 Olympics. The other candidates are Germany, India, Qatar, South Korea, South Africa and Türkiye.

The interested parties have until 31 October 2026 to formally indicate their interest. They will then present their projects to the IOC’s Future Host Commission in November.

Budapest at the centre of Hungary’s bid

Olympic bids are formally submitted by cities rather than national governments. Hungary has identified Budapest as the main host location for its project.

The other interested parties have also named their proposed host cities: Germany has put forward Munich, India Ahmedabad, Qatar Doha, Türkiye Istanbul, South Korea Seoul and South Africa Cape Town. Qatar’s proposal could also involve neighbouring countries in hosting events.

The IOC says potential hosts will be assessed on several factors, including their venue masterplan, athlete experience, funding strategy, political and public support, ability to deliver the Games and plans for a long-term legacy.

The projects will also be assessed on how well they fit local development plans and the goals of the Olympic movement.

The Olympics Park in Budapest, Hungary. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

If you missed it: Will Budapest miss out? India throws its hat into the ring for the 2036 Olympic Games

When will the host be chosen?

The selection process will take several years. The current interested parties will present their projects to the Future Host Commission in November 2026. By March 2027, the IOC is expected to complete feasibility assessments and open a more detailed Strategic Dialogue with the candidates.

The IOC Executive Board will then narrow down the field. In December 2028, the selected Preferred Hosts will enter a final Targeted Dialogue with the IOC and provide detailed plans and financial and legal guarantees.

The 2036 Olympic host is expected to be elected by IOC members in mid-2029.

The IOC says no additional candidates will be considered for the 2036 Games after 31 October 2026.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

A long-standing Budapest ambition

A Budapest Olympics has been a long-standing ambition in Hungarian politics, particularly under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

Budapest previously submitted a bid for the 2024 Olympics, but the application was withdrawn in 2017 after the Momentum movement collected around 266,000 signatures for a referendum on the proposal.

Since then, Hungary has continued to develop major sports infrastructure, including the Puskás Arena, MVM Dome, National Athletics Centre and Duna Arena. Budapest has also hosted major international sporting events, including the World Aquatics Championships and World Athletics Championships, as well as European Championship football matches.

These developments have frequently been cited as evidence that Hungary now has much of the infrastructure needed to host an Olympic Games.

The Puskás Arena in Budapest. Photo: BKK

What does Budapest’s current Olympic plan look like?

Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony has previously said he does not oppose the idea of hosting the Olympics in principle, but has attached conditions to any potential bid.

In September, Karácsony said that the capital’s Olympic concept does not require state spending during the current parliamentary term and does not include the construction of new stadiums. He described the proposal primarily as an urban development strategy focused on improving infrastructure in Budapest and across Hungary.

Under the concept, he said, an eventual Olympic Games would be organised together with as many major cities and other municipalities outside Budapest as possible.

However, Karácsony has also stressed that major projects such as the Olympics are difficult to discuss while Budapest is locked in financial disputes with the central government.

The Tisza government has not yet stated its position

Péter Magyar, now Hungary’s prime minister, previously expressed reservations about an Olympic bid. In 2024, he said Hungary did not need an Olympics under the circumstances at the time, while arguing that the event could become a national project if it had broad public support.

Magyar also previously said that the Tisza Party would only seriously consider an Olympic bid if the government provided additional funding for healthcare, education and social services, restored funding to Budapest and organised a national referendum on the issue.

World.title: PM Magyar announces wealth and small-business tax details
World.content:
Hungary will introduce a new wealth tax on assets worth more than HUF 1 billion from 2027, while the government plans to significantly broaden access to the KATA small-business tax scheme and remove a special tax allowance for professional athletes, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Tuesday.

In a video posted on social media, Magyar outlined changes to three areas of taxation: the new wealth tax, KATA and EKHO, a simplified tax scheme used by certain professionals including journalists, artists, performers and athletes.

Wealth tax to target assets worth over HUF 1 billion

The new wealth tax will come into force on 1 January 2027 and will have two rates. People with wealth exceeding HUF 1 billion will pay 1% on the portion above the HUF 1 billion threshold, while assets exceeding HUF 100 billion will be subject to a 1.5% rate, according to Magyar’s announcement.

The tax will cover a person’s overall wealth, including property, investments and company holdings. Assets held abroad or placed in wealth-management structures will also be covered.

Loans will be deductible from the taxable base. Taxes already paid on property and vehicles will also be deductible from the wealth tax itself, with the government saying this is intended to help avoid double taxation.

The government plans to introduce detailed rules for calculating the value of assets, primarily based on their actual market value. This will apply to both real estate and company holdings. The tax will be paid once a year through self-assessment. The first declaration will be based on taxpayers’ assets at the end of 2026 and will be due by 31 August 2027.

Only people whose wealth per person reaches HUF 1 billion will have to file a declaration. The Hungarian Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) is expected to provide a calculator to help taxpayers determine their taxable wealth. Magyar also criticised attempts to lobby against the new tax, saying people with less than HUF 1 billion in wealth would have nothing to do under the new system.

KATA to become available to more small businesses

The government is also planning a major overhaul of KATA, Hungary’s simplified tax scheme for small businesses. The changes would once again allow part-time entrepreneurs, pensioners and university students running businesses alongside their studies to use KATA.

KATA taxpayers would also once again be able to invoice companies and other organisations, rather than being restricted to invoicing private individuals. The government expects more than 100,000 additional small businesses could become eligible for the scheme as a result. (1 euro = 366 forints)

However, the monthly fixed tax will increase. For full-time KATA taxpayers, the monthly amount will rise to HUF 100,000. Those using KATA alongside another job will pay HUF 50,000 per month.

There will be a transitional arrangement for those who invoice exclusively private individuals. They will pay HUF 75,000 per month in 2027, with the HUF 100,000 rate applying from 2028.

The government says the higher tax is partly intended to improve social security protection for KATA taxpayers. The amount used to calculate their sick pay, maternity benefits and future pension will also be increased.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

15% tax on certain business income

The revised KATA system will also introduce a 15% tax on income earned from invoicing companies and other organisations. However, the fixed KATA tax already paid will count towards this liability. As a result, a full-time KATA taxpayer will not face an effective additional tax burden on company income until their annual company revenue exceeds HUF 8 million, according to Magyar’s explanation.

The annual KATA revenue limit will also increase from HUF 18 million to HUF 22 million.

The government argues that the changes will make KATA available to a much wider group of small businesses while maintaining it as a relatively simple and predictable form of taxation.

The HUF 100,000 monthly rate represents a substantial nominal increase from the HUF 50,000 rate introduced when KATA was launched in 2013. However, the tax rate has not changed since then, while Hungary has experienced roughly 80% inflation over the period. In today’s money, the original HUF 50,000 would be worth around HUF 88,000–89,000.

Professional athletes to lose special EKHO allowance

The government will also change the rules for EKHO, or simplified contribution taxation. Under the current system, the general annual income limit for EKHO is HUF 60 million, but professional athletes have been allowed to use the preferential system on income of up to HUF 500 million.

That special limit will be abolished from 2027, Magyar said. Professional athletes will instead be subject to the same HUF 60 million annual limit as other professions eligible for EKHO.

Magyar said there was no justification for professional footballers earning HUF 10–20 million, and sometimes HUF 50 million, per month to have substantially different tax rules from journalists, actors or other professionals using EKHO.

The government said it supports Hungarian sport and wants to see successful Hungarian clubs and athletes, but intends to remove what it considers unjustified exceptions from the tax system.

World.title: Former FM Szijjártó travelled to Russia every few months, spending more time there than in Germany
World.content:
Former Hungarian Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó travelled to Russia 16 times during his final four-year term in office – roughly once every three to four months – while visiting the country more often than Germany, according to detailed Foreign Ministry data obtained by 24.hu.

The figures show that Szijjártó travelled extensively during his 2022–2026 term, visiting 96 sovereign states, or almost half of all UN member countries. He made a total of 342 foreign trips involving 468 destinations. The former minister has since joined Chinese carmaker BYD.

Russia was a more frequent destination than Germany

Szijjártó’s 16 trips to Russia stand out in the data, particularly given the country’s war against Ukraine and Germany’s position as Hungary’s most important economic partner. The Russian trips were spread across his four years in office, meaning Szijjártó travelled to Russia on average every three to four months.

The figure does not include meetings with Russian officials held outside Russia. Szijjártó visited Luxembourg, where EU meetings are frequently held, the same number of times. His 16 trips to Russia, however, exceeded the number of times he travelled to Germany during the period.

Have you read this? Former Hungarian foreign minister Szijjártó questioned over BYD role in closed-door security hearing

Brussels was his most frequent destination

Belgium was Szijjártó’s most frequently visited country, with 38 trips, mainly to Brussels for EU and NATO-related meetings. The United States was second with 31 visits. Several of these trips included meetings at Donald Trump’s Florida residence.

Neighbouring Serbia ranked third, with Szijjártó travelling there 25 times during his term. Overall, his foreign travel covered 96 countries – equivalent to 49.7% of the world’s 193 UN member states.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

590 days spent abroad

The data also provides insight into just how much time Szijjártó spent travelling. Out of the nearly 1,450 days covered by his previous government’s term, he spent 590 days on foreign trips.

Despite the extensive travel schedule, Szijjártó often spent little time abroad, favouring short visits and returning home quickly. According to the data, he actually spent more nights sleeping on aircraft than in foreign accommodation.

The Foreign Ministry spent a total of HUF 512 million on accommodation for foreign trips during the period, of which HUF 53.9 million was attributed to Szijjártó.

The most expensive trip cost HUF 262 million

The data also reveals substantial differences in the cost of individual trips. Szijjártó’s most expensive foreign trip cost HUF 262 million, with the Foreign Ministry’s previous travel data showing that chartered aircraft accounted for a particularly significant share of spending on his foreign visits.

The latest figures come after 24.hu previously reported on the ministry’s spending on private aircraft for Szijjártó’s foreign travel, including almost HUF 300 million spent on private planes that ultimately did not take off.

World.title: EUR 8 million AI data centre planned in Transylvanian town with large Hungarian community
World.content:
A new artificial intelligence (AI) data centre worth more than EUR 8 million is being developed in Reghin, Transylvania, with the first NVIDIA servers expected to become operational before the end of the year.

The project, led by Romanian IT company Expert IT, will initially install 56 high-performance NVIDIA B300 graphics processing units (GPUs) across seven servers, G4Media reported. The company is also considering a much larger expansion involving another 512 GPUs. The investment is part of a wider EUR 10 million development planned by Expert IT on a 1.7-hectare site in Reghin, Mureș County.

56 NVIDIA GPUs to power AI models

The first phase of the project will cost more than EUR 8 million and involves not only the servers and GPUs but also the electricity supply and cooling infrastructure needed to operate them.

Expert IT chief executive Mihai Farcaș Dan said the 56-GPU order is the largest purchase of its kind in Romania this year. The company has already completed discussions about a potential expansion involving a further 512 graphics cards.

“The servers are due to become operational this year and are intended for developing large models,” Farcaș Dan told Radio Târgu Mureș.

The company has been developing its investment plans in Reghin for around 12 years, with AI becoming an increasingly important focus over the past three to four years. Details of how the first phase of the investment is being financed have not yet been disclosed.

AI could help doctors diagnose patients faster

One of the project’s main areas of focus will be healthcare. Expert IT is considering working with Romanian clinics and universities to develop AI systems capable of supporting communication between doctors and patients, assisting medical professionals and analysing medical imaging.

The company hopes such systems could eventually help speed up diagnoses in areas such as oncology and cardiology, where rapid identification of serious conditions can be particularly important.

The planned AI models could, for example, analyse large datasets and medical images to identify patterns and support doctors in reaching a diagnosis more quickly. The project could therefore involve healthcare and academic institutions from several parts of Romania.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Transylvania is becoming an AI data centre hotspot

The Reghin project is far from the only major AI-related data centre development underway in Transylvania. In Luna, Cluj County, US-based DriverAI and Romanian partner Leviatan Group are planning an 80-megawatt facility known as the Quantum AI Data Center.

The first phase has been estimated at around US$1 billion, with the centre intended primarily to provide computing capacity for running and training AI models. That project is still in the preparation stage, however, and the selected site is currently involved in a legal dispute following a challenge by a business using an adjacent plot.

Mureș County is also preparing another major data centre in Vidrasău. The Mureș County Council and Mureș Industrial Park are planning a facility costing almost RON 240 million (around EUR 45 million).

The approximately 1,700-square-metre centre would provide data storage, processing and server hosting, as well as computing capacity for artificial intelligence applications. Funding for the project has reportedly already been secured.

Meanwhile, the George Emil Palade University of Medicine, Pharmacy, Science and Technology of Târgu Mureș is developing its own high-performance computing infrastructure.

Its nearly RON 60 million (EUR 11.2 million) DEEP_AI project will support research based on artificial intelligence, machine learning and large-scale data analysis, including work on communications security and the detection of cyberattacks.

Romania wants to become a regional AI hub

The developments in Transylvania are part of a much wider push to expand Romania’s AI infrastructure. According to Telex, Romania is also planning the Black Sea AI Gigafactory, a huge project designed to establish the country as a regional centre for artificial intelligence. The planned facilities in Cernavodă and Doicești would eventually host more than 100,000 AI processors.

One of the biggest challenges facing such projects is securing enough electricity to power the enormous computing capacity required by modern AI systems.

World.title: Commercial ship sinks after drone attack off Bulgaria, Hungary’s PM reacts
World.content:
A commercial ship sank and another was damaged in a drone attack in the Black Sea off Bulgaria early Tuesday, with Hungary’s Prime Minister Péter Magyar expressing solidarity with Bulgaria following the incident.

The attack took place in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, around 80 nautical miles (approximately 130 kilometres) east of Cape St Athanasius and the town of Byala, according to Dnevnik.bg. The identities of the attackers have not yet been officially established, although there are reports that the drones may have been Russian.

One ship sank, crew missing

The attack reportedly took place at around 3 AM and involved two cargo vessels: the Togo-flagged ALFA WATAN and the Palau-flagged ABLE.

According to Maritime.bg, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the ALFA WATAN sank following the attack. A nearby Bulgarian vessel headed towards the site after the explosion, but so far rescuers have found only an overturned boat, three overturned life rafts and life jackets. The crew of the sunken vessel remains missing and the search operation is continuing. Authorities have not yet released information about the ship’s cargo.

The second vessel, which was carrying wheat, was also hit and caught fire. Its 18-person crew consisted of 11 Turkish and seven Indian nationals. All of them managed to abandon the vessel and were rescued. Two sailors were injured and taken by speedboat to the port of Varna. One suffered burns, while the other sustained a head injury.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Bulgaria launches emergency response

Bulgarian authorities immediately launched a response following the overnight attack. Radev convened a meeting involving representatives of the defence, interior, transport and environment ministries, the president’s office and the country’s security services.

The prime minister described the attack as completely unacceptable and a serious violation of international law and maritime regulations. The exact origin of the drones is under investigation.

Authorities are also monitoring another vessel, the EMIL, which has been drifting without a crew since August due to a malfunctioning steering system. A military aircraft carried out reconnaissance over the vessel two days before the latest incident.

Bulgarian authorities are tracking its movement to ensure it does not enter the country’s territorial waters or pose a threat to the coastline. They are also monitoring the possibility of pollution or an oil spill.

If you missed it: Hungary to stop blocking next stage of Ukraine’s EU accession talks, Financial Times reports

Another Black Sea ship was attacked a day earlier

The incident came just one day after another suspected drone attack on a grain carrier in the Black Sea, this time in Romania’s exclusive economic zone in international waters, Index reported. Romanian authorities sent several rescue vessels and helicopters to the scene. One person was killed and another is still missing following that incident.

Péter Magyar expresses Hungary’s solidarity

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar also reacted to the attack on Tuesday. In a Facebook post, Magyar said Hungary stands in full solidarity with Bulgaria following the incident.

“At dawn, two commercial ships were hit by a drone attack in Bulgaria’s territorial waters in the Black Sea. One ship sank, and the attack, whose origin is currently unknown, has injured people. Hungary assures Bulgaria of its full solidarity.”

The Hungarian prime minister did not speculate about who was responsible for the attack.

World.title: Good news for buyers: Hungarian housing market is turning, Budapest prices fall for 2nd month
World.content:
Hungary’s housing market appears to be losing momentum, with nationwide house prices stagnating in September while prices in Budapest fell for the second consecutive month, according to the latest housing price index from ingatlan.com.

The slowdown marks a notable shift after a period of rapid price growth. Since mid-2015, it has happened only three times before that all eight Hungarian regions simultaneously recorded slower price growth or falling prices compared with the previous month.

Budapest prices fall again

Nationwide, house prices rose by 0.4% in August but remained unchanged in September. Annual price growth also slowed sharply, from 11.2% in August to 8.2% in September.

The change has been even more pronounced in Budapest. Prices fell by 0.7% in August and a further 0.2% in September. Despite the recent declines, homes in the capital were still 3.3% more expensive than a year earlier.

“The price surge of last year peaked in November 2025, when we measured annual price increases of 18.4% nationwide and 24.1% in Budapest,” said László Balogh, chief economic expert at ingatlan.com.

“By September this year, the pace of nationwide price growth had fallen to less than half of that level, while in Budapest it had dropped to roughly one-seventh.”

According to Balogh, the figures indicate that price growth is slowing, although prices remain high. The nationwide market is currently stagnating, while Budapest is already seeing a modest decline. Annual nationwide house price growth has not been this low since December 2024. In Budapest, the latest figure represents the weakest annual growth recorded since February 2024.

If you missed it: Hungarian house prices soar over 10% in a year – But then came a sharp quarterly drop

Some regions are already seeing falling prices

The slowdown is not limited to the capital. In September, prices fell by 0.6% month-on-month in Pest County and by 1.2% in the Northern Great Plain. In the Southern Great Plain, where prices had jumped by 2.2% in August, growth slowed to just 0.1% in September.

Meanwhile, prices rose by 1.5% in Central Transdanubia, 0.9% in Southern Transdanubia and 0.6% in Northern Hungary. Prices in Western Transdanubia remained unchanged.

Just a few months ago, annual price growth was at least 10% across all Hungarian regions. By September, however, only three regions remained above that threshold: Central Transdanubia, Southern Transdanubia and the Southern Great Plain.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Why is the housing market slowing down?

One factor behind the slowdown is the unusually high price base from last year. When Hungary’s Otthon Start home-buying programme launched in September 2025, nationwide house prices jumped by 2.8% in a single month. This September, they remained unchanged.

However, affordability also appears to be playing an increasingly important role. As homes have become more expensive, fewer potential buyers can afford to enter the market, according to Balogh. The changing balance between supply and demand is particularly telling. The supply of newly built homes has reached a five-year high, while demand has fallen significantly.

The Otthon Start programme initially gave demand a major boost, contributing to widespread price increases. Developers and sellers, however, were slower to respond by increasing supply. By the time more new homes reached the market, prices had risen so much that some potential buyers could no longer afford them.

Six Budapest districts are now cheaper than last year

The latest figures also reveal significant differences between Budapest districts. At the beginning of October, the median price per square metre for second-hand flats and houses in Budapest stood at HUF 1.41 million (EUR 3,860), around 2% higher than a year earlier.

However, prices were already lower than last year in six districts:

District IX: down 2.7%

down 2.7% District III: down 1.9%

down 1.9% District V: down 1.8%

down 1.8% District XII: down 1.7%

down 1.7% District XI: down 1.5%

down 1.5% District XIII: down 0.5%

At the other end of the scale, prices rose by 10–12% in Districts XXII, XVII, XXIII and XVIII. District V remained Budapest’s most expensive area, with a median price of HUF 1.99 million per square metre. District I followed at HUF 1.87 million, while District XII stood at HUF 1.75 million. District XXIII was the most affordable, with a median price of HUF 958,000 per square metre.

World.title: If you drive a car like this in Hungary, you have until 30 November to change its number plate
World.content:
More than 32,000 plug-in hybrid vehicles in Hungary still have green number plates that they are no longer entitled to use. Their owners have until 30 November to replace them, according to a statement from the Digital Government Agency (DMÜ) sent to MTI on Monday.

The DMÜ is urging owners and operators of the affected vehicles not to leave the process until the final weeks. The number plate change can be initiated at any government window (kormányablak) in Hungary.

Which cars are affected?

The DMÜ recalled that since 1 September 2024, only vehicles classified in environmental categories 5E (fully electric) and 5Z (zero-emission) have been eligible for light green number plates.

Cars in environmental categories 5N (plug-in hybrid electric vehicles with an increased range) and 5P (plug-in hybrid electric vehicles) that were previously issued green number plates can continue using them only until 30 November.

After that date, if the vehicle is stopped during a road inspection, the authorities will confiscate the number plate and registration document and initiate the vehicle’s withdrawal from traffic. This will remain in effect until a new number plate is issued, either through a re-registration or a change of vehicle type.

According to the DMÜ, there are currently 32,325 plug-in hybrid vehicles in Hungary that still have green number plates and are either in circulation or temporarily withdrawn from traffic.

Have you heard? Budapest Assembly ends free parking for electric cars

How much will the number plate change cost?

The operators of affected vehicles have two options. They can request a new-character number plate, which costs HUF 17,475 (EUR 48), including the issue of the new number plate and registration document. Alternatively, they can request a number plate with the same characters, for which the administrative fee is HUF 16,605 (EUR 45.2).

The key difference is that with a same-character number plate change, existing contractual arrangements linked to the previous registration number do not need to be amended because of the change. These include compulsory motor third-party liability insurance, comprehensive insurance (CASCO), and certain parking and access permits. However, the process requires two in-person visits.

What happens to motorway e-vignettes?

A valid motorway e-vignette can still be used after the number plate change. However, if the vehicle receives a new-character number plate, the e-vignette must be transferred to the new registration number through the toll-road customer service of Magyar Közút Nonprofit Zrt.

Drivers also do not have to pay the vehicle acquisition tax retrospectively because of the previous benefits associated with the green number plate. The DMÜ has published detailed information about the procedure and frequently asked questions on its website.

World.title: Hungarian footballer Milos Kerkez on the list of “Ukraine’s enemies”
World.content:
Hungarian international footballer Milos Kerkez has been added to a controversial website’s list of alleged “enemies of Ukraine” following a social media post by his father.

Kerkez caught up in controversy

The Liverpool left-back was reportedly added to the Mirotvorec (Peacemaker) database following Hungary’s 1–0 Nations League defeat to Ukraine last Friday. The match ended in a tense confrontation after Ukrainian substitute Oleksandr Nazarenko was sent off. Players from both sides became involved in a heated exchange, during which Kerkez clashed verbally with Ukrainian midfielder Viktor Tsyhankov. Both players were shown yellow cards.

After the match, Kerkez’s father, Sebastijan Kerkez, shared footage of the incident on Instagram, adding the song “Russian Paradise” by Russian rap group AK-47 to the video. The choice of music reportedly caused outrage among Ukrainian audiences. Mirotvorec subsequently listed both Kerkez and his father, accusing the footballer of supporting Russian aggression, writes HVG.hu.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

The Hungarian international rejects the accusation

The player has strongly distanced himself from the accusation, telling Hungarian media that he has never supported aggression. “I have never supported and do not support any aggression,” Kerkez said, adding that the incident on the pitch was simply about defending Hungary’s captain and his friend.

“I am not the type of person who accepts anything that could harm others”, Kerkez claimed. He also stressed that his father’s actions should not be attributed to him. “My father is not me. I cannot take responsibility for his actions,” the footballer said.

Website not linked to Ukrainian government

The Mirotvorec database is not an official Ukrainian government platform. According to Hungarian reports, the operators of the website remain unclear, and it has been viewed in diplomatic circles as a controversial and potentially problematic initiative. Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán also condemned the listing of Hungarian citizens and stressed that the website should not be confused with an official Ukrainian state channel.

Read also: Szoboszlai sends strong message to journalists – but can a national team captain do this?

World.title: Bulgarian PM and Opposition Quarrel Over Black Sea Drone Attack
World.content:
Bulgaria’s opposition has criticised the government over its response to a drone attack on two foreign commercial cargo vessels on Tuesday in Bulgaria’s zone in the Black Sea.

The strike occurred at around 3 a.m. about 70 nautical miles east of the town of Byala and sank a Palau-flagged ship. A Togo-flagged ship was damaged by fire. The total number of sailors injured in the strike is unclear.

Prime Minister Rumen Radev called the attack “a crude violation of international law” but is yet to name the aggressor.

“It’s clear the drones were either Russian or Ukrainian,” he told media, adding that “worse cases have happened before”, without clarifying what events he was referring to.

Radev later stated: “As I have long said before, if this [Ukraine] war is not ended on time, it will continue to expand its territorial reach, become more brutal, increase the risks and turn into a global conflict.”

Acting President Iliana Iotova, formerly vice to Radev during his 2016-2026 presidential mandate, signed a decree to assemble Bulgaria’s security council on Wednesday. But Radev indirectly downplayed the need for such a decision, saying: “It would make people speculate with all kinds of nonsense.”

Opposition members criticised Radev for not naming Russia as the aggressor, alleging it was symptomatic of his sympathy for the Kremlin, following his reluctance for years to aid Ukraine – an agenda allegedly shared by Iotova, a runner in upcoming presidential elections on October 25.

“Although the budget for the military has doubled, there’s no adequate protection for Bulgarian citizens. There’s no real President, no real leader,” Assen Vassilev, co-leader of the opposition party We Continue the Change, told media.

“It is clearly a strike from Russia but Radev is not brave enough to say it,” said Ivaylo Mirchev, of Democratic Bulgaria, who asked why Radev had seemed more concerned when a non-threatening decoy drone was found near the border with Romania.

Sixteen crew members of the struck vessels, comprising Turkish and Indian nationals, have meanwhile been evacuated.

One who identified as a Turkish citizen told media on the Bulgarian shore: “I think the Russians threw at us a naval mine, there was a fire, not like one from a drone, since it came from underneath. I think it’s a Russian [attack] because we were carrying Ukrainian cargo.”

No government official has commented on the nature of the cargo carried by the vessels, or on whether there is a likely connection to Ukraine.

Two crew members sustained serious injuries – one with severe burns and another with head trauma – and were transported to the military hospital in Varna for treatment. Rescue missions are ongoing.

On September 18, Bulgaria announced it would start further supplying infrastructure facilities with drone-countermeasure systems, the move announced days after a fire ​broke out at a weapons depot, raising concerns about the security of munitions manufacturers.

World.title: Serbian Student Targeted by Spyware Attack Sues Authorities
World.content:
Lawyers representing student activist Jelena Kontic filed a criminal complaint on Tuesday with the Prosecutor’s Office for High-Tech Crime over the installation of Pegasus spyware on her phone, allegedly by Serbian security forces.

“The complaint was filed against individuals within the Security Information Agency [the state intelligence service] and the police whose identities have yet to be established, as well as responsible individuals at NSO Group, the Israeli company that manufactures Pegasus,” a Serbian digital rights NGO, SHARE Foundation, said in a press release.

Kontic is one of 14 members of the student movement, opposition politicians and activists who were targeted with advanced spyware. SHARE Foundation and The Citizen Lab, a research unit of the University of Toronto, revealed the alleged attacks on September 2.

SHARE Foundation added that Kontic’s case is the first confirmed successful Pegasus spyware infection in Serbia.

Given the precedence, Kontic told BIRN that “she expects the forensic examination of her phone and the processing of the case to present a challenge for the prosecution”.

Kontic only learned that she had been targeted when she received a notification from Apple. Forensic analysis confirmed that her device had been compromised remotely through a so-called “zero-click” attack.

“The attack exploited a vulnerability in the iMessage app on her iPhone, without her knowledge or any interaction on her part,” SHARE Foundation added.

The complaint covers five criminal offences: unauthorised collection of personal data, unauthorised interception and recording, creation and introduction of computer viruses, unauthorised access to a protected computer, and abuse of office.

Kontic’s lawyers, as quoted by SHARE Foundation, argued that the prosecutor’s office was required to act as soon as the case became public, and that the offences are punishable by imprisonment.

BIRN asked the High-Tech Crime Prosecution in September whether it had opened an investigation into the alleged attacks, but it did not respond.

But one day after the student movement published the information about the 14 people targeted with spyware, on September 3, the Security Information Agency dismissed the claims as “trivial sensationalism”.

Serbia’s Commissioner for Information of Public Importance and Personal Data Protection told BIRN on September 17 that it had not opened a case, as it lacked vital information.

“The Commissioner has not initiated a new proceeding, as at this time he does not have specific information and evidence concerning the circumstances of individual cases that would make it possible to establish grounds for action within his jurisdiction,” it said.

Kontic is part of the students’ movement that has become the main opponent of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party.

The movement was created after the fatal collapse of part of Novi Sad railway station in November 2024 triggered mass protests. The movement later formed the Student List, which is running in the parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25.

World.title: Kosovo Protesters Against Hague Court Gather Again After Clashes
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Protesters led by the Kosovo Liberation Army War Veterans’ Organisation started to reassemble outside parliament in Pristina on Tuesday after violent clashes the previous evening.

Angered by the convictions of four wartime KLA leaders including ex-President Hashim Thaci, they want MPs to pass legislation limiting the powers of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers war crimes court.

MPs on Monday voted to amend the law on the Hague-based court, which is part of Kosovo’s justice system, to say it may not impose jail sentences exceeding 15 years. But the amendment still needs a parliamentary committee review before it can return for a second reading.

After the parliamentary session ended, protesters demanded MPs vote on a second reading the same day. They blocked MPs from leaving the chamber and forcibly pushed ruling Vetevendosje party MP Fahrush Rexhepi back inside the parliament’s perimeter.

They then burned garbage bins and threw fireworks and explosives at the government building, but without damaging it. Clirim Haziri, organiser of the “Not in My Name” protest, declared that no MP would leave “without stepping over our bodies”.

Police said three persons were arrested and six police officers were injured. Naser Syla, from the University Clinical Centre of Kosovo, on Monday evening said 12 people had received medical assistance, including one police officer.

Peaceful protests have been continuing since the Specialist Chambers issued a first-instance verdict convicting the four former KLA leaders of war crimes on September 16.

The so-called special court sentenced former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and three other former leaders of the KLA, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi, to 25, 25 18 and 13 years in prison respectively for war crimes.

They were found guilty of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder from April 1998 to June 20, 1999, in Kosovo and several locations in Albania.

Other amendments passed on Monday include for the jail sentences to be served in Kosovo. Based on the current law, “the Specialist Chambers may order the transfer of a convicted person to a third country for service of his or her sentence of imprisonment”.

They also allow for Kosovo’s President to grant pardons, for the work of the court to be subjected to monitoring by international organisations, and for a constitutional review of the law to be conducted by the Constitutional Court of Kosovo.

The court is a hybrid tribunal. Although it is part of Kosovo’s judiciary, it is staffed with internationals and located in The Hague. It was established in 2015 under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies because of concern of potential witness intimidation if the processes were to be held domestically in Kosovo.

The court has a mandate to try crimes committed from January 1, 1998, to December 31, 2000, based on a Council of Europe report by Swiss Senator Dick Marty, which made allegations of war crimes and organ trafficking by KLA fighters.

An EU Special Investigative Task Force, led by former US prosecutor Clint Williamson, concluded that there was enough evidence to indict suspects for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but not enough to bring charges for organ trafficking.

The amendments to the law would also change the mandate of the court to only cover crimes allegedly committed after the Kosovo war ended, from July 1, 1999, until December 31, 2000.

The draft also says the court will not have jurisdiction over acts not committed in relation to the allegations of organ-trafficking in the Marty report – for which it has already been established that there is not enough evidence for trials.

Following the first-reading vote in parliament on Monday, the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, founded by Thaci, demanded that the second reading be held that same day.

This proposal was rejected by the Speaker, Albulena Haxhiu, who said it was not on the agenda and who insisted that the party leaders – PM Albin Kurti and leader of Vetevendosje and Bedri Hamza of the PDK, meet first.

Hamza and Kurti held a meeting on Monday, but it did not result in an agreement.

Kurti said the top priority was electing a state President. During the parliament session, Kurti said: “A law regarding the Hague court is necessary, but so is a President of Kosovo. Proceeding with one without the other could be highly detrimental. We cannot claim to be defending Kosovo’s interests in The Hague while allowing an institutional vacuum to develop within Kosovo.”

Parliament’s deputy speaker from the PDK, Vlora Citaku, disagreed. She said after the parliament session that voting on the new law was “a national obligation, whereas the election of the president is a matter of agreement”.

World.title: From Streets to Polling Stations: Serbia’s Student Movement Takes Electoral Test
World.content:
When Serbia’s students began blockading their universities after the fatal collapse of the canopy at the railway station in Novi Sad in November 2024, entering parliament was not part of the plan.

Their demands were directed at Serbia’s institutions: publication of documentation relating to the station reconstruction, prosecution of those accused of attacking students commemorating the victims, the dropping of charges against arrested students, and increased funding for higher education.

“At that point, we did not even know what the electoral process involved. We simply wanted justice,” said Milica Najdanovic, a student at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering.

Five months of university blockades and mass protests changed the calculation. Concluding that their original demands would not be met, the students added another: early parliamentary elections.

World.title: One Click, Money Gone: Albania Battles Spike in Cyber Fraud
World.content:
It all started with a text message in May. Gentjana Driza was waiting for a delivery from e-commerce marketplace Temu when she received a message apparently from Albania Post, telling her to pay a small customs fee.

The message contained a link. Driza clicked on it and was taken to a series of forms. According to her complaint to the police, she believed the request genuinely came from Albania Post, so she followed the instructions and entered her personal and banking details.

She soon realised she had been scammed. Notifications began appearing on her banking app showing substantial transfers from her account. The transactions continued even after she contacted her bank and blocked her card.

Over the next three days, around 100,000 lek (1,085 euros) was taken from Driza’s account. The exact amount remained unclear, as transactions continued to be processed.

World.title: Nationalist Parties Celebrate Wins in Bosnia Election, But Many Voters Stay Home
World.content:
“It was not a surprise because we as citizens cannot free ourselves from the ethno-national frameworks,” political analyst Tanja Topic told BIRN after Bosnia’s dominant nationalist parties claimed victory on October 4 in the general election.

The [Bosniak] Party of Democratic Action, SDA, the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ BiH, and the [Serb] Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD, each remained the strongest force in their respective ethnic camps, while many voters stayed at home – and a new challenger shook up the Bosniak field.

Topic said most voters clearly looked past the corruption, crime, nepotism and clientelism on which power rests, as each wave of national homogenisation follows another, leaving the country stuck in a vicious circle.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament Moves Towards Changing Law to Curb Hague Special Court
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



The first reading of the special court law amendment at the Kosovo parliament, October 5, 2026. Photo: Antigone Isufi/BIRN.

Kosovo MPs on Monday voted to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers so the Hague-based court, part of Kosovo’s justice system, may not impose a sentence of imprisonment exceeding 15 years. The amendment has not been adopted yet, as it must undergo a parliamentary committee review and return for a second reading.

Outside parliament, protesters who had staged an all-night vigil in front of the legislature chanted: “Vote [for] the law.”

The vote comes amid anger in Kosovo after the court sentenced former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and three other former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi, to 25, 25 18 and 13 years in prison respectively for war crimes on September 16.

The four were found guilty of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder from April 1998 to June 20, 1999, in Kosovo and several locations in Albania.

Critics have, among others, claimed that the court did not apply the “lex mitior” principle, which allows defendants to be sentenced under the most favourable law of the time that the crime was committed. According to the applicable law of former Yugoslavia, the maximum prison sentence is 15 years.

The amendments include for the sentences to be served in Kosovo. Based on the current law, “the Specialist Chambers may order the transfer of a convicted person to a third country for service of his or her sentence of imprisonment”.

The amendments also grant Kosovo’s President power to grant pardons, the work of the court to be subjected to monitoring by international organisations, and for a constitutional review of the law to be conducted by the Constitutional Court of Kosovo.

It is not certain whether a second reading will take place on Monday.

Bedri Hamza, chair of the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, which Thaci founded, and which proposed the amendments, said before the vote that the law does not belong to his party, even if it “is a PDK initiative”.

The verdict, which is to be appealed, caused outrage in Kosovo and people have been protesting daily ever since.

It also led to the initiative to change the law on the court. The court is a hybrid tribunal – although it is part of Kosovo’s judiciary, it is staffed with internationals and located in The Hague.

It was established in 2015 under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies because of concern of potential witness intimidation if the processes were to be held domestically in Kosovo.

The court has a mandate to try crimes committed from January 1, 1998, to December 31, 2000, based on a Council of Europe report by Swiss Senator Dick Marty, which made allegations of war crimes and organ trafficking by KLA fighters.

An EU Special Investigative Task Force, led by former US prosecutor Clint Williamson, concluded that there was enough evidence to indict suspects for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but not enough to bring charges for organ trafficking.

The amendments of the law aim to change the mandate of the court to only cover crimes allegedly committed after the Kosovo war, from July 1, 1999 until December 31, 2000. The draft amendment says that the court will not have jurisdiction over acts that were not committed in relation to the allegations of organ-trafficking in the Dick Marty report – for which it has already been established that there is not enough evidence for trials.

On Monday, before the law was put to a vote, Prime Minister Albin Kurti reminded MPs that the country faces another crisis, over the election of a President.

“A law regarding the Hague court is necessary, but so is a President of Kosovo. Proceeding with one without the other could be highly detrimental. We cannot claim to be defending Kosovo’s interests in The Hague while allowing an institutional vacuum to develop within Kosovo,” he said.

Tuesday is the constitutional deadline for Kosovo to elect a President and finalise the formation of institutions deriving from the June 7 elections. If a President is not elected, the country faces its fourth parliamentary elections in less than two years.

Even if the law amendments pass the second reading, they will be enforced only after the appeals panel at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers issues a verdict for Thaci and the three others.

World.title: Serbs Abroad May Have to Vote Overnight Under New Election Rule
World.content:
Serbs voting abroad in upcoming elections will have to follow polling hours based on Central European Time under a new decision adopted in the early hours of Monday morning by the Republic Electoral Commission, RIK, which has set standardised voting hours of 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.

The decision means that while some polling stations abroad will operate simultaneously with those in Serbia if they are in the same time zone, voters in some countries, including the United States, Australia and Indonesia, may have to cast ballots during local nighttime hours.

The proposal was passed by 20 RIK members in favour, while seven voted against. Several RIK members criticised the move, arguing it could make it harder for Serbian citizens abroad to exercise their right to vote. They also questioned why the Foreign Ministry, which initiated the proposal, had become involved in determining polling hours.

RIK member Ivan Sebek said such an arrangement had never been introduced since Serbia began organising voting abroad, and no previously reported problem justified it. “You are further restricting voters’ rights and effectively cutting the time available to exercise their right to vote in half,” Sebek said.

Other RIK members raised concerns about voters’ safety when voting at night. Vladimir Dragas called it “completely illegal” and warned it could anger some diaspora voters, forced to cast their ballots in the middle of the night.

The decision comes as the governing Serbian Progressive Party faces its strongest challenge since it came to power in 2012, from the recently-established opposition Student List, which grew out of the student-led protest movement. Some commentators have suggested there is strong support for the students’ cause among diaspora Serbians.

The change in voting times has worried some Serbian voters around the world.

Marija, who lives in China, speaking to BIRN on condition of anonymity, said the opening hours of the Serbian embassy on election day would be inconvenient, lasting from 2 p.m. until 3 a.m. Another issue is that, for the whole of China, only one polling station has been approved, in Beijing.

“Considering that China is a huge territory, the travelling distance we are talking about is huge … Don’t forget families who need to add two hours per flight, book accommodation, eat in Beijing, and come back home the same day. Also, local laws are very strict when it comes to people gathering, especially around the San Li Tun area [where most of the embassies are],” she explained.

Marija said diaspora voters had already faced various difficulties since the elections were announced.

“When we initially contacted the authorities about our request to vote abroad, we did not receive timely responses to our emails. In some cases, we had to wait a day or two for an answer. There were also significant delays concerning the documents we were supposed to receive from our local authorities in Serbia confirming we were eligible to vote outside the country, particularly here in China,” she said.

She said they had been expecting polling stations to be opened wherever at least 100 citizens had registered. However, only one polling station, in Beijing, was ultimately approved.

The same issue has emerged in Australia, where polling stations were approved only in Melbourne and Sydney, even though more than 100 Serbian voters have registered also in Perth and Brisbane.

Nemanja Djurovic told BIRN that voters from Brisbane have been directed to vote in Melbourne, even though Sydney is closer.

He added that the decision to open polling stations in only these two cities would result in many people not voting, as travel is a financial burden, and some citizens, like pregnant women, will not be able to take the flights that are necessary.

“The state is effectively slapping Serbian citizens living in Brisbane and Perth in the face. We are deeply disappointed and feel like second-class citizens because our rights are being openly ignored. The state is sending us a clear message that it does not want the diaspora to vote,” Nemanja said.

He added that the voting hours could significantly affect turnout in Australia, as polling there would take place from 5 p.m. on Sunday until 6 a.m. on Monday, when many people would already be preparing for work.

“Public transport stops running around midnight, while some bus services stop even earlier. This will significantly reduce turnout,” he predicted.

“The authorities want to prevent the first results coming from diaspora polling stations in the east from being negative for them,” he added.

World.title: Support for Young People in Croatia to Buy First Property Approved
World.content:
October the 6th, 2026 – 39 million euros in support measures have been approved for young people in Croatia to purchase their first property.

The Ministry of Physical Planning, Construction and State Property has announced that the Agency for Legal Transactions and Real Estate Brokerage (APN) received a total of 7,925 applications for tax refund on the purchase or construction of a first residential property by the 2nd of October 2026.

Poslovni reports that of the applications received, 6,561 have already been processed, 5,122 have been approved, 274 have been sent for additional documentation, while 1,165 applications have been rejected. Accordingly, a total payment of almost 39 million euros has been approved, while the average support per family amounts to 7,581 euros, the statement says.

This is a support measure intended for young citizens and families aimed at facilitating the resolution of the housing issue. The largest number of approved applications comes from the City of Zagreb (2,068), followed by Zagreb County (490), Split-Dalmatia County (487)… Among cities, Zagreb leads (2,068), followed by Split (282), Rijeka (214), Velika Gorica (167), Zadar (138), Osijek (131), Karlovac (101), Zaprešić (89), Solin (64), Varaždin (63), Slavonski Brod (61), Vinkovci (59), Pula (55), Samobor (54), Dugo Selo and Koprivnica (45), and Dubrovnik (42).

The average age of applicants is 32 years of age; the youngest are 18 and the oldest are 44 years of age. Regarding the size of the property, the average area is 72 square metres. The smallest property for which support was approved is located in Primorje-Gorski Kotar County and has 14 square metres, while the largest property by area, measuring 259 square metres, was recorded in Istria County. The average property price is 2,168 euros per square metre. The highest recorded price of 5,263 euros per square metre relates to a property in Dubrovnik-Neretva County, while the property with the lowest price, 83 euros per square metre, was purchased in Brod-Posavina County.

World.title: Incident at Split Airport: Air Serbia Plane Evacuated, Man Arrested
World.content:
October the 6th, 2026 – An unusual incident at Split Airport saw an Air Serbia plane bound for Belgrade evacuated and a man arrested.

Index reports that an incident occurred on an otherwise entirely normally scheduled Air Serbia aircraft that was due to take off for Belgrade yesterday afternoon. All passengers had to be evacuated on Monday afternoon at Split Airport due to a bomb threat. The police quickly arrived following the statement made by a man who then detained the passenger. The flight was scheduled for 15:20 but left only hours later.

Vinko Paić, one of the passengers on board the flight, described the bizarre situation on the aircraft. He said that several police officers entered the plane on the tarmac, some in uniform and some in civilian clothes. “Through the window I saw a police vehicle pull up next to the plane. They took out a grey-haired gentleman who was sitting in the 3rd or 4th row,” Paić explained. Since the passengers initially had absolutely no idea what was going on, Paić asked a flight attendant what it was about. She briefly replied: “He mentioned the word bomb.”

Paić added that several passengers left the aircraft of their own accord out of fear. Shortly afterwards, around 15:40, the pilot announced over the intercom that everyone had to leave for a security check of the aircraft. The police then thoroughly checked all of the passengers, all of their luggage and the entire aircraft. After no explosives were found, the aircraft was cleared for its flight from Split to Belgrade.
