World.title: Azerbaijan, Georgia discuss prospects for further bilateral cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. The prospects for further developing Azerbaijani-Georgian cooperation were discussed on October 6.

This was reported in a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

According to the Ministry, the discussion took place during a meeting between Jeyhun Bayramov, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan, and George Zakarashvili, the newly appointed Ambassador of Georgia to Azerbaijan.

Minister Jeyhun Bayramov congratulated the ambassador on his appointment and wished him success in his diplomatic efforts aimed at further strengthening relations between the two countries.

During the meeting, it was emphasized that the traditionally friendly and good-neighborly relations between Azerbaijan and Georgia, as well as the existing high-level ties, play an important role in advancing bilateral cooperation.

The meeting addressed the current state and prospects for further developing the partnership between Azerbaijan and Georgia, as well as economic and trade relations, energy security, transportation and communications projects, defense and security, and other areas of cooperation. It was emphasized that relations based on mutual trust are of particular importance for ensuring the stability and development of the region. The importance of mutual support within international organizations was also noted.

The parties noted the regional and global significance of joint projects in the energy and transportation sectors, including the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan Pipeline, the Southern Gas Corridor, the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars Railway, and the Middle Corridor, as well as “green energy” projects such as the undersea power cable in the Black Sea.

Minister Jeyhun Bayramov provided the ambassador with detailed information on the current situation in the region during the post-conflict period, the large-scale reconstruction efforts underway in the liberated territories, as well as the Azerbaijani-Armenian peace process and the normalization of relations.

Ambassador George Zakarashvili, expressing his gratitude for the warm welcome, emphasized that serving in this position is a great honor and responsibility for him. He stated that he would make every effort to further expand the strategic partnership between Georgia and Azerbaijan during his term of office.

The meeting also included an exchange of views on other bilateral and regional issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Kuwait's KPI discuss oil, gas, and aviation fuel cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. Kazakhstan's Ambassador to Kuwait Yerzhan Yelekeyev and Kuwait Petroleum International (KPI) President Shafi Taleb Al-Ajmi discussed potential areas for further practical cooperation during a meeting, Kazakhstan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

According to the Ministry, in the course of the meeting, the sides discussed prospects for bilateral cooperation in the oil and gas and petrochemical sectors.

Particular attention was paid to cooperation in aviation fuel, including potential engagement with Kazakh airlines and airports, as well as prospects for developing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The sides also considered cooperation in the retail sale of petroleum products, including the development of modern filling stations and related infrastructure in Kazakhstan, taking into account KPI's international experience under the Q8 brand.

Following the meeting, the sides agreed to continue working jointly on specific areas and projects of mutual interest, with the participation of relevant Kazakh organizations and companies.

Kuwait Petroleum International, established in 1983, is the international downstream arm of state-owned Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC) and operates under the Q8 brand.

The company operates in oil refining, petrochemicals, aviation fuel, and retail petroleum products. KPI's international retail network comprises more than 4,500 filling stations, including through joint ventures, and has a presence in Italy, Spain, Portugal, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Sweden and Vietnam.

KPI also participates in major oil refining and petrochemical projects in Italy, Vietnam, and Oman.

World.title: Aktau forum discusses Azerbaijan-Kazakhstan partnership prospects (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. The international forum “The Caspian Macroregion: The Architecture of Political Partnership Between Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan,” held in Aktau, discussed prospects for Azerbaijan-Kazakhstan partnership and continued with panel discussions.

This was reported by the State Commission for Diaspora Affairs.

In addition, it was reported that the panel discussions addressed the prospects for developing cooperation between Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan in the political, legal, transportation, and humanitarian spheres, as well as issues related to strengthening relations in the Caspian region.

The panel discussions were moderated by experts Eldar Jafarov, Emin Jabbarov, Elvin Talishinski, and Orkhan Yolchuyev.

The first panel, titled “Legal Foundations of Integration,” discussed the legal foundations of cooperation between the two countries, the role of universities in developing legal culture and public diplomacy, as well as issues related to the environmental safety of the Caspian Sea in the context of the development of the Middle Corridor.

During the second session, dedicated to “Transport Diplomacy and the Middle Corridor,” participants exchanged views on the geopolitical significance of the Caspian Sea, the role of transport diplomacy in regional cooperation, and the Middle Corridor’s contribution to strengthening ties between Central Asia and the South Caucasus.

The third session was devoted to the topic “The Role of the Diaspora and Public Diplomacy in Strengthening Azerbaijani-Kazakh Relations.” During the discussions, participants addressed issues of information and cultural diplomacy, the role of the diaspora, the shared historical and cultural values of the two countries, and the development of cooperation within the framework of the Organization of Turkic States.

At the end of the forum, participants were presented with certificates and a commemorative photo was taken.

Meanwhile, the event was held with the support of the State Committee for Diaspora Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan, organized by the Sh. Yessenov Khazar State University of Technology and Engineering and the “Azerbaijan Center” Public Foundation, with the support of the Consulate General of Azerbaijan in Aktau.

World.title: Former German spy chief arrested over alleged espionage and treason
World.content:
Former German foreign intelligence chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of attempted treason for allegedly paying to access secret documents and using them to prepare an analysis for a foreign spy service, federal prosecutors said.

Prosecutors did not identify the foreign intelligence service, and it was not immediately clear whether the analysis reached its intended recipient.

"Hanning is strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, obtaining state secrets, attempted treason and espionage," the prosecutor's office said in a statement.

Five years after his seven-year tenure as head of the BND intelligence service ended in 2005, Mr Hanning agreed with a former BND office manager to receive confidential intelligence information in exchange for payment, according to prosecutors.

The office manager, identified as Manfred D. in line with privacy rules, was also arrested on Tuesday and both were due to appear before a judge at the Federal Court of Justice.

'No compromises'

Prosecutors said Manfred D. is suspected of having supplied around 2,000 documents over the years, including classified material intended solely for internal use within the BND and senior-level intelligence briefings at the chancellery.

August Hanning was previously based at the BND headquarters in Berlin. (Reuters: Liesa Johannssen)

According to prosecutors, Mr Hanning used classified information supplied by D. to prepare an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service and for years shared political information with a representative of the spy agency.

According to information obtained by the SZ newspaper, the case does not involve Russia.

BND President Martin Jaeger said the agency had launched extensive internal investigations as soon as suspicions emerged, adding that "there can be no compromises on internal security".

Hanning did not respond to a request for comment from Reuters. The chancellery declined to comment.

Past spy scandals

Mr Hanning's arrest is the latest in a series of notorious espionage scandals in Germany.

West German Chancellor Willy Brandt was forced to resign in 1974 after it was revealed that an East German spy had worked as his close aide for nearly two years. In 1990, a senior West German counter-intelligence official was exposed for spying for East Germany throughout the 1980s and was later convicted of treason.

More recently, former domestic intelligence chief Hans-Georg Maassen said in 2024 he was now being monitored by the security agency he once ran over alleged right-wing political extremism, which he denied.

Reuters

World.title: De Minaur retires injured, handing China Open title to Djokovic
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has been left shattered by having to pull out injured from a thrilling China Open final duel with Novak Djokovic in Beijing after both men needed medical treatment.

Djokovic had just won a marathon first set in a tie break after 67 minutes in Tuesday's showdown when calling for the trainer for more treatment on his ongoing physical struggles.

Medvedev disqualified in Beijing Drama at the China Open as Daniil Medvedev is disqualified for hitting a spectator with a tennis ball, while Australia's Alex de Minaur reaches the final after his opponent retires due to injury.

But after he'd been treated on court, there was more surprise immediately afterwards as Australian No.1 de Minaur also required an off-court medical timeout for what appeared to be a groin injury.

De Minaur returned, his left thigh heavily strapped, only to play an excellent first game to hold serve in the second set but then glumly approached the net to shake hands with his Serbian opponent, explaining that he couldn't carry on.

It was a sad end to what had been a brilliant, lung-busting contest, with the amazing 39-year-old Djokovic claiming victory at 7-6 (7-3) 0-1 to claim the 102nd title of his career.

"I don't feel great ... I want to say sorry to all the amazing fans," said De Minaur at the trophy presentation.

"I didn't want to finish like this... hopefully see you next year," added the 27-year-old fifth seed.

An exhausted Djokovic also needed treatment during the break and was surprised when De Minaur signalled the end of the match.

Novak Djokovic won with a final score of 7-6 (7-3) 0-1 to claim the 102nd title of his career (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov)

"I'm really sorry for the way you had to finish today and I really hope that you can recover quickly," Djokovic told De Minaur.

"This year has been quite challenging for me, lots of ups and downs, physical and health issues," he added.

"So I just tried to find a good feeling on the court, and obviously I know that when I'm striking the ball well I can still compete at the highest level."

AAP/Reuters

World.title: 'No future': Thousands gather in France as high school protests continue
World.content:
Tens of thousands of demonstrators have been marching in cities across France in support of protests by school pupils demanding more education funding, increasing pressure on the government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.

In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs marked with "The state has killed national education" and other messages, in largely peaceful rallies.

In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march through the city.

But in Strasbourg, Lyon and Rennes, the demonstrations at times turned violent, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles.

The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Mr Macron's nearly decade-long tenure.

Students in Paris hold a banner which reads "We burn trash, you burn our future". (Reuters: Abdul Saboor)

In Nantes, thousands marched behind a huge banner that read: "Schools with no money, country with no future".

The Interior Ministry estimated that 86,000 people took part in demonstrations outside Paris on Tuesday morning, local time.

More were gathering in the capital for a protest scheduled for the afternoon.

More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,100 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.

The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France.

Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Mr Macron, who cannot run for a third consecutive term.

Against that backdrop, pupils' complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.

Riot police face high school students as they gather before a demonstration against under-resourced schools in Paris. (AP: Aurelien Morissard)

"You say 'young people are the future,' so listen to them," read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.

Ministry offers online portal for complaints

Some protesters have tipped rubbish bins and bicycles on their sides to create makeshift barricades.

Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police.

Classes were totally or partially suspended Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.

Riot police use water cannon as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Rennes. (AP: Jeremias Gonzalez)

Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Tuesday defended policing methods used against high schoolers, despite a growing list of gruesome injuries blamed on officers' riot-control weapons.

The latest was a 15-year-old boy who lost a hand on Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade.

Mr Nunez said the police response has been proportionate in "almost all cases".

The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fuelling defiance and angering some parents and teachers.

Mr Nunez said protests transformed at times into rioting, requiring police intervention.

He said 715 officers have been injured.

Student protests have drawn attention to rundown classrooms

Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centring on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools despite the promise of France's national motto: "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity".

Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats.

Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads.

French high school students' compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.

AP/AFP/Reuters

World.title: Customers' personal details may have been accessed in hack, Asos says
World.content:
Asos says customer's personal information may have been accessed through "unauthorised activity", hours after shoppers were sent a phone alert saying the online fashion retailer had been hacked.

Users of the Asos mobile app were sent an alarming phone notification on Tuesday night, with the headline "ASOS HACKED".

"We have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it," the message read.

Snowflake is a cloud-based data platform that companies, like Asos, use to store, process and analyse data including transactions.

The push notification users of the Asos app were sent on Tuesday night. (Supplied.)

Snowflake's website said it had more than 12,000 customers around the world.

Asos has apologised to those who received the "unauthorised" push notification and advised customers not to "click or engage with the link it contained".

"We're investigating the unauthorised activity and have taken immediate action to restrict access," the UK-based company said in a statement.

"Based on what we know at this stage, basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed.

"However, we do not believe that any payment-card information or account passwords have been impacted."

Asos said it was working with internal and external specialist advisors and relevant authorities to investigate the breach.

Asos' share price slumped more than 10 per cent on the London Stock Exchange following the alert.

ABC/AFP

World.title: Nobel Prize in Physics honours work on 'ghost messengers from space'
World.content:
Francis Halzen has won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole and his discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.

Born in Belgium, the 82-year-old scientist is affiliated with the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the US.

"This year's prize is about ghostly messengers from space," Ellen Moons, secretary general of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a news conference, on Tuesday morning, local time.

The Academy noted that Mr Halzen's "vision and scientific leadership" had been fundamental for the observatory, which it described as "a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors".

Using the observatory, researchers can capture neutrinos — rare subatomic particles — "from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe".

Trio win Nobel medicine prize for brain activity research The prize went to scientists working on the mechanisms the brain uses to switch the activity of individual nerve cells on or off.

"This Nobel Prize is about a giant ice cube positioned at the South Pole of our globe. The ice cube enables the detection of neutrinos," Professor Eva Olsson, a member of the Nobel Committee for Physics, told reporters.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor, ($1.718 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates, or an organisation.

"It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn't expect it," Mr Halzen told the news conference by telephone shortly after the prize was announced.

"But it's a great pleasure to hear about this prize."

Last year, three scientists won the Nobel Prize in Physics for research on the strange behaviour of subatomic particles called quantum tunnelling that enabled the ultra-sensitive measurements achieved by MRI machines and laid the groundwork for better cellphones and faster computers.

The announcements of this year's prizes began Monday, local time, with the Nobel Prize in Medicine being awarded to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.

This week, the awards for chemistry and literature will also be handed out.

The perhaps most keenly anticipated award — the Nobel Peace Prize — is due to be announced on Friday, local time.

AP/AFP

World.title: Nickel miner fined $810k over boilermaker's spinal injury
World.content:
A Canadian mining company has been fined $810,000 for safety failures that left a West Australian mine worker severely injured.

The man was working at the Ravensthorpe Nickel Mine, 500 kilometres south-east of Perth, in March 2023 when he was struck by an unsecured piece of equipment and suffered serious spinal injuries.

It is the latest in a string of work safety convictions for mine operator FQM Australia Nickel, a subsidiary of Canadian mining giant First Quantum Minerals, which faced the Albany Magistrates Court for sentencing on Tuesday.

The court heard the injured worker had started work at the mine as a mechanical boilermaker just 17 days prior to the incident.

He was carrying out maintenance on an industrial conveyor system, alongside two other workers, when he was hit by a heavy plant component known as a "Roman shield" and pinned in place.

The worker underwent spinal fusion surgery and 12 months of physiotherapy after the incident, and suffers from ongoing sleep and pain management issues.

FQM shuttered its mine on WA's south coast in October 2017 due to a fall in nickel prices. (AAP: Marion Rae)

The court heard one of the workers present was a supervisor, who had been in the position for three days.

The prosecutor with the Department of Local Government, Industry Regulation and Safety, Mark Blundell, said the collective lack of experience meant the risks were not identified, and FQM failed to instruct the workers to properly secure the component, warn them of the risks of uncontrolled movement, or tell them to stay clear of the line of fire.

"You have an allocated supervisor who, according to the company, is not qualified in [Job Hazard Analysis]," he said.

" It's damning on the accused's position, to compare the crew and the company's supervisor. "

'Worsening pattern of conduct'

Sentencing the company, Magistrate Rosemarie Myers said FQM's prior convictions had to be taken into account.

The company was fined $35,000 in 2020 after a ruptured tank spilled more than 10,000 litres of hot acidic slurry at the Ravensthorpe mine, mirroring a similar 2014 incident where a spill temporarily trapped three people in a control room at the site.

Later in 2025, FQM was fined $19,000 after a telehandler rolled, endangering two workers.

Mr Blundell urged the magistrate to consider the company's past conduct.

"When compared to the previous four convictions, this is worse," he said.

The Ravensthorpe nickel operation was once the biggest employer in the small coastal town but folded a year after the incident. (Andrea Hayward: AAP)

" The fine should ensure duty holders keep employees free of well-known hazards. "

Following the incident, FQM engaged a specialist safety consultant, introduced more comprehensive job hazard analyses, and enhanced training programs for new employees and supervisors.

The company has been ordered to pay more than $11,000 in costs.

The Ravensthorpe nickel operation was once the biggest employer in the small coastal town but folded a year after the incident, with fewer than 50 employees now left at the site under care and maintenance.

World.title: Veteran news anchor Richard Morecroft dies, aged 70
World.content:
Veteran news anchor Richard Morecroft has died, aged 70.

Morecroft presented ABC's NSW 7pm news bulletin from 1983 to 2002.

Before moving to Sydney, Morecroft presented the ABC News SA bulletin.

He also hosted Letters and Numbers on SBS, as well as popular children's current affairs show Behind the News on ABC.

A spokesperson confirmed the death on Tuesday night, saying Morecroft had died "at a time of his choosing, on the south coast of NSW".

"He was diagnosed with cancer earlier this year and was grateful to go peacefully, with his partner of 36 years, Alison Mackay, beside him," they said in an Instagram post.

"We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly."

Hundreds have paid tribute to Morecroft on social media, with Australian Story presenter Leigh Sales describing Morecroft as a "gentle man".

"He was pure class in every way," she said.

"I consider myself a lucky person indeed to have been his friend.

"I remember I started in the Sydney newsroom as a junior reporter ... and he went out of his way to welcome me ... touch base with me and to make sure that I was going OK.

" Just an absolutely divine human being. "

'A big loss'

Sales said Morecroft had been a "reassuring presence in people's homes" for decades.

"He was full of life, he adored nature, he loved art, he loved people, he was just kind and caring, through and through," she said.

She said she saw Morecroft about a month ago when he was "dealing with bad news in a very stoic way and dignified manner".

"It's just a big loss," she said.

ABC managing director Hugh Marks said Morecroft was "one of the great broadcasters of his generation".

"His intelligence, warmth and professionalism, beamed into homes across Australia for almost two decades, made him a trusted presence in the lives of Australians and an enduring part of the ABC's history," he said in a statement.

"Our thoughts are with his family, friends and former colleagues."

ABC NSW 7pm News presenter Jeremy Fernandez said Morecroft was in person "as affable, generous, and clever as he appeared on-air".

"Richard was a model of how to wear success and popularity with grace and humility," he said.

"He didn't let the business of news and media dim his love and enthusiasm for people, art, the environment, and the world.

"I’m so deeply saddened by his passing."

'The newsreader's newsreader'

Former ABC News Breakfast presenter Michael Rowland said Morecroft was one of his role models.

"I looked up to him enormously," he said.

"He was the newsreader's newsreader.

"When he said something, you absolutely believed him because it was heartfelt and that was something that he took with him until his final days.

"You put Richard Morecroft in front of a TV camera, and you didn't have to worry because he was the voice of authority.

"Whether he was presenting a serious news bulletin or hosting a quiz show, he was the man."

ABC Radio Sydney listeners also paid tribute to the popular presenter, with one saying they grew up watching Morecroft on television.

"I love the way he presented the news," the listener said.

"What a great guy he was."

World.title: Hundreds protest against Australia's largest defence expo in Perth
World.content:
More than 600 people have marched through Perth city to peacefully protest Australia's biggest land defence expo, which opened in the state capital today two years after violent clashes marred demonstrations against the same event in Melbourne.

Chanting anti-war slogans, protesters against the Land Forces event held various placards and signs that read "there is no future in war" and "warmongers not welcome".

Protesters at Yagan Square against the Land Forces Expo. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

The planned protest, held by 35 organisations, began in Yagan Square before marching to Elizabeth Quay, which is near where the expo is being held at the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre.

The demonstration was surrounded by a heavy police presence, with vans and other vehicles on stand-by.

WA Police have been given special powers as part of the security for the event. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

At the start of the march, Noongar elders held a traditional smoking ceremony, which was followed by a group of dancers performing a flash mob to Edwin Starr's famous anti-war anthem "War".

Dancers take part in the flash mob. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

'Choose peace'

Several Palestinian flags were held aloft, as well as signs criticising the military industry that included "Guns=Death" and "End arms trade with Israel".

"I think the world's at a crossroads. We've got to choose between peace and we've got to choose between war," said one protester, Paddy Cullen.

The protesters were critical of the expo and the military industry. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

"Just think of what 11 million dollars could have been put towards in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis," said demonstrator Danica Scott, referring to the extra $11.5 million given to police to provide security for the expo.

Will Shanahan is on the excluded persons list. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

Climate protester Will Shanahan, who is on the excluded persons list, said he attended the protest to highlight the overlap between military activity and environmental damage.

"The military is so destructive of the environment," they said.

A traditional smoking ceremony held at Yagan Square. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

Extra powers

The biennial Land Forces conference, featuring industry representatives from 60 countries, is being held between October 6 and 8 at Perth's Convention and Exhibition Centre, featuring almost 1,000 exhibiting organisations.

WA police were given 10 days of temporary extra powers for the event, which included the ability to ban "excluded persons" from the expo and its dedicated security zone outside the convention centre.

A new facial recognition system currently being trialled by WA police will likely be used to help enforce those bans.

In the lead-up to Land Forces, police deemed Greens staffer Matilda Lane-Rose an excluded person, but she was now permitted to enter the event's area for a "short window" on Tuesday to film content, after she lodged a complaint in the Supreme Court.

Police Minister Reece Whitby has described the police response as the "biggest police operation" in the state.

An armoured vehicle on display at Perth's Land Forces expo. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

When the expo was held in Melbourne in 2024, there were ugly scenes as protesters clashed with police.

Hundreds of officers were called in and 24 police members were injured, while dozens of protesters were arrested in Victoria's capital, where officers arrested people for offences like assault, obscuring or hindering police, arson and blocking roadways.

World.title: Demon was taking it up to Djokovic in the Beijing final. Then this happened
World.content:
SportTennisATP Tour Demon was taking it up to Djokovic in the Beijing final. Then this happened Marc McGowan October 7, 2026 — 1:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur’s bid to win a maiden Beijing title has ended suddenly – and in heartbreak – retiring one game into the second set of the final against Novak Djokovic with a groin injury. Djokovic, who extended his perfect Beijing tournament record to 34 matches with a seventh title in the Chinese capital on Tuesday night, edged out de Minaur in a 67-minute opening set that required a tiebreak to split them before both players took medical timeouts. Alex de Minaur congratulates Beijing champion Novak Djokovic after retiring from their final with an injury. AP Photo/Andy Wong The Serbian tennis legend, 39, received a massage on his diaphragm region, as he has several times throughout the week, before de Minaur left the court for his own treatment. It is believed the Australian world No.9 called for the trainer after losing the first point in the tiebreak.



Related Article ATP Tour Medvedev disqualified for hitting fan with ball, De Minaur reaches China final De Minaur returned with strapping high on his left leg, and his service speed was significantly down on resumption. He rolled in a serve then struck a forehand winner to hold, but instantly shook his head before crossing the net to shake Djokovic’s hand and end the contest while trailing 7-6 (7-3), 0-1. It was a shattering end to de Minaur’s week after a welcome return to form amid an up-and-down season, including early exits at Roland-Garros (third round) and the US Open (second round) as he fights to retain his top-10 ranking and secure a spot at the end-of-year ATP finals. He cut a forlorn figure during the post-match ceremony, apologising to the Beijing crowd for the abrupt ending to the final after both semi-finals also ended prematurely for contrasting reasons.



“I don’t feel great,” de Minaur said. “Look, first of all, congratulations to you [Djokovic], your team. It was pretty amazing, as a fan of the sport, to watch the tennis you produced this whole week, so I’m wishing you nothing but the best, so well done. De Minaur had produced a strong performance in the opening set pre-injury. Getty Images “As for me, I want to say sorry to all the amazing fans who came to watch this match. I didn’t want to finish like this, so I’m really sorry … it’s been a great week, and I’m sure there’s plenty more to come.” The unfortunate circumstances meant it was a subdued celebration for Djokovic, who captured the last of his Beijing titles 11 years ago, but played his best tennis in some time to defeat the likes of Alexander Zverev and Daniil Medvedev en route to the final.



Related Article Analysis

Tennis Australia Lleyton Hewitt says Australian tennis is struggling. Is he right? “I don’t think it happened ever in my career that I have semis and finals without finishing the match,” Djokovic said. “I want to celebrate because I think I’ve played one of the best weeks in the last couple of years. At the same time, he [de Minaur] retired the match at the beginning of the second, so it doesn’t feel right and respectful to jump around, and be joyful. “But deep inside, I’m very proud of this achievement. “It’s been a challenging year, and many times, I questioned whether I wanted to keep on playing this way, feeling this way on the court. This week has proven me wrong once again and given me a great confidence boost for the rest of the season.”



De Minaur started the event with long odds to qualify for the ATP finals in Turin, but resuscitated his hopes with gutsy three-set victories over Quentin Halys then Andrey Rublev that advanced him to the Beijing semi-finals. Hubert Hurkacz (adductor) then retired while a set and 3-2 down to de Minaur in their semi-final, while Djokovic booked the other final spot when Medvedev was defaulted for accidentally hitting a spectator with a ball. Alex de Minaur retired from his Beijing final against Novak Djokovic due to injury. Getty Images Medvedev will forfeit his prizemoney and 200 ranking points from the tournament as part of his sanction. That is relevant because only the top eight players qualify for Turin, with Medvedev (3020 points) in eighth, ahead of Djokovic (2830) and de Minaur (2690).



There is an extra spot up for grabs after world No.1 Jannik Sinner, who has not played since Wimbledon because of a knee injury, announced on Tuesday that he would not contest another tournament this year. “Me, together with the doctors, have decided that I need a course of treatment for my knee,” Sinner said in an Instagram video. As for de Minaur, it is unclear how serious his setback is. He infamously suffered a proximal adductor avulsion – a rare and severe groin and hip fibre cartilage tear, connected to the adductor – late in his fourth-round win over Arthur Fils at Wimbledon 2024 that resulted in him withdrawing before his quarter-final against Djokovic.



View post on X De Minaur played a strong first set in the Beijing final, and it took a remarkable Djokovic backhand passing shot winner to prevent the Australian going up a break in the fifth game. He played an uncharacteristically loose tiebreak, but that may have owed to his injury. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Cameron Green out of Durban Test, Connolly and Maddinson in duel for spot
World.content:
Updated SportCricketAustralian cricket Cameron Green out of Durban Test, Connolly and Maddinson in duel for spot Daniel Brettig Updated October 6, 2026 — 10:45pm ,first published 6:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Durban: Cameron Green is out of the first Test against South Africa and won’t be able to bowl for the entire series, opening the door for Cooper Connolly or Nic Maddinson for a possible call-up on what’s expected to be a turning pitch at Kingsmead this week. Head coach Andrew McDonald confirmed Green was out of the series opener on Tuesday night, after suffering an abdominal injury while batting in the ODI series. McDonald added that if Green did play in the remaining two Tests, it would be for his batting alone. Cooper Connolly celebrates scoring a one-day century for Australia in Bangladesh in June. AP Photo/Mosaraf Hossain “It is an odd one, it had our medical team scrambling,” McDonald said of Green’s abdominal strain suffered while batting, which is more common in tennis than cricket. “It’s not a rotational muscle, it’s a stabilising muscle … there is a path where he can play in this series. “We’d be solely focused on getting him to return as a batter, we wouldn’t be putting that demand on him to return as a bowler, I think that would be too high risk.”



Recently turning 23, Connolly has been a consistent presence in Australian squads over the past 18 months, granted multiple opportunities to learn – and to fail – in foreign conditions as he moulds his game. Connolly is likely up against the more seasoned Maddinson, 34, for a spot in the absence of Josh Inglis (broken finger). Selectors George Bailey and McDonald will thus have a clear choice between youth and experience. The pair took a first look at the surface on Tuesday. Andrew McDonald and George Bailey inspecting the pitch at Kingsmead on Tuesday. Daniel Brettig “If you look before [his cancer treatment], quality player, can bat at the top, can bat in the middle,” McDonald said of Maddinson. “We’re going to get challenged with spin, and those subcontinent tours we’ve had in the past, he’s been well and truly in our thoughts.



“It may not have been obvious for others, but we felt the player we needed to replace Josh Inglis, can bat at the top and bat in the middle.” Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Grave doubts for Green: Selection intrigue for Australia with all-rounder unlikely for first Test With his left-arm spin as a useful second string, Connolly has firm views about how he wants to play, and fellow left-hander Travis Head looms large in his thinking. “He’s unbelievable. Over the last couple of years, I’ve watched him play Test cricket, and he’s been that aggressive and changed games. And that’s something I want to be,” Connolly said. “There might be time and a place where the game is asking something else, but I watch him a little bit and try to understand how he goes about it. “We’re slightly different players, but that’s sort of how I want to approach my game. Similar to Trav, I want to take the game on. I want to score runs, I want to impose myself. I want to be aggressive. I want to put the bowlers back under pressure.



“Speaking to Trav over the last year and a bit, just understanding how he wants to go about it and how he thinks out there. I think Trav’s someone that stands out for me, how I want to play my game.” Connolly was just 21 when he made his Test debut in Sri Lanka in early 2025, and at the time he was still wrestling with how to handle spin bowling in the initial phase of his innings. He’s used those experiences to learn, beginning a routine of making regular batting notes at home in Perth before each assignment. “I’ll sit down at home in Perth ... and write down what I want to achieve out of this,” he said. “I first started it before the [2026] IPL because I’d obviously had a tough period before then. It was just [contemplating] what do I want to get out of this, whether I’m playing or not playing. How can I come back a better cricketer? “And if I play, what’s my method, and how do I want to do it? What are some key words that are going to help me approach every innings the same, so it’s not searching for things in every innings. It’s consistency throughout the whole series. Australians Cooper Connolly and Xavier Bartlett were able to share the taste of victory for Punjab in the IPL this year. AP



“I think I went in to Sri Lanka a little bit raw and trying to still play the same way, where it sometimes doesn’t work because it spins a little bit more, and you get beaten and stumped or something like that. Committing to a method, for me, in those conditions has been the big one.” Tellingly, the routine caught the interest of white-ball skipper Mitchell Marsh, who told Connolly he wished he had been similarly fastidious as a younger player. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket A year ago, Nic Maddinson was battling testicular cancer. Now he’s in line for a Test recall “‘Bison’ (Marsh) said to me ‘the one thing I regret is not writing down notes when I was your age because it’s something to look back on when things were going well’,” Connolly said. “Understanding that yeah, these things that you look back on and have helped you progress to the cricketer you are now, you look back and you go, OK, that’s how I played the game then, and you don’t lose that. “That’s probably the one thing that stood out when Bison said that to me. I was like, yeah, that’s not a bad idea, and I’ve already been doing it, but it’s just something that sort of needed a little bit of reinforcing to understand that the older guys actually wish they did it when they were younger.”



Like Steve Smith 15 years ago, Connolly understands that his spin bowling might help him in a tight selection squeeze, but maintains that ultimately it will be his batting that flourishes. “I see myself as a batting all-rounder,” he said. “I didn’t used to put a lot of time into it. I just thought left-arm spin was pretty easy, but there’s actually a bit more to spin bowling.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Tens of thousands protest housing crisis as Spain calls early election
World.content:
WorldEuropeSpain Tens of thousands protest housing crisis as Spain calls early election David Crowe October 6, 2026 — 9:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A rally over the cost of housing has turned into a violent protest on Spanish streets after masked demonstrators turned on police and set fire to cars and rubbish bins, one day after Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election amid widening social unrest. Protesters confronted police and lit fires in central Barcelona after 20,000 people gathered for a largely peaceful demonstration over the cost of housing, seen as a dominant issue for the November 29 parliamentary election. The protest came hours after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced an early general election. AP Photo/Emilio Morenatti Sanchez called the election on Sunday after the parliament rejected his proposed housing reforms – including rent caps – in the wake of large protests on housing when a landlord evicted an 87-year-old woman from her home. The violence in Barcelona on Monday highlighted the power of the protest movement after weeks of rallies and a stalemate in parliament over how to tackle housing shortages and rising rents.



While the protest organisers claimed 120,000 attended the gathering in Barcelona on Monday, the Guardia Urbana police estimated the crowd at about 20,000. The police said 30 officers were injured and 13 people were arrested. The violence erupted after many of the peaceful protestors had dispersed and activists stepped up their actions near the main thoroughfare in Barcelona, the Passeig de Gracia. News photographers on the scene witnessed some protestors waving banners for the POUM, the Workers Party of Marxist Unification, a party that traces its history to the Spanish Civil War of the 1930s. A protester holds a flag next to trash cans on fire during clashes with police following a demonstration over Spain’s housing crisis. AP Photo/Emilio Morenatti The city’s tenants union, Sindicat de Llogateres, organised the rally to call for a general strike over housing to force action by governments to reduce costs. Sanchez called the election with a promise to act on affordable housing, public services, and social rights.



“Spain must continue advancing, and for that, we need citizens to bolster our strength in parliament,” he said. “It’s time to mobilise. It’s time to fight. On November 29, we’re going to make history. Again.” Sanchez, the leader of the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, has ruled since 2018 and won several elections despite predictions of his defeat because of the rise of parties on the right. At the coming election, however, he begins the campaign lagging behind the People’s Party and its leader, Alberto Nunez Feijoo. The Sanchez government’s housing plans were rejected in parliament last Friday when opponents from the right blocked changes including rent caps and limits on purchasing real estate for corporations.



Tens of thousands of people joined the mass protest. AP Photo/Emilio Morenatti Feijoo and the People’s Party are promising an alternative plan that includes building 250,000 new homes a year and claiming this would help create 600,000 jobs. “If Spaniards give me their trust, my priority, my success, will be housing policy,” said Feijoo on Sunday. The People’s Party has about 33 per cent support and the Socialists have around 26 per cent support in recent polls. The Sanchez government is planning to go ahead with the housing policy changes despite the parliamentary setback, with moves on Tuesday in Madrid – late on Tuesday, AEST – to put them into force.



Culture Minister Ernest Urtasun said the decrees on housing would be sent for approval by a reduced body of caretaker legislators who remain in place after parliament was dissolved for the election. Related Article Housing crisis They broke down an 87-year-old’s door with a battering ram. Then Spain erupted The ⁠standing body of 69 members, when including lower ​house speaker Francina Armengol from Sanchez’s Socialist Party, has a ​slim majority in favour of the measures. The housing decrees would ​be implemented temporarily until a new parliament is formed, broadcaster TVE reported. The trigger for the unrest was the attempted eviction of 87-year-old ​Maricarmen Abascal in central Madrid last month after her building was bought by a real estate firm, setting off the concerns about corporate ownership.



Her case triggered nationwide protests and catapulted the issue ‌to the top of the agenda, even overshadowing immigration, which had dominated headlines for weeks following a mass migrant crossing in Ceuta. World.title: Behind the scenes at Perth’s most controversial expo
World.content:
Updated NationalWADefence Behind the scenes at Perth’s most controversial expo Hamish Hastie Updated October 6, 2026 — 9:24pm ,first published 3:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hundreds of people have marched through Perth’s CBD to protest Australia’s biggest defence expo, which opened at the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre on Tuesday. It is the first time the Land Forces expo has been held in WA, and is the first such event since the Victorian expo in 2024, where protesters clashed with police. Protesters march through Perth’s CBD on Tuesday evening. WAtoday Those ugly scenes triggered an extraordinary response from the Cook government ahead of this year’s event, including $11.5 million for security and a controversial act of parliament giving WA Police powers to ban activists from entering a security zone around the convention centre. Heavily armed public order police were concentrated on entrances to the convention centre and attendees were asked to show passes and IDs before entering the convention centre grounds.



About a half a dozen protesters holding upside-down red ensign flags gathered outside the security zone on Tuesday morning and were talked to by police. On Tuesday evening, a larger rally organised by the WA Anti-War Collective was held at Yagan Square, with hundreds of people gathering to hear from speakers including Greens MLC Sophie McNeill before marching down William Street to to Elizabeth Quay, just outside the security zone. Protesters are spoken to by police on Tuesday morning. Hamish Hastie Streets around the Perth CBD were brought to a standstill as the protesters moved down the central street, but the evening was largely incident-free, with organisers urging the crowd to remain peaceful and avoid anything that would get them arrested. Inside the event, some of the biggest defence companies in the world including Boeing and BAE Systems, are among the 964 exhibitors.



The Australian Army, Defence West and Department of Defence also have stands at the event, and the Chief of Army Symposium is being held concurrently in the Riverside Theatre. Related Article Opinion

Defence War is big business, but what about Perth’s small businesses? Kate Hulett Contributor A theme emerging within the expo is the prominence of autonomy and AI in defence technology. Thales, the makers of Australia’s famed Bushmaster vehicles, unveiled a remote and autonomous diesel-electric hybrid vehicle, the BladeHAUL. Australia has provided 120 Bushmasters to Ukraine, and Thales’ vice president lands, Andrew Downes, said the company drew inspiration from the unmanned warfare happening on the frontlines in the country’s war with Russia.



The BladeHAUL is a box that can carry up to 10 tonnes on top and is configured to easily fit a sea container. Downes said it could carry anything from a field hospital to long-range missiles, and had the capability of a Bushmaster but cost less than the $2-$3 million price tag for one of those. “It’s deliberately designed to be procured in mass because we know these platforms,” he said. CMAX Advisory’s Tyson Sara Hamish Hastie “You unfortunately do lose them in combat. The whole point of the exercise is to take humans out of harm’s way, so the price point is much cheaper than a vehicle like the Bushmaster, for example.”



Tyson Sara, from defence advisory group CMAX Advisory, brought over several weapons manufacturers to the event. Related Article Updated

Protests WA Greens staffer’s Land Forces ban overturned He said the immediate theme apparent from the expo revolved around AI an autonomy. “We’re seeing a lot of work in different platforms and different systems, different software that goes to that autonomy mission, and I think that’s probably a big underlying theme of what you’ll see around the show,” he said. Greens MP Sophie McNeill is one of the staunchest critics of the Cook Government’s support of the expo and the money spent on the security operation.



She attended the first day, which she said was to see what her taxpayers dollars were paying for. She said the event made her “feel ill”. “It is an event that is all about increasing militarisation in our world,” she said. “It is all about these massive corporations making huge profits to sell these weapons that kill people and as you walk around this show, there’s all this talk about investment opportunities and military capabilities, but there’s no talk of the reality of where this ends up,” she said. “I’ve seen what happens. I’ve seen the other side of these missiles.”



McNeill also called for event organisers to remove Israeli government-owned Rafael Advanced Defense Systems from the event. The MP will also speak at the protest in Yagan Square on Tuesday evening. McNeill’s staffer Matilda Lane-Rose, who is on WA Police’s exclusion list, entered the security zone on Tuesday morning to film social media content of McNeill’s attendance. Lane-Rose secured an exemption to her ban from the security zone on Monday after challenging it in the Supreme Court. The exemption allowed Lane-Rose, a climate activist who was fined last year for her involvement in a protest outside former Woodside boss Meg O’Neill’s home, to enter the security zone from 8am to 6pm on Tuesday.



Lane-Rose intends to pursue the ban in the Supreme Court, but her matter won’t be heard until next week after the expo has concluded. Sara, who also attended the Victorian expo in 2024, said protest was part and parcel of the nature of defence and the military. “I think everyone wishes that there wasn’t a need to have to use armed force in the defence of our interests,” he said. “But one of the features of a democracy is that you need to defend it, and one of the features of a democracy is that you’re allowed to say what you like about that.”

World.title: Some of Brisbane’s best ribbony, hand-slapped noodles head northside
World.content:
Eating outFood Some of Brisbane’s best ribbony, hand-slapped noodles head northside These thick, chilli oil-coated noodles have been a Sunnybank hit. Now they’re in Chermside too, along with flaky, perfectly baked Chinese pork burgers. Matt Shea October 6, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Amy Huy wants to tell you about Xi’an. She wants to tell you about its opera and its Terracotta Army, and its 14-kilometre Ming Dynasty-era city wall. She produces a phone and swipes to a promotional video of the city, the capital of Shaanxi province in China’s north. She and husband Boqiao Li used to live there, she says pointing – that neighbourhood, just there. Terrific Noodles’ striking frontage sticks out at Westfield Chermside. Markus Ravik “Xi’an has more than 3000 years of history,” Yu says. “It’s the origin of the Silk Road … Beijing only had five dynasties, Xi’an had 13. We are so proud of this city.” Every ounce of that enthusiasm seems to have been channelled into Terrific Noodles. First it was Sunnybank, with a restaurant at Market Square that opened three years ago. Now it’s on the other side of town in Chermside.



Related Article 14.5 / 20 Review The laneway contender for Brisbane’s most underrated restaurant It’s decked out with vibrant murals by a Xi’an artist and gallery owner Yu refers to as Mr Ma, and an enormous front window that allows passers-by to gawk at the chefs as they slap their thick biang biang noodle dough on the kitchen counter. The restaurant is basically two people transforming a longing for their hometown into a celebration for Brisbane diners. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up The Market Square restaurant, despite a slow first few months, has been an enormous hit – head there at peak time and good luck getting a table (although they tend to turn over very fast), with punters drawn by the noodle dishes’ big portions and big flavours, as well as generously stuffed, super-flaky rou jia mo (Chinese pork burgers). The Chermside restaurant features a larger internal dining room compared to the Sunnybank original. Markus Ravik It was a Westfield leasing executive who reached out to Huy and Li about a second store, but at Garden City rather than Chermside.



“I felt [Garden City] was too close to Sunnybank,” Huy says. “I thought, ‘if we’re going to open a second store, it must be north’. We wanted to introduce our food to a new audience up here.” Terrific Noodles feels like the latest in a new wave of tenants designed to underscore Chermside’s credentials as a food destination. In the past two years it’s also welcomed a David’s Noodle & Hotpot and a Scugnizzi, although the latter was short-lived. Braised beef noodle soup. Markus Ravik Huy says the restaurant has been busy since soft launching towards the end of September, and particularly since its official opening in early October. Walking through the door are both newcomers to Xi’an cuisine and homesick migrants. “[Li] is so stubborn,” Huy says. “He said he wasn’t going to adapt any flavours: ‘I can introduce other [flavours] to suit people’s expectations, but traditional is traditional’. People can tell – it’s real, from Xi’an. I’ve had a few people speak to me in the local dialect and say they’ve never tried anything in Brisbane this authentic.”



The restaurant features a wide selection of rou jia mo. Markus Ravik The menu at the Chermside restaurant is mostly the same as the Sunnybank original, split into noodle soups, dry noodle dishes, cold noodle dishes, a bunch of rou jia mo, and a selection of cold sides. The portions are, as usual, huge. Soups include a golden noodle soup with beef brisket and Chinese sauerkraut, a spicy and sour beef noodle soup, and a pork bone broth noodle soup. Noodles with pork mince, tomato and chopped vegetables. Markus Ravik There’s a stack of options on the biang biang dry noodles menu, including braised beef rib; sauteed chicken; mash potato, pork mince and sauce; and chilli with pork mince.



And the cold noodle dishes include noodles with sesame sauce; noodles with shredded chicken, cucumber in a chilli and sesame sauce; and cold noodles with a special chilli oil. Terrific’s hand-prepared noodles come thick and glossed in chilli oil. Markus Ravik By far the most popular noodles across the menu are the wheat-based biang biang noodles, but there are also spinach biang biang noodles, thinner hand-pulled noodles, and vermicelli. Dumplings will be added to the menu in the coming weeks. The restaurant has been an enormous hit since opening this month. Markus Ravik



Drinks are the same straightforward selection of sodas and juice variations that regulars will know from Market Square, and includes an Ice Peak tangerine soda imported from Xi’an. There’s also a seasonally rotating selection of sparkling sodas, which currently include grapefruit and lychee flavours. “I really love Australian diners because they are so open to different cultures,” Huy says. “Like, some of the pho in Brisbane is just as good as Vietnam. Boqiao and I went back to Xi’an recently and ordered cold noodles – my favourite as a child – and I feel like ours is just as good, so we’re very proud.” Open daily 11am-9pm Shop FC611, Level 2, Westfield Chermside, Gympie Road, Chermside instagram.com/terrificnoodles

World.title: Veteran ABC newsreader Richard Morecroft dies aged 70
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCancer Veteran ABC newsreader Richard Morecroft dies aged 70 Emily Kaine and Aine Ryan Updated October 6, 2026 — 9:10pm ,first published 8:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former ABC newsreader Richard Morecroft has died at the age of 70 following a cancer diagnosis. The veteran reporter anchored the ABC’s nightly NSW news bulletin for nearly two decades from the 1980s to the early 2000s. “Sadly, our beloved Richard died today, at a time of his choosing, on the South Coast of NSW,” a statement shared on his Instagram account said. Richard Morecroft alongside his partner Alison Mackay in 2022. Fairfax Media “He was diagnosed with cancer earlier this year and was grateful to go peacefully, with his partner of 36 years, Alison Mackay, beside him. We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly.” Morecroft moved from England to Adelaide with his family at the age of 10. He studied English and drama at the University of Adelaide and worked at the university’s radio station before landing a job at the ABC.



Richard Morecroft pictured in May of 1983. Paul Wright/Fairfax Media He presented the Adelaide News bulletin before hosting ABC News NSW from 1983 until 2002. Morecroft also hosted the quiz show Letters and Numbers on SBS between 2010 and 2012. His career spanned more than 20 years, including reporting stints in Canberra. He was also a staunch environmental activist and was a long-time trustee for the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), a governor of the Taronga Foundation and a director of the Zoological Parks Board of NSW. Morecroft was also an acclaimed landscape photographer. His work hangs on the walls of Parliament House in Canberra.



He met his long-term partner, Alison Mackay, in Far North Queensland in 1990 while he was on holiday at Cape Tribulation. They kept in touch through handwritten fountain-pen letters for two years before Mackay moved to Sydney. Morecroft had shared updates on his Instagram account earlier in the year about his long stay in the Chris O’Brien Lifehouse in Sydney for cancer treatment. Tributes have already started to flow in from veteran news presenters who worked alongside Morecroft at the ABC, including Leigh Sales and Michael Rowland. Related Article Good Weekend How former TV presenter Richard Morecroft found love through a fountain pen “The best way I can describe Richard is that he was a gentleman, and a gentle man. He was pure class in every way - a kind, warm and generous colleague, as well as being a consummate professional. I had so much admiration and regard for him and I consider myself a lucky person indeed to have been his friend,” Sales wrote in a comment on the Instagram post.



Rowland added: “I’m so sorry to hear this. Richard was a superb newsreader and a lovely man. My condolences to Alison and the rest of Richard’s family and friends.” ABC News presenter Joe O’Brien, in a post on social media, said: “Richard set the respected standard for others to follow. And more importantly was a warm, encouraging guy too.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Demon was taking it up to Djokovic in the Beijing final. Then this happened
World.content:
SportTennisATP Tour Demon was taking it up to Djokovic in the Beijing final. Then this happened Marc McGowan October 7, 2026 — 1:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur’s bid to win a maiden Beijing title has ended suddenly – and in heartbreak – retiring one game into the second set of the final against Novak Djokovic with a groin injury. Djokovic, who extended his perfect Beijing tournament record to 34 matches with a seventh title in the Chinese capital on Tuesday night, edged out de Minaur in a 67-minute opening set that required a tiebreak to split them before both players took medical timeouts. Alex de Minaur congratulates Beijing champion Novak Djokovic after retiring from their final with an injury. AP Photo/Andy Wong The Serbian tennis legend, 39, received a massage on his diaphragm region, as he has several times throughout the week, before de Minaur left the court for his own treatment. It is believed the Australian world No.9 called for the trainer after losing the first point in the tiebreak.



Related Article ATP Tour Medvedev disqualified for hitting fan with ball, De Minaur reaches China final De Minaur returned with strapping high on his left leg, and his service speed was significantly down on resumption. He rolled in a serve then struck a forehand winner to hold, but instantly shook his head before crossing the net to shake Djokovic’s hand and end the contest while trailing 7-6 (7-3), 0-1. It was a shattering end to de Minaur’s week after a welcome return to form amid an up-and-down season, including early exits at Roland-Garros (third round) and the US Open (second round) as he fights to retain his top-10 ranking and secure a spot at the end-of-year ATP finals. He cut a forlorn figure during the post-match ceremony, apologising to the Beijing crowd for the abrupt ending to the final after both semi-finals also ended prematurely for contrasting reasons.



“I don’t feel great,” de Minaur said. “Look, first of all, congratulations to you [Djokovic], your team. It was pretty amazing, as a fan of the sport, to watch the tennis you produced this whole week, so I’m wishing you nothing but the best, so well done. De Minaur had produced a strong performance in the opening set pre-injury. Getty Images “As for me, I want to say sorry to all the amazing fans who came to watch this match. I didn’t want to finish like this, so I’m really sorry … it’s been a great week, and I’m sure there’s plenty more to come.” The unfortunate circumstances meant it was a subdued celebration for Djokovic, who captured the last of his Beijing titles 11 years ago, but played his best tennis in some time to defeat the likes of Alexander Zverev and Daniil Medvedev en route to the final.



Related Article Analysis

Tennis Australia Lleyton Hewitt says Australian tennis is struggling. Is he right? “I don’t think it happened ever in my career that I have semis and finals without finishing the match,” Djokovic said. “I want to celebrate because I think I’ve played one of the best weeks in the last couple of years. At the same time, he [de Minaur] retired the match at the beginning of the second, so it doesn’t feel right and respectful to jump around, and be joyful. “But deep inside, I’m very proud of this achievement. “It’s been a challenging year, and many times, I questioned whether I wanted to keep on playing this way, feeling this way on the court. This week has proven me wrong once again and given me a great confidence boost for the rest of the season.”



De Minaur started the event with long odds to qualify for the ATP finals in Turin, but resuscitated his hopes with gutsy three-set victories over Quentin Halys then Andrey Rublev that advanced him to the Beijing semi-finals. Hubert Hurkacz (adductor) then retired while a set and 3-2 down to de Minaur in their semi-final, while Djokovic booked the other final spot when Medvedev was defaulted for accidentally hitting a spectator with a ball. Alex de Minaur retired from his Beijing final against Novak Djokovic due to injury. Getty Images Medvedev will forfeit his prizemoney and 200 ranking points from the tournament as part of his sanction. That is relevant because only the top eight players qualify for Turin, with Medvedev (3020 points) in eighth, ahead of Djokovic (2830) and de Minaur (2690).



There is an extra spot up for grabs after world No.1 Jannik Sinner, who has not played since Wimbledon because of a knee injury, announced on Tuesday that he would not contest another tournament this year. “Me, together with the doctors, have decided that I need a course of treatment for my knee,” Sinner said in an Instagram video. As for de Minaur, it is unclear how serious his setback is. He infamously suffered a proximal adductor avulsion – a rare and severe groin and hip fibre cartilage tear, connected to the adductor – late in his fourth-round win over Arthur Fils at Wimbledon 2024 that resulted in him withdrawing before his quarter-final against Djokovic.



View post on X De Minaur played a strong first set in the Beijing final, and it took a remarkable Djokovic backhand passing shot winner to prevent the Australian going up a break in the fifth game. He played an uncharacteristically loose tiebreak, but that may have owed to his injury. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.
