World.title: Cameron Green out of Durban Test, Connolly and Maddinson in duel for spot
World.content:
Updated SportCricketAustralian cricket Cameron Green out of Durban Test, Connolly and Maddinson in duel for spot Daniel Brettig Updated October 6, 2026 — 10:45pm ,first published 6:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Durban: Cameron Green is out of the first Test against South Africa and won’t be able to bowl for the entire series, opening the door for Cooper Connolly or Nic Maddinson for a possible call-up on what’s expected to be a turning pitch at Kingsmead this week. Head coach Andrew McDonald confirmed Green was out of the series opener on Tuesday night, after suffering an abdominal injury while batting in the ODI series. McDonald added that if Green did play in the remaining two Tests, it would be for his batting alone. Cooper Connolly celebrates scoring a one-day century for Australia in Bangladesh in June. AP Photo/Mosaraf Hossain “It is an odd one, it had our medical team scrambling,” McDonald said of Green’s abdominal strain suffered while batting, which is more common in tennis than cricket. “It’s not a rotational muscle, it’s a stabilising muscle … there is a path where he can play in this series. “We’d be solely focused on getting him to return as a batter, we wouldn’t be putting that demand on him to return as a bowler, I think that would be too high risk.”



Recently turning 23, Connolly has been a consistent presence in Australian squads over the past 18 months, granted multiple opportunities to learn – and to fail – in foreign conditions as he moulds his game. Connolly is likely up against the more seasoned Maddinson, 34, for a spot in the absence of Josh Inglis (broken finger). Selectors George Bailey and McDonald will thus have a clear choice between youth and experience. The pair took a first look at the surface on Tuesday. Andrew McDonald and George Bailey inspecting the pitch at Kingsmead on Tuesday. Daniel Brettig “If you look before [his cancer treatment], quality player, can bat at the top, can bat in the middle,” McDonald said of Maddinson. “We’re going to get challenged with spin, and those subcontinent tours we’ve had in the past, he’s been well and truly in our thoughts.



“It may not have been obvious for others, but we felt the player we needed to replace Josh Inglis, can bat at the top and bat in the middle.” Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Grave doubts for Green: Selection intrigue for Australia with all-rounder unlikely for first Test With his left-arm spin as a useful second string, Connolly has firm views about how he wants to play, and fellow left-hander Travis Head looms large in his thinking. “He’s unbelievable. Over the last couple of years, I’ve watched him play Test cricket, and he’s been that aggressive and changed games. And that’s something I want to be,” Connolly said. “There might be time and a place where the game is asking something else, but I watch him a little bit and try to understand how he goes about it. “We’re slightly different players, but that’s sort of how I want to approach my game. Similar to Trav, I want to take the game on. I want to score runs, I want to impose myself. I want to be aggressive. I want to put the bowlers back under pressure.



“Speaking to Trav over the last year and a bit, just understanding how he wants to go about it and how he thinks out there. I think Trav’s someone that stands out for me, how I want to play my game.” Connolly was just 21 when he made his Test debut in Sri Lanka in early 2025, and at the time he was still wrestling with how to handle spin bowling in the initial phase of his innings. He’s used those experiences to learn, beginning a routine of making regular batting notes at home in Perth before each assignment. “I’ll sit down at home in Perth ... and write down what I want to achieve out of this,” he said. “I first started it before the [2026] IPL because I’d obviously had a tough period before then. It was just [contemplating] what do I want to get out of this, whether I’m playing or not playing. How can I come back a better cricketer? “And if I play, what’s my method, and how do I want to do it? What are some key words that are going to help me approach every innings the same, so it’s not searching for things in every innings. It’s consistency throughout the whole series. Australians Cooper Connolly and Xavier Bartlett were able to share the taste of victory for Punjab in the IPL this year. AP



“I think I went in to Sri Lanka a little bit raw and trying to still play the same way, where it sometimes doesn’t work because it spins a little bit more, and you get beaten and stumped or something like that. Committing to a method, for me, in those conditions has been the big one.” Tellingly, the routine caught the interest of white-ball skipper Mitchell Marsh, who told Connolly he wished he had been similarly fastidious as a younger player. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket A year ago, Nic Maddinson was battling testicular cancer. Now he’s in line for a Test recall “‘Bison’ (Marsh) said to me ‘the one thing I regret is not writing down notes when I was your age because it’s something to look back on when things were going well’,” Connolly said. “Understanding that yeah, these things that you look back on and have helped you progress to the cricketer you are now, you look back and you go, OK, that’s how I played the game then, and you don’t lose that. “That’s probably the one thing that stood out when Bison said that to me. I was like, yeah, that’s not a bad idea, and I’ve already been doing it, but it’s just something that sort of needed a little bit of reinforcing to understand that the older guys actually wish they did it when they were younger.”



Like Steve Smith 15 years ago, Connolly understands that his spin bowling might help him in a tight selection squeeze, but maintains that ultimately it will be his batting that flourishes. “I see myself as a batting all-rounder,” he said. “I didn’t used to put a lot of time into it. I just thought left-arm spin was pretty easy, but there’s actually a bit more to spin bowling.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Tens of thousands protest housing crisis as Spain calls early election
World.content:
WorldEuropeSpain Tens of thousands protest housing crisis as Spain calls early election David Crowe October 6, 2026 — 9:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A rally over the cost of housing has turned into a violent protest on Spanish streets after masked demonstrators turned on police and set fire to cars and rubbish bins, one day after Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election amid widening social unrest. Protesters confronted police and lit fires in central Barcelona after 20,000 people gathered for a largely peaceful demonstration over the cost of housing, seen as a dominant issue for the November 29 parliamentary election. The protest came hours after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced an early general election. AP Photo/Emilio Morenatti Sanchez called the election on Sunday after the parliament rejected his proposed housing reforms – including rent caps – in the wake of large protests on housing when a landlord evicted an 87-year-old woman from her home. The violence in Barcelona on Monday highlighted the power of the protest movement after weeks of rallies and a stalemate in parliament over how to tackle housing shortages and rising rents.



While the protest organisers claimed 120,000 attended the gathering in Barcelona on Monday, the Guardia Urbana police estimated the crowd at about 20,000. The police said 30 officers were injured and 13 people were arrested. The violence erupted after many of the peaceful protestors had dispersed and activists stepped up their actions near the main thoroughfare in Barcelona, the Passeig de Gracia. News photographers on the scene witnessed some protestors waving banners for the POUM, the Workers Party of Marxist Unification, a party that traces its history to the Spanish Civil War of the 1930s. A protester holds a flag next to trash cans on fire during clashes with police following a demonstration over Spain’s housing crisis. AP Photo/Emilio Morenatti The city’s tenants union, Sindicat de Llogateres, organised the rally to call for a general strike over housing to force action by governments to reduce costs. Sanchez called the election with a promise to act on affordable housing, public services, and social rights.



“Spain must continue advancing, and for that, we need citizens to bolster our strength in parliament,” he said. “It’s time to mobilise. It’s time to fight. On November 29, we’re going to make history. Again.” Sanchez, the leader of the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, has ruled since 2018 and won several elections despite predictions of his defeat because of the rise of parties on the right. At the coming election, however, he begins the campaign lagging behind the People’s Party and its leader, Alberto Nunez Feijoo. The Sanchez government’s housing plans were rejected in parliament last Friday when opponents from the right blocked changes including rent caps and limits on purchasing real estate for corporations.



Tens of thousands of people joined the mass protest. AP Photo/Emilio Morenatti Feijoo and the People’s Party are promising an alternative plan that includes building 250,000 new homes a year and claiming this would help create 600,000 jobs. “If Spaniards give me their trust, my priority, my success, will be housing policy,” said Feijoo on Sunday. The People’s Party has about 33 per cent support and the Socialists have around 26 per cent support in recent polls. The Sanchez government is planning to go ahead with the housing policy changes despite the parliamentary setback, with moves on Tuesday in Madrid – late on Tuesday, AEST – to put them into force.



Culture Minister Ernest Urtasun said the decrees on housing would be sent for approval by a reduced body of caretaker legislators who remain in place after parliament was dissolved for the election. Related Article Housing crisis They broke down an 87-year-old’s door with a battering ram. Then Spain erupted The ⁠standing body of 69 members, when including lower ​house speaker Francina Armengol from Sanchez’s Socialist Party, has a ​slim majority in favour of the measures. The housing decrees would ​be implemented temporarily until a new parliament is formed, broadcaster TVE reported. The trigger for the unrest was the attempted eviction of 87-year-old ​Maricarmen Abascal in central Madrid last month after her building was bought by a real estate firm, setting off the concerns about corporate ownership.



Her case triggered nationwide protests and catapulted the issue ‌to the top of the agenda, even overshadowing immigration, which had dominated headlines for weeks following a mass migrant crossing in Ceuta. With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Behind the scenes at Perth’s most controversial expo
World.content:
Updated NationalWADefence Behind the scenes at Perth’s most controversial expo Hamish Hastie Updated October 6, 2026 — 9:24pm ,first published 3:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hundreds of people have marched through Perth’s CBD to protest Australia’s biggest defence expo, which opened at the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre on Tuesday. It is the first time the Land Forces expo has been held in WA, and is the first such event since the Victorian expo in 2024, where protesters clashed with police. Protesters march through Perth’s CBD on Tuesday evening. WAtoday Those ugly scenes triggered an extraordinary response from the Cook government ahead of this year’s event, including $11.5 million for security and a controversial act of parliament giving WA Police powers to ban activists from entering a security zone around the convention centre. Heavily armed public order police were concentrated on entrances to the convention centre and attendees were asked to show passes and IDs before entering the convention centre grounds.



About a half a dozen protesters holding upside-down red ensign flags gathered outside the security zone on Tuesday morning and were talked to by police. On Tuesday evening, a larger rally organised by the WA Anti-War Collective was held at Yagan Square, with hundreds of people gathering to hear from speakers including Greens MLC Sophie McNeill before marching down William Street to to Elizabeth Quay, just outside the security zone. Protesters are spoken to by police on Tuesday morning. Hamish Hastie Streets around the Perth CBD were brought to a standstill as the protesters moved down the central street, but the evening was largely incident-free, with organisers urging the crowd to remain peaceful and avoid anything that would get them arrested. Inside the event, some of the biggest defence companies in the world including Boeing and BAE Systems, are among the 964 exhibitors.



The Australian Army, Defence West and Department of Defence also have stands at the event, and the Chief of Army Symposium is being held concurrently in the Riverside Theatre. Related Article Opinion

Defence War is big business, but what about Perth’s small businesses? Kate Hulett Contributor A theme emerging within the expo is the prominence of autonomy and AI in defence technology. Thales, the makers of Australia’s famed Bushmaster vehicles, unveiled a remote and autonomous diesel-electric hybrid vehicle, the BladeHAUL. Australia has provided 120 Bushmasters to Ukraine, and Thales’ vice president lands, Andrew Downes, said the company drew inspiration from the unmanned warfare happening on the frontlines in the country’s war with Russia.



The BladeHAUL is a box that can carry up to 10 tonnes on top and is configured to easily fit a sea container. Downes said it could carry anything from a field hospital to long-range missiles, and had the capability of a Bushmaster but cost less than the $2-$3 million price tag for one of those. “It’s deliberately designed to be procured in mass because we know these platforms,” he said. CMAX Advisory’s Tyson Sara Hamish Hastie “You unfortunately do lose them in combat. The whole point of the exercise is to take humans out of harm’s way, so the price point is much cheaper than a vehicle like the Bushmaster, for example.”



Tyson Sara, from defence advisory group CMAX Advisory, brought over several weapons manufacturers to the event. Related Article Updated

Protests WA Greens staffer’s Land Forces ban overturned He said the immediate theme apparent from the expo revolved around AI an autonomy. “We’re seeing a lot of work in different platforms and different systems, different software that goes to that autonomy mission, and I think that’s probably a big underlying theme of what you’ll see around the show,” he said. Greens MP Sophie McNeill is one of the staunchest critics of the Cook Government’s support of the expo and the money spent on the security operation.



She attended the first day, which she said was to see what her taxpayers dollars were paying for. She said the event made her “feel ill”. “It is an event that is all about increasing militarisation in our world,” she said. “It is all about these massive corporations making huge profits to sell these weapons that kill people and as you walk around this show, there’s all this talk about investment opportunities and military capabilities, but there’s no talk of the reality of where this ends up,” she said. “I’ve seen what happens. I’ve seen the other side of these missiles.”



McNeill also called for event organisers to remove Israeli government-owned Rafael Advanced Defense Systems from the event. The MP will also speak at the protest in Yagan Square on Tuesday evening. McNeill’s staffer Matilda Lane-Rose, who is on WA Police’s exclusion list, entered the security zone on Tuesday morning to film social media content of McNeill’s attendance. Lane-Rose secured an exemption to her ban from the security zone on Monday after challenging it in the Supreme Court. The exemption allowed Lane-Rose, a climate activist who was fined last year for her involvement in a protest outside former Woodside boss Meg O’Neill’s home, to enter the security zone from 8am to 6pm on Tuesday.



Lane-Rose intends to pursue the ban in the Supreme Court, but her matter won’t be heard until next week after the expo has concluded. Sara, who also attended the Victorian expo in 2024, said protest was part and parcel of the nature of defence and the military. “I think everyone wishes that there wasn’t a need to have to use armed force in the defence of our interests,” he said. “But one of the features of a democracy is that you need to defend it, and one of the features of a democracy is that you’re allowed to say what you like about that.”

World.title: Some of Brisbane’s best ribbony, hand-slapped noodles head northside
World.content:
Eating outFood Some of Brisbane’s best ribbony, hand-slapped noodles head northside These thick, chilli oil-coated noodles have been a Sunnybank hit. Now they’re in Chermside too, along with flaky, perfectly baked Chinese pork burgers. Matt Shea October 6, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Amy Huy wants to tell you about Xi’an. She wants to tell you about its opera and its Terracotta Army, and its 14-kilometre Ming Dynasty-era city wall. She produces a phone and swipes to a promotional video of the city, the capital of Shaanxi province in China’s north. She and husband Boqiao Li used to live there, she says pointing – that neighbourhood, just there. Terrific Noodles’ striking frontage sticks out at Westfield Chermside. Markus Ravik “Xi’an has more than 3000 years of history,” Yu says. “It’s the origin of the Silk Road … Beijing only had five dynasties, Xi’an had 13. We are so proud of this city.” Every ounce of that enthusiasm seems to have been channelled into Terrific Noodles. First it was Sunnybank, with a restaurant at Market Square that opened three years ago. Now it’s on the other side of town in Chermside.



Related Article 14.5 / 20 Review The laneway contender for Brisbane’s most underrated restaurant It’s decked out with vibrant murals by a Xi’an artist and gallery owner Yu refers to as Mr Ma, and an enormous front window that allows passers-by to gawk at the chefs as they slap their thick biang biang noodle dough on the kitchen counter. The restaurant is basically two people transforming a longing for their hometown into a celebration for Brisbane diners. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up The Market Square restaurant, despite a slow first few months, has been an enormous hit – head there at peak time and good luck getting a table (although they tend to turn over very fast), with punters drawn by the noodle dishes’ big portions and big flavours, as well as generously stuffed, super-flaky rou jia mo (Chinese pork burgers). The Chermside restaurant features a larger internal dining room compared to the Sunnybank original. Markus Ravik It was a Westfield leasing executive who reached out to Huy and Li about a second store, but at Garden City rather than Chermside.



“I felt [Garden City] was too close to Sunnybank,” Huy says. “I thought, ‘if we’re going to open a second store, it must be north’. We wanted to introduce our food to a new audience up here.” Terrific Noodles feels like the latest in a new wave of tenants designed to underscore Chermside’s credentials as a food destination. In the past two years it’s also welcomed a David’s Noodle & Hotpot and a Scugnizzi, although the latter was short-lived. Braised beef noodle soup. Markus Ravik Huy says the restaurant has been busy since soft launching towards the end of September, and particularly since its official opening in early October. Walking through the door are both newcomers to Xi’an cuisine and homesick migrants. “[Li] is so stubborn,” Huy says. “He said he wasn’t going to adapt any flavours: ‘I can introduce other [flavours] to suit people’s expectations, but traditional is traditional’. People can tell – it’s real, from Xi’an. I’ve had a few people speak to me in the local dialect and say they’ve never tried anything in Brisbane this authentic.”



The restaurant features a wide selection of rou jia mo. Markus Ravik The menu at the Chermside restaurant is mostly the same as the Sunnybank original, split into noodle soups, dry noodle dishes, cold noodle dishes, a bunch of rou jia mo, and a selection of cold sides. The portions are, as usual, huge. Soups include a golden noodle soup with beef brisket and Chinese sauerkraut, a spicy and sour beef noodle soup, and a pork bone broth noodle soup. Noodles with pork mince, tomato and chopped vegetables. Markus Ravik There’s a stack of options on the biang biang dry noodles menu, including braised beef rib; sauteed chicken; mash potato, pork mince and sauce; and chilli with pork mince.



And the cold noodle dishes include noodles with sesame sauce; noodles with shredded chicken, cucumber in a chilli and sesame sauce; and cold noodles with a special chilli oil. Terrific’s hand-prepared noodles come thick and glossed in chilli oil. Markus Ravik By far the most popular noodles across the menu are the wheat-based biang biang noodles, but there are also spinach biang biang noodles, thinner hand-pulled noodles, and vermicelli. Dumplings will be added to the menu in the coming weeks. The restaurant has been an enormous hit since opening this month. Markus Ravik



Drinks are the same straightforward selection of sodas and juice variations that regulars will know from Market Square, and includes an Ice Peak tangerine soda imported from Xi’an. There’s also a seasonally rotating selection of sparkling sodas, which currently include grapefruit and lychee flavours. “I really love Australian diners because they are so open to different cultures,” Huy says. “Like, some of the pho in Brisbane is just as good as Vietnam. Boqiao and I went back to Xi’an recently and ordered cold noodles – my favourite as a child – and I feel like ours is just as good, so we’re very proud.” Open daily 11am-9pm Shop FC611, Level 2, Westfield Chermside, Gympie Road, Chermside instagram.com/terrificnoodles

For subscribers Matt Shea is Food and Culture Editor at Brisbane Times. He is a former editor and editor-at-large at Broadsheet Brisbane, and has written for Escape, Qantas Magazine, the Guardian, Jetstar Magazine and SilverKris, among many others.

World.title: Veteran ABC newsreader Richard Morecroft dies aged 70
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCancer Veteran ABC newsreader Richard Morecroft dies aged 70 Emily Kaine and Aine Ryan Updated October 6, 2026 — 9:10pm ,first published 8:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former ABC newsreader Richard Morecroft has died at the age of 70 following a cancer diagnosis. The veteran reporter anchored the ABC’s nightly NSW news bulletin for nearly two decades from the 1980s to the early 2000s. “Sadly, our beloved Richard died today, at a time of his choosing, on the South Coast of NSW,” a statement shared on his Instagram account said. Richard Morecroft alongside his partner Alison Mackay in 2022. Fairfax Media “He was diagnosed with cancer earlier this year and was grateful to go peacefully, with his partner of 36 years, Alison Mackay, beside him. We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly.” Morecroft moved from England to Adelaide with his family at the age of 10. He studied English and drama at the University of Adelaide and worked at the university’s radio station before landing a job at the ABC.



Richard Morecroft pictured in May of 1983. Paul Wright/Fairfax Media He presented the Adelaide News bulletin before hosting ABC News NSW from 1983 until 2002. Morecroft also hosted the quiz show Letters and Numbers on SBS between 2010 and 2012. His career spanned more than 20 years, including reporting stints in Canberra. He was also a staunch environmental activist and was a long-time trustee for the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), a governor of the Taronga Foundation and a director of the Zoological Parks Board of NSW. Morecroft was also an acclaimed landscape photographer. His work hangs on the walls of Parliament House in Canberra.



He met his long-term partner, Alison Mackay, in Far North Queensland in 1990 while he was on holiday at Cape Tribulation. They kept in touch through handwritten fountain-pen letters for two years before Mackay moved to Sydney. Morecroft had shared updates on his Instagram account earlier in the year about his long stay in the Chris O’Brien Lifehouse in Sydney for cancer treatment. Tributes have already started to flow in from veteran news presenters who worked alongside Morecroft at the ABC, including Leigh Sales and Michael Rowland. Related Article Good Weekend How former TV presenter Richard Morecroft found love through a fountain pen “The best way I can describe Richard is that he was a gentleman, and a gentle man. He was pure class in every way - a kind, warm and generous colleague, as well as being a consummate professional. I had so much admiration and regard for him and I consider myself a lucky person indeed to have been his friend,” Sales wrote in a comment on the Instagram post.



Rowland added: “I’m so sorry to hear this. Richard was a superb newsreader and a lovely man. My condolences to Alison and the rest of Richard’s family and friends.” ABC News presenter Joe O’Brien, in a post on social media, said: “Richard set the respected standard for others to follow. And more importantly was a warm, encouraging guy too.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Health NZ chases $70m in unpaid health bills from tourists and migrants
World.content:
Tourists and migrants have run up bills of more than $70 million in unpaid public healthcare.

Health New Zealand says it's likely at least a quarter of that debt will not be recoverable, as it writes a similar amount off each year.

In one case a man had a $174,000 debt to Health NZ which he incurred after not disclosing his pre-existing renal diagnosis to Immigration New Zealand (INZ), nor two criminal convictions in his visa application.

Most visitors with visas lasting less than 12 months are not eligible for public healthcare. While all applicants must have an acceptable standard of health to be issued a visa, medical checks are usually only carried out on prospective migrants staying longer than that.

All others are urged to get travel insurance, but it is only a prerequisite for certain visas, including international students, some working holidaymakers and parent visas.

Health NZ chief financial officer Bevan McKenzie said the latest unpaid debt figure was higher than 2022/23's costs of $45.6m, possibly because of travel growth since the pandemic. It's also a large increase on the $18m of bad debt incurred by ineligible patients at the country's 20 then-DHBs in the year 2019 to 2020. Counties Manukau topped that list of affected areas, followed by Auckland, Southern and Waitematā DHBs.

Health NZ chief financial officer Bevan McKenzie. Supplied / Health NZ

"The amount written off varies from year to year; however, our experience is that between 25 and 30 percent of outstanding debts will typically be written off as unrecoverable," said McKenzie. "Health NZ uses a range of recovery actions, including invoices and reminders, payment arrangements, engagement with sponsors or insurers, and referral to debt collection agencies.

"Where sponsorship arrangements exist, Health NZ may seek assistance from the sponsor in meeting the debt. However, sponsors are not always financially able to meet these obligations. Clinical decisions are not based on financial circumstances and care is provided irrespective of a patient's eligibility or immediate ability to pay."

Health NZ used an external debt collection agency with international reach to support recovery efforts, he said.

"[Cost] recovery can be affected by overseas residency, patients leaving New Zealand, incomplete contact information, personal financial difficulty, limited insurance cover, and cross-border enforcement constraints." ·

Immigration minister Erica Stanford stays informed about some of the more expensive cases, which include the $85,000 costs of medically evacuating a Korean overstayer who had a stroke. The cost of her healthcare was not disclosed, but her treatment included two surgeries and lengthy rehabilitation.

Criminal cases

In a case brought to Stanford's attention, a man did not disclose his diabetes or end-stage renal disease to INZ.

When it found out, INZ granted him a 12-month visa as an exception to instructions. It had found out he had two undeclared criminal convictions, although the details were withheld in information supplied to RNZ.

Payment arrangements with the hospital were made by family members in late 2023 but by March 2025 the total amount due was $174,746. His GP confirmed he had ongoing treatment for terminal renal failure and had also since received palliative surgery after being diagnosed with advanced gastric cancer.

"INZ is still not satisfied that the applicants meet the instruction for the grant of a visitor visa under medical treatment category. However, INZ intends to grant the applicants the visitor visa under medical treatment category for 12 months as an exception to instructions to allow the principal applicant to remain in New Zealand for life preserving treatment," said officials at the time.

A Tongan man with four previous undisclosed convictions was also granted a 12-month visa to continue dialysis for end-stage renal failure.

The 57-year-old national could not receive the required dialysis treatment in Tonga, and was on haemodialysis treatments three times a week at Manukau Super Clinic.

"This treatment is a permanent and life-sustaining treatment. The applicant's medical treatment is not funded by his home government and treatment costs are not covered under New Zealand's Official Development Assistance programme. The applicant has provided evidence of a payment agreement for the debt outstanding between the applicant and Health New Zealand."

Another man needed kidney dialysis for the rest of his life, treatment was not available in his home country.

The 53-year-old arrived in New Zealand in June 2024 on a visitor visa, subsequently becoming unwell and being admitted to hospital. INZ approved his visa and that of family, who were supporting him during his treatment.

Immigration minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Dialysis costs

Clinical decisions are not based on someone's ability to pay.

Officials identified seven cases of people seeking urgent care for dialysis and/or renal failure soon after arriving on visitor visas in the year to December 2024.

"These individuals did not declare any adverse health information in their visitor visa applications and INZ does not require medical certificates to be provided for stays of less than 12 months.

"Looking closer at these cases, it has been noted that at least two of the individuals were confirmed to have been aware of their health issues prior to arriving and had provided false information to INZ in their application. Others were formally diagnosed after arrival in New Zealand. All individuals were receiving treatment for end stage renal failure within a month of arriving in New Zealand."

They all applied for medical treatment visas to remain in New Zealand to continue receiving renal care.

New Zealand has reciprocal agreements with the UK and Australia to provide limited, free healthcare to each other's citizens, and some treatment is also provided to certain Pacific citizens depending on their circumstances.

To be granted a medical treatment visa, for example for renal dialysis, they must be funded by either their home government or through New Zealand's Official Development Assistance Programme under the Medical Treatment Scheme, administered by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

"There are no renal care services available in [redacted country/region] and none of the seven individuals identified were receiving funding via these mechanisms for their treatment in New Zealand," said officials' notes to Stanford.

"Summary of this review will be shared with Ministry of Health and Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, along with internal INZ Pacific teams."

Ministers have been warned specifically about renal care costs for several years. INZ told its appeal tribunal in 2018 that demand pressure from patients ineligible for New Zealand healthcare was leading to rationing of New Zealanders' dialysis treatment. At the time National Renal Advisory Board said patients were not at risk of reduced care.

More recently, kidney patients in Christchurch were also being warned dialysis treatment may have to be rationed because of staffing shortages and a lack of hospital space.

World.title: National's proposed foreign aid cut could make NZ 'invisible' on world stage - expert
World.content:
An international aid and development expert says National's proposed $431 million cut to the foreign aid budget could see New Zealand becoming "invisible" at the international stage and cut off from important global conversations.

The National Party wants to redirect foreign aid money into funding for new medicines if it leads the new government; aid to the Pacific would be protected.

Christopher Luxon on Tuesday said National believed that "we should put our country and our people first" and used the example of indigenous farmer workshops in Patagonia as the kind of foreign aid that would be cut.

Massey University's associate professor Gerard Prinsen said the move would be a bad idea in terms of geopolitical and business interests, and that New Zealand could be retreating into a corner of the world only looking at the Pacific - "[The Pacific] are indeed our neighbours, but the world is bigger than the Pacific," he said.

Currently, nearly 60 percent of New Zealand's Official Development Assistance funding goes to the Pacific, in an aid budget of about $1.2 billion in the 2025/2026 fiscal year.

Prinsen said New Zealand may lose personal networks and business networks with countries in Africa and Latin American, and possibly compromise its voice at the United Nations (UN) level if the cut went ahead.

Massey University's associate professor Gerard Prinsen. Supplied / Massey University

"We contribute to quite a lot of UN bodies, if we cut back our contribution then we are no longer at the table, so people will forget what NZ thinks, what NZ has to offer, we become invisible at the international stage," he said.

He said this could mean being not being invited to certain UN conferences and losing touch with the latest developments on important issues - such as the impact of artificial intelligence on education, which would be discussed at UNESCO forums.

Not attending these events meant New Zealand would be relying on papers to be published by the agencies, which could mean being six months or a year behind the international debate on these issues, said Prinsen.

He said New Zealand currently contributed to over 40 UN bodies, and that he'd be interested to see how the aid budget could be reduced without affecting those contributions.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon and health spokesperson Simeon Brown have been approached for comment.

Regarding interntional aid to Africa, Prinsen said New Zealand's contribution was already "miniscule" - amounting to less than 1 percent of its aid budget - and that further reducing it would lead to New Zealand disappearing from the view of African nations.

"I think it's important to realise that the African population will grow to be the third largest in 10 year's time, so that's a huge market, and nobody would've heard of New Zealand.

"New Zealand will not be participating, will have no personal networks, we will be a small island in the Pacific that maybe looks good on the tourist folder, but that's about it," he said.

Prinsen said decision makers should also keep in mind the importance of bilateral relations between New Zealand and major African nations such as Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa.

He said it's "silly" for the prime minister to use Patagonia as an example, as a place where many people would not have heard of.

Prinsen said aid programmes helped New Zealand to build relationships with other nations, and he couldn't see how cutting hundreds of million of dollars in foreign aid could be worth losing contacts with the world.

Foreign Minister Winston Peters. RNZ / Nick Monro

Foreign Minister Winston Peters called National's foreign aid cut campaign promise dangerous and desperate, particularly during one of the most uncertain global times in history.

"It is irresponsible for National to jeopardise the relationships we have in the very markets we need to grow our economy," he said.

World.title: Lake Wakatipu bush fire expected to continue 'quite strongly'
World.content:
A huge vegetation fire on the southern shores of Lake Wakatipu is likely to have worsened overnight amid high winds.

The blaze, which has been burning since Tuesday morning, was not contained or controlled when firefighters suspended operations on Tuesday night.

Assistant District Commander Nic McQuillan said strong nor-westerly winds were fuelling the fire, which had escalated in the McKinlays Creek area.

"There are areas where the fire will burn itself out, but we are expecting it to still be going quite strongly first thing in the morning," he said on Tuesday night.

The geography of McKinlays Creek was a ravine, causing it to act like a chimney, funnelling wind and fire upwards, making it difficult for firefighters to access the area, he said.

"So the wind funnels up it and draws the fire with it - essentially the smoke and the fire is drawn up the valley and out the top of the mountains, which makes it very hot and impressive in terms of what we're seeing.

"Helicopter operations have been hindered by the amount of smoke being generated and the fact that the McKinlays Creek area is acting like a chimney, which means that we can only get into the bottom part of it."

McQuillan estimated the fire had affected more than 1000 hectares by late Monday night, calling the growth caused by winds Tuesday afternoon "massive".

Efforts to protect the historic Walter Peak homestead and other buildings in its vicinity were successful, and there were no longer concerns for the homestead building, McQuillan said.

The fire was not contained or controlled when firefighters suspended operations on Tuesday night. Supplied / Tom Kelly

Earlier, Walter Peak tour operator RealNZ said people had been evacuated and experiences were cancelled.

McQuillan said the most likely cause of the fire was a burn off that reignited a week later.

"This burn off was out, but when the conditions are right, they'll reignite by themselves. If you are intending to have a burn off or you are intending to have an outdoor fire, make sure it is fully extinguished.

"It's not just a case of let it burn itself out and walk away, put it out, make sure it's wet."

He said the upcoming El Niño weather pattern, which is likely to bring more frequent and stronger winds, made this even more critical.

"The wind is a guaranteed factor in the El Niño coming up, and that's a hugely contributing factor to how fire grows and develops and the speed it travels.

"So whether the conditions are wet or dry, the wind is coming, and it will cause us problems especially around fires that haven't been put out properly."

Residents should keep their doors and windows shut as heavy smoke drift will travel as conditions shift, and boat users were urged to stay well off shore to allow helicopters with monsoon buckets to operate throughout the day.

World.title: VentureFruit launches family of apples bred to cope with hotter growing conditions
World.content:
A family of apples bred to cope with hotter growing conditions has been launched by VentureFruit, T&G Global's variety-management and commercialisation business.

ADORE is an umbrella brand covering several apple varieties developed through the Hot Climate Partnership, a breeding programme involving organisations in New Zealand and Catalonia.

The programme would initially include HOT03A1 and a second, unnamed variety that ripened four to six weeks earlier, with more varieties under development.

VentureFruit general manager Morgan Rogers said putting the apples under one brand would allow growers to choose the variety - or mix of varieties - that worked best for their climate and harvest season.

"The exciting thing about ADORE and what makes it quite unique is we're releasing ADORE as an umbrella brand for a suite of varieties," he said.

The apples were being put through their paces in hotter, tougher growing conditions. But Rogers said coping with heat was only part of the test.

They also had to produce yields at least as good as existing varieties, keep their quality and sell for enough to make them worthwhile for growers.

"The climate resilience really is a grower-based benefit. But what we're doing at the same time is making sure the fruit can compete with those super-premium and premium varieties around the world, and that consumers still really enjoy the fruit at that price point," Rogers said.

VentureFruit has tested the apples' taste, appearance and texture with consumers in Europe and Asia.

About 120 hectares have already been licensed in Catalonia through FruitFutur. Rogers said HOT03A1 was expected to reach European consumers over the next few years, while planting material was being tested for possible releases elsewhere.

The apples were also being trialled in New Zealand. However, the trees were still young and Rogers said it would be several years before there were meaningful local results.

Growers and marketers would need licences to use the ADORE name and plant its varieties, rather than being able to grow them freely.

T&G said the global premium apple market was expected to grow from US$13 billion in 2025 to US$19 billion by 2030 - average annual growth of 7.6 percent.

The Hot Climate Partnership began in 2002 and brings together Catalonia's Institute of Agrifood Research and Technology, New Zealand's Bioeconomy Science Institute, Catalonian grower group FruitFutur and VentureFruit.

ADORE follows the September consumer launch in Vietnam of JOLI, a large, full-flavoured apple bred in New Zealand and commercialised globally by VentureFruit.

World.title: Chris v Chris: Are they still playing in the major party league?
World.content:
Analysis - Three years ago, Christopher Luxon headed into his first head-to-head debate with Chris Hipkins on the back of a poll that had National on 37 points and able to form a government with ACT alone.

Labour under then-Prime Minister Chris Hipkins was on a downward spiral on 27 percent in that same 1News-Verian poll and had no path to power.

Fast-forward three years and both parties headed into Tuesday night's debate with two fresh new polls.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406343796112

RNZ-Reid Research's results had National on 26 percent and Labour on 31, while 1News-Verian had a much tighter race with just one point in it and both parties just under 30.

Those results spell early retirement and unemployment for a decent number of National Party MPs currently enjoying the government benches.

MMP has evolved so much in the past three elections that the combined Labour-National vote has gone from 81 percent at the 2017 election to just 57 in Tuesday's RNZ-Reid Research poll.

So-called minor parties have grown in both size and influence, capturing the imagination of voters that traditionally voted blue or red.

Increasingly polling is suggesting another new party - Opportunity - has a good chance of making it into Parliament and being a potential kingmaker.

There's now a very real possibility that the next government could be made up of four political parties.

That has happened before under Sir John Key's National government in 2008, but because he chose to welcome the Māori Party into the fold, not because he had to.

The minor parties of 2026 have leverage and power going into any coalition talks well beyond any previous election years.

It makes a head-to-head between Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins far more redundant in this political age.

The two Chrises greet each other. TVNZ/Harley Peters

They can't fully commit to any of the promises they make because the slate is almost entirely wiped clean after 7 November when political parties sit down to discuss what a future government might look like.

Luxon has ruled out working with Opportunity after the election because of its land tax policy and National campaigning on no new taxes.

On Tuesday night he repeatedly refused to answer whether he would pick the phone up if he needed the party to be prime minister.

Instead, he repeated his previous comments about an untenable land tax, and then told reporters after the debate the question was a "hypothetical" that didn't need an answer.

To be clear, that's not a no.

At times in the debate the leaders could have been put in a time machine and transported back to three years ago, so similar were some of the issues and answers to them.

The cost of living crisis continued to be the overwhelming theme, a healthcare system under pressure and patients waiting too long in emergency departments hadn't improved, and neither Chris had fully grasped the meaning of a yes or no question.

There was no big revelation or pledge - on the latter neither party has the headroom in their fiscal plans to do so.

It's unlikely undecided voters watching were swayed one way or the other by the end of it.

That's not to say the two Chrises performed badly.

They were both across their briefs, and while they had some nervous energy at the outset both settled into a comfortable rhythm and got their key messages across.

While Hipkins managed to land a few blows on Luxon over his failure to discipline New Zealand First's Winston Peters and Shane Jones over racist remarks, Luxon in return made a strong argument on education and had Hipkins concede he had done what Labour couldn't and got India across the line on a free trade agreement.

The biggest controversy of the night was the pair being asked to pick between the All Blacks and the Warriors with Luxon going Team ABs while Hipkins chose to "Up the Wahs".

Both would have gone to bed happy with their performance and grateful they didn't say or do anything they deeply regretted.

World.title: Election 2026: Luxon faces Hipkins in first leaders' debate
World.content:
Audio player for " RNZ National " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1749767%2Felection-2026-luxon-faces-hipkins-in-first-leaders-debate

RNZ national

RNZ's latest political poll - the first during the election campaign - came out just hours before the two major party leaders faced off in TVNZ's debate.

National's campaign chair Simeon Brown acknowledged little more than that the election will be a tight one off the back of its crushing poll result.

On Tuesday evening, Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins had their first opportunity to go head-to-head on the issues that matter most to New Zealanders in TVNZ's leader debate.

World.title: What we learned from the first leaders' debate
World.content:
Well, we learned Chris Hipkins would rather the Warriors win the NRL Premiership than the All Blacks win the Rugby World Cup next year, we learned Christopher Luxon has never pulled a sickie, and we learned both leaders want to learn more te reo Māori.

But in terms of the more substantial scraps, commitments, common ground, and policy outcomes from the TVNZ leaders' debate, RNZ has put together this handy recap.

Relive all the action in our live blog.

A cost of living election

Both parties have talked about this being a cost of living election, and its place as the first main debate topic confirmed that.

Luxon started by talking up National's plan to lift the economy, with an obligatory "no new taxes", while Hipkins said Luxon had stood on the same spot three years ago and promised to fix the cost of living.

"Are you better off than you were three years ago?"

Asked whether the average New Zealander was better off under National, Luxon said it would be worse under Labour.

"What we have to do is not band-aid solutions, and we actually have to tackle the fundamental economic challenges we have. That means lowering costs for New Zealanders, and it also means growing this economy, and that's how we set it up for people to do well."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406343796112

Hipkins said Labour's policies in aged care and public transport would help, and were fully-funded.

"Christopher has just said that life is getting easier for New Zealanders. The vast majority of New Zealanders watching this today, they will be at home shouting at the TV, saying, 'Don't you understand?'"

Hipkins said Labour would also freeze petrol taxes for a whole term, with Luxon saying it was not funded (a criticism he levelled at Hipkins many times during the debate).

"Stop telling things that aren't true. This is why people don't trust you," Hipkins responded.

Both leaders agreed New Zealand should be a high-wage economy, with Luxon afterwards ruling out a freeze to the minimum wage (an ACT policy).

"We're going to increase minimum wage each and every year in line with inflation, more or less," he said after the debate.

The health of our health system

Both leaders guaranteed more nurses, with Luxon saying 2200 would be hired in the coming year, while Hipkins pointed to Labour's guarantee to give every nursing graduate a job.

Luxon said health was "incredibly challenging" but the government had put in record investment, and was hiring more nurses and making progress on its health targets, particularly on wait times in emergency departments.

Asked what difference Labour's three free GP visits would make when it's difficult to see a GP now, Hipkins said Labour would provide low-interest loans to new GPs.

The two also argued how many nurses were hired, with Luxon insisting 2100 had been hired under this government, while Hipkins said it was 54 in the last two years, with the rest funded by the previous Labour-led government.

Hipkins also committed to re-instating the smokefree generation legislation, and while he expressed concern over the number of young New Zealanders getting addicted to vaping, he did not offer a solution.

TVNZ/Harley Peters

Education, education, education

Education was where the two really started to fire up, with Luxon calling Hipkins the "worst education minister New Zealand has ever had", and jeering "oh, great flip flop" when Hipkins expressed his support for the ban on cellphones in schools.

After Hipkins confirmed Labour would bring back the old school lunch scheme, Luxon repeated his criticism that it was unfunded, to which Hipkins responded it was in Labour's fiscal plan.

"You would be able to make the same claim if you actually had a fiscal plan," he said.

Hipkins also committed to again scrapping charter schools, as Labour had done when taking office last time.

"But they're working. They're getting great results for those kids," Luxon responded.

What appeared to be a new commitment, that Labour would scrap the required hour of reading, writing, and maths, was later clarified.

"Give schools the discretion," was Hipkins' response during the debate.

"We still want kids to be learning reading, writing, and maths, but I want to give the teachers the flexibility to do that in a way that engages kids," was his response afterwards.

TVNZ/Harley Peters

Taxes and billionaires

Both leaders agreed New Zealand's tax system was not fair, with Luxon putting an emphasis on less tax, while Hipkins said the system put too much emphasis on salary and wage earners.

They were asked to commit to not increasing any existing taxes next term, with both saying yes.

"He's putting up fuel tax by 25 cents a litre, so that's simply not true," Hipkins said, referencing the planned deferral, and then incremental increases, to fuel excise duty, which Labour would scrap.

After Luxon guaranteed GST would not go up, Hipkins said John Key had promised the same and then raised it.

"You're not debating John Key, you're debating Chris Luxon," the National leader responded.

Luxon later said he misheard the original question, telling media afterwards he thought he was being asked about no new taxes.

"We're not lifting GST, we're not lifting income tax. Any increase in fees and levies we'll do very efficiently, but that was the point where I got a bit overexcited."

Where the two were able to find common ground is that neither were able to give a straight answer on whether it was morally acceptable for any one person to be a billionaire.

TVNZ/Harley Peters

An opportunity for Opportunity

With Luxon being reminded of polling that showed National needing to pick up its support, he was again pressed on his decision to rule out the Opportunity Party.

Asked if he was unable to form a government without Opportunity come 8 November, and if he would pick up the phone, he again confirmed National had ruled Opportunity out.

"I have been crystal clear with who we could or couldn't work with. I've laid that out from the very beginning of the year. I've been clear about Opportunity."

He was quizzed by media afterwards, but batted questions away.

Hipkins targeted National's existing coalition partners, lumping in ACT's policy to freeze the minimum wage as National's, and attacking Luxon for not taking stronger action against Winston Peters and Shane Jones.

"You did nothing about it. You did not stand up for migrant communities when Winston Peters and Shane Jones said absolutely racist things about them."

Luxon insisted he had called out "comments from Winston Peters and other political leaders that are racist", and said it was incumbent on all political leaders to watch their rhetoric.

"If any minister in a government I led expressed the sort of racist sentiment that he's put up with, I would sack them immediately," Hipkins responded.

TVNZ/Harley Peters

How did they rate their performance?

The undecided voters in TVNZ's audience gave Hipkins the win, on 49 percent versus Luxon's 24 percent (a further 27 percent remain undecided).

Both Luxon and Hipkins emerged from their first leaders' debate of 2026 pleased with their respective performances.

"It's the first time we've done it in a wee while, so I was pretty happy with it overall," said Hipkins.

"That was fun," Luxon said.

When it was put to him the audience had sided with Hipkins, Luxon was unbothered.

World.title: Firefighters battling large vegetation fire in Queenstown stand down for night
World.content:
Firefighters tackling a large vegetation fire in Queenstown have stood down for the night.

The fire, which has been burning on steep slopes above the shores of Lake Wakatipu since Tuesday morning, is not yet contained or controlled.

Assistant District Commander Nic McQuillan said the size of the fireground had increased from about 146 hectares to about 390 hectares.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406338317112

Kevin Pilbrow

Efforts to protect the historic Walter Peak homestead and other buildings in its vicinity have been successful, McQuillan said.

Earlier, Walter Peak tour operator RealNZ said people had been evacuated and experiences were cancelled.

Firefighters from Queenstown, Frankton, Glenorchy and Mossburn worked on the western flank to consolidate the perimeter, alongside six helicopters, until sunset when operations were suspended.

Kevin Pilbrow

Kevin Pilbrow

Those in areas affected by drifting smoke, including Hanleys Farm and Jacks Point, should keep doors and windows shut to avoid smoke overnight, McQuillan said.

Ground and air operations would resume in the morning, with more than a dozen firefighters supported by helicopters with monsoon buckets, and another directing the air attack.

World.title: Jannik Sinner to miss rest of tennis season with knee injury
World.content:
World number one Jannik Sinner will not compete again in 2026 after opting to continue his recovery ‌from a knee injury that has kept him out of action ‌since his ⁠triumphant Wimbledon campaign in July.

"Me, together with the doctors, have decided that I need a course of treatment for my knee, which means that the 2026 season is officially over," Sinner said in a video message on Instagram.

" I also need to think about my long-term career so I will do everything possible to get back 100 per cent. "

Sinner has not played since beating Alexander Zverev in the All England Club final on July 12, with the 25-year-old missing the North American hardcourt swing, the US Open as well as the ongoing slate of tournaments in Asia.

He will now miss the European indoor hardcourt swing as well as the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin, where he won the title in the last two years.

Sinner's team said in a statement that he would follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee.

"The decision has been made to have the treatment now to give Jannik the necessary time to recover before beginning preparations for 2027."

Sinner's absence could open the door for Zverev to finish the year at the top of the world rankings.

The German world number two has cut the gap to Sinner after winning the French Open and US Open titles.

World.title: Zach Merrett staying 'open-minded' after high-profile AFL move to Hawks
World.content:
Boom AFL recruit Zach Merrett is open-minded over what role he will play at Hawthorn under coach Sam Mitchell.

More than a year after the bombshell revelation that the Hawks were trying to lure Merrett from Essendon, a deal was finally struck for the former Bombers captain when the trade period opened on Monday.

Essendon will receive the number 15 and 25 picks in this year's national draft, as well as Hawthorn's 2028 second-round selection.

The bitter rivals were unable to reach a deal for Merrett in trade talks a year ago.

Merrett would obviously boost Hawthorn's midfield, but he noted on Tuesday in a club interview that he could also play in defence or across half-forward.

"It is funny that Gia and I are back together," he said of former Essendon assistant coach Daniel Giansiracusa, who is now at the Hawks.

"We worked for three years on trying to be the most flexible player in the competition, being able to play a number of different roles.

"I have no preconceived ideas with Sam. We're going to be pretty open-minded, to what that could look like.

Loading Instagram content

"There are already so many incredible players out there for the Hawks, so wherever I fit in, I will make sure I make that work — whether that's back, forward, mid, or wing, or whatever it looks like."

Merrett has toured Hawthorn's Dingley headquarters and met with captain Jai Newcombe.

"It's been a bit overwhelming, the last 24 hours," Merrett said.

"To see the whole facility and to get so many incredible messages, I feel extremely welcomed, and so is my family."

Last Thursday Merrett became the third player to win Essendon's best and fairest award seven times, alongside Dick Reynolds and Bill Hutchison.

"It was a really hard decision, it was probably something I weighed up for six to nine months," Merrett said of the move.

"It felt like Hawthorn was going to be the best place for me and my family, moving forward, to keep achieving, to achieve out of footy.

"I also have so much respect and love for Essendon as well, so it is a unique feeling, a little bit.

"But I'm keen to move forward, get stuck into work."

Hawthorn, whose season ended with an epic preliminary final loss to premiers Brisbane, are also expected to recruit key forward Ben King from Gold Coast.

World.title: Women's stars call on Cricket Australia to fix scheduling
World.content:
Senior women's players have called on Cricket Australia to push to return some of their games to the peak of summer, fearing the current schedule will hurt the sport's growth among girls.

Australia begin their home summer against Bangladesh on Friday, marking the first of three ODIs in Brisbane before three T20s against New Zealand in Sydney.

All three of the Sydney matches fall on school nights.

They will then not play on home soil until they host New Zealand for ODIs in March, in what looms as a sign of things to come for the world's number one-ranked team.

Australian women's cricket team Upcoming games ODI vs Bangladesh, Brisbane: October 9, 1:50pm AEST

ODI vs Bangladesh, Brisbane: October 11, 1:50pm AEST

ODI vs Bangladesh, Brisbane: October 14, 1:50pm AEST

T20I vs New Zealand, North Sydney: October 18, 6:15pm AEST

T20I vs New Zealand, North Sydney: October 20, 6:15pm AEST

T20I vs New Zealand, North Sydney: October 22, 6:15pm AEST

Under the current ICC schedule, there will be no WBBL or international women's cricket during the school holidays in Australia for at least the next three years, with all fixtures in the shoulder seasons.

"We don't want to be the sport that falls behind because we're just getting it wrong," veteran wicketkeeper-bat Beth Mooney told AAP.

"We're just pushing it uphill, because we're in a bad timeslot and it's a bad time of year for parents.

"They're not dragging their kid out to watch a 7pm T20 on a Tuesday night or whatever it is.

"That's going to stop girls getting into the game, because parents aren't going to take them."

Mooney's comments come after Australia's most-capped player Ellyse Perry expressed similar concerns earlier last month.

Australian players have for a long time had some frustrations over the schedule, particularly around the same consistency in men's cricket.

This summer has been impacted by the ICC moving the Champions' Trophy to India, leaving no international women's games at all in Perth.

But multiple players have also expressed concerns to AAP over India being able to claim the January window for its lucrative WPL, fearing it will only expand into a larger window. This year it runs January 14 to February 7.

Australia wins Women's T20 World Cup Australia has won the ICC Women's T20 World Cup in commanding style, defeating England by seven wickets in the final at Lord's.

They are concerned the national team is at risk of being out of sight and out of mind, stunting momentum after another T20 World Cup win.

One push is for more home matches to be scheduled in December around the Christmas window, with Australia to tour Sri Lanka through that period this year.

"We're not getting crowds, it's not marketed well. There is no big-ticket item where people go, 'The Australian women's team play here [at this time] every year,'" Mooney said.

"We want to be relatable athletes. And if we're not front and centre of the summer it makes it pretty difficult when it's meant to be a summer sport.

"We don't need to compete with the men. They play the day-night Test at some point. We can have T20s before that.

"Or we can play night T20s when there is a men's Test on."

Australia's coach Shelley Nitschke said it was "obviously disappointing" not to play at home in December or January, while captain Sophie Molineux argued home games in December would be "really special" for her team.

"It would also help see fans come through," Molineux said.

"I completely understand that the schedules are getting bigger and busier."

AAP

World.title: Jaymie Graham named new North Melbourne AFL coach
World.content:
North Melbourne has named Fremantle assistant coach Jaymie Graham as the new coach for the AFL side.

A statement from club president Sonja Hood on Tuesday said Graham was the new senior coach, succeeding four-time premiership coach Alastair Clarkson, who was sacked by the Kangaroos earlier this year.

Graham spent five seasons at the Dockers as an assistant to Justin Longmuir.

The Kangaroos finished the 2026 season — Clarkson's fourth season in charge — in 14th spot with nine wins.

Speaking at his first press conference, Graham thanked the club for having faith in him.

Having missed out on a number of coaching opportunities before landing the North Melbourne job, he said he was nervous and proud to take charge of the Kangaroos.

"This opportunity came up, things happen for a reason. I feel I belong here already," he said.

"There's no ceiling on where we want to get to. There's clearly some talent on this list, but there's also some work to do."

Graham described himself as a "systems-based and relationships-based coach".

"People don't care how much you know, until they know how much you care."

Club CEO Jen Watt confirmed the panel tasked with finding the new coach had unanimously picked Grham.

Earlier, in the club statement, Hood told members Graham had "the resilience to handle the relentless toils of the football environment, carrying the exact kind of grit we value at North Melbourne.

"As a coach, Jaymie is a process-driven leader with a quiet, grounded presence, sharp attention to detail, and a clear football vision," she said.

"Outside of his exceptional character, he joins us with a proven skill set. He played a key role in West Coast's 2018 premiership success, and more recently he was the line coach for one of the competition's best forward lines at Fremantle as part of a high-performing program.

"He is widely respected across the industry as a developer of talent and a connector of people — someone who builds strong player relationships instantly and earns respect through his actions."

The announcement marks a change in direction, with a young untested AFL senior coach — who has been a caretaker or interim coach for three games in total at West Coast and Fremantle, after a period in charge of East Perth in the WAFL — after the end of the Clarkson era.

The Kangaroos were criticised for the tone of their press conference in early September announcing Clarkson's departure.

Alastair Clarkson leaves North North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney explain why the club is parting ways with Alastair Clarkson with a year to run on his deal.

At the time, Hood said Clarkson's replacement needed to be "a coach who can coach for the modern game".

"It'll be a coach who knows what they're doing, and it'll be a coach who's the best fit for this football club," she said.

Football manager Todd Viney said in the press conference there were "still some gaping holes in our game plan".

Fremantle paid tribute to Graham in a statement, wishing him well for his new role and thanking him for his "five outstanding seasons" at the club.

"Jaymie has had a significant impact not only on our player group — but the entire football department and broader club," Fremantle executive general manager of football Joe Brierty said.

"It is well documented that Jaymie has had ambitions of becoming a senior coach in his own right one day, and we couldn't be prouder or happier for him to take an opportunity he's worked so hard for."

World.title: Mary Fowler withdraws from Matildas squad for Germany, Haiti games
World.content:
Matildas star Mary Fowler has been withdrawn from the Australian squad for two upcoming internationals, due to personal circumstances.

A release from Football Australia on Tuesday morning said the decision had been taken following discussions between Fowler, Manchester City and Matildas staff.

Fowler has been in solid form, coming on as a sub to spark a comeback win for Manchester City over WSL rivals Arsenal on Monday morning, Australian time.

Fowler's City still perfect in WSL Mary Fowler's landmark 100th game for Manchester City is a bright spot for the beleaguered club, with a big win over Arsenal keeping them with a perfect record on top of the WSL.

There was no talk of injury after the game.

Fowler's partner, Nathan Cleary, is recovering in Sydney after leg surgery.

The Penrith Panthers NRL star went into the preliminary final against Newcastle with a broken foot, before suffering a compound fracture and a dislocated ankle in a hip-drop tackle, requiring emergency surgery.

Fowler has been replaced in the Australian squad by Charlton Athletic midfielder Leah Davidson. Davidson has made four appearances for the Matildas since her international debut in 2024.

The Matildas are playing two international friendlies in Europe as they continue preparations towards next year's FIFA Women's World Cup.

Australia split a two-match series with Mexico in June, with one win each.

Now the Matildas will face Germany in Karlsruhe on Saturday morning, Australian time before taking on Haiti in France on October 13.

World.title: Hawks make King offer official as Tigers swing move for Freo winger
World.content:
Hawthorn has officially lodged the paperwork in its bid to sign Gold Coast forward Ben King as a free agent.

King, who has played 143 games for the Suns, has reportedly been offered a seven-year deal worth $9 million by the Hawks.

As King is a restricted free agent, Gold Coast reserves the right to force Hawthorn into a trade by matching the contract offer to the 26-year-old.

The Suns have a 72-hour window to match the contract offer. If they do not choose to do so, they are expected to receive a band one compensation pick from the AFL in November's draft.

A band one pick would land directly after Gold Coast's first-round selection (currently No.6) in this year's draft, but it remains to be seen whether the Suns will want more in return in exchange for their all-time leading goalkicker.

Hawthorn is limited in what assets it could provide Gold Coast in the way of draft capital in exchange for King after sending multiple picks to Essendon in exchange for Zach Merrett on the opening day of the trade period.

Gold Coast is interested in young Hawthorn forward Aidan Schubert, but is adamant any deal for Schubert would be independent of a deal involving King.

Elsewhere on day two, Richmond bolstered its young list by trading for Fremantle winger Nathan O'Driscoll in exchange for a fourth-round selection (currently No.61) in this year's draft.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the action from day two of the trade period.

World.title: Demon faces Djokovic in China final after Medvedev disqualified
World.content:
Alex de Minaur will face Novak Djokovic in the China Open final after the Serb's semifinal opponent, Daniil Medvedev, was disqualified ‌for hitting a loose ball into the crowd and causing a spectator to suffer an eye injury.

The Australian number one progressed from his semifinal after Poland's Hubert Hurkacz retired injured when trailing in the second set.

Djokovic was leading 7–5, 5–3 in Beijing and serving for the match when the incident happened.

After a forehand volley winner from Djokovic, the ball bounced off the advertising boards to Medvedev, who smacked a backhand that sailed into the stands.

A male spectator (obscured) was struck in the eye after Daniil Medvedev hit a ball into the stands during his China Open semifinal. (AP: Andy Wong)

It hit a spectator in the front row behind him.

The spectator clutched his left eye and appeared to be in ‌pain as he walked out, assisted by stadium staff.

"Terribly sorry to ‌the spectator, first ⁠of all," Medvedev told reporters. "I'm trying to get in touch with him, if he wants it. Hopefully I can apologise in person and see how he feels."

The Russian world number five said he did not cause the incident intentionally.

"The ball was bouncing back, so I tried to, like, just hit it anywhere, so it doesn't go out from the court. When I saw the result, I mean, I felt horrible because, again, I don't think I was ever close to such a situation."

Medvedev, 30, has a history of on-court behaviour issues. He was fined 6,000 euros ($9,600) after he smashed his racquet seven times during a 6–0, 6–0 loss to Matteo Berrettini at this year's Monte Carlo Masters.

"I was shocked, to be honest … I hope that person is not ‌badly injured," said Djokovic, who was disqualified from the US Open in 2020 under similar circumstances.

"On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil because I know exactly how it feels to be disqualified in a big match … ‌I'm sure that Daniil didn't want to do this intentionally."

Alex de Minaur was a set up on Hubert Hurkacz in the China Open semifinal when Hurkacz was forced to withdraw due to injury. (Getty Iimages: Eurasia Sport/Hermann Chu)

De Minaur will be seeking to become the first person to beat Djokovic in 34 matches at the China Open. He has a 1–3 head-to-head record with the Serb.

The winner will leave Beijing ninth in the race to qualify for November's eight-man ATP Finals, with the gap to Medvedev in eighth reduced as the Russian will lose the 200 points he had gained in Beijing.

There are two ATP Masters 1000 events to come, in Shanghai and Paris, but ninth may be enough with Jannik Sinner's availability uncertain.

On Saturday, the world number one, who last played at Wimbledon, pulled out of Shanghai, which begins on Wednesday. The Italian has a knee problem.

De Minaur was up 6–4, 3–2 and 40–0 when Hurkacz retired with an apparent adductor injury after showing mobility problems.

The world number nine had broken a tentative Hurkacz in his opening two service games before holding to lead 4–0, then withstood a comeback to take the first set 6–4.

Another break in the third game of the second set helped de Minaur build a 3–1 lead. Hurkacz fought desperately to hold serve in the following game, surviving four break points and a marathon deuce game, but was unable to battle much longer.

In Tokyo, defending champion Carlos Alcaraz overcame early wobbles on his serve ‌to outclass fellow Spaniard Jaume Munar 5–7, 6–3, 6–1 ‌and reach the Japan Open final.

He will play Jiri Lehecka, who beat Valentin Vacherot 6-4, 6-2.

AAP/AP

World.title: Why NRL grand final 'freak' is making Wallabies lick their lips
World.content:
It was not just the 80,000 spectators crammed inside Sydney's Olympic stadium, nor the millions of TV viewers in Australia, who were left in awe of Mark Nawaqanitawase's performance in the NRL grand final.

Last night, across the Tasman in New Zealand, the Wallabies eagerly watched on as Nawaqanitawase added to his highlight reel by scoring two tries in the Sydney Roosters' nail-biting 19-18 victory over Newcastle.

Roosters win classic NRL grand final A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final.

The fact that some of the Wallabies were Nawaqanitawase's ex-teammates helped explain the interest.

But knowing the dual international is switching codes once again, in time for next year's Rugby World Cup, also had Wallabies players licking their lips in anticipation.

"He'll be massive. He's just been a freak," Wallabies prop Allan Alaalatoa told reporters in Auckland today.

"What he's done in the last two years in league is probably unheard of.

"He's gone over there in the space of two years and pretty much done everything, and now he's coming back."

Following the Wallabies' disastrous Rugby World Cup campaign three years ago, Nawaqanitawase announced he would move to the NRL ahead of the 2025 season.

He was given clearance to join the Roosters earlier than scheduled, and made his NRL debut in the final round of the 2024 premiership.

Mark Nawaqanitawase (left) scored twice for the Roosters in the NRL grand final.

To suggest Nawaqanitawase made an impact in rugby league is an understatement.

He took the NRL by storm in his first full season, which was capped off when he debuted for Australia in last year's Ashes series in England.

Nawaqanitawase was selected in NSW's successful State of Origin squad this year and played a crucial role in helping the Roosters capture their first NRL premiership since 2019.

His athleticism and aerial skills on the wing contributed to an astonishing strike rate of 47 tries in as many NRL matches.

Nawaqanitawase has hit the pause button on his NRL career for now, having signed with Japanese rugby club Saitama Wild Knights on a two-year deal.

He will be available for Wallabies selection, although the 26-year-old is unlikely to feature in November's Nations Championship Tests against England, Scotland and Wales.

After impressing for the Wallabies in 11 Test appearances between 2022-23, he is expected to make a smooth transition once he returns to rugby.

Having him play alongside the likes of Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Max Jorgensen in a Wallabies' backline is a tantalising prospect; however, coach Les Kiss says there are "no promises and no guarantees".

Mark Nawaqanitawase played 11 Tests for the Wallabies before switching codes in 2024. (Getty Images: Aurelien Meunier)

Kiss is justified in declaring Nawaqanitawase will not walk straight back into the Wallabies squad.

But his presence will create competitive pressure among candidates for the Wallabies' wing spots ahead of the Rugby World Cup, which Australia is hosting.

"He'll just naturally start demanding more from other people because of the type of competition that is in the squad," said Alaalatoa, as the Wallabies prepare for Saturday's Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park.

"I think that only adds health to the group, and it brings the best out of people in his position because of the type of player that he is and what he's shown on some of the biggest stages in Australia.

"I think that is the type of value he'll add to our group."

Nawaqanitawase is set to debut for Saitama Wild Knights in the Japan Rugby League One competition in December.

Not surprisingly, his immediate focus is helping the Roosters celebrate the club's NRL and NRLW premiership victories.
